As I was writing this book, my friend and mentor, Dr. Tracey Bretag, was encouraging me every step of the way. The book went into production just before she passed away. We carry on our work and our commitment to academic integrity in her absence, inspired by her commitment to ethical teaching, learning, and living.

Preface

Preface
The process of writing a book begins long before the first words are ever typed. At least, that’s how it has been for me. I suppose my obsession with citing, referencing, and source attribution began when I was a doctoral student. My PhD supervisor, Dr. J. Tim Goddard, had a particular way of teaching his graduate students how to do a literature review, which I have not seen written down anywhere before or since. He would tell us, “Imagine you are coming to a conversation circle where people are talking about your subject. The conversation has been going on for many years, maybe even centuries. The people who are in this circle can be from any point in history. When you join the circle, you sit down and listen to the voices of those who have come before you. Listen closely to what they have to say, and try to understand their point of view. Then pay attention to the relationship between the people in the circle. Who wrote on the topic first? Who influenced whom? Who disagrees with whom, and why? How has the conversation shifted over time? What have people been saying recently? Your job when you first join this circle is to listen, and to understand. In time, you will contribute your own voice to the conversation, but you don’t start by talking. You start by listening” (T. Goddard, oral teachings. Multiple dates from 2005 onward). Of course, by “listen,” he meant “read.”

He would tell us, “Imagine you are coming to a conversation circle where people are talking about your subject. The conversation has been going on for many years, maybe even centuries. The people who are in this circle can be from any point in history. When you join the circle, you sit down and listen to the voices of those who have come before you. Listen closely to what they have to say, and try to understand their point of view. Then pay attention to the relationship between the people in the circle. Who wrote on the topic first? Who influenced whom? Who disagrees with whom, and why? How has the conversation shifted over time? What have people been saying recently? Your job when you first join this circle is to listen, and to understand. In time, you will contribute your own voice to the conversation, but you don’t start by talking. You start by listening” (T. Goddard, oral teachings. Multiple dates from 2005 onward). Of course, by “listen,” he meant “read.”
Originally from the north of England, Tim’s career was deeply affected by working with Indigenous populations in a number of countries. His way of teaching us how to understand and undertake a literature review was no doubt influenced by Indigenous perspectives and teachings. It was based on the sacred tradition of sharing circles in Indigenous cultures.

Originally from the north of England, Tim’s career was deeply affected by working with Indigenous populations in a number of countries. His way of teaching us how to understand and undertake a literature review was no doubt influenced by Indigenous perspectives and teachings. It was based on the sacred tradition of sharing circles in Indigenous cultures.
Tim’s approach focused on people and relationship-building. He taught us that starting with the sources first was backward. He was insistent thatpeoplewrite the books and journal articles that we read and cite, and so we must start with the people, rather than with the sources. Tim’s approachdiffered from many textbooks and websites that offer instructions for conducting a literature review.

Tim’s teachings have stayed with me, and now I pass along a similar approach to my own students, using the story of how Tim taught me as a starting point. Because his approach focuses on thepeoplewho made contributions to the field rather than thesources, a literature review is framed as a conversation that has been ongoing long before we take up our work as students. It challenges us to situate ourselves within this circle, within the traditions of our discipline and within a community of scholars. The notion of situating oneself in the work is a practice that one develops as a qualitative researcher. We are trained to engage in critical reflexivity about our identity, our subjectivity, and our own biases, as well as our intersubjective relationships with others (Walshaw, 2011). I begin this work by sharing my positionality as an educator, researcher, and advocate.

I was born on Treaty 3: Between the Lake Purchase Territory, in southern Ontario, Canada, to parents of British heritage, neither of whom graduated high school. We lived below the poverty line, and my mother was particularly emphatic that education was crucial to improving one’s life. I was a first-generation university student. I earned a Bachelor of Arts (Honours) in English Literature from Saint Mary’s University in Halifax, Nova Scotia, the city where I spent much of my childhood, after moving around quite a lot throughout my early years.

I was born on Treaty 3: Between the Lake Purchase Territory, in southern Ontario, Canada, to parents of British heritage, neither of whom graduated high school. We lived below the poverty line, and my mother was particularly emphatic that education was crucial to improving one’s life. I was a first-generation university student. I earned a Bachelor of Arts (Honours) in English Literature from Saint Mary’s University in Halifax, Nova Scotia, the city where I spent much of my childhood, after moving around quite a lot throughout my early years.
Following that, thanks to the generosity of the Spanish embassy, which granted me a scholarship to study in Spain one summer, I spent time at the Universidad Complutense in Madrid, learning Spanish as a foreign language. In addition to Spanish, my study of languages has included French and German at the college level. Although I maintain minimal proficiency in French and have all but lost any of my proficiency in German, I have sufficient reading ability to help me puzzle through some of the original sources in additional languages I have consulted in the preparation of this book.

I completed a Master of Arts in Spanish, specializing in literature, followed by a PhD in educational leadership, policy, and governance. This place has been my home for more than half my life, and I am writing this book as a recently tenured professor at the same institution that granted my graduate degrees.
As a doctoral student, I struggled to learn the citing and referencing standards of the American Psychological Association (APA). I had been steeped in the conventions of the Modern Language Association (MLA) while obtaining my literature degrees. Linguists have a term for the mistakes that people make when they are learning a new language and their previous languages influences the one that they are learning. They call it “language interference.” As a PhD student, I experienced “citation interference.” For the first few years, I was constantly including MLA conventions in my writing. Tim would gently, but insistently, keep referring me back to theAPA Manual.Although he was adamant about starting our scholarly work by focusing on the people who wrote the sources we read, he was equally unrelenting about ending with impeccable APA citations and references. He knew that demonstrating our proficiency with the details of APA conventions would be one of the various criteria by which the overall quality of our work would be judged by other professors and thesis examiners. Even if he didn’t agree with that criterion in principle, he recognized it to be a reality of higher eduation scholarship, so he stood firm on the importance of citing and referencing standards.

As a doctoral student, I struggled to learn the citing and referencing standards of the American Psychological Association (APA). I had been steeped in the conventions of the Modern Language Association (MLA) while obtaining my literature degrees. Linguists have a term for the mistakes that people make when they are learning a new language and their previous languages influences the one that they are learning. They call it “language interference.” As a PhD student, I experienced “citation interference.” For the first few years, I was constantly including MLA conventions in my writing. Tim would gently, but insistently, keep referring me back to the
APA Manual.
Although he was adamant about starting our scholarly work by focusing on the people who wrote the sources we read, he was equally unrelenting about ending with impeccable APA citations and references. He knew that demonstrating our proficiency with the details of APA conventions would be one of the various criteria by which the overall quality of our work would be judged by other professors and thesis examiners. Even if he didn’t agree with that criterion in principle, he recognized it to be a reality of higher eduation scholarship, so he stood firm on the importance of citing and referencing standards.
Over time, I became more proficient with APA conventions, though I have often wondered why we couldn’t just have a universal citing and referencing system that was easy to use. If the point is to recognize the contributions of those who came before us, why do we need to get caught up in the technical minutiae of referencing and citing? That is not a question I attempt to answer in this book, though I remain cognizant that it is an important one to contemplate. I do, however, tackle other tough topics related to plagiarism and academic integrity in higher education. It is not my intention to solve all the problems related to plagiarism or breaches of integrity; there are too many, and they are too complex for any one person to fix. Besides, it is in my nature to be a little suspicious of anyone who claims to have all the answers, and as a scholar, I have always been reluctant to claim that I have any answers at all.

It is not my intention to solve all the problems related to plagiarism or breaches of integrity; there are too many, and they are too complex for any one person to fix. Besides, it is in my nature to be a little suspicious of anyone who claims to have all the answers, and as a scholar, I have always been reluctant to claim that I have any answers at all.
Having said that, with this book, I add my voice to the circle of those who have come before me. I have contributed already, though articles, conference presentations, and perhaps most important, conversations, but a book is considered a major undertaking in one’s career. It is a task that I have not taken lightly. As I was undertaking this project, a couple of senior scholars in the field, whom I respect very much and whose work I have read and reread numerous times, posed a question. Whether it was a curiosity, a challenge, or some combination of both, I do not know. They asked, “What will you contribute that is new?” The question has echoed in my head throughout the writing process, serving as a reminder that works that are only derivative are less useful and less interesting than those that bringsomething new to the conversation. It will be up to those who are already part of this knowledge circle, as well as those who join it in the future, to decide if this book brings something new to the field, but writing it with that purpose in mind has been my goal.

Introduction

Introduction
Plagiarism remains a complex and pressing issue at every level of education. Despite decades of research, educators, librarians, student services professionals, and policymakers continue to encounter and address plagiarism (Altbach, 2015; Colella-Sandercock & Alahmadi, 2015; Eaton, Guglielmin, & Otoo, 2017; Leonard, Schwieder, Buhler, Beaubien Bennett, & Royster, 2015). Until recently, researchers were adamant that plagiarism has been on the rise (Park, 2003). A variety of studies have shown that academic misconduct, including plagiarism, rose continuously from the 1940s to the early part of the twenty-first century (Alschuler & Blimling, 1995; Ludeman, 1988; Park, 2003).

Plagiarism remains a complex and pressing issue at every level of education. Despite decades of research, educators, librarians, student services professionals, and policymakers continue to encounter and address plagiarism (Altbach, 2015; Colella-Sandercock & Alahmadi, 2015; Eaton, Guglielmin, & Otoo, 2017; Leonard, Schwieder, Buhler, Beaubien Bennett, & Royster, 2015). Until recently, researchers were adamant that plagiarism has been on the rise (Park, 2003). A variety of studies have shown that academic misconduct, including plagiarism, rose continuously from the 1940s to the early part of the twenty-first century (Alschuler & Blimling, 1995; Ludeman, 1988; Park, 2003).
There are indications that traditional cut-and-paste plagiarism may be decreasing (Curtis & Tremayne, 2019; Curtis & Vardanega, 2016; McCabe, 2016). This could be due in part to an increase in the use of commercial text-matching software (also called “plagiarism detection software”), but this does not mean that overall academic misconduct is decreasing. In 2019, the BBC conducted an investigative report that showed that the contract cheating industry, once known as “term paper mills,” is estimated to be worth at least $1 billion worldwide (BBC News, 2019). Through my informal conversations with colleagues, however, we believe this to be a low estimate, but because this black market for academic work exists mainly online, and often offshore, it has been impossible to get a clear idea of the actual size of the industry. We know that copy-and-paste plagiarism is just the tip of the iceberg. Educators need to be aware of other forms of unethical writing, such as the use of online academic outsourcing services, predatory file-sharing sites, and paraphrasing software, all of which have a similar effect—namely, pushing the idea that writing is an endproduct, rather than a demonstration of the learning process. These are just a few of the tough topics I tackle in this book.

In 2019, the BBC conducted an investigative report that showed that the contract cheating industry, once known as “term paper mills,” is estimated to be worth at least $1 billion worldwide (BBC News, 2019). Through my informal conversations with colleagues, however, we believe this to be a low estimate, but because this black market for academic work exists mainly online, and often offshore, it has been impossible to get a clear idea of the actual size of the industry. We know that copy-and-paste plagiarism is just the tip of the iceberg. Educators need to be aware of other forms of unethical writing, such as the use of online academic outsourcing services, predatory file-sharing sites, and paraphrasing software, all of which have a similar effect—namely, pushing the idea that writing is an end
product
, rather than a demonstration of the learning process. These are just a few of the tough topics I tackle in this book.

Intended Audience

Intended Audience
The audience for this book is not limited to one particular group, such as academic librarians. Instead, the book is directed at everyone who is attentive to issues relating to plagiarism and academic ethics in higher education. This includes, but is not limited to, faculty members, librarians, writing center tutors, student services professionals, and even higher education policy makers. As I emphasize throughout the book, academic integrity requires a multistakeholder approach, and therefore, this book is written for a broad audience that includes students and future academics and higher education professionals.

InChapter 3, I examine several reasons why people plagiarize and the various complicating factors that affect the act of plagiarism. I look at topics such as unethical translation, cryptomnesia, and the role that textuality and intentionality play. I also consider how students and professors see plagiarism differently, and why these differences further complicate our understanding of what plagiarism is.

I draw from work done in the field of the scholarship of teaching and learning (SoTL), showing its applicability to plagiarism and academic integrity. Specifically, I show how the 4M Framework can help us to understand academic integrity from micro (individual), meso (departmental), macro (institutional), and mega (societal) perspectives (Friberg, 2016; Kalu et al., 2018; Kenny, Watson, & Desmaris, 2016; Poole & Simmons, 2013; Simmons, 2016; Williams et al., 2013).

REFLECTIONS ON REFERENCING

REFLECTIONS ON REFERENCING
As someone who researches plagiarism and academic ethics, I am sensitive not only to the topics that I address in this book, but also how I cite and reference my sources. I know all too well that there are disciplinary differences with regard to referencing. In my field of education, scholars are sometimes criticized for overreferencing. I might be guilty of that in this book, but I offer a rationale in my own defense. It is encumbent upon academic integrity advocates to serve as role models in terms of their ethical treatment of source material, so I have made painstaking efforts to leave a trail of referencing bread crumbs for the reader who wishes to follow up and learn more from the source material that I have used in researching and preparing this work.

A Brief History of Plagiarism

A Brief History of Plagiarism
There is no singular or absolute definition of plagiarism. Others before me have written historical perspectives on plagiarism specifically, and academic misconduct more broadly (Bertram Gallant, 2008; Carter, 2005; Davis, Drinan, & Bertram Gallant, 2009; Grossberg, 2009; Hoffer, 2004; Howard, 1995, 1999; Mallon, 1989; Randall, 2001; Sutherland-Smith, 2008). Their works have informed and influenced this chapter, which offers an updated overview of this history, contextualized for those who work in higher education contexts.

There is no singular or absolute definition of plagiarism. Others before me have written historical perspectives on plagiarism specifically, and academic misconduct more broadly (Bertram Gallant, 2008; Carter, 2005; Davis, Drinan, & Bertram Gallant, 2009; Grossberg, 2009; Hoffer, 2004; Howard, 1995, 1999; Mallon, 1989; Randall, 2001; Sutherland-Smith, 2008). Their works have informed and influenced this chapter, which offers an updated overview of this history, contextualized for those who work in higher education contexts.
Many authors have looked to the etymology of the wordplagiarismto explain its modern definition. In 1828, F. E. J. Valpy publishedAn Etymological Dictionary of the Latin Language,which definedplagiumas “the crime of kidnapping” (Valpy, 1828, p. 345). TheOxford English Dictionary(OED, n.d.) offers a similar etymological path, noting the Latin rootplagiumas being “a kidnapping,” explaining that the Latin word was derived from the Greekplagion. The OED also notes that the meaning ofplagiarismin the sense of kidnapping is now obsolete, having evolved to mean “literary theft” (Park, 2003, p. 472). There is merit in the idea of plagiarism being “intellectual burglary” (Maddox, 1995, p. 721) because the idea of plagiarism has evolved to extend far beyond literary theft.

to explain its modern definition. In 1828, F. E. J. Valpy published

which defined
plagium
as “the crime of kidnapping” (Valpy, 1828, p. 345). The
Oxford English Dictionary

plagium
as being “a kidnapping,” explaining that the Latin word was derived from the Greek
plagion
. The OED also notes that the meaning of
plagiarism
in the sense of kidnapping is now obsolete, having evolved to mean “literary theft” (Park, 2003, p. 472). There is merit in the idea of plagiarism being “intellectual burglary” (Maddox, 1995, p. 721) because the idea of plagiarism has evolved to extend far beyond literary theft.
The etymological link to Greek may not be accidental, as stories about plagiarism date back to ancient Greek scholars. John Maddox, editor of the journalNature, recounted a story told by Dr. Frederick Newsome in 1995 at a national meeting of the Office of Research Integrity of the U.S. PublicHealth Services, which collaborated with various other prestigious organizations, such as the American Association for the Advancement of Science and the American Bar Association, to host a major conference on plagiarism. Maddox told Newsome’s riveting story of Pythagoras. Newsome explained that Pythagoras left Greece to travel to Egypt to study with priests there. Pythagoras later returned to Greece to share ideas about “the square of the hypotenuse of a right triangle and the significance of the simple geometrical shapes that became the hallmark of the Pythagorean School” (Maddox, 1995, p. 721). In doing so, Pythagoras upset the Egyptians, who maintained that the Greek scholar had taken credit for their ideas without giving them proper attribution.

The etymological link to Greek may not be accidental, as stories about plagiarism date back to ancient Greek scholars. John Maddox, editor of the journal
Nature
, recounted a story told by Dr. Frederick Newsome in 1995 at a national meeting of the Office of Research Integrity of the U.S. Public
Health Services, which collaborated with various other prestigious organizations, such as the American Association for the Advancement of Science and the American Bar Association, to host a major conference on plagiarism. Maddox told Newsome’s riveting story of Pythagoras. Newsome explained that Pythagoras left Greece to travel to Egypt to study with priests there. Pythagoras later returned to Greece to share ideas about “the square of the hypotenuse of a right triangle and the significance of the simple geometrical shapes that became the hallmark of the Pythagorean School” (Maddox, 1995, p. 721). In doing so, Pythagoras upset the Egyptians, who maintained that the Greek scholar had taken credit for their ideas without giving them proper attribution.
This story is interesting because it relates to the theft of ideas, rather than text. This would seem to point to a flaw related to how the Englishplagiarismevolved from the Latinplagium, and the earlier Greekplagion, to focus narrowly on the theft of words rather than the use of ideas of another party without attribution. The evolution of the wordplagiarismin English and its definition did not take into account the notion of unattributed ideas, even though one of the earliest examples that we have of plagiarism, dating back to the ancient Greeks, is clearly about taking others’ ideas—not their literary works—and claiming them as one’s own without attribution. If this is the case, then no wonder that it has been nearly impossible to defineplagiarismin absolute terms.

In addition to ideas, “jokes about out-and-out literary theft go all the way back to Aristophanes … but what we call plagiarism was more of a matter for laughter than litigation” (Mallon, 1989, p. 4). In other words, the first recorded instances of plagiarism date back thousands of years.

THE PRINTING PRESS AS A DISRUPTIVE TECHNOLOGY

THE PRINTING PRESS AS A DISRUPTIVE TECHNOLOGY
Returning to this notion of literary theft, a brief discussion is warranted about how the emergence of plagiarism is historically situated, and specifically about the influence the printing press had on both the democratization of knowledge and plagiarism. Elizabeth Eisenstein, in her two volumes on the how the printing press was a major change agent in human history, offers a detailed exploration of the impact of the printing press not only for scholars, but for society at large (Eisenstein, 1979). She offers insights into how the press allowed books to be produced, distributed, and read on a wider scale. In turn, this affected people’s interest not only in reading and writing, but in having that writing shared and making money from it. It might not have always been possible to make a living from writing then (just as it is not always possible today), but the idea of telling better stories to sell more books catalyzed plagiarism among authors of thetime. One cannot fully understand the development of plagiarism without considering how the printing press changed notions of knowledge sharing, learning, and authorship.

Elizabeth Eisenstein, in her two volumes on the how the printing press was a major change agent in human history, offers a detailed exploration of the impact of the printing press not only for scholars, but for society at large (Eisenstein, 1979). She offers insights into how the press allowed books to be produced, distributed, and read on a wider scale. In turn, this affected people’s interest not only in reading and writing, but in having that writing shared and making money from it. It might not have always been possible to make a living from writing then (just as it is not always possible today), but the idea of telling better stories to sell more books catalyzed plagiarism among authors of the
time. One cannot fully understand the development of plagiarism without considering how the printing press changed notions of knowledge sharing, learning, and authorship.
Early in her first volume, Eisenstein elaborates on how Johannes Gutenberg’s invention in the mid-1400s revolutionized how we learn, think, and understand knowledge. She cautions against trying to understand the development of printed transmission with precise detail because contradictions and complexities around the history of both hand-scribed and early printed texts result in a history that was problematic, amorphous, and full of contradictions, particularly in the first century or so after the printing press became more prevalent, which happened in the late 1400s and early 1500s. Eisenstein (1979) notes that “one must wait until a full century after Gutenberg before the outlines of new world pictures begin to emerge into view” (p. 33).

The Case of Joseph Hall: One of the Earliest Documented Cases of Plagiarism in English

The Case of Joseph Hall: One of the Earliest Documented Cases of Plagiarism in English
Eisenstein explores the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries in some depth in her book. It comes as no surprise then, that the OED traces one of the early uses of the wordplagiarismin English to the same period when the impact of the printing press becomes more fully documented and understood. The OED notes that one of the earliest uses ofplagiarismin the English language was found in 1598, in the writings of Joseph Hall, the Bishop of Norwich, who was a religious writer and satirist. Hall was born in 1574 and earned a master’s degree in 1596, after which he joined the university as a lecturer at Cambridge for two years (McCabe, 2008). Richard McCabe’s (2008) biography of Hall documents one of the earliest known public plagiarism disputes. McCabe notes that Hall’s publication,Virgidemiarum, was considered to be the first collection of formal satire verse published in England, but it resulted in a public and vigorous dispute with John Marston. McCabe traces the lineage of the argument through Davenport’s 1949 edited volume of Hall’s satires, explaining that Marston publicly accused Hall of plagiarism by “pasting a satiric epigram into all of the copies ofThe Metamorphosis of Pigmalions Image‘that came to the Stationers at Cambridge’ (A. Davenport, ed.,The Poems of Joseph Hall, 1949, xxix)” (as cited in McCabe, 2009). What is fascinating about this is that McCabe studied the work of Davenport, who was a scholar of Hall’s work. McCabe’s work provides an excellent demonstration of acknowledging one’s intellectual predecessors in order to establish something new.

Virgidemiarum
, was considered to be the first collection of formal satire verse published in England, but it resulted in a public and vigorous dispute with John Marston. McCabe traces the lineage of the argument through Davenport’s 1949 edited volume of Hall’s satires, explaining that Marston publicly accused Hall of plagiarism by “pasting a satiric epigram into all of the copies of
The Metamorphosis of Pigmalions Image

, 1949, xxix)” (as cited in McCabe, 2009). What is fascinating about this is that McCabe studied the work of Davenport, who was a scholar of Hall’s work. McCabe’s work provides an excellent demonstration of acknowledging one’s intellectual predecessors in order to establish something new.
In this case, the “something new” was the documentation of one of the earliest-known public debates over plagiarism. Joseph Hall’s volume onthis topic was produced in 1599. This predates what had previously been noted in the OED as the first mention of plagiarism. In his volume on the history of plagiarism, Thomas Mallon (1989) noted that the OED of the late 1980s traced the first use of the word back to Ben Johnson. The OED of 2019 that I consulted while writing this book showed that Johnson did not use the word until 1602, four years after the lesser-known Hall. It is possible that when Mallon wrote his book in the 1980s, the Johnson reference was indeed the earliest known mention of “plagiary,” and that since then, literary historians such as McCabe (2009) dug even deeper, so today we have updated knowledge that simply was not available at the time that Mallon was conducting his research.

this topic was produced in 1599. This predates what had previously been noted in the OED as the first mention of plagiarism. In his volume on the history of plagiarism, Thomas Mallon (1989) noted that the OED of the late 1980s traced the first use of the word back to Ben Johnson. The OED of 2019 that I consulted while writing this book showed that Johnson did not use the word until 1602, four years after the lesser-known Hall. It is possible that when Mallon wrote his book in the 1980s, the Johnson reference was indeed the earliest known mention of “plagiary,” and that since then, literary historians such as McCabe (2009) dug even deeper, so today we have updated knowledge that simply was not available at the time that Mallon was conducting his research.
This is an example of how scholarship works. We aim to trace back our knowledge as far as we can given the resources, tools, and evidence available to us at any given time. This observation is no doubt influenced by Eisenstein (1979), who talked about how “modern scholars” (p. 6) uncover new old inventions (or in this case, literary works) almost as fast as new ones are produced. The irony that Eisenstein wrote her book ten years before Mallon did should not be lost on us. Neither is it lost on me that I sit at my desk writing this brief history precisely forty years after Eisenstein’s book was published, and thirty years after Mallon’s. In that time, much has changed in how scholars and students conduct research and share knowledge, with the Internet being arguably the most significant disrupter in how knowledge is shared since the printing press.

THE INFLUENCE OF THE INTERNET

THE INFLUENCE OF THE INTERNET
Eisenstein (1979) wrote, “The more rapidly new inventions proliferate, the less conspicuous earlier ones tend to become” (p. 20). She recounted how countless other new technologies that emerged during the Renaissance overshadowed the impact of the printing press, which seemed to get less and less attention in historical journals that traced the history of technological developments during that time. Whether she knew how applicable her words would be to the emergence of the Internet as a revolutionizing force in how knowledge of all kinds would be shared is impossible to say, but if she followed the news during her most productive scholarly years, it is possible she could have observed the emergence of the Internet in its earliest forms in the 1960s and early 1970s.

Eisenstein (1979) wrote, “The more rapidly new inventions proliferate, the less conspicuous earlier ones tend to become” (p. 20). She recounted how countless other new technologies that emerged during the Renaissance overshadowed the impact of the printing press, which seemed to get less and less attention in historical journals that traced the history of technological developments during that time. Whether she knew how applicable her words would be to the emergence of the Internet as a revolutionizing force in how knowledge of all kinds would be shared is impossible to say, but if she followed the news during her most productive scholarly years, it is possible she could have observed the emergence of the Internet in its earliest forms in the 1960s and early 1970s.
Ten years prior to the publication of Eisenstein’s book on the printing press, the technology that evolved into the Internet was born. According to Leonard Kleinrock (2009), who was among the group of students from University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) who developed the technology, it all began on October 29, 1969 at 10:30 p.m. The student group hadbeen recruited to work at the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA), which was created by the U.S. Department of Defense in response to the Soviet Union’s Sputnik, which was the first artificial satellite to orbit the Earth. ARPA was situated out of a laboratory at UCLA. The first transmission the research team sent was transmitted from UCLA to the Stanford Research Institute (SRI), 400 miles away. The idea was to see if one computer could communicate with another. The plan was for the ARPA team to send the letters “L-O-G” and for SRI to respond with “I-N.” But the ARPA computer crashed after only two letters, so all that was transmitted was “L-O.”

Kleinrock (2009, 2019) reported that e-mail was introduced two years later, and from there, the Internet evolved. At the time, none of the developers of the Internet ever imagined the unethical or even illegal ways in which it would end up being used. In 2019, on the fiftieth anniversary of the Internet, Kleinrock reflected that
the ethos that defined the culture we were building was characterized by words such as ethical, open, trusted, free, shared. None of us knew where our research would lead, but these words and principles were our beacon. We did not anticipate that the dark side of the internet would emerge with such ferocity. (Kleinrock, 2019)

Kleinrock (2009) points out that the strengths of the Internet, such as the open sharing of information, lead to some of its weaknesses, among which are the unethical use of information and the appropriation of others’ words, ideas, and other digital creations without attribution or permission.

At the same moment in history when the Internet infrastructure was becoming more widespread and commercialized in 1992, Jean-Marie Dru, chairman of the international advertising agency, TBWA, coined the termcreative disruption.This term refers to an approach to business and marketing that advocates for radical and creative innovation (Nora, 2016).

At the same moment in history when the Internet infrastructure was becoming more widespread and commercialized in 1992, Jean-Marie Dru, chairman of the international advertising agency, TBWA, coined the term
creative disruption.
This term refers to an approach to business and marketing that advocates for radical and creative innovation (Nora, 2016).
That same year (i.e., 1992) the online service AskERIC was launched (Sutton, 2001). It was offered by the Education Resources Information Center (ERIC), whose development was sponsored by the Institute of Education Sciences of the U.S. Department of Education (Sutton, 2001; Weiner, 2008). Although ERIC started in the 1960s as a bibliographic archive, it continued to develop over the decades. In 1992, AskERIC was considered “a pioneering e-mail-based question-answer service” (Sutton, 2001, p. 21). A year later, ERIC became one of the first 100 sites on the World Wide Web (Sutton, 2001). Today, ERIC remains one of the most widely consulted publicly available educational databases. The early 1990s represented a time of massive shifting in terms of how technology was developing, knowledge was shared, and business was conducted, and all of it was connected to the World Wide Web, which was developing during that time.The Internet was to the second half of the twentieth century what the printing press was to the second half of the fifteenth: the most creatively disruptive change to how knowledge is shared across large numbers of people.

The Internet was to the second half of the twentieth century what the printing press was to the second half of the fifteenth: the most creatively disruptive change to how knowledge is shared across large numbers of people.
The copy-and-paste and general sharing culture that has evolved since the development of the Internet has been of interest to educators and researchers for decades now (Blum, 2009, 2016; Rogerson & Basanta, 2016; Teixeira da Silva, 2016). There is an ethical component to how information is shared over the Internet, and young people in particular encounter different expectations when they are among their peers than when they are in an educational setting (Blum, 2009). The kind of digital sharing that is generally accepted as permissible in social settings can be considered plagiarism in an educational or research context.

There is an ethical component to how information is shared over the Internet, and young people in particular encounter different expectations when they are among their peers than when they are in an educational setting (Blum, 2009). The kind of digital sharing that is generally accepted as permissible in social settings can be considered plagiarism in an educational or research context.
Today’s scholars of plagiarism are divided on whether the Internet is responsible for increases in plagiarism. Just after the turn of the millennium, Scanlon and Neumann (2002) conducted a survey of 698 students across nine postsecondary institutions and found no evidence that students plagiarized more using the Internet than they did using traditional paper sources. They suggested that if students were inclined to plagiarize, they would do so regardless of whether the source material appeared online or in print.

Today’s scholars of plagiarism are divided on whether the Internet is responsible for increases in plagiarism. Just after the turn of the millennium, Scanlon and Neumann (2002) conducted a survey of 698 students across nine postsecondary institutions and found no evidence that students plagiarized more using the Internet than they did using traditional paper sources. They suggested that if students were inclined to plagiarize, they would do so regardless of whether the source material appeared online or in print.
However, findings such as this do not stop others from disagreeing. One scholar argues that “the online environment is accelerating the decline in academic ethics” (Ison, 2015, p. 151). Another argues that it is not the Internet, but the general moral failure of society that is to blame, suggesting “that the biggest single factor in escalating academic dishonesty is the failure of parents and teachers to diligently teach, enforce, advocate and model personal integrity” (Josephson, 2005, p. 10). Still others point out that there is no empirical evidence to show that the Internetitselfis responsible for an increase in plagiarism, but “the speed of sharing and copying information online can lead to theperceptionthat the Internet causes plagiarism” (Panning Davies & Howard, 2016, p. 592, emphasis added).

Another argues that it is not the Internet, but the general moral failure of society that is to blame, suggesting “that the biggest single factor in escalating academic dishonesty is the failure of parents and teachers to diligently teach, enforce, advocate and model personal integrity” (Josephson, 2005, p. 10). Still others point out that there is no empirical evidence to show that the Internet
itself
is responsible for an increase in plagiarism, but “the speed of sharing and copying information online can lead to the
perception
that the Internet causes plagiarism” (Panning Davies & Howard, 2016, p. 592, emphasis added).
The reality is that we may never be able to gather empirical evidence about whether the online environment is the cause of increases in plagiarism. The reason for this is that the overall amount of information being shared on the Internet is massive, and the rate at which it is being shared seems to increase exponentially every day. What we cannot show is whether the amount of plagiarism, relative to the amount of overall knowledge freely available to the general public, has changed at all. When the printing press was developed, the number of books available increased dramatically, but the total number of books was still ultimately a finite number. Today, it is all but impossible to calculate how many new websitesand pages are added, deleted, or changed on a daily basis. What scholars and educators agree on is that since the advent of the Internet in the early 1990s, access to information has changed forever. By extrapolation, how students learn has also changed.

Changing Perspectives in Higher Education: Focus on Academic Integrity

Changing Perspectives in Higher Education: Focus on Academic Integrity
Plagiarism has long been considered a particular type of academic misconduct, but the overall concept of dishonesty in learning contexts spans a variety of additional objectionable behaviors, including but not limited to cheating, fabrication or falsification of research data, and unauthorized collaboration. To situate this brief history of plagiarism within the higher education context, we can examine the history of academic misconduct, considering plagiarism a particular kind of misconduct that is situated within the broader context of academic integrity and its breaches.

Plagiarism has long been considered a particular type of academic misconduct, but the overall concept of dishonesty in learning contexts spans a variety of additional objectionable behaviors, including but not limited to cheating, fabrication or falsification of research data, and unauthorized collaboration. To situate this brief history of plagiarism within the higher education context, we can examine the history of academic misconduct, considering plagiarism a particular kind of misconduct that is situated within the broader context of academic integrity and its breaches.
Scholars who look at the history of academic misconduct have documented cases of exam cheating dating back to the early seventh century, during the Sui dynasty in China, when examinations were first introduced (Blum, 2009; Lang, 2013). The discussion of plagiarism among the literary elite of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries began to extend beyond literary circles to learning contexts as education become more widespread during the Industrial Revolution.

Scholars who look at the history of academic misconduct have documented cases of exam cheating dating back to the early seventh century, during the Sui dynasty in China, when examinations were first introduced (Blum, 2009; Lang, 2013). The discussion of plagiarism among the literary elite of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries began to extend beyond literary circles to learning contexts as education become more widespread during the Industrial Revolution.
A nineteenth-century scholar named Thomas Gallwey (1879) wrote about plagiarism in theIrish Monthly,a publication that began as a devotional magazine in 1873 and later evolved into a literary scholarly journal until its publication ceased in 1954 (Irish Monthly, n.d.). By that time, academic misconduct was a topic of interest for both researchers and educational administrators.

A nineteenth-century scholar named Thomas Gallwey (1879) wrote about plagiarism in the
Irish Monthly,
a publication that began as a devotional magazine in 1873 and later evolved into a literary scholarly journal until its publication ceased in 1954 (
Irish Monthly
, n.d.). By that time, academic misconduct was a topic of interest for both researchers and educational administrators.
In her bookAcademic Integrity in the Twenty-First Century: A Teaching and Learning Imperative, Tricia Bertram Gallant (2008) traces the use of “integrity” when referring to student conduct back to the early 1960s, which coincided with the largest study on academic misconduct up to that point. A multi-institutional study by W. J. Bowers (1964),Student Dishonesty and Its Control in College, is still considered a seminal work in this field. The study shares the results of questionnaires that Bowers sent to over 600 deans and 500 student body presidents about academic misconduct in Amercian colleges. The results showed that over half of American college students engaged in some form of academic misconduct, with only a small proportion being caught and facing consequences for their actions. Later, over 5,000 students from ninety-nine colleges across the United States participated in the follow-up, in which more than 50 percent ofthem admitted to some form of academic misconduct, including plagiarism. Worthy of note is that Bowers conducted his data collection in 1962—precisely thirty years prior to the commercialization of the Internet and the term “creative disruption” being coined. This research on student academic dishonesty (Bowers, 1964, 1966) was considered its own kind of creative disruption at the time it was published because he did what no one before him had attempted—perform large-scale research across dozens of colleges in order to understand and uncover the realities of academic misconduct in Amercian higher education at the time.

This research on student academic dishonesty (Bowers, 1964, 1966) was considered its own kind of creative disruption at the time it was published because he did what no one before him had attempted—perform large-scale research across dozens of colleges in order to understand and uncover the realities of academic misconduct in Amercian higher education at the time.
His work remained the most prominent work in the field for the better part of thirty years, until Donald McCabe and colleagues began researching academic misconduct on a wide scale in the United States in the 1990s (McCabe, 1992, 1993; McCabe & Treviño, 1993). McCabe and Bowers (1994) copublished a paper thirty years after Bowers’s seminal study was released, which provides us with evidence not only of Bowers’s influence on McCabe, but their ultimate collaboration.

o, 1993). McCabe and Bowers (1994) copublished a paper thirty years after Bowers’s seminal study was released, which provides us with evidence not only of Bowers’s influence on McCabe, but their ultimate collaboration.
By then, a group of researchers, including McCabe, had established the Center for Academic Integrity (CAI) in 1992, effectively launching what became known as the “academic integrity movement” (Davis, Drinan, & Bertram Gallant, 2008, p. 28). McCabe arguably launched the field of academic integrity as an area of research on a large scale, and this center became the first hub of its kind for educators, advocates, and scholars. The establishment of CAI can be situated within larger technoglobal developments at the time. Its creation occurred during the same year that Jean-Marie Dru coined the term “creative disruption” to explain new ways of approaching business and marketing, and the same year that the AskERIC service was launched, just as the Internet was developing into a widespread and freely available tool. The establishment of CAI occurred at the same time in history as massive technological changes across the world were transforming how students learned, how teachers taught, and how research was conducted.

The quarter-century that followed saw intense development in the field of academic integrity in terms of research, learning, teaching, and educational administration on a global scale. A number of scholarly journals emerged, becoming a cornerstone for research. TheJournal of Academic Ethicswas launched in 2003 “to provide a venue for dialogue about the ethical issues facing universities in the 21st century” (Poff & Michalos, 2003, p. 1). In November of that same year, the inaugural Asia-Pacific Educational Integrity Conference (APEIC) was held at the University of South Australia, which led to the development and launch of theInternational Journal for Educational Integritytwo years later (Bretag & Marsden, 2005). Then,Education and Ethicswas launched (Smith, 2006). All three journals remain in publication today.

The quarter-century that followed saw intense development in the field of academic integrity in terms of research, learning, teaching, and educational administration on a global scale. A number of scholarly journals emerged, becoming a cornerstone for research. The
Journal of Academic Ethics
was launched in 2003 “to provide a venue for dialogue about the ethical issues facing universities in the 21st century” (Poff & Michalos, 2003, p. 1). In November of that same year, the inaugural Asia-Pacific Educational Integrity Conference (APEIC) was held at the University of South Australia, which led to the development and launch of the
International Journal for Educational Integrity
two years later (Bretag & Marsden, 2005). Then,
Education and Ethics
was launched (Smith, 2006). All three journals remain in publication today.
During the first decade of the twenty-first century, a flurry of books was published on academic integrity, many with a focus on higher education and some specifically addressing plagiarism (Bertram Gallant, 2008; Blum, 2009; Carroll, 2007; Eisner & Vicinus, 2008; Lampert, 2008; Lathrop & Foss, 2000, 2005; Sutherland-Smith, 2008; Twomey, White, & Sagendorf, 2009). During the same decade, Donald McCabe expanded his research and collaborations to Canada (Christensen Hughes & McCabe, 2006a, 2006b) and other countries, including Mexico, Australia, Singapore, Egypt, Morocco, and countries in Europe (ICAI, 2017). To close out the decade, the Center for Academic Integrity was renamed the International Center for Academic Integrity (ICAI) in 2010 to reflect its expanding reach and membership (ICAI, 2017), effectively signaling to the world that integrity was a topic of global importance in educational contexts and beyond.

During the same decade, Donald McCabe expanded his research and collaborations to Canada (Christensen Hughes & McCabe, 2006a, 2006b) and other countries, including Mexico, Australia, Singapore, Egypt, Morocco, and countries in Europe (ICAI, 2017). To close out the decade, the Center for Academic Integrity was renamed the International Center for Academic Integrity (ICAI) in 2010 to reflect its expanding reach and membership (ICAI, 2017), effectively signaling to the world that integrity was a topic of global importance in educational contexts and beyond.
The second decade of the twenty-first century (2010–2019) brought further changes to the ways that we contemplate, discuss, teach, and understand what it means to learn ethically and conduct oneself with integrity. In 2016, Tracey Bretag’s edited volumeHandbook of Academic Integritywas released. Spanning in excess of 1,000 pages, with contributions from more than ninety authors from across the world, the volume stands as the single most comprehensive treatment of topics ranging from plagiarism to peer-to-peer file sharing to corruption in educational contexts. Only a few months after its publication, the man who had become affectionately known as the “grandfather of academic integrity,” Donald McCabe, passed away; his chapter in Bretag’s handbook was one of his final contributions to the field that he helped to build. In 2020, Tracey Bretag passed away, leaving another legacy of research and advocacy contributions to the field.

CONCLUSIONS

CONCLUSIONS
Although scholars and educators alike have been careful to point out that plagiarism and cheating are not the same (Curtis & Vardenega, 2016), the former remains a topic of deep concern in educational contexts and in society generally. As we move deeper into the twenty-first century, the meaning ofplagiarismcontinues to evolve. Educators, scholars, and librarians are now working in a post-McCabe and post-Bretag era, as questions grow about how technology will continue to challenge our thinking, learning, and development as the human species. This coincides with the rapid development of artificial intelligence and new technologies that are quickly moving beyond the Internet. This book addresses the intersection and intertwining of plagiarism with other aspects of educational ethics and explores updated notions of what it means to plagiarize and how our thinking might evolve to keep up with the times.

plagiarism
continues to evolve. Educators, scholars, and librarians are now working in a post-McCabe and post-Bretag era, as questions grow about how technology will continue to challenge our thinking, learning, and development as the human species. This coincides with the rapid development of artificial intelligence and new technologies that are quickly moving beyond the Internet. This book addresses the intersection and intertwining of plagiarism with other aspects of educational ethics and explores updated notions of what it means to plagiarize and how our thinking might evolve to keep up with the times.
In this chapter, I have outlined a brief history of plagiarism and academic misconduct in the English-speaking world. I have limited my discussion to this context for the sake of brevity; however, it is important to acknowledge that neither the concept nor the history of plagiarism are limited to English-speaking countries. Scholars have delved into the history and development of plagiarism in other languages, such as French (Donahue, 2008; Falaky, 2010), German (Weber-Wulff, 2014), Latin (McGill, 2012), Persian (Sadeghi, 2019), Portuguese (Krokoscz, 2014), Spanish (Perromat Augostín, 2010), and no doubt many others. These works are worth deeper consideration for scholars, educators, and educational professionals concerned with the development of plagiarism in broader global terms. In the next chapter, I explore what a modern definition of plagiarism might look like, but before doing so, I expore how both the termplagiarismand the concepts that underpin it have evolved over time.

Contextualizing and Defining Plagiarism in Higher Education

Contextualizing and Defining Plagiarism in Higher Education
It seems that there is at least one story about plagiarism in the news every week. The media often sensationalizes plagiarism, particularly when celebrities or other public figures are implicated. Media stories attract the attention of the public and often generate intense emotional reactions (Valentine, 2006). Unfortunately, journalists often confuse plagiarism with other concepts, such as copyright, trademarks, and intellectual property in the broad sense. Although these concepts can be related to plagiarism, the various concepts are not interchangeable. The confusion may lie in the fact that plagiarism is a complex phenomenon that continues to be difficult—if not impossible—to define in terms that are absolute, or even precise (Carroll, 2007; Eaton, 2017; Howard, 2000, Luke & Kearins, 2012; Price, 2002). Concepts beyond plagiarism fall outside the scope of this book, which addresses plagiarism and academic integrity in higher education contexts rather than in industry or in broader public spheres.

Media stories attract the attention of the public and often generate intense emotional reactions (Valentine, 2006). Unfortunately, journalists often confuse plagiarism with other concepts, such as copyright, trademarks, and intellectual property in the broad sense. Although these concepts can be related to plagiarism, the various concepts are not interchangeable. The confusion may lie in the fact that plagiarism is a complex phenomenon that continues to be difficult—if not impossible—to define in terms that are absolute, or even precise (Carroll, 2007; Eaton, 2017; Howard, 2000, Luke & Kearins, 2012; Price, 2002). Concepts beyond plagiarism fall outside the scope of this book, which addresses plagiarism and academic integrity in higher education contexts rather than in industry or in broader public spheres.
In this chapter, I situate plagiarism as a particular type of misconduct within postsecondary education and explore what that means in today’s terms. I offer a more modern framing of plagiarism that may be useful when explaining the concept to students and may assist administrators seeking to update institutional academic integrity policies and procedures.

In this chapter, I situate plagiarism as a particular type of misconduct within postsecondary education and explore what that means in today’s terms. I offer a more modern framing of plagiarism that may be useful when explaining the concept to students and may assist administrators seeking to update institutional academic integrity policies and procedures.
CONCEPTUAL FRAMING OF PLAGIARISM

CONCEPTUAL FRAMING OF PLAGIARISM
Before digging into a definition, it is worthwhile to explore why it might be useful to have one at all. This sets the stage for a more informed exploration of what a definition could look like. Educators, administrators, and others might view plagiarism through one of three lenses: (1) as a policy or regulatory issue, (2) as a teaching and learning issue, or (3) as a moral issue (Adam, 2016; Adam et al., 2017; Kaposi & Dell, 2012). I briefly examine plagiarism through each of these lenses, showing how they are interrelated (seeFigure 2.1). Then I consider how higher education institutions can begin to work toward more robust definitions that take different disciplinary knowledge into account.

Plagiarism through a Policy Lens

Plagiarism through a Policy Lens
In universities and colleges, plagiarism is often considered a particular kind of academic misconduct. The terms “academic misconduct” and“academic dishonesty” are often used interchangeably, though the former imposes less judgment on behavior, whereas the latter implies intentionality and deceit (suggesting moral failure), which we know from decades of research is not always the case when students plagiarize. For that reason, we see the term “academic dishonesty” less often nowadays. Although the term has not fallen entirely out of use yet, it may over time.

Institutional policy directs members of educational communities on how to address plagiarism after it has happened. I use the term “policy” inclusively to describe a variety of formal institutional policy statements, as well as secondary and complementary policy instruments that are used to guide their implementation, such as procedures, guidelines, forms, and checklists (Bretag & Mahmud, 2016; Clark, Griffin, & Martin, 2012; Freeman, 2013; Stoesz et al., 2019).

Institutional policy directs members of educational communities on how to address plagiarism after it has happened. I use the term “policy” inclusively to describe a variety of formal institutional policy statements, as well as secondary and complementary policy instruments that are used to guide their implementation, such as procedures, guidelines, forms, and checklists (Bretag & Mahmud, 2016; Clark, Griffin, & Martin, 2012; Freeman, 2013; Stoesz et al., 2019).
Academic misconduct policy often names or attempts to define a suite of behaviors that fall under a broad umbrella called “academic misconduct.” Plagiarism and cheating are often named as different behaviors in policy documents, precisely because there can be differences between them (Curtis & Vardenega, 2016; Stoesz et al., 2019). Policy might also include other kinds of unacceptable behaviors, such as data fabrication or falsification, impersonation for exams, or other forms of contract cheating (for a detailed exploration of these topics, seeChapter 8).

Academic misconduct policy often names or attempts to define a suite of behaviors that fall under a broad umbrella called “academic misconduct.” Plagiarism and cheating are often named as different behaviors in policy documents, precisely because there can be differences between them (Curtis & Vardenega, 2016; Stoesz et al., 2019). Policy might also include other kinds of unacceptable behaviors, such as data fabrication or falsification, impersonation for exams, or other forms of contract cheating (for a detailed exploration of these topics, see
Chapter 8
).
The shift toward talking about academic integrity, instead of “misconduct” or “dishonesty,” has increased in recent decades. Academic integrity is viewed as a set of values that members of educational communities are expected to uphold, including virtues such as courage, fairness, honesty, respect, responsibility, and trust (Christensen Hughes & McCabe, 2006a, 2006b; International Center for Academic Integrity, 2014; McCabe, 1993). Academic integrity “is more than the absence of misconduct” (Christensen Hughes & McCabe, 2006b, p. 51). As Julia Christensen Hughes (2017) points out, values drive behavior. Policy is generally concerned with behavior and accepted norms for conduct within the boundaries of the institution.

The shift toward talking about academic integrity, instead of “misconduct” or “dishonesty,” has increased in recent decades. Academic integrity is viewed as a set of values that members of educational communities are expected to uphold, including virtues such as courage, fairness, honesty, respect, responsibility, and trust (Christensen Hughes & McCabe, 2006a, 2006b; International Center for Academic Integrity, 2014; McCabe, 1993). Academic integrity “is more than the absence of misconduct” (Christensen Hughes & McCabe, 2006b, p. 51). As Julia Christensen Hughes (2017) points out, values drive behavior. Policy is generally concerned with behavior and accepted norms for conduct within the boundaries of the institution.
When there is cause for policy to be implemented, it is because people have behaved badly, not because they have bad values. When we talk about academic integrity from a policy perspective, we talk about “breaches of integrity” or “violations of integrity.” The word “integrity” comes from the same Latin root (integritas) as the word “integrate,” meaning to make something whole. In contrast, a “breach” implies that something that was previously whole has been compromised. A “critical failure” is something that has occurred that requires immediate attention. Using this kind of language shows that institutional expectations have not been met. A breach of integrity is as much of a concern as a breach of privacy, data, contract, or records containing personal information. Ethical breaches of all kinds in higher education are serious matters.

When we talk about academic integrity from a policy perspective, we talk about “breaches of integrity” or “violations of integrity.” The word “integrity” comes from the same Latin root (
integritas
) as the word “integrate,” meaning to make something whole. In contrast, a “breach” implies that something that was previously whole has been compromised. A “critical failure” is something that has occurred that requires immediate attention. Using this kind of language shows that institutional expectations have not been met. A breach of integrity is as much of a concern as a breach of privacy, data, contract, or records containing personal information. Ethical breaches of all kinds in higher education are serious matters.
Policies help educators and administrators answer the question, “OK, I have found that a student has behaved badly, so now what do I do?” The word “policy” comes from the same Greek root (politeia, later imported into Latin aspolitia), from which the English word “police” is derived. Policies are designed to help those in positions of authority follow judicial procedure, enforce rules, and administer discipline to those who break the rules. When this kind of “policing” lens is used, it can result in an adversarial relationship between students, educators, and administrators (Bertram Gallant, 2008a; Eisner & Vicinus, 2008; Serviss, 2016). To help alleviate this, experts have begun to advocate including students as stakeholders in the process of developing, communicating, and administering policy (Bretag et al., 2011; Bretag & Mahmud, 2016; Freeman, 2013). Treating students as stakeholders—and even partners—in matters relating to academic integrity helps to mitigate adversarial relationships between students and faculty.

Plagiarism through an Educational Lens

Plagiarism through an Educational Lens
Academic integrity has been called a “teaching and learning imperative” (Bertram Gallant, 2008a). The idea of instructional practices to teach what some have called “plagiarism prevention” (Strittmatter & Bratton, 2016, p. 107) have existed for decades, but terms such as this can strike fear into students, as learning is focused on avoiding punishment rather than skill development or critical thinking. Bertram Gallant (2008a) challenges us to reframe the question, “How do we stop students from cheating?” to “How do we ensure students are learning?” If students are constantly fearful of being accused of plagiarism, it is unlikely that they will be able to focus on learning. Fear-driven and authoritarian pedagogy, once the norm, is now considered antithetical to modern teaching and learning approaches (Hargreaves, 2015; Hargreaves, Elhawary, & Mahgoub, 2018).

Academic integrity has been called a “teaching and learning imperative” (Bertram Gallant, 2008a). The idea of instructional practices to teach what some have called “plagiarism prevention” (Strittmatter & Bratton, 2016, p. 107) have existed for decades, but terms such as this can strike fear into students, as learning is focused on avoiding punishment rather than skill development or critical thinking. Bertram Gallant (2008a) challenges us to reframe the question, “How do we stop students from cheating?” to “How do we ensure students are learning?” If students are constantly fearful of being accused of plagiarism, it is unlikely that they will be able to focus on learning. Fear-driven and authoritarian pedagogy, once the norm, is now considered antithetical to modern teaching and learning approaches (Hargreaves, 2015; Hargreaves, Elhawary, & Mahgoub, 2018).
One fear-based approach to teaching students about plagiarism merits discussion. It is the idea that textual plagiarism can be defined by a finite number of words lifted from a text without proper attribution. This is a myth that was completely busted by Rebecca Moore Howard (2000) more than twenty years ago. She traces this practice to the logical positivism of the 1960s, explaining how it originated in the fifth edition of theHarbrace Handbookfrom 1962, which advised writers to place three or more words within quotation marks. The handbook was first released in 1941 by John C. Hodges, a professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and became ubiquitous across American campuses (University of Tennessee, Knoxville, 2012). By 1962, the fifth edition could be found in college classrooms across the United States and beyond (Hodges & Whitten, 1962).

One fear-based approach to teaching students about plagiarism merits discussion. It is the idea that textual plagiarism can be defined by a finite number of words lifted from a text without proper attribution. This is a myth that was completely busted by Rebecca Moore Howard (2000) more than twenty years ago. She traces this practice to the logical positivism of the 1960s, explaining how it originated in the fifth edition of the
Harbrace Handbook
from 1962, which advised writers to place three or more words within quotation marks. The handbook was first released in 1941 by John C. Hodges, a professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and became ubiquitous across American campuses (University of Tennessee, Knoxville, 2012). By 1962, the fifth edition could be found in college classrooms across the United States and beyond (Hodges & Whitten, 1962).
Although the advice was offered as a way to encourage ethical citation practices, it was subverted such that the reverse of the original approach was taken up. Educators and policymakers grabbed on to the idea that if three or more words were written from a source without quotation marks, it must be plagiarism. This approach was ill conceived, but it was seductive to both educators and policymakers because it took a complex idea and simplified it to the point of being reductionist. It led to an “if-then” fallacy of logic that was deeply flawed: if a student wrote three or more words without placing them within quotation marks, then that amounted to plagiarism. This led to a widespread, often unquestioned practice of having students placeanypassage of three words or more within quotation marks.

This approach was ill conceived, but it was seductive to both educators and policymakers because it took a complex idea and simplified it to the point of being reductionist. It led to an “if-then” fallacy of logic that was deeply flawed: if a student wrote three or more words without placing them within quotation marks, then that amounted to plagiarism. This led to a widespread, often unquestioned practice of having students place
any
passage of three words or more within quotation marks.
That 1962 edition was coauthored by Mary Whitten, who carried on with the work after Hodges’s death in 1967. Coincidentally, 1962 was the year when William Bowers was collecting the data for his seminal study, which was not published until two years later and which went on to change our understanding of plagiarism and other academic misconduct from that point forward. It is possible that Bowers’s work influenced revisions to subsequent editions of the handbook that followed.

That 1962 edition was coauthored by Mary Whitten, who carried on with the work after Hodges’s death in 1967. Coincidentally, 1962 was the year when William Bowers was collecting the data for his seminal study, which was not published until two years later and which went on to change our understanding of plagiarism and other academic misconduct from that point forward. It is possible that Bowers’s work influenced revisions to subsequent editions of the handbook that followed.
Ten years after Hodge’s passing, the eighth edition of the handbook was released (Hodges & Whitten, 1977). Rebecca Moore Howard (2000) explains that by then, the idea of associating plagiarism with a particular number of words had been dropped entirely. This was because in part, the idea had been scorned by scholars who asserted that notions of text and plagiarism could not be addressed in such reductionist and formulaic terms (Howard, 2000). It has not appeared in the handbook since.

Ten years after Hodge’s passing, the eighth edition of the handbook was released (Hodges & Whitten, 1977). Rebecca Moore Howard (2000) explains that by then, the idea of associating plagiarism with a particular number of words had been dropped entirely. This was because in part, the idea had been scorned by scholars who asserted that notions of text and plagiarism could not be addressed in such reductionist and formulaic terms (Howard, 2000). It has not appeared in the handbook since.
Nevertheless, the idea that plagiarism can be defined as a finite number of words lifted from another’s text without attribution persists, despite scholars having agreed for half a century that such an oversimplified approach is utterly unacceptable. An updated approach to this flawed logic would say that there is an acceptable “originality score” generated by text-matching software (e.g., Turnitin) that would determine whether plagiarism has occurred. There have been reports of universities automatically failing students whose theses contain more than a particular percentage of text-matching, as identified by software (Zuo, 2019). The percentage is inevitably an arbitrary number, not based on any empirical research but more likely an administrative estimation of what is considered tolerable. Similar to the “finite number of words” approach from the 1960s, the “acceptable percentage of text-matching” one is equally reductionist and grossly oversimplified. As Alice Drum (1986) points out, “avoiding plagiarism is not simply a matter of following accepted rules” (p. 242). Avoiding plagiarism is about learning ethical citation and referencing practices and teaching students to value not only what they know, but how they know it and whose work they learned from.

Similar to the “finite number of words” approach from the 1960s, the “acceptable percentage of text-matching” one is equally reductionist and grossly oversimplified. As Alice Drum (1986) points out, “avoiding plagiarism is not simply a matter of following accepted rules” (p. 242). Avoiding plagiarism is about learning ethical citation and referencing practices and teaching students to value not only what they know, but how they know it and whose work they learned from.
Because the idea of plagiarism is complex, the ways in which we address it must be attentive to nuance and multiple factors, which can all come into play at once. An educational approach to plagiarism puts student learning at the forefront. It includes curriculum development, direct instruction, and assessment design, as well as formative and summative feedback that focuses intensely on student learning in ways that are proactive and learner-centered. This is no small feat for educators who have heavy course loads and jam-packed syllabi with more content than teaching hours.

Because the idea of plagiarism is complex, the ways in which we address it must be attentive to nuance and multiple factors, which can all come into play at once. An educational approach to plagiarism puts student learning at the forefront. It includes curriculum development, direct instruction, and assessment design, as well as formative and summative feedback that focuses intensely on student learning in ways that are proactive and learner-centered. This is no small feat for educators who have heavy course loads and jam-packed syllabi with more content than teaching hours.
Faculty members must take some responsibility for ensuring that students understand what they expect from them and why. When I work with colleagues in educational development settings, I engage them in conversations about the role they play in helping students learn about integrity. One of the key messages I share is that just because there is a statement in the course syllabus that indicates students are expected to abide by institutional expectations to act with integrity, that does not absolve faculty members of the responsibility of explicitly communicating their expectations to students. In other words, it is up to faculty members to explicitly communicate to students how they expect them to enact the values of integrity in their classes.

Faculty members must take some responsibility for ensuring that students understand what they expect from them and why. When I work with colleagues in educational development settings, I engage them in conversations about the role they play in helping students learn about integrity. One of the key messages I share is that just because there is a statement in the course syllabus that indicates students are expected to abide by institutional expectations to act with integrity, that does not absolve faculty members of the responsibility of explicitly communicating their expectations to students. In other words, it is up to faculty members to explicitly communicate to students how they expect them to enact the values of integrity in their classes.
The nature of academic misconduct policy in education has often taken a “Gotcha!” approach (Howard, 2001; Jendrek, 1989; Price, 2002), in which the focus has been on punishing students after they have been found responsible for engaging in misconduct rather than taking a proactive approach to prevent it (Eaton, Guglielmin, & Otoo, 2017). Seen from this perspective, one could argue that plagiarism could be situated along a continuum, with education dedicated to prevention at one end and policy and disciplinary actions at the other. Such a position could be useful to engage people in conversations about how and why institutions must adopt teaching and learning approaches in addition to policy ones. But in and of itself, a continuum is not enough because it is often the gray area in the middle of the continuum that presents the most difficulty. That is the point at which an educator [usually a professor, but sometimes a teaching assistant (TA)] either suspects or identifies plagiarism. At that moment, we have the sense that integrity has been breached. Educational and preventative approaches have failed, and we move from the part of the continuum concerned with education to the part of the continuum where policy is consulted and then implemented. Then questions begin to arise: Is this plagiarism? If yes, was it intentional, or did the student just lack adequate citing and referencing skills?

The nature of academic misconduct policy in education has often taken a “Gotcha!” approach (Howard, 2001; Jendrek, 1989; Price, 2002), in which the focus has been on punishing students after they have been found responsible for engaging in misconduct rather than taking a proactive approach to prevent it (Eaton, Guglielmin, & Otoo, 2017). Seen from this perspective, one could argue that plagiarism could be situated along a continuum, with education dedicated to prevention at one end and policy and disciplinary actions at the other. Such a position could be useful to engage people in conversations about how and why institutions must adopt teaching and learning approaches in addition to policy ones. But in and of itself, a continuum is not enough because it is often the gray area in the middle of the continuum that presents the most difficulty. That is the point at which an educator [usually a professor, but sometimes a teaching assistant (TA)] either suspects or identifies plagiarism. At that moment, we have the sense that integrity has been breached. Educational and preventative approaches have failed, and we move from the part of the continuum concerned with education to the part of the continuum where policy is consulted and then implemented. Then questions begin to arise: Is this plagiarism? If yes, was it intentional, or did the student just lack adequate citing and referencing skills?
This question of unintentional versus intentional plagiarism has been discussed at length by educators and scholars (Adam, 2016; Elander et al., 2010; Jensen, 2012; Paterson, Taylor, & Usick, 2003; Walker, 2008). It isnow widely accepted that not all incidences of student plagiarism are deliberate. When it is intentional, it viewed as more egregious than when it is due to a lack of knowledge or skills (Jensen, 2012). Whether a student intended to plagiarize is important because it points beyond a two-dimensional continuum, with teaching and learning (prevention) and policy (punishment) at opposite ends, to a three-dimensional model, in which morality can play a role.
