now widely accepted that not all incidences of student plagiarism are deliberate. When it is intentional, it viewed as more egregious than when it is due to a lack of knowledge or skills (Jensen, 2012). Whether a student intended to plagiarize is important because it points beyond a two-dimensional continuum, with teaching and learning (prevention) and policy (punishment) at opposite ends, to a three-dimensional model, in which morality can play a role.
Academic Integrity through a Moral Lens

Academic Integrity through a Moral Lens
Some argue that the concept of plagiarism has its roots in Judeo-Christian values (Colon, 2001; Eaton, 2017; Park, 2003; Standler, 2012), but others situate it within a human rights context (Freedman, 1994). What is clear is that there is discourse around plagiarism having moral implications, particularly when it is done knowingly. Having said that, it is important to resist the temptation to demonize students who plagiarize. This can lead down the path of oversimplification that has been prevalent for too long in the discourse around academic misconduct. This has led to a “moral panic” (Bertram Gallant, 2008b, p. 2). In turn, this has created an adversarial relationship between students and their teachers, as well as educational administrators (Eisner & Vicinus, 2008). The results are ethical binaries and moral dichotomies (Bertram Gallant, 2008a; Valentine, 2006), which position those who plagiarize as immoral and those who do not as morally superior. Plagiarism is often represented in the media as a moral dilemma in the press (Valentine, 2006), which exacerbates reductionist views of an inherently complex phenomenon.

Some argue that the concept of plagiarism has its roots in Judeo-Christian values (Colon, 2001; Eaton, 2017; Park, 2003; Standler, 2012), but others situate it within a human rights context (Freedman, 1994). What is clear is that there is discourse around plagiarism having moral implications, particularly when it is done knowingly. Having said that, it is important to resist the temptation to demonize students who plagiarize. This can lead down the path of oversimplification that has been prevalent for too long in the discourse around academic misconduct. This has led to a “moral panic” (Bertram Gallant, 2008b, p. 2). In turn, this has created an adversarial relationship between students and their teachers, as well as educational administrators (Eisner & Vicinus, 2008). The results are ethical binaries and moral dichotomies (Bertram Gallant, 2008a; Valentine, 2006), which position those who plagiarize as immoral and those who do not as morally superior. Plagiarism is often represented in the media as a moral dilemma in the press (Valentine, 2006), which exacerbates reductionist views of an inherently complex phenomenon.
Further, students constitute only one component of the larger educational system, and academic integrity is fundamental to the entire university system. As such, an organizational or systems approach is needed in which “institutional structures and cultures support integrity” (Bertram Gallant, 2008b, p. 7). The idea that postsecondary institutions, and universities in particular, must uphold integrity is a fundamental aspect of the higher education leadership discourse. Besvinick (1983, p. 569) noted, “Universities are perceived as epitomizing intellectual and social honesty, and they are expected to strive continually for that form of perfection.” Besvinick goes on to say that intellectual good and social good are intertwined at higher education institutions. We can extrapolate from this that when educators and policymakers uphold expectations for intellectually ethical conduct, they are upholding the notion that those who are members of the university (including students) have a social responsibility to act ethically. Besvinick notes, “The integrity of a university is measured by its ability to join both the intellectual good and the social good” (1983,p. 568). Those words hold just as true today and could also be extended to other kinds of postsecondary institutions, too. Upholding academic integrity cannot only be about the application of policy after misconduct has occurred; it must also address institutional and societal expectations that students, as well as everyone else on campus, conduct themselves in ethical ways that demonstrate integrity.

Besvinick notes, “The integrity of a university is measured by its ability to join both the intellectual good and the social good” (1983,
p. 568). Those words hold just as true today and could also be extended to other kinds of postsecondary institutions, too. Upholding academic integrity cannot only be about the application of policy after misconduct has occurred; it must also address institutional and societal expectations that students, as well as everyone else on campus, conduct themselves in ethical ways that demonstrate integrity.
Although I have presented each of these conceptual lenses separately, by now it should be obvious that they are interconnected. Individually, none of the lenses presents a complete picture. By layering the lenses on top of one another, though, the complexity of the issue comes into focus. We understand that responsible ethical conduct in higher education involves instruction, policy application, and the acknowledgment that the institution itself plays a fundamental role in upholding integrity among its various stakeholders. With that established, I turn to addressing how we can begin to define plagiarism in higher education contexts.

TOWARD A CONTEMPORARY DEFINITION OF PLAGIARISM

TOWARD A CONTEMPORARY DEFINITION OF PLAGIARISM
When people use the term “plagiarism,” they may assume that others share the same idea of what it means. Building on the history of plagiarism that I explored inChapter 1, the word has lacked a clear definition for centuries. Oversimplifications abound, but plagiarism is complex and has no singular definition. As a result, faculty members, staff, and students may be confused about what actually counts as plagiarism (Bricault, 2007; Brown & Howell, 2001). From a scholarly perspective, plagiarism has been defined as “stealing (by copying) the words or ideas of someone else and passing them off as one’s own without crediting the source” (Park, 2003, p. 472). Others have defined the concept similarly, with a focus on text and ideas (Fialkoff, 1993). Still others assert that the idea of theft should be dismissed altogether (Helgesson & Ericksson, 2015). The only thing that scholars seem to agree on is that there is no singular or absolute definition of plagiarism. It would be arrogant of me to suggest that I could define plagiarism when others before me have deemed that to be an impossible task (Howard, 2000). Instead of attempting to do the impossible, instead I offer some considerations of how plagiarism might be better understood and unpacked in higher education. I explore ways that faculty and administrators can think beyond preexisting notions of stereotypes of what plagiarism is and begin to reconceptualize it in ways that make sense for today’s learners.

Others have defined the concept similarly, with a focus on text and ideas (Fialkoff, 1993). Still others assert that the idea of theft should be dismissed altogether (Helgesson & Ericksson, 2015). The only thing that scholars seem to agree on is that there is no singular or absolute definition of plagiarism. It would be arrogant of me to suggest that I could define plagiarism when others before me have deemed that to be an impossible task (Howard, 2000). Instead of attempting to do the impossible, instead I offer some considerations of how plagiarism might be better understood and unpacked in higher education. I explore ways that faculty and administrators can think beyond preexisting notions of stereotypes of what plagiarism is and begin to reconceptualize it in ways that make sense for today’s learners.
Traditional definitions of plagiarism have not evolved to meet modern teaching and learning contexts where digital engagement is a key element of learning. Today’s students differ from previous generations in profound ways when it comes to how they understand the ownership and distributionof knowledge, data, and content (Blum, 2009; Evering & Moorman, 2012). We know one thing for certain: plagiarism in the twenty-first century extends beyond text and ideas.

Traditional definitions of plagiarism have not evolved to meet modern teaching and learning contexts where digital engagement is a key element of learning. Today’s students differ from previous generations in profound ways when it comes to how they understand the ownership and distribution
of knowledge, data, and content (Blum, 2009; Evering & Moorman, 2012). We know one thing for certain: plagiarism in the twenty-first century extends beyond text and ideas.
Nontext-based plagiarism has been the topic of much discussion among academic integrity scholars (Blythman, Orr, & Mullin, 2007; Bradley, 2011; Chuda et al., 2012; Culwin, MacLeod, & Lancaster, 2001; Foltýnek, Meuschke, & Gipp, 2019; Porter, 2009; Simon, 2016; Sutherland-Smith, 2008). Despite that, many higher education institutions continue to focus on text-based plagiarism in policies, procedures, and learning supports for students. For this reason, I will delve into some of the complexities of how plagiarism has evolved beyond its traditional definition of literary theft to include broader considerations such as musical scores, computer code, and other creative, technical, and intellectual output (Batane, 2010; Carroll, 2007; Marsden, Carroll, & Neill, 2005; Simon, 2016). In the section that follows, I offer examples about how to understand plagiarism in today’s world, but I caution that they are not intended as absolutes. That would only further propagate an oversimplification of an issue that is becoming increasingly complex. I offer these explorations as a way to challenge outdated ideas, provoke thought, and generate dialogue among faculty, administrators, students, and others with an interest in education.

Framework for a Twenty-First-Century Definition of Plagiarism

Framework for a Twenty-First-Century Definition of Plagiarism
Figure 2.2offers a visual representation of how we might begin to expand our ideas about plagiarism in higher education. This representation includes elements that have traditionally been considered plagiarism (text and ideas), but adds new dimensions, such as data, code, music, design, and art. Some of these categories overlap, and next I discuss each of them in more detail to differentiate among them. I can add that in my analysis of twenty Canadian universities, only four explicitly included all these elements in their institutional policies addressing plagiarism (Eaton, 2017). I expect that similar results could be also found in the United States, the United Kingdom, and other countries. That is why it is important to expand our ideas about what constitutes plagiarism so that we can ultimately help our students focus on learning in ethical ways in changing contexts.

Text

Text
Textual plagiarism involves written prose, including but not limited to essays, manuscripts, articles, theses, books, and personal communications (e.g., letters and e-mails). Textual plagiarism can also apply to digital textsuch as blogs, microblogs, online articles, discussion board posts, social media status updates and posts, and tweets. This is not an exhaustive list, but rather one intended to generate ideas and conversations about how our notions of “text” have changed since the advent of the printing press, and later the Internet. There is no doubt that the ways in which text is presented in digital form will continue to evolve, so it is important for educators and administrators to keep an open mind about what we mean when we talk about “text.”

A Twenty-First Century Understanding of Plagiarism
Because most text today is produced in digital form, the cut-and-paste practice of lifting digital material has been practiced for decades (Oliphant, 2002; Teixeira da Silva, 2016). Although some have dubbed this practice “cyber-plagiarism” (Oliphant, 2002; Holi, 2013), the reality is that we do not need fancy names for what is essentially the same practice that has existed for centuries. Besides, cases of plagiarism remain where text hasbeen transcribed by hand from a print-only source or a hand-scribed manuscript, and all of it can fall under the same name of “textual plagiarism.”

Although some have dubbed this practice “cyber-plagiarism” (Oliphant, 2002; Holi, 2013), the reality is that we do not need fancy names for what is essentially the same practice that has existed for centuries. What is important is that today, writing is produced in a variety of ways that may not have existed when professors were students. For example, students using other students’ discussion board posts from online courses without attribution could be considered a form of plagiarism. The problem is solved by having students learn when and how to give attribution to others for their work. It is essential for educators to communicate to students that it is the appropriation of others’ textwithoutadequate attribution that provides cause for concern that plagiarism has occurred.

Ideas

Ideas
The area of ideas is perhaps the most difficult kind of plagiarism to address, in part because it can be tricky to prove. In industry, “idea theft,” as Lewis (2013, p. 739) calls it, is rampant. In a survey of more than 950 journalists, over 74 percent rejected the belief that the ideas for stories should be attributed, despite originality being prized within the profession (Lewis, 2013). In his article, Lewis talks about how idea plagiarism might be worthy of more attention in higher education, “which places a premium on original thinking” (p. 741).

The area of ideas is perhaps the most difficult kind of plagiarism to address, in part because it can be tricky to prove. In industry, “idea theft,” as Lewis (2013, p. 739) calls it, is rampant. In a survey of more than 950 journalists, over 74 percent rejected the belief that the ideas for stories should be attributed, despite originality being prized within the profession (Lewis, 2013). In his article, Lewis talks about how idea plagiarism might be worthy of more attention in higher education, “which places a premium on original thinking” (p. 741).
The idea of “original thinking” in higher education becomes problematic because in educational contexts, we expect students to scaffold their learning. That means building on ideas and knowledge that one has internalized as part of the learning process. The idea of scaffolding can be traced back to Vygotsky (1978), though according to Maybin, Mercer, and Stierer (1992), the actual term “scaffolding” was introduced by Bruner (1985). The point is that “certain kinds of support which learners receive in their interaction with parents, teachers, and other ‘mentors’ as they move towards new skills, concepts, or levels of understanding” (Maybin, Mercer, & Stierer, 1992, p. 21), otherwise known as “scaffolding,” has been around since before many of today’s learners were even born.

The idea of “original thinking” in higher education becomes problematic because in educational contexts, we expect students to scaffold their learning. That means building on ideas and knowledge that one has internalized as part of the learning process. The idea of scaffolding can be traced back to Vygotsky (1978), though according to Maybin, Mercer, and Stierer (1992), the actual term “scaffolding” was introduced by Bruner (1985). The point is that “certain kinds of support which learners receive in their interaction with parents, teachers, and other ‘mentors’ as they move towards new skills, concepts, or levels of understanding” (Maybin, Mercer, & Stierer, 1992, p. 21), otherwise known as “scaffolding,” has been around since before many of today’s learners were even born.
However, it is important to acknowledge that “the scaffolding concept remains at an abstract level and is not easily translated into a practical classroom context” (Maybin, Mercer, & Stierer, 1992, p. 23). It could be argued that the concept of scaffolding could be at odds with the notion of original thinking, and there is already robust discussion in the literature about whether there is such a thing as an original idea at all (e.g., Helgesson & Ericksson, 2015; Lewis, 2013).

Professors, research lab managers, teaching assistants (TAs), and administrators can find themselves in a mess when a student is accused of plagiarizing someone else’s ideas when those ideas have not previouslybeen written down. If the ideas were written down and there is a record of it, then text enters into the equation as well. But ideas can be presented at conferences or in personal conversations (Helgesson & Ericksson, 2015), for example. If the ideas have been only been discussed or have only existed in some other nontraceable form, then unravelling the details about who had the original idea can be an exercise in frustration.

been written down. If the ideas were written down and there is a record of it, then text enters into the equation as well. But ideas can be presented at conferences or in personal conversations (Helgesson & Ericksson, 2015), for example. If the ideas have been only been discussed or have only existed in some other nontraceable form, then unravelling the details about who had the original idea can be an exercise in frustration.
This sense of frustration can lead those who are responsible for reporting or investigating academic misconduct to be tempted to ignore or dismiss suspected cases of idea plagiarism. This is an inappropriate and unethical response because taking others’ ideas without acknowledging their source is not benign—there is an intellectual injury to those whose ideas have been misappropriated (Lewis, 2013).

This sense of frustration can lead those who are responsible for reporting or investigating academic misconduct to be tempted to ignore or dismiss suspected cases of idea plagiarism. This is an inappropriate and unethical response because taking others’ ideas without acknowledging their source is not benign—there is an intellectual injury to those whose ideas have been misappropriated (Lewis, 2013).
One response to alleged cases of idea theft is to have the student engage in an activity to trace the origin of the idea. The idea of an intellectual genealogy (Roediger, 2005) is a kind of forensic activity in which a person endeavors to identify and then list those who mentored and influenced them. This kind of activity is not only self-reflective, it also teaches students to become aware of the importance of giving attribution to those who came before them. Even when ideas are original, we are influenced by those whose works we have read, those with whom we have had conversations, and those who have mentored us in a variety of ways. This kind of approach can be more restorative than punitive, and if done carefully, it can help students to understand the importance of attribution as part of their learning process.

Code

Code
In this section, I specifically address plagiarism of source code because it is a particularly complex topic in the field of computer science and computer engineering in higher education (and beyond). Notwithstanding the fact that I am not a coder, I recognize the importance of including a discussion about code plagiarism in a chapter that attempts to modernize our understanding of what plagiarism exactly is. Plagiarism of source code been recognized among scholars as deserving of special attention since before the turn of the millennium (Bowyer & Hall, 1999; Sutherland-Smith, 2008), as well as since (Abraham & Milligan, 2008; Arwin & Tahaghoghi, 2006; Carroll, 2007; Culwin et al., 2001; Prechelt, Malpohl, & Philippsen, 2002; Sutherland-Smith, 2008).

In this section, I specifically address plagiarism of source code because it is a particularly complex topic in the field of computer science and computer engineering in higher education (and beyond). Notwithstanding the fact that I am not a coder, I recognize the importance of including a discussion about code plagiarism in a chapter that attempts to modernize our understanding of what plagiarism exactly is. Plagiarism of source code been recognized among scholars as deserving of special attention since before the turn of the millennium (Bowyer & Hall, 1999; Sutherland-Smith, 2008), as well as since (Abraham & Milligan, 2008; Arwin & Tahaghoghi, 2006; Carroll, 2007; Culwin et al., 2001; Prechelt, Malpohl, & Philippsen, 2002; Sutherland-Smith, 2008).
Although computer codes are referred to as “languages,” when it comes to academic integrity and plagiarism, it is important to distinguish between the kind of text I have addressed up to now and “writing from many other forms that are still written in textual characters but not insuch a way as to form prose”—that is to say, it is important to address text that is “not a representation of ideas in words, sentences, and paragraphs,” as is the case with computer code (Simon, 2016, p. 764). In academic disciplines related to coding, students are not only required to solve problems, but at more advanced levels, they are also expected to develop code or software that is their own original work (Chuda et al., 2012).

Although computer codes are referred to as “languages,” when it comes to academic integrity and plagiarism, it is important to distinguish between the kind of text I have addressed up to now and “writing from many other forms that are still written in textual characters but not in
such a way as to form prose”—that is to say, it is important to address text that is “not a representation of ideas in words, sentences, and paragraphs,” as is the case with computer code (Simon, 2016, p. 764). In academic disciplines related to coding, students are not only required to solve problems, but at more advanced levels, they are also expected to develop code or software that is their own original work (Chuda et al., 2012).
Identifying unauthorized replication of source code may not be as straightforward as one might think, as subtle differences and derivations can occur that can cause a professor to conclude that perhaps a particular student was not really the creator of the code (Chuda et al., 2012). One study showed that 42 percent of 313 computer science students surveyed believed that code they had created had been plagiarized by others (Chuda et al., 2012). The same study showed that 100 percent of faculty members and 94 percent of students considered “copying, modifying, or presenting another’s source code as plagiarism” (Chuda et al., 2012, p. 24).

Identifying unauthorized replication of source code may not be as straightforward as one might think, as subtle differences and derivations can occur that can cause a professor to conclude that perhaps a particular student was not really the creator of the code (Chuda et al., 2012). One study showed that 42 percent of 313 computer science students surveyed believed that code they had created had been plagiarized by others (Chuda et al., 2012). The same study showed that 100 percent of faculty members and 94 percent of students considered “copying, modifying, or presenting another’s source code as plagiarism” (Chuda et al., 2012, p. 24).
In her book on plagiarism and the Internet, Wendy Sutherland-Smith (2008) traces how the protection of source code was a topic at the 1971 meeting of the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works. The Convention dates back to 1886 for member-nations and has been updated numerous times since. Sutherland-Smith points out how member-countries are guided and bound by the Convention in the development of their own copyright laws. Thus the protection of computer code under copyright law has been considered for about half a century, but academic misconduct relating to computer code has still yet to be acknowledged by some college academic misconduct policies. This points to how far behind colleges and universities can be when it comes to updating their understanding of what counts as academic misconduct.

Sutherland-Smith points out how member-countries are guided and bound by the Convention in the development of their own copyright laws. When we talk about academic integrity and code, we can think of broad applications: software, apps, algorithms, game development, and other kinds of intellectual products that involve source code of some kind. It is important for higher education scholars, educators, and administrators to recognize that not only can plagiarism be an issue when it comes to code, but detection and investigation of cases can be just as complex in these instances as they are in text-based plagiarism. The use of tools such as JPlag and MOSS (which stands for “Measure of Software Similarity”) have long been recognized as useful in helping educators recognize when a deeper investigation might be warranted (Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, n.d.; Prechelt et al., 2002).

Credit is due to computer scientists for initiating the fundamental paradigm shift in terms of how we think about plagiarism. It is thanks to them that the rest of higher education now recognizes and acknowledges that plagiarism happens in non-text-based disciplines. It is also worth noting that it was computer scientists who challenged the rest of higher educationto look beyond term-paper mills as the only way that academic work can be outsourced. The term “contract cheating” was coined by two computer scientists in the United Kingdom (Clarke & Lancaster, 2006), a term that has become ubiquitous across higher education to refer to academic outsourcing of all kinds.

Data

Data
Theft of data is sometimes considered plagiarism, though it often falls under other categories of academic or research misconduct in institutional definitions. Research laboratories are also learning environments where students build skills and knowledge through hands-on training. I include data here because the early definitions of plagiarism were centered around notions of theft. The idea of taking something that one did not create oneself is central to plagiarism, and this includes both raw data and analyzed results. A central tenet to this argument is that misconduct has occurred when someone else’s work has been taken and used without permission or without giving the source credit for it. Data theft differs from fabrication or falsification of research data, which are other forms of research misconduct.

Theft of data is sometimes considered plagiarism, though it often falls under other categories of academic or research misconduct in institutional definitions. Research laboratories are also learning environments where students build skills and knowledge through hands-on training. I include data here because the early definitions of plagiarism were centered around notions of theft. The idea of taking something that one did not create oneself is central to plagiarism, and this includes both raw data and analyzed results. A central tenet to this argument is that misconduct has occurred when someone else’s work has been taken and used without permission or without giving the source credit for it. Data theft differs from fabrication or falsification of research data, which are other forms of research misconduct.
A case of someone misappropriating someone else’s data or results and presenting it as their own is a clear-cut case of misconduct. Sadly, many cases of data plagiarism are not straightforward. When data are collected in a lab environment or as part of a research team, it can be unclear who owns the data, how and when it can be used, and by whom. In situations like this, student researchers, as well as postdoctoral fellows, professional research associates, clinicians, study coordinators, and others, can all be working on the same project and can be coming in and out of a laboratory at all hours to perform various tasks, all under the direction of a principal investigator, who is often also a faculty member.

A case of someone misappropriating someone else’s data or results and presenting it as their own is a clear-cut case of misconduct. Sadly, many cases of data plagiarism are not straightforward. When data are collected in a lab environment or as part of a research team, it can be unclear who owns the data, how and when it can be used, and by whom. In situations like this, student researchers, as well as postdoctoral fellows, professional research associates, clinicians, study coordinators, and others, can all be working on the same project and can be coming in and out of a laboratory at all hours to perform various tasks, all under the direction of a principal investigator, who is often also a faculty member.
In cases like this, it behooves the principal investigator to take the time to explain to the team members what their expectations are around data storage, retention, and use, as well as how and when results can be shared and who needs to be given credit. These expectations can vary from one lab to another, and there is no single prescription for handling data ethically. Many universities will have a central research office to assist with such matters, but I cannot overemphasize how important it is for principal investigators to engage all team members in ongoing, open, and explicit conversations about ethical conduct and expectations. Even though taking the time to have these conversations can seem like time taken away from the actual research itself, the investment of time can pay off in spades if it prevents a case of misconduct from happening in the first place.Documenting these conversations in team meeting notes can further help to legitimize and clarify what constitutes ethical conduct in research settings.

Music

Music
In this section, as well as the two that follow, I discuss plagiarism in what could be considered traditionally artistic disciplines. I have separated them for the purposes of this discussion, but there is much overlap between them. Music could be considered art, of course, as could design, but within the context of higher education, it could be argued that there are various disciplinary and intellectual genealogies (Roediger, 2005) that merit a deeper discussion of these as distinct areas for consideration.

In this section, as well as the two that follow, I discuss plagiarism in what could be considered traditionally artistic disciplines. I have separated them for the purposes of this discussion, but there is much overlap between them. Music could be considered art, of course, as could design, but within the context of higher education, it could be argued that there are various disciplinary and intellectual genealogies (Roediger, 2005) that merit a deeper discussion of these as distinct areas for consideration.
In the case of music, cases of plagiarism are often discussed in the news. The music industry is a commercial enterprise that is concerned with issues that extend beyond the kind of plagiarism that we find in higher education. The commercial aspects of musical plagiarism become entangled with intellectual property, copyright, and other legal aspects of creation that do not apply in the same way in higher education contexts. There is a robust body of literature on music plagiarism and litigation (Keyt, 1988; Knopper, 2015; Müllensiefen & Pendzich, 2009), but almost no scholarly research about academic integrity in music education (Simon, 2016). This has led to an overall lack of guidance for music educators who wants to teach their students how to engage in ethical music composition, as well as how and when to pursue a possible case of plagiarism.

In the case of music, cases of plagiarism are often discussed in the news. The music industry is a commercial enterprise that is concerned with issues that extend beyond the kind of plagiarism that we find in higher education. The commercial aspects of musical plagiarism become entangled with intellectual property, copyright, and other legal aspects of creation that do not apply in the same way in higher education contexts. There is a robust body of literature on music plagiarism and litigation (Keyt, 1988; Knopper, 2015; M
ü
llensiefen & Pendzich, 2009), but almost no scholarly research about academic integrity in music education (Simon, 2016). This has led to an overall lack of guidance for music educators who wants to teach their students how to engage in ethical music composition, as well as how and when to pursue a possible case of plagiarism.
Design

Design
Higher education disciplines that focus on design include, but are not limited to, industrial design, engineering, architecture, fashion, and interior design. Overall rates of academic misconduct have been found to be especially high in engineering fields, compared with other disciplines, with up to 96 percent of students admitting to various forms of cheating (McCabe, 1997) This not only applies to plagiarism, but other forms of misconduct as well, such as cheating on exams. Very little is known about the prevalence of plagiarism or misconduct in other design-based disciplines. What these fields have in common, however, is a focus on collaborative learning, where students often work in pairs or groups to complete their work.

Higher education disciplines that focus on design include, but are not limited to, industrial design, engineering, architecture, fashion, and interior design. Overall rates of academic misconduct have been found to be especially high in engineering fields, compared with other disciplines, with up to 96 percent of students admitting to various forms of cheating (McCabe, 1997) This not only applies to plagiarism, but other forms of misconduct as well, such as cheating on exams. Very little is known about the prevalence of plagiarism or misconduct in other design-based disciplines. What these fields have in common, however, is a focus on collaborative learning, where students often work in pairs or groups to complete their work.
Although it is easy to talk about single-authored work in text-based disciplines, in other fields where scaffolded learning and creativity become indistinguishable, identifying and addressing plagiarism can become almost impossible. Similar to the misappropriation of ideas or data that can happen in labs, in fields where collaborative creativity is prized, much of thelearning can happen in design studios or collaborative learning spaces where students are working side by side or together (Walker, 2009), to the extent that learning and creating become inseparable. In these fields, it is especially important for students to document their ideas, emerging designs, and the development of their work through notes, journals, or portfolios.

Although it is easy to talk about single-authored work in text-based disciplines, in other fields where scaffolded learning and creativity become indistinguishable, identifying and addressing plagiarism can become almost impossible. Similar to the misappropriation of ideas or data that can happen in labs, in fields where collaborative creativity is prized, much of the
learning can happen in design studios or collaborative learning spaces where students are working side by side or together (Walker, 2009), to the extent that learning and creating become inseparable. In these fields, it is especially important for students to document their ideas, emerging designs, and the development of their work through notes, journals, or portfolios.
In design-based disciplines, faculty members can find it challenging to know where the students’ ideas begin and end, as well as how much of what they produce is their own individual work as opposed to the result of collaboration. The subject-matter experts in these fields must determine what counts as plagiarism in these subjects and then clearly communicate their expectations to students. What we can say for sure is that educators and experts are paying more attention to plagiarism in design-based disciplines, including but not limited to engineering, architecture, industrial design, video games, and fashion (Bailey, 2020; Ridgley, Schindler-Lynch, & Lynch, 2019; Ridgley et al., 2020).

Art

Art
I have included art in its own category because finding ways to identify and address plagiarism in the fine arts is becoming increasingly important (Bowman, 2007; Garrett & Robinson, 2012). The field of fine arts is diverse, as it includes but is not limited to:

I have included art in its own category because finding ways to identify and address plagiarism in the fine arts is becoming increasingly important (Bowman, 2007; Garrett & Robinson, 2012). The field of fine arts is diverse, as it includes but is not limited to:
- Visual, spatial, and graphic arts, which often include creative products produced in two dimensions, such as painting, drawing, and graphic arts.

- Plastic and decorative arts, which often include creative products produced in three dimensions, such as sculpture, modeling, enamelwork, and furniture design. (There is some overlap here with the design category mentioned in the first point.)

- Performing arts, which often includes embodied artistic expression, such as theater, dance, film, and music (the last of which was covered in its own category in the “Music” section).

- Culinary arts, which can include a hybrid of scientific and artistic knowledge, combining food science, chemistry, nutrition, gastronomy, and food preparation and presentation.

- Digital art of all kinds, including but not limited to graphics, illustrations, memes, and videos.

Visual, spatial, and graphic arts, which often include creative products produced in two dimensions, such as painting, drawing, and graphic arts.
Plastic and decorative arts, which often include creative products produced in three dimensions, such as sculpture, modeling, enamelwork, and furniture design. (There is some overlap here with the design category mentioned in the first point.)
Performing arts, which often includes embodied artistic expression, such as theater, dance, film, and music (the last of which was covered in its own category in the “Music” section).
Culinary arts, which can include a hybrid of scientific and artistic knowledge, combining food science, chemistry, nutrition, gastronomy, and food preparation and presentation.
Digital art of all kinds, including but not limited to graphics, illustrations, memes, and videos.
These are broad descriptions. The list is not intended to be exhaustive, and there are many forms of fine arts not mentioned here. No doubt, scholars in each of these areas would enjoy debating and critiquing the categorizations I have presented, and by no means do I intend to suggest absolutedefinitions. Instead, I offer these as loose organizations to help the reader puzzle through unique aspects of academic integrity in these disciplines that may differ from other fields.

These are broad descriptions. The list is not intended to be exhaustive, and there are many forms of fine arts not mentioned here. No doubt, scholars in each of these areas would enjoy debating and critiquing the categorizations I have presented, and by no means do I intend to suggest absolute
definitions. Instead, I offer these as loose organizations to help the reader puzzle through unique aspects of academic integrity in these disciplines that may differ from other fields.
One reason why I have grouped them together is that aesthetics and philosophy provide a foundation for the study and creation of fine arts in particular ways. Another reason is that for centuries, the teaching and learning of fine arts has included students learning by imitation, a practice intended to instill a sense of reverence and respect among students for those who came before them, while simultaneously teaching them foundational concepts and skills of the discipline (Walker, 2009, p. 49). This can make it especially problematic for students to discern where others’ ideas end and where theirs begin, with inspiration woven throughout (Ridgley et al., 2020. In turn, that makes it complicated for educators and administrators to determine what might be plagiarism, as opposed to what might be influence, or what, in prose-based disciplines, is referred to as “intertextuality.” Ryerson University (n.d.) has produced an open-access online guide to best practices for preventing visual plagiarism, which offers practical guidance for students and instructors about what such plagiarism is and how to avoid it.

This can make it especially problematic for students to discern where others’ ideas end and where theirs begin, with inspiration woven throughout (Ridgley et al., 2020. CONCLUSIONS

CONCLUSIONS
In this chapter, I have presented an expanded view of what might be considered plagiarism in twenty-first-century higher education. The ideas are not without their limitations, and they are not exhaustive. I recognize that I have focused on university contexts, and there is a need for an extended conversation about academic integrity in the trades and polytechnic contexts. Having said that, the central message here is that it is imperative for educators and policymakers to challenge outdated notions of plagiarism that focus only on text or ideas. There is a need to deeply and critically consider how students learn and how they show evidence of that learning through a variety of outputs, regardless of how those outputs are created. In turn, it is the responsibility of higher education institutions to provide adequate and modern learning resources, services, policies, and procedures that are better aligned with how today’s students learn.

In this chapter, I have presented an expanded view of what might be considered plagiarism in twenty-first-century higher education. The ideas are not without their limitations, and they are not exhaustive. I recognize that I have focused on university contexts, and there is a need for an extended conversation about academic integrity in the trades and polytechnic contexts. Having said that, the central message here is that it is imperative for educators and policymakers to challenge outdated notions of plagiarism that focus only on text or ideas. There is a need to deeply and critically consider how students learn and how they show evidence of that learning through a variety of outputs, regardless of how those outputs are created. In turn, it is the responsibility of higher education institutions to provide adequate and modern learning resources, services, policies, and procedures that are better aligned with how today’s students learn.

Intentionality, Textuality, and Other Complicating Factors

Intentionality, Textuality, and Other Complicating Factors
There are many reasons why people plagiarize and various ways it can occur. Because this book is focused on higher education, I direct my discussion toward student plagiarism, recognizing that some of it may be applicable to professors, researchers, and others as well. Inchapter 2, I addressed how we might think about defining and conceptualizing plagiarism in various disciplines. I would be remiss if I did not discuss the range of acts that can be classified as plagiarism, at least in text-based disciplines, and then attempt to explain why such acts happen. I begin in this chapter by describing what counts as plagiarism. From there, I discuss the differences in how students and professors perceive plagiarism. Finally, I tackle the reasons why students plagiarize, which can range from simple and straightforward to complex and confounding justifications.

Finally, I tackle the reasons why students plagiarize, which can range from simple and straightforward to complex and confounding justifications.
PLAGIARISM: A RANGE OF ACTS

PLAGIARISM: A RANGE OF ACTS
One reason why plagiarism has been difficult to define in absolute terms is that it is not a single act; there is a range of behaviors that can be classified as plagiarism (Elander et al., 2010; Howard, 2001; McCabe et al., 2001; Park, 2003). Of course, experts disagree on whether some of these acts should be considered plagiarism at all, but I will get to that later. In this section, I outline examples of some acts that have been classified as plagiarism. I notethat others before me have undertaken similar exercises in classifying acts of plagiarism (e.g., Hexham, 1992, 2013; Loui, 2002; Park, 2003; Wilhoit, 1994), and I draw from their work. Further, I have deliberately avoided ranking these acts in terms of severity to avoid creating a hierarchy that could be weaponized and used as a tool to punish students. The discussion that follows is meant to help the reader understand some of the nuances and complexities of what has—or could be—classified as plagiarism in text-based work from an educational perspective, rather than a punitive one.

Citing and Referencing Errors

Citing and Referencing Errors
Citing and referencing are often considered together, but they are different aspects of demonstrating to the reader (e.g., the professor) the sources that one has consulted. As I have pointed out elsewhere (Eaton, 2013), in academic writing, citations are used in the body of the the text itself, whereas references are a complete list of sources included at the end of a written work. There are disciplinary and stylistic differences in terminology. The list might be called “References,” “Reference List,” “Works Cited,” or “Bibliography,” for example. There are nuanced differences among these terms, which become more relevant as one develops as a scholar and academic writer, but for the average undergraduate student, it is enough to know that differences exist, and what these elements have in common is their shared purpose of leaving a trail of bibliographic bread crumbs for someone to follow in order to know what source material was consulted. In some disciplines, such as law, a strong tradition of footnoting exists, whereas in other disciplines, such as those that follow the American Psychological Association (APA) style guide (e.g., psychology, education, and other fields), footnoting is discouraged.

Citing and referencing are often considered together, but they are different aspects of demonstrating to the reader (e.g., the professor) the sources that one has consulted. As I have pointed out elsewhere (Eaton, 2013), in academic writing, citations are used in the body of the the text itself, whereas references are a complete list of sources included at the end of a written work. There are disciplinary and stylistic differences in terminology. The list might be called “References,” “Reference List,” “Works Cited,” or “Bibliography,” for example. There are nuanced differences among these terms, which become more relevant as one develops as a scholar and academic writer, but for the average undergraduate student, it is enough to know that differences exist, and what these elements have in common is their shared purpose of leaving a trail of bibliographic bread crumbs for someone to follow in order to know what source material was consulted. In some disciplines, such as law, a strong tradition of footnoting exists, whereas in other disciplines, such as those that follow the American Psychological Association (APA) style guide (e.g., psychology, education, and other fields), footnoting is discouraged.
Errors and omissions with citing and referencing include a wide variety of acts, including but not limited to the following:

Errors and omissions with citing and referencing include a wide variety of acts, including but not limited to the following:
- Failing to cite or reference an entire source

- Citing a source in the body of a paper, but not including it in the list of references

- Including sources in the references that are not cited in the text

- Failing to use quotation marks appropriately or accurately

- Noting the name of the original author or creator of a work, but without including attribution to an original source

- Changing the original text slightly (e.g., substituting a particular word with a synonym), without attributing the original

- Incomplete or inaccurate footnotes

Failing to cite or reference an entire source
Citing a source in the body of a paper, but not including it in the list of references
Including sources in the references that are not cited in the text
Failing to use quotation marks appropriately or accurately
Noting the name of the original author or creator of a work, but without including attribution to an original source
Changing the original text slightly (e.g., substituting a particular word with a synonym), without attributing the original
Incomplete or inaccurate footnotes
There are disciplinary differences that can affect how these are understood. In some fields, it is acceptable to include works consulted in the list of references even if they are not directly cited in the body of the work. There are also disciplinary differences and debates about what counts as common knowledge and might not require referencing another original work to support it. Each of these must be understood from within the subject area in which a person is working.

Poor Paraphrasing

Poor Paraphrasing
Problems with poor paraphrasing are discussed and debated at length in the plagiarism literature. Considerations of poor paraphrasing cannot ethically be divorced from intentionality, or even pedagogy. Poor paraphrasing has been described as an academic literacies or writing development issue (Howard, 1995; McGowan, 2005; Pecorari, 2016). One form of poor paraphrasing is patchwriting, which happens when a student copies from an original source, changes a few words, and alters the grammar slightly, which has been positioned as a writing development process, not a form of plagiarism (Howard, 1995).

Problems with poor paraphrasing are discussed and debated at length in the plagiarism literature. Considerations of poor paraphrasing cannot ethically be divorced from intentionality, or even pedagogy. Poor paraphrasing has been described as an academic literacies or writing development issue (Howard, 1995; McGowan, 2005; Pecorari, 2016). One form of poor paraphrasing is patchwriting, which happens when a student copies from an original source, changes a few words, and alters the grammar slightly, which has been positioned as a writing development process, not a form of plagiarism (Howard, 1995).
Those for whom English is an Additional Language (EAL) are noted as being academically vulnerable when it comes to writing development (Pecorari, 2003, 2015, 2016; Rezanejad & Rezaei, 2013). I discuss EAL students in more depth inchapter 9, on diversity, equity, and inclusion, so I will limit my treatment of that topic here. Suffice to say that paraphrasing as an academic literacies and writing development issue is discussed at length in the literature. I recommend the work of Rebecca Moore Howard (1995, 2000, 2001) and Diane Pecorari (Pecorari, 2003, 2015, 2016; Pecorari & Petrić, 2014), two leading scholars with deep expertise in paraphrasing in student writing.

ć
, 2014), two leading scholars with deep expertise in paraphrasing in student writing.
I offer the following examples with the caveat that a deeper understanding of paraphrasing requires careful consideration beyond a simple classification of acts that might be considered plagiarism. Having said that, in the interest of helping to answer the question of “What counts as plagiarism?” I present these examples with caution:

I offer the following examples with the caveat that a deeper understanding of paraphrasing requires careful consideration beyond a simple classification of acts that might be considered plagiarism. Having said that, in the interest of helping to answer the question of “What counts as plagiarism?” I present these examples with caution:
- Paraphrasing or summarizing that fails to acknowledge or give attribution to the original source

- Rewriting of the original text without acknowledgment of the source material

- The use of paraphrasing software without acknowledgment of the source material (Rogerson & McCarthy, 2017)

Paraphrasing or summarizing that fails to acknowledge or give attribution to the original source
Rewriting of the original text without acknowledgment of the source material
The use of paraphrasing software without acknowledgment of the source material (Rogerson & McCarthy, 2017)
What is common among these examples is lack of attribution to the source material. This lack of attribution is a key point for postsecondary students as part of their overall academic literacy and research skill development.

What is common among these examples is lack of attribution to the source material. This lack of attribution is a key point for postsecondary students as part of their overall academic literacy and research skill development.
Variations on Cut-and-Paste Plagiarism

Variations on Cut-and-Paste Plagiarism
When most people hear the word “plagiarism,” the simple act of cutting and pasting from an original source is what comes to mind; however, it can be more manipulative. Some examples include:

When most people hear the word “plagiarism,” the simple act of cutting and pasting from an original source is what comes to mind; however, it can be more manipulative. Some examples include:
- Using the copy and paste functions of a word processing program to copy a portion or the entirety of an original text without attribution.

- Transcribing (i.e., retyping) material from an original source that cannot be copied and pasted easily, and then not providing attribution to the original source.

- Running an original source that cannot be copied because it is in an unreadable format through optical character recognition (OCR) software to make it copyable, and then copying and pasting the source material without attribution. This includes taking screen shots of material that is in a format that is not easily copyable and then running it through OCR software to make it easier to cut and paste.

Using the copy and paste functions of a word processing program to copy a portion or the entirety of an original text without attribution.
Transcribing (i.e., retyping) material from an original source that cannot be copied and pasted easily, and then not providing attribution to the original source.
Running an original source that cannot be copied because it is in an unreadable format through optical character recognition (OCR) software to make it copyable, and then copying and pasting the source material without attribution. This includes taking screen shots of material that is in a format that is not easily copyable and then running it through OCR software to make it easier to cut and paste.
OCR software was once difficult to obtain, but that is no longer the case. Files that are supposedly protected from copying and pasting are easily converted into a readable (and copyable) format in a matter of seconds.

OCR software was once difficult to obtain, but that is no longer the case. Files that are supposedly protected from copying and pasting are easily converted into a readable (and copyable) format in a matter of seconds.
Unauthorized Translation

Unauthorized Translation
A book that tackles tough topics in plagiarism and academic integrity would be incomplete without addressing the circumstances under which translation is a form of plagiarism. Inadequate language proficiency can lead some students to plagiarize (Rezanejad & Rezaei, 2013) in a way that can include unauthorized translations, but that does not mean that all forms of academic translation are unethical.

A book that tackles tough topics in plagiarism and academic integrity would be incomplete without addressing the circumstances under which translation is a form of plagiarism. Inadequate language proficiency can lead some students to plagiarize (Rezanejad & Rezaei, 2013) in a way that can include unauthorized translations, but that does not mean that all forms of academic translation are unethical.
I offer an example from personal experience. I completed a master’s degree in Spanish (which for me is a foreign language), followed by fifteen years teaching the language, so my knowledge of the role that translation plays in learning is both experiential and academic. I remember a particular e-mail exchange at the beginning of my master’s program which focused on Hispanic literature, with one of my professors, Dr. Rachel Schmidt, who has remained a mentor and is now a colleague. The exchange is now only in my memory; the exact details are long since lost, and so I cannot cite them. The course was onDon Quixote, a text on which Dr. Schmidt is an internationally renowned scholar. Dr. Schmidt made it clear that because it was a graduate-level course, she was starting with the assumption that we had readDon Quixotein its entirety and as such, we would not be studying the text itself, but rather the literary theory surrounding the work.

I remember a particular e-mail exchange at the beginning of my master’s program which focused on Hispanic literature, with one of my professors, Dr. Rachel Schmidt, who has remained a mentor and is now a colleague. The exchange is now only in my memory; the exact details are long since lost, and so I cannot cite them. The course was on
Don Quixote
, a text on which Dr. Schmidt is an internationally renowned scholar. Dr. Schmidt made it clear that because it was a graduate-level course, she was starting with the assumption that we had read
Don Quixote
in its entirety and as such, we would not be studying the text itself, but rather the literary theory surrounding the work.
I panicked. As a speaker of Spanish as a foreign language, I was familiar with the basic story, but I had not read the text during my undergraduate years. Knowing that Cervantes and Shakespeare were more or less contemporaries, I anticipated that the language of the original Spanish would be difficult to navigate without guidance. That was exacerbated by the fact that I was studying in an additional language. I immediately set out to find a translation ofDon Quixotein English so that I could at least be familiar with more of the details of the story. The minute orientation was over, I raced home. I cracked open my Penguin Classic English translation of the work late Friday afternoon, before classes started the next week. I did not emerge from my rented room until early Monday morning, except to take bathroom breaks and take quick bites of toast or a bowl of instant noodles.

Don Quixote
in English so that I could at least be familiar with more of the details of the story. The minute orientation was over, I raced home. I cracked open my Penguin Classic English translation of the work late Friday afternoon, before classes started the next week. I did not emerge from my rented room until early Monday morning, except to take bathroom breaks and take quick bites of toast or a bowl of instant noodles.
I read over 1,000 pages that weekend to prepare for class the following Monday. I am ashamed to say how woefully and utterly unprepared I was. I came home that first day of class, went straight to my room, and sobbed. I was completely out of my depth. Looking back, I am grateful for the kindness and generosity of Dr. Schmidt. I am sure that it was obvious to her that I was struggling. What I lacked in academic preparation, I made up for in tenacity and perseverance. I made it through my degree, though not without a significant impact on my emotional and mental well-being.

I came home that first day of class, went straight to my room, and sobbed. I was completely out of my depth. Looking back, I am grateful for the kindness and generosity of Dr. Schmidt. I made it through my degree, though not without a significant impact on my emotional and mental well-being.
That experience made me empathetic to students for whom English is not a first language who come to Western institutions to study, only to be blindsided by expectations that they could not have imagined and finding themselves ill prepared for what awaits them. My experience with studying in an additional language also gives me a particular bias toward translation. Some educators believe that when students write in their first language and then translate their own work into the language of instruction where they are studying, the students are committing academic misconduct. I could not disagree more. I believe vehemently that producing original work in one’s own native language and then translating it for the purposes of assessment in the language of instruction should not, under any circumstances, be considered plagiarism. It is a form of academic coping, not misconduct. I would further contend that any students who find themselves in the position of not being able to produce academic work in the language of instruction and resort to translation as a means to survive academically are not only learning, they are likely pushing their cognitive load beyond what is reasonable.

There are undoubtedly some forms of translation that could be considered plagiarism, such as when it is done for the express purpose of bypassing text-matching (i.e., plagiarism detection) software. There are undoubtedly some forms of translation that could be considered plagiarism, such as when it is done for the express purpose of bypassing text-matching (i.e., plagiarism detection) software. Free online machine translation (MT) services have been widely available since the mid-1990s, offering quick and easy ways for writers to translate academic work (Somers et al., 2006). Examples include:
- Translating someone else’s published work and then claiming it as one’s own, without attributing the original source. This is clearly unethical. This can happen not only with text, but also with images, figures, charts, data, and other scholarly works (Loui, 2002).

- Translating the work of another student who completed similar coursework in another language, and then submitting the translation as one’s own original work.

- Buying or otherwise outsourcing academic work in one language and then translating it into the language of instruction. This is a form of contract cheating, which happens in numerous languages (Eaton & Dressler, 2019).

- Translation of one’s own previous work that has already undergone assessment or been previously published. This becomes a form of self-plagiarism by translation and is a form of “double-dipping,” in which the creator attempts to gain credit or acknowledgment more than once for what is essentially the same work. This has been documented more as a form of research misconduct than student academic misconduct (Joob & Wiwanitkit, 2017), and novice researchers must be taught that this practice is not acceptable. One way around this is to declare that the work was previously published or assessed, thereby being transparent about the origin of the work and eliminating any deception or perception of deception.

- Using automated translation software (e.g., Google Translate) to backtranslate/retranslate work. This might involve, for example, starting with an original English work (e.g., a paper submitted by a previous student in the same course), using free online MT services to translate it into another language, and then backtranslating it into English. The resulting work will be a different English-language version of the work, as the process of translation will result in subtle differences that make the reproduction sufficiently different from the original as to potentially deceive the person marking the paper or using text-matching software. There are those who put significant effort into retranslating and backtranslating work to avoid detection. The clever fraudster will translate the work more than once, choosing a language from a number of language groups for each translation, so as to avoid detection (e.g., English→Japanese→German→Russian→English). Plenty of Internet videos offer step-by-step instructions on how to do this. One important risk of multiple translations of a work is that the end product could be so unintelligible that it might not be of sufficient quality to earn a passing grade. That aside, this is a form of unethical translation that is not uncommon.

The point is that unethical academic translation happens when there is no intellectual effort on the part of the student (Somers et al., 2006). Even if a student has used MT and then tidied it up, it can be considered a “derived translation” (Somers et al., 2006, p. 43), in which there has been little substantive intellectual engagement with the content. Drawing from the work of Bertram Gallant (2008), the driving question to ask is: are students learning? If students are engaging with the content in a deep and meaningful way, then pursuing a case of plagiarism may not be warranted. If, on the other hand, translation has happened as a way to circumvent learning, there may definitely be cause for an academic misconduct investigation to probe further. Such cases can be difficult to investigate.

Cryptomnesia

Cryptomnesia
There is inconsistency about how cryptomnesia is defined. Building on Taylor’s (1965) work, Marsh and Bower (1993) defined cryptomnesia as “the unconscious influence of memory that causes current thoughts to be (wrongly) experienced as novel or original inventions” (p. 673). Individuals who experience cryptomnesia “believe that their newly produced ideas, songs, or solutions to a problem are original, but in reality, such ‘novel’ products already had been presented by others and, in fact, had been experienced by these individuals at an earlier time” (Roig, 2001, p. 308). Therefore, cryptomnesia could be considered a particular subcategory of unintentional plagiarism.

There is inconsistency about how cryptomnesia is defined. Building on Taylor’s (1965) work, Marsh and Bower (1993) defined cryptomnesia as “the unconscious influence of memory that causes current thoughts to be (wrongly) experienced as novel or original inventions” (p. 673). Individuals who experience cryptomnesia “believe that their newly produced ideas, songs, or solutions to a problem are original, but in reality, such ‘novel’ products already had been presented by others and, in fact, had been experienced by these individuals at an earlier time” (Roig, 2001, p. 308). Therefore, cryptomnesia could be considered a particular subcategory of unintentional plagiarism.
Of particular interest with this form of plagiarism is that it has been studied not only by educational scholars, but also by psychologists. Psychological studies on cryptomnesia sometimes examine the role of memory function (e.g., Bink, Marsh, & Hicks, 1999; Bink et al., 1999b; Heesacker, Petty, & Cacioppo, 1983; Tenpenny et al., 1998). Psychologists note that unconscious plagiarism might occur when participants do not use all the information that they have stored in their memory, called “source information” (Bink et al., 1999b, p. 295). Older memories are often weaker, making it more difficult to retrieve relevant details (Bink et al., 1999a). Some psychologists have contended that the more credible the information, the more likely it is to be reimagined as original material later (Bink et al., 1999b; Heesacker et al., 1983).

Psychologists note that unconscious plagiarism might occur when participants do not use all the information that they have stored in their memory, called “source information” (Bink et al., 1999b, p. 295). Older memories are often weaker, making it more difficult to retrieve relevant details (Bink et al., 1999a). Some psychologists have contended that the more credible the information, the more likely it is to be reimagined as original material later (Bink et al., 1999b; Heesacker et al., 1983).
An additional factor to consider is that when individuals are under greater stress levels, or the demands on their attention are increased (e.g., divided attention) at the time they first encountered the source information, the more likely it is that memory coding and storage processes can be compromised (Johnson, Hashtroudi, & Lindsay, 1993). Also noteworthy is that people who experience cryptomnesia are more likely to appropriatesource material that is originally created by someone of the same gender (Stark, Perfect, & Newstead, 2005; Macrae et al., 1999).

An additional factor to consider is that when individuals are under greater stress levels, or the demands on their attention are increased (e.g., divided attention) at the time they first encountered the source information, the more likely it is that memory coding and storage processes can be compromised (Johnson, Hashtroudi, & Lindsay, 1993). Also noteworthy is that people who experience cryptomnesia are more likely to appropriate
source material that is originally created by someone of the same gender (Stark, Perfect, & Newstead, 2005; Macrae et al., 1999).
The terms “patchwriting,” “unconscious plagiarism,” and “non-prototypical plagiarism” (Jamieson, 2016, p. 503) have all been used to refer to cryptomnesia. Patchwriting can be either intentional or unintentional (Jamieson, 2016), and some view patchwriting as a possible transitional strategy to developing more sophisticated scholarly writing skills (Howard, 1995). But patchwriting should not be conflated with cryptomnesia, which is more often classified as a form of unintentional, unconscious, or inadvertent plagiarism (Brown & Halliday, 1991; Brown & Murphy, 1989; Carpenter, 2002; Defeldre, 2005; Macrae et al., 1999; Stark et al., 2005; Taylor, 1965). These varying perspectives show some of the complexities surrounding cryptomnesia and how the term is understood. Using terms such as “patchwriting,” which can refer to either intentional or unintentional coping strategies is likely inaccurate. It is important to remember that “unintended verbatim plagiarism is a rare occurrence” (Taylor, 1965, p. 1111). What seems to be more prevalent is the appropriation of another person’s ideas or overall concepts, sometimes with an adaptation of or an improvement to the ideas presented in the original source material (Moss, White, & Lee, 2017; Perfect & Stark, 2008; Stark & Perfect, 2005, 2008).

Patchwriting can be either intentional or unintentional (Jamieson, 2016), and some view patchwriting as a possible transitional strategy to developing more sophisticated scholarly writing skills (Howard, 1995). But patchwriting should not be conflated with cryptomnesia, which is more often classified as a form of unintentional, unconscious, or inadvertent plagiarism (Brown & Halliday, 1991; Brown & Murphy, 1989; Carpenter, 2002; Defeldre, 2005; Macrae et al., 1999; Stark et al., 2005; Taylor, 1965). These varying perspectives show some of the complexities surrounding cryptomnesia and how the term is understood. Using terms such as “patchwriting,” which can refer to either intentional or unintentional coping strategies is likely inaccurate. It is important to remember that “unintended verbatim plagiarism is a rare occurrence” (Taylor, 1965, p. 1111). What seems to be more prevalent is the appropriation of another person’s ideas or overall concepts, sometimes with an adaptation of or an improvement to the ideas presented in the original source material (Moss, White, & Lee, 2017; Perfect & Stark, 2008; Stark & Perfect, 2005, 2008).
Psychologists have determined that some circumstances under which cryptomnesia is more likely to happen include when (1) there is a lengthy period of time between the appearance of original and credible source material and when it resurfaces in a form believed to be a new idea; (2) extreme stress or divided attention; and (3) the original source material was created by someone of the same gender. Although cryptomnesia exists as a psychological phenomenon, due to its rarity and difficulty to prove, in the absence of an assessment from a qualified psychologist, a claim of cryptomnesia is unlikely to be entertained by those who make determinations about student academic misconduct. In terms of student plagiarism, claims of cryptomnesia are likely indefensible in student academic misconduct investigations and hearings, precisely because it can be difficult (if not impossible) to show, even on the balance of probabilities.

Self-Plagiarism

Self-Plagiarism
I have dedicated an entire chapter to this topic later in this book (Chapter 6), so I merely introduce it here. Self-plagiarism is another contested notion among educators and policymakers. As with translation, the fundamental concept underpinning self-plagiarism is whether students have made an intellectual investment in their own learning. If they are simply recycling or reusing previously submitted work without learning anythingnew, then there could be a cause for further investigation. Examples of self-plagiarism in student work could include the following:

I have dedicated an entire chapter to this topic later in this book (
Chapter 6
), so I merely introduce it here. Self-plagiarism is another contested notion among educators and policymakers. As with translation, the fundamental concept underpinning self-plagiarism is whether students have made an intellectual investment in their own learning. If they are simply recycling or reusing previously submitted work without learning anything
new, then there could be a cause for further investigation. Examples of self-plagiarism in student work could include the following:
- Submitting the same assignment for more than one course without the knowledge or permission of the instructors involved. This can be thought of as “double-dipping” (receiving double the academic credit for the same submitted work, without any new learning happening).

- Submitting the same assignment for the same course if the student withdrew the first time and then reregistered at a later time. Again, a key point is that if no new learning has occurred, the submission of the same work could be considered double-dipping for academic credit.

Contract Cheating

Contract Cheating
As with self-plagiarism, this is a complex topic to which I dedicate a chapter later in this book (Chapter 8), so here I will only lay some groundwork for it. Readers may be more familiar with the phrases “term paper mill,” “essay mill,” or “ghostwriter,” which have existed for decades. Clarke and Lancaster (2006), two computer science professors from the United Kingdom, coined the term “contract cheating” as a more inclusive phrase, to show that it is not only term papers, but all kinds of academic work, that are outsourced to third parties. Examples of academic outsourced work include but are not limited to (Bretag et al., 2019a, 2019b; Clarke & Lancaster, 2006; Eaton & Dressler, 2019; Ellis et al., 2019):

), so here I will only lay some groundwork for it. Readers may be more familiar with the phrases “term paper mill,” “essay mill,” or “ghostwriter,” which have existed for decades. Clarke and Lancaster (2006), two computer science professors from the United Kingdom, coined the term “contract cheating” as a more inclusive phrase, to show that it is not only term papers, but all kinds of academic work, that are outsourced to third parties. Examples of academic outsourced work include but are not limited to (Bretag et al., 2019a, 2019b; Clarke & Lancaster, 2006; Eaton & Dressler, 2019; Ellis et al., 2019):
- Term papers (including essays and other written projects)

- Graduate capstone projects and theses (including doctoral dissertations)

- Slide decks for presentation

- Coding assignments and projects

- Foreign-language assignments

- Exam impersonation (both in person and online)

- Completion of an entire course by a third party

HOW STUDENTS AND FACULTY VIEW PLAGIARISM DIFFERENTLY

HOW STUDENTS AND FACULTY VIEW PLAGIARISM DIFFERENTLY
There are different views and research data about how students view plagiarism. Students might be terrified about being caught for plagiarizing, an anxiety that can stem from not understanding what is expected, leadingto the potential that their learning may be disrupted or negatively affected (Adam, 2016; Adam et al., 2017; Ashworth, Bannister, & Thorne, 1997; Leask, 2006). Students can find plagiarism among their peers to be morally reprehensible and unfair to those who put honest effort into their learning (Ashworth et al., 1997). Some students might blame the institution for plagiarism or student cheating, particularly if there appear to be no consequences for those who are engaging in dishonest behaviors (Ashworth et al., 1997). Others have suggested that students may not view plagiarism as a serious offense (Austin et al., 2006; Austin, Simpson, & Reynen, 2005; Blum, 2009, 2016; Mahmud, Bretag, & Foltýnek, 2019) or may not believe it to be as serious an offense as their professors do (Austin et al., 2006; Hudd et al., 2009, Kwong et al., 2010; Macdonald & Carroll, 2006; Pincus & Schmelkin, 2003). There is no single perspective on plagiarism that applies universally to all learners. It is also clear that if faculty members ignore or turn a blind eye to plagiarism or other forms of academic misconduct, students are more likely to engage in it (Coren, 2011; Jendrek, 1989).

UNDERSTANDING THE COMPLEXITY OF TEXTUALITY

UNDERSTANDING THE COMPLEXITY OF TEXTUALITY
When we start with the assumption that plagiarism is a complex issue, we can approach each instance as a puzzle for which there may be numerous pieces to explain what is happening and why. This approach has been gaining popularity since the 1990s, when the literature of “plagiaries” (Adam, 2016, p. 521) became more popular. Advocates of this approach call for an understanding of the relationship between the self, the writing (or other forms of knowledge sharing, as in nontext-based disciplines), the original work, memory, and learning (Adam, 2016; Howard, 1995; Pennycook, 1996).

When we start with the assumption that plagiarism is a complex issue, we can approach each instance as a puzzle for which there may be numerous pieces to explain what is happening and why. This approach has been gaining popularity since the 1990s, when the literature of “plagiaries” (Adam, 2016, p. 521) became more popular. Advocates of this approach call for an understanding of the relationship between the self, the writing (or other forms of knowledge sharing, as in nontext-based disciplines), the original work, memory, and learning (Adam, 2016; Howard, 1995; Pennycook, 1996).
Plagiaries scholars are dominated by compositionists, philologists, and other literary and liberal arts scholars. Those with an appreciation of twentieth-century philosophy will appreciate the discussions of Roland Barthes (1977), Mikhail Bakhtin (1981, 1986), and Michel Foucault (1972, 1977). Those interested in how these theorists and others contributed to our understanding of textuality and plagiarism can look to the work of Ali Abasi and Barbara Graves (2008), Roz Ivanič(1998), Betty Leask (2006), Rebecca Moore Howard (1995), and Wendy Sutherland-Smith (2008), among others.

Although these deep considerations of the nature of the self in relation to the text are relevant and insightful, they are firmly rooted in the domain of scholars for whom language is not only a means of communication, but also a field of study.
