Many educators and other higher education stakeholders have to deal with the practicalities of student plagiarism from a hands-on perspective, without the benefit of theoretical training or expertise in concepts relating to authorship or intertextuality.
One thing that all members of the learning community can agree on is that plagiarism is often complex. There can be much more going on than first meets the eye. Therefore, starting from the position that there are many pieces to the puzzle, some of which may be obscured from view, can help us resist the temptation of assuming that all plagiarism is deliberate.

INTENTIONAL VERSUS UNINTENTIONAL PLAGIARISM

INTENTIONAL VERSUS UNINTENTIONAL PLAGIARISM
Although intentionality becomes important during an investigation and management of a case of plagiarism, it is important to understand from the start that not all plagiarism is a malicious or intentional act. The intentionality becomes important from a case management and policy perspective because it can affect the type and harshness of the sanction imposed on a student (Adam, 2016). It is important to preface this section by emphasizing that it is important—essential even—to resist binary views of plagiarism. It would be just as easy as it is erroneous to conclude that intentional plagiarism is heinous, whereas unintentional plagiarism is less egregious.

The intentionality becomes important from a case management and policy perspective because it can affect the type and harshness of the sanction imposed on a student (Adam, 2016). It would be just as easy as it is erroneous to conclude that intentional plagiarism is heinous, whereas unintentional plagiarism is less egregious.
Intentional Plagiarism

Intentional Plagiarism
When many people think of plagiarism, their mind goes directly to thinking about it as a deliberate and deceitful act. In turn, this can quickly lead to judgment and the urge to police and punish the deviant act (Adam, 2016). It is easy to position plagiarism within a moral frame when it is intentional.

When many people think of plagiarism, their mind goes directly to thinking about it as a deliberate and deceitful act. In turn, this can quickly lead to judgment and the urge to police and punish the deviant act (Adam, 2016). It is easy to position plagiarism within a moral frame when it is intentional.
Plagiarism should be declared to be deliberate only if the student has had ample opportunity to learn how to avoid plagiarizing (Carroll, 2016). This would include learning institutional and instructional expectations and being given explicit training on how to cite and reference properly. Instructors who assume that students should already know how to avoid plagiarizing by the time they arrive in their class could be contributing to the plagiarism. Instructional assumptions are the enemy of evidence-based decisions about whether plagiarism has occurred. Plagiarism should be declared to be deliberate only if the student has had ample opportunity to learn how to avoid plagiarizing (Carroll, 2016). This would include learning institutional and instructional expectations and being given explicit training on how to cite and reference properly. Instructors who assume that students should already know how to avoid plagiarizing by the time they arrive in their class could be contributing to the plagiarism. Instructional assumptions are the enemy of evidence-based decisions about whether plagiarism has occurred. A determination that plagiarism is deliberate should be an evidence-based decision, not a presumption. Some indicators to assist in making this determination might include:
- Evidence of deceit or deception—There are a number of indicators that might signal intentionality, such as padded reference lists, fabricated references, and work that has knowingly been completed in part or in whole by someone else (Carroll, 2016).

- Second or subsequent incidence—Evidence that the student has been previously caught for plagiarism and has had an opportunity to learn how to do better is one indicator that the student knows what is expected and understands what is being done is wrong (Carroll, 2016).

- Belligerence or lack of remorse—There is a small percentage of students who will plagiarize “just for fun” (Rezanejad & Rezaei, 2013, p. 285), though these are in the minority.

Unintentional Plagiarism

Unintentional Plagiarism
Unintentional plagiarism is also called “accidental plagiarism” (Kier, 2013, 2014) or “inadvertent plagiarism” (Howard et al., 2010; McDonald & Adl, 2019). Although unintentional plagiarism has often been attributed to underdeveloped writing or citation skills, Howard (1995) challenges us to move beyond deficit-based conclusions about why this kind of plagiarism occurs. Patchwriting can (and probably should) also be viewed as a “transitional strategy in the student’s progress toward membership in a discourse community” (Howard, 1995, p, 788). This approach challenges entrenched notions that plagiarism was something to be fixed, punished, or both (Howard, 1995, 2000). This later led to Howard (2000) declaring that plagiarism defies definition and is infinitely more complex and nuanced than many policy documents would have us believe. Even today, many articles and books (including this one) start with an attempt to define plagiarism, despite Howard’s (2000) arguments that educators, particularly those involved in teaching writing, should “discard the termplagiarismaltogether,” advocating that patchwriting should be “removed entirely from the juridical category of plagiarism” (p. 475).

INDIVIDUAL VERSUS CONTEXTUAL FACTORS

INDIVIDUAL VERSUS CONTEXTUAL FACTORS
There are numerous factors that can put students at greater risk of plagiarizing or engaging in other forms of academic malpractice. Experts have classified these broadly into individual and contextual factors (Bertram Gallant, 2008; Bretag, 2016; McCabe & Treviño, 1993). It is also worth noting that there is a difference between the factors that can be predictive of academic misconduct, as opposed to those that are predictive of an individual being reported for it (Bertram Gallant, Binkin, & Donohue,2015). Students in certain groups, such as international students, are more likely to be reported for cheating than their domestic peers, for example (Bretag, 2019).

Individual Factors

Individual Factors
Individual factors are those pertaining to each student, as a person. Although humans are always connected to one another, the organizations in which they learn and the society in which they live, there are risk factors that pertain more to the individual than the broader context in which they are situated. The list of factors that can predict or affect plagiarism and other cheating behaviors is long (Bertram Gallant, 2015; Bretag et al., 2019a, 2019b; McCabe & Treviño, 1993; Tremayne & Curtis, 2020). Here, I highlight a few of the factors that are discussed most often in this research:

Individual factors are those pertaining to each student, as a person. Although humans are always connected to one another, the organizations in which they learn and the society in which they live, there are risk factors that pertain more to the individual than the broader context in which they are situated. The list of factors that can predict or affect plagiarism and other cheating behaviors is long (Bertram Gallant, 2015; Bretag et al., 2019a, 2019b; McCabe & Trevi
ñ
o, 1993; Tremayne & Curtis, 2020). Here, I highlight a few of the factors that are discussed most often in this research:
- Maturity:Younger students can be at higher risk of engaging in academic misconduct (Bertram Gallant et al., 2015; Tremayne & Curtis, 2020). The effect of the student’s year in college (e.g., freshman, junior, etc.) has been shown to be less of a determinant in cheating behaviors (Bertram Gallant, 2015). So, for example, a mature first-year student might be less likely to engage in academic misconduct than their younger peers. The reasons for this are unclear, but it could have to do with the idea that moral development continues throughout one’s youth and early adulthood.

- Unfamiliarity with institutional expectations: It could also be that first-year students are less familiar with institutional expectations for how to conduct themselves. As they spend more time at a school, they become more acculturated to the social and academic norms of the institution. This lack of familiarity with institutional expectations could also be a factor for those who come from other countries to study at a particular school, which could be amplified further if the student’s language proficiency in the language of instruction is limited.

- Grade point average: Students who struggle academically have been shown to self-report cheating behaviors more often than high-achieving students (Bertram Gallant et al., 2015; Bunn, Caudill, & Gropper, 1992; McCabe & Treviño, 1993). It is worth noting that students with a lower grade point average (GPA) might be more willing to self-report their behaviors than higher-achieving students who might have more to lose (Bertram Gallant et al., 2015).

- Sex and gender identity:The evidence about whether birth sex and gender identity are predictors of academic cheating behavior isinconclusive (Bertram Gallant et al., 2015; McCabe & Treviño, 1993; Perry, Kane, Bernesser, & Spicker, 1990). There is no conclusive evidence to suggest that maleness or femaleness, or nonbinary, transgender, or cisgender identity, is associated with a greater or lesser likelihood of engaging in academic misconduct. Some have suggested that males may be overrepresented in the reported groups of students who engage in academic misconduct (Bretag et al. 2019b), which could point to reporting bias rather than actual differences in behavior. Although birth sex and gender identity were explored as possible factors to determine individual propensity to engage in plagiarism or other forms of academic misconduct in the twentieth century (Whitley, Nelson, & Jones, 1999), there is less and less evidence to suggest this is actually the case, as once thought.

- Personality and behavior:Type A individuals who are highly competitive and achievement oriented might cheat to attain success(McCabe & Treviño, 1993; Perry et al., 1990; McCabe, 2016). Type A students might also be more likely to place high importance on grades, leading some to entertain cheating as a means to achieve their goal of getting better grades (Perry et al., 1990). Some students believe that they must do whatever it takes to get an A grade (McCabe, 2016). The anxiety brought on by the sense of academic achievement as an indicator of self-worth might be another factor that leads some students to feel that they have no other option but to cheat.

- Self-regulation and self-control: Students who demonstrate higher levels of self-control may be less likely to plagiarize and cheat (Reisig & Bain, 2016; Tremayne & Curtis, 2020). Those who have better self-regulatory learning behaviors, such as time management, may also engage less in academic misconduct.

Some of these individual factors appear contradictory. For example, the individual factors of the high-achieving personality versus the person with a low GPA seem to oppose one another. It is important to avoid the temptation to profile students or jump to conclusions because of one or more possible risk factors. Instead, it might be more useful to develop educational supports that focus on teaching and learning (Bertram Gallant et al., 2015). For example, academic integrity induction programs to support students’ understanding of the institutional expectations around integrity could be helpful. Ongoing writing and tutoring supports on campus can help struggling students attain a higher GPA and learn better self-regulation skills, such as time management. Mental health supports for those experiencing anxiety or poor self-esteem can help students develop healthier approaches to dealing with learning stress.

Contextual Factors

Contextual Factors
Contextual factors are external to students but can affect their choices and their behaviors. Examples include the following:

Contextual factors are external to students but can affect their choices and their behaviors. Examples include the following:
- Pressure to perform:Students who are subjected to unrealistic expectations from parents or other caregivers may engage in academic misconduct to achieve the grades expected of them by family members (Bertram Gallant et al., 2015; McCabe, 2016).

- Competition for grades:Learning environments that encourage students to compete for grades (e.g., grading on a bell curve) might create conditions in which students feel compelled to cheat as a means of academic survival (Singhal, 1982). This phenomenon has been anecdotally dubbed the “cheat to compete” syndrome.

- Perception of peers:Students’ perceptions of their peers have been shown to be a major factor in whether they engage in academic misconduct (McCabe, 2016). The cheat to compete syndrome can be further catalyzed by their perception that “everyone is doing it.”

- Honor codes:Academic misconduct has been shown to be less prevalent at honor code institutions (McCabe & Treviño, 1993; McCabe et al., 1999).

- Faculty and institutional responses:If students perceive that their instructors and their institution are uninterested in academic misconduct or willfully turn a blind eye to it, students may interpret this as condoning cheating (Bunn et al., 1992; McCabe & Treviño, 1993; Thomas, 2017). Similarly, institutions that put systems in place to deter and respond to academic misconduct send the message that cheating is taken seriously, which can help to deter cheating (Singhal, 1982; McCabe & Treviño, 1993).

One or more of these, in almost infinite combinations, can affect students. None of them is a guarantee that students will engage in academic misconduct. Little is known about how these factors might interact with each other, although it is likely that both personal and contextual factors can be at play at any given time (Tremayne & Curtis, 2020). Although these lists highlight some of the more common factors established in the literature, they are not exhaustive.

CONCLUSIONS

CONCLUSIONS
In this chapter, I have explored some of the numerous complexities around why students engage in plagiarism and academic misconduct ingeneral. A takeaway for the reader is that there are no easy answers. Plagiarism is not a single act, but rather a range of acts. Students and faculty members’ views on what counts as plagiarism or academic misconduct, as well as the seriousness of those acts, vary wildly. To complicate matters further, numerous individual and contextual factors can affect whether students engage in academically dishonest behaviors. Inchapter 4, I address how and why a multistakeholder approach is essential to upholding and enacting academic integrity.

4
A Multistakeholder Systems Approach to Plagiarism: The 4M Framework

A Multistakeholder Systems Approach to Plagiarism: The 4M Framework
In this chapter, I take up the idea that upholding academic integrity requires a multistakeholder approach. Others have made the same argument, noting that students cannot be the only ones held responsible for preventing plagiarism or academic misconduct in general (Bertram Gallant, 2008; Carroll, 2007; Macdonald & Carroll, 2006; TEQSA, 2017). The word “integrity” comes from the Latinintegrāre(Hoad, 1993), from which we also derive the phrase “to integrate,” meaning “to make whole.” Although this book is focused on plagiarism, we cannot talk about plagiarism without talking about academic integrity; and we cannot talk about academic integrity without talking about the educational ecosystem. The discussion would be incomplete without addressing the learning organization (school, college, university) as an entity that exists within a broader educational system and within society itself.

Others have made the same argument, noting that students cannot be the only ones held responsible for preventing plagiarism or academic misconduct in general (Bertram Gallant, 2008; Carroll, 2007; Macdonald & Carroll, 2006; TEQSA, 2017). The word “integrity” comes from the Latin
integrāre
(Hoad, 1993), from which we also derive the phrase “to integrate,” meaning “to make whole.” Although this book is focused on plagiarism, we cannot talk about plagiarism without talking about academic integrity; and we cannot talk about academic integrity without talking about the educational ecosystem. The discussion would be incomplete without addressing the learning organization (school, college, university) as an entity that exists within a broader educational system and within society itself.
Sidney Besvinick, who served as the associate provost at the University of Miami, argued that “a university does not exist in a vacuum. It must be concerned with what ought to be. It is a social entity and must take cognizance of its own impact upon the society of which it is a part and of the legitimate demands that society may make of it” (Besvinick, 1983, p. 568). Here, Besvinick is arguing that although truth (however that may be defined) is “neither good nor evil” (1983, p. 568), the process of knowledge seeking and creation that happens in universities is not anamoral act. Universities have a social responsibility to act in socially responsible ways.

Sidney Besvinick, who served as the associate provost at the University of Miami, argued that “a university does not exist in a vacuum. It must be concerned with what ought to be. It is a social entity and must take cognizance of its own impact upon the society of which it is a part and of the legitimate demands that society may make of it” (Besvinick, 1983, p. 568). Here, Besvinick is arguing that although truth (however that may be defined) is “neither good nor evil” (1983, p. 568), the process of knowledge seeking and creation that happens in universities is not an
amoral act. Universities have a social responsibility to act in socially responsible ways.
He notes that, “the integrity of a university is measured by its ability to join both the intellectual good and the social good.… into a consistent and harmonious pattern. A university must create knowledge, transmit knowledge, and make its wisdom available to the society that supports it or it is incomplete and not an integrated whole” (1983, p. 568). He continues that “universities are perceived as epitomizing intellectual and social honesty and they are expected to strive continually for that form” (1983, p. 569). All of this discussion about the social responsibilities of a university could also be applied to community colleges, polytechnics, public schools and just about any other learning institution.

All of this discussion about the social responsibilities of a university could also be applied to community colleges, polytechnics, public schools and just about any other learning institution.
Historically, there has been little evidence of a consistent model for plagiarism prevention education across, or sometimes even within, institutions. Sometimes the work of prevention falls to learning specialists or tutors at campus writing centers, student services liaisons, librarians, or library staff. This lack of consistency makes it difficult to figure out which models of plagiarism prevention education are most effective, but it is clear that different individuals on campus play a role in supporting students’ success. These individuals, however, do not work in isolation. Students are affiliated with programs, as are individual faculty members. Programs are housed within departments. Additional learning supports are housed within other units on campuses such libraries or student affairs. Administrative units such as the registrar’s office or the academic integrity or appeals office operate alongside these other units. The individual units comprise the institution, which exists within the broader higher community, which are often overseen by government legislative or quality assurance bodies. In this chapter, I argue for an integrated multistakeholder approach to academic integrity, focused on supporting students’ learning (prevention) first and foremost, while acknowledging larger institutional mandates to address academic integrity violations (policy implementation).

USING THE 4M FRAMEWORK FOR ACADEMIC INTEGRITY

USING THE 4M FRAMEWORK FOR ACADEMIC INTEGRITY
The 4M Framework offers a concrete way to understand how and why different stakeholders play a role in upholding and enacting academic integrity. Scholars have advocated for a teaching and learning approach to academic integrity and plagiarism prevention for a long time (Bertram Gallant, 2008; Eaton et al., 2019; Williams et al., 2013). The 4M Framework was developed in the scholarship of teaching and learning (SoTL) community to help people understand how teaching and learning inquiry is connected to the larger educational landscape (Friberg, 2016; Kalu et al., 2018;Kenny et al., 2016; Poole & Simmons, 2013; Simmons, 2016; Williams et al., 2013). The framework consists of four nested organizational levels. Each level offers a lens through which educators, scholars and others can frame an inquiry. Themicrolevel represents the individual perspective within the organization. Themesolevel represents the departmental or unit level within an organization. Themacrolevel represents the institution or organization. Finally, themegalevel connects the institution to the broader educational and social contexts and communities. A key point is that each level is interconnected and inseparable from the others (seeFigure 4.1).

In the sections that follow, I explore each of these levels individually, noting that plagiarism, as well as academic misconduct in general, affect every level of the learning organization (Frenken, 2013). The explorations that follow are by no means exhaustive. It would be impossible to review every individual role on every campus, or every possible organizationalunit and structure, if for no other reason that campuses differ in how they self-organize, including how roles and responsibilities are assigned. The point is not to present an exhaustive list, but rather to highlight some of the more common examples in each level. A useful exercise for an academic integrity training session on campus would be to have participants reflect on what their own individual role is, and then situate their own professional practice in relation to others on their team, as well as within the various other levels of the framework.

THE MICRO LEVEL: THE INDIVIDUAL

THE MICRO LEVEL: THE INDIVIDUAL
In this section, I highlight some of the key individual actors within the postsecondary learning organization who play a role in upholding and enacting academic integrity.

In this section, I highlight some of the key individual actors within the postsecondary learning organization who play a role in upholding and enacting academic integrity.
The Role of Students

The Role of Students
I begin with students because many institutions take the stance that upholding and enacting academic integrity, which include preventing plagiarism, is primarily a student responsibility. At some institutions, themodus operandiis that students are exclusively responsible for preventing plagiarism in their own work (Whiteman & Gordon, 2001). In such cases, the role of the professors and administrators is to intervene only when a case of alleged misconduct has already happened. Although assessment design might enter the conversation, the responsibility for plagiarism rests with the students (Whiteman & Gordon, 2001). Such an approach only serves to exacerbate various adversarial relationships on campus (e.g., students versus professors, professors versus administrators, students versus administrators) that have been discussed at length in the literature (Davis, Drinan, & Bertram Gallant, 2009; Eisner & Vicinus, 2008; Israel & Drenth, 2016; Serviss, 2016a).

Although assessment design might enter the conversation, the responsibility for plagiarism rests with the students (Whiteman & Gordon, 2001). Such an approach only serves to exacerbate various adversarial relationships on campus (e.g., students versus professors, professors versus administrators, students versus administrators) that have been discussed at length in the literature (Davis, Drinan, & Bertram Gallant, 2009; Eisner & Vicinus, 2008; Israel & Drenth, 2016; Serviss, 2016a).
An overemphasis on the responsibility of the individual student can be seen in institutional policies, procedures, and processes that specify, sometimes with exacting language, that it is the sole responsibility of the individual student to act with integrity and avoid academic misconduct. I am not suggesting that students should be exempted from individual responsibility. Clearly, each individual within the learning organization has responsibilities. However, there can be an embedded myopia when it comes to insisting that the responsibility of students outweighs that of professors or others within the institution. There is an underlying assumption, embedded within the culture of many Western learning organizations, that each person is an autonomous and independent individual who must be solely responsible for her or his own actions.

This deeply embedded cultural bias toward individualism can be seen in activities such as individual assessments and exams. The line between legitimate collaboration and unsanctioned collusion remains a point of frustration in education, with unauthorized collaboration being one of the most prevalent forms of academic misconduct (McGowan, 2016). This could be due, in part, to culturally embedded notions of individualism that position the individual learner as somehow working in isolation from others. This is a bizarre viewpoint that assumes that each learner is a compartmentalized unit, and that learning happens in a bubble in which learners are sequestered within their own individual microcosms. The bias toward individualism is rarely stated explicitly; instead, it is evidenced through actions, teaching and assessment practices, policies, and regulations. This bias toward individualism is at odds with current trends in learning and business that emphasize the value of collaboration and teamwork (Senge, 2006). It is also at odds with established learning theories that support the idea that learning is an inherently social activity that is interconnected with other individuals, as well as larger social units within a broader system (Keaton & Bodie, 2011).

Students are not only learners; they are also important stakeholders. Including students in policy development, academic integrity violation and appeal hearings, and training is an important way for the institution as a whole to demonstrate that it values student involvement in the overall development of an ethical campus culture (McCabe, Butterfield, & Treviño, 2012). Ideally, student involvement should be embedded into institutional governance. For example, the terms of reference for an academic integrity policy development committee should explicitly state that student representation on the committee must reflect the student body itself. If a university has both undergraduate and graduate programs, then both groups of students should be included and represented on institutional committees and other ad hoc bodies, such as appeal board hearing panels. This is an example of the interplay between the individual and the institutional levels of a postsecondary learning organization.

The Role of Faculty Members

The Role of Faculty Members
Compared with the large body of research that has focused on students, scholars have paid less attention to the attitudes, perceptions, and experiences of faculty. This may be, in part, because the news has not been good. For example, a survey of over 850 faculty members from the United States, 40 percent admitted to ignoring academic misconduct (Coren, 2011). In this section, I explore the reasons for this and propose practical ways to support faculty as proactive partners in student learning.

Compared with the large body of research that has focused on students, scholars have paid less attention to the attitudes, perceptions, and experiences of faculty. This may be, in part, because the news has not been good. For example, a survey of over 850 faculty members from the United States, 40 percent admitted to ignoring academic misconduct (Coren, 2011). In this section, I explore the reasons for this and propose practical ways to support faculty as proactive partners in student learning.
Faculty members are role models when it comes to conveying ethical values to students (Austin, Simpson, & Reynen, 2005; Speight, 2016). Professors must take a proactive role in helping students to understand institutional and disciplinary norms for upholding and enacting academic integrity. Of course, faculty members are subject-matter experts, but this does not absolve them of the responsibility of teaching students about the expectations for ethical learning, which include but are not limited to citing, referencing, and understanding what it means to learn and demonstrate that learning in ethical ways. I have emphasized elsewhere that the professor’s job includes proactive pedagogical approaches to academic integrity, not merely reporting violations after they have happened (Eaton et al., 2017).

I have emphasized elsewhere that the professor’s job includes proactive pedagogical approaches to academic integrity, not merely reporting violations after they have happened (Eaton et al., 2017).
I say all of this as a tenured faculty member with a research appointment. I understand very well the pressures on professors to focus on research and publishing. Nevertheless, I remain firm in my commitment to providing quality learning experiences for my students because I see it as a fundamental responsibility of being a professor. And we cannot provide quality learning experiences to students if we do not incorporate conversations and instruction about ethics and integrity into our classes.

It is also incumbent upon those with the privilege of full-time and secure employment to advocate for those whose roles may be more precarious, such as teaching assistants (TAs) or colleagues who serve as contingent faculty. Because this book is about tackling tough topics in academic integrity, I take up these delicate and controversial issues because we need more and deeper conversations and action on our campuses about how to ensure that all members of our learning communities are supported to uphold integrity.

Contingent Faculty

Contingent Faculty
Contingent faculty, also called “contingent academic staff,” “adjuncts,” “sessionals,” “lecturers,” and “contract teachers,” can be at a particular disadvantage when it comes to upholding and promoting academic integrity. Contingent faculty lack job security and benefits, are typically underpaid and horrifyingly overworked, and are regularly excluded from academic activities reserved for those who are tenure-track or tenured, such as eligibility to apply for grants or even being able to attend department meetings or social gatherings (AAUP, 2014, 2018; Crossman, 2019; Speight, 2016). The American Association of University Professors (AAUP, 2014, 2018) reports that the percentage of faculty who are off the tenure track and without permanent employment has been steadily increasing, and this trend is likely to continue. The situation in other countries is similar.

Contingent faculty, also called “contingent academic staff,” “adjuncts,” “sessionals,” “lecturers,” and “contract teachers,” can be at a particular disadvantage when it comes to upholding and promoting academic integrity. Contingent faculty lack job security and benefits, are typically underpaid and horrifyingly overworked, and are regularly excluded from academic activities reserved for those who are tenure-track or tenured, such as eligibility to apply for grants or even being able to attend department meetings or social gatherings (AAUP, 2014, 2018; Crossman, 2019; Speight, 2016). The American Association of University Professors (AAUP, 2014, 2018) reports that the percentage of faculty who are off the tenure track and without permanent employment has been steadily increasing, and this trend is likely to continue. The situation in other countries is similar.
Contingent faculty are disadvantaged with regard to academic integrity because they may not have the time to engage deeply with students and may not have access to the same professional development and training opportunities as full-time educators (Bertram Gallant, 2018; McCabe, Butterfield, & Treviño, 2012). They may also not receive adequate training or support about how to report violations (Crossman, 2019; McCabe et al., 2012). If they do report misconduct, they may find themselves in the position of having to spend numerous hours of uncompensated time to gather evidence and prepare a case file as part of the reporting process, which sometimes can even extend past the end date of their teaching contract (Crossman, 2019). The impact of student evaluations of teaching can create added stress for contingent faculty. If their future employment depends in part on the results of their teaching evaluations, and they fear that their scores may decrease if they report a suspected case of plagiarism or other misconduct, they may be disinclined to report for fear of losing their livelihood (Crossman, 2019; McCabe et al., 2012).

The impact of student evaluations of teaching can create added stress for contingent faculty. If their future employment depends in part on the results of their teaching evaluations, and they fear that their scores may decrease if they report a suspected case of plagiarism or other misconduct, they may be disinclined to report for fear of losing their livelihood (Crossman, 2019; McCabe et al., 2012).
Unbundling of the traditional faculty role occurs when faculty members’ contracts are based on payment in exchange for piecemeal work (AAUP, 2018; Kezar, De Paola, & Scott, 2019). Under such circumstances, each individual task is worth a particular amount of money. Each hour of class time taught, each assignment graded, each meeting attended, and other teaching and administrative duties are allocated a certain amount of money. Rarely is support for academic integrity given financial priority (or even consideration) in such arrangements. This can leave faculty members who are struggling to survive wondering if reporting breaches of integrity is worth it. Even if one values academic integrity personally, there is literally no return on investing in one’s time or effort to uphold student academic integrity.

Under such circumstances, each individual task is worth a particular amount of money. Each hour of class time taught, each assignment graded, each meeting attended, and other teaching and administrative duties are allocated a certain amount of money. Rarely is support for academic integrity given financial priority (or even consideration) in such arrangements. This can leave faculty members who are struggling to survive wondering if reporting breaches of integrity is worth it. Even if one values academic integrity personally, there is literally no return on investing in one’s time or effort to uphold student academic integrity.
I am not suggesting that there should be a reward system for those who report academic misconduct. That could easily mutate into a kind of academic witch hunt that further propagates adversarial relationships between students and teachers, as well as between students and the larger institution. Instead, compensation could be offered first for proactive activities that support ethical learning and teaching. This could include offering explicit academic integrity education lessons, providing students with individual coaching sessions to help them improve their writing and academic skills, and taking part in professional development activities to help educators learn more about effective assessment and teaching with integrity. Only after the proactive activities have been undertaken and recognized would a faculty member receive additional compensation to engage in activities related to reporting academic integrity violations. Overall, faculty members can be champions of integrity, advocates for more marginalized members of the campus community, and above all else, role models for students.

The Role of Teaching Assistants and Postdocs

The Role of Teaching Assistants and Postdocs
TAs and postdoctoral fellows (postdocs) have been among the most neglected academic integrity stakeholders. TAs in particular are often “thrown in at the deep end with the hope that he or she can swim” (Speight, 2016, p. 59). This applies to all aspects of the teaching assistantship, but it is especially true when it comes to understanding how to navigate the complex landscape of academic integrity. TAs and postdocs need explicit training and support about how to approach academic integrity and misconduct in the courses that they are employed to support (Serviss, 2016b). All too often, the professor assigned to actually teach the course absolves themself of the responsibility to provide mentorship and supervision to TAs, passing off responsibilities for various aspects of the course to the TAs without them having the full authority of a faculty member (Speight, 2016; Twomey et al., 2009).

TAs and postdoctoral fellows (postdocs) have been among the most neglected academic integrity stakeholders. TAs in particular are often “thrown in at the deep end with the hope that he or she can swim” (Speight, 2016, p. 59). This applies to all aspects of the teaching assistantship, but it is especially true when it comes to understanding how to navigate the complex landscape of academic integrity. TAs and postdocs need explicit training and support about how to approach academic integrity and misconduct in the courses that they are employed to support (Serviss, 2016b). All too often, the professor assigned to actually teach the course absolves themself of the responsibility to provide mentorship and supervision to TAs, passing off responsibilities for various aspects of the course to the TAs without them having the full authority of a faculty member (Speight, 2016; Twomey et al., 2009).
TAs and postdocs are often expected to engage in oversight and proctoring activities, such as grading papers, overseeing labs, and invigilating exams. Naturally, when one is undertaking these activities, it is likely that one will observe a breach of integrity at some point. It is reasonable to expect TAs to report an academic integrity violation, and it is unethical to require, or even suggest, that TAs ignore cases of misconduct. However, it is unacceptable to ask TAs to bear the entire burden of responsibility for case management or evidence-gathering (Eaton, 2019). The same goes for postdocs.

TAs and postdocs are often expected to engage in oversight and proctoring activities, such as grading papers, overseeing labs, and invigilating exams. Naturally, when one is undertaking these activities, it is likely that one will observe a breach of integrity at some point. It is reasonable to expect TAs to report an academic integrity violation, and it is unethical to require, or even suggest, that TAs ignore cases of misconduct. However, it is unacceptable to ask TAs to bear the entire burden of responsibility for case management or evidence-gathering (Eaton, 2019). The same goes for postdocs.
The larger institution (at the macro level) must be responsible, at least in part, to provide support for reporting and case management (Stevenson et al., 2004). Departments also play a role in ensuring that TAs and postdocs understand discipline-specific aspects of academic integrity. It is important to acknowledge that it is not sufficient to provide one-time or periodic training workshops to TAs and postdocs and then expect them to know how to deal with academic integrity violations. This kind of “set it and forget it” approach does not help them learn how to deal with the complexities of violations when they occur. TAs and postdocs benefit from ongoing formal and informal training and mentoring throughout their terms (Seals et al., 2014; Serviss, 2016b).

Departments also play a role in ensuring that TAs and postdocs understand discipline-specific aspects of academic integrity. It is important to acknowledge that it is not sufficient to provide one-time or periodic training workshops to TAs and postdocs and then expect them to know how to deal with academic integrity violations. This kind of “set it and forget it” approach does not help them learn how to deal with the complexities of violations when they occur. TAs and postdocs benefit from ongoing formal and informal training and mentoring throughout their terms (Seals et al., 2014; Serviss, 2016b).
TAs and postdocs are likely to be among the next generation of professors, so it is imperative that their acculturation into academic life includes support for learning how to uphold academic integrity as part of their role. At the same time, TAs should not be expected to bear the brunt of dealing with academic integrity violations alone. They need support from the professors who are assigned to the course, as well as from department heads and others in positions of authority who can protect, guide, and mentor them. Similarly, postdocs need support from department heads andadministrators to help them learn what is expected of them in terms of their teaching responsibilities.

The Role of the Academic Librarian and Library Staff

The Role of the Academic Librarian and Library Staff
Academic librarians and library staff play a unique role on campus in terms of plagiarism prevention. They are called on to support faculty, students, and other campus members (Schifter Caravello, 2007). The role of the librarian and library staff with regard to academic integrity has evolved considerably since the turn of the millennium (Kloda & Nicholson, 2007). In the twentieth century, librarians were often responsible for helping faculty members detect and prove cases of plagiarism by finding the original source material that had had been plagiarized (Kloda & Nicholson, 2007; Oliphant, 2002; Wood, 2004). As learning technologies have developed and funding has decreased, librarians have sought out new ways to share their unique expertise on campus, shifting their role from that of detective to that of integrity partner for education, prevention, research skill and information literacy development, and ethical use of information (Auer & Krupar, 2001; Chen & Van Ullen, 2011; Kloda & Nicholson, 2007; Nicosia, 2019). Many academic librarians also conduct outreach activities by providing student-centered classroom instruction in discipline-specific courses (Kloda & Nicholson, 2007). Some go as far as extending their outreach to community engagement by providing instruction to high school students to help prepare them for their success when they go to college (Morrow, 2018).

Academic librarians and library staff play a unique role on campus in terms of plagiarism prevention. They are called on to support faculty, students, and other campus members (Schifter Caravello, 2007). The Role of the Higher Education Professional (HEPRO)

The Role of the Higher Education Professional (HEPRO)
Higher education professionals (HEPROs) are a heterogeneous group who “are not primarily active in teaching and research, but prepare and support decisions of university management” (Schneijderberg & Merkator, 2013, p. 53). Academic integrity HEPROs include those who focus on student judicial affairs (Eerkes, 2010), manage and work at honor code or academic integrity offices (AIOs) (McCabe & Treviño, 2002), provide academic development and learning support (Hendricks & Quinn, 2000), serve as ombuds, and manage and staff academic appeals offices, to name a few functions. Academic integrity HEPROs also provide education to studentsthat is either preventative, remedial, or both (Saunders & Butts, 2011). Sometimes these individuals also have the responsibility of documenting students’ completion of mandatory remedial work after a case of academic or nonacademic misconduct (Eerkes, 2010).

HEPROs may support “organizational change and decision-making” (Kehm, 2015, p. 101), and as such, when it comes to matters of academic integrity, it is crucial that they not only be consulted, but intentionally and authentically involved at every step. Individuals in these roles “typically operate as boundary spanners” (Usick, 2020, p. 85), whose expertise can go beyond simply providing services to students to navigating the various levels of institutional complexity. HEPROs often do not hold academic appointments, though, which leaves them vulnerable to being shunned by those who do. It is essential that administrators and academic staff not only acknowledge and support the legitimacy of academic integrity HEPROs, but consistently recognize the value they contribute to building a campuswide culture of integrity.

Other Campus Staff

Other Campus Staff
From the staff working in the information privacy office to departmental secretaries, many employees in the learning organization play a role in upholding academic integrity. Staff who can—and do—contribute to building an overall culture of integrity on campus should not be overlooked simply because their job title or function does not seem at first glance to be related. Even custodial staff can be empowered to remove flyers and ads promoting essay mills or other contract cheating services (TEQSA, 2017).

THE ROLE OF ADMINISTRATORS

THE ROLE OF ADMINISTRATORS
Individuals in leadership roles, from the president to department heads, forge the links among the various organizational levels. I include administrators at the micro level because as individuals, they hold power and authority within the larger contexts in which they work. The ways in which they exercise their power and authority can affect other individuals within the system, as well as the system itself.

I include administrators at the micro level because as individuals, they hold power and authority within the larger contexts in which they work. The ways in which they exercise their power and authority can affect other individuals within the system, as well as the system itself.
Executive and Senior Leaders

Executive and Senior Leaders
It is important for those in positions of high authority and leadership to clearly communicate this message: integrity matters at our school. Leaders at this level can embed words such as “integrity,” “ethics,” and “honesty”into their speeches and written communications to the public and to the student body. This is important because, as one colleague said to me, “if it’s important to the president, it’s important to me.” Presidents, chancellors, provosts, and others at the executive level play a key role in communicating messages to the public about institutional values (McCabe et al., 2012). Senior leaders play a key role “in catalyzing and supporting change by articulating a compelling vision; communicating the importance of making a shift; setting explicit guidelines for success; and providing appropriate financial, structural, strategic, and procedural resources” (Kenny et al., 2016, pp. 87–88).

Senior leaders play a key role “in catalyzing and supporting change by articulating a compelling vision; communicating the importance of making a shift; setting explicit guidelines for success; and providing appropriate financial, structural, strategic, and procedural resources” (Kenny et al., 2016, pp. 87–88).
Others in the organization will take their cues from senior leaders, so conveying consistent messages about how the institution is committed to integrity will help others take up the work. Of course, the words need to be backed up by systems, processes, and supports, or else they ring hollow. When appropriate and effective systems are in place, the messaging can ensure that the established policies, procedures, and processes are implemented.

Deans, Associate Deans, and Department Heads

Deans, Associate Deans, and Department Heads
The titles may vary from one institution to the next, but deans, associate deans, and department heads are the link between the senior leaders and the meso-level units. These people are responsible for ensuring that policies and procedures are implemented and followed. They also have the power to support instructors, TAs, staff, and others who interface directly with the students. Leaders at this level have the responsibility to allocate the budget, time, and resources to ensure that those who work directly with students receive appropriate and adequate training and have opportunities for professional development. It is essential that leaders at the departmental level ensure that breaches of integrity are not ignored, but instead are addressed in fair and just ways.

THE MESO LEVEL: FACULTIES, DEPARTMENTS, AND OTHER UNITS

THE MESO LEVEL: FACULTIES, DEPARTMENTS, AND OTHER UNITS
Individuals comprise the various larger units within the learning community, so each of the levels that extend out from the center necessarily include the people who make up the faculty, departments, or other units in the postsecondary organization. There was a time when the organizational structure of universities and colleges was neater and tidier than it is today, at least in North America. Although some are still organizationally straightforward, many are changing and adapting in response to shrinking budgetsand increasing demands. There might be a public perception that the university is divided into faculties (e.g., science, humanities, fine arts, and medicine), which are then further divided into departments that offer courses on particular topics. For example, a faculty of science might be further subdivided into departments such as biology, chemistry, physics, and so on. However, nondepartmentalized faculties are becoming increasingly common. Instead, a nondepartmentalized faculty structure can be organized by program area, often established in response to market demand. Nondepartmentalized faculties are cheaper to run because instead of a department head, there may be an associate dean, or some other equivalent position, assigned to each broad program area, and fewer administrative staff are needed to support the day-to-day operations to run programs.

Regardless of how meso-level units exist within the larger organization, they still have unit-level responsibilities to uphold and promote academic integrity. I use the term “faculty” and “department” to refer to academic units in charge of teaching undergraduate and graduate courses, with departments being subsumed under a larger faculty structure. I use the term “unit” to refer to areas that do not bear responsibility for teaching academic courses, such as the library, student affairs, and others. I recognize that these differences in how postsecondary organizations are structured may differ even more outside of North American contexts. I trust that readers will be able to transfer the concepts that I discuss here to their own particular institution, using the ideas to generate conversations with students, colleagues, and others to advance academic integrity.

Faculties and Academic Departments

Faculties and Academic Departments
Faculties and departments bear the primary responsibility for planning and delivering academic programs. Various roles, mechanisms, teaching and learning functions, and governance elements interact at these levels to promote academic integrity. From faculty-level deans to department heads and others in leadership positions, down through the various academics, TAs, and departmental administrators and secretaries, students will interact with the individuals within these meso-level units most often during their academic journeys. Therefore, it is important that the leadership of these units not only share aspirational messages about the importance of integrity, but also provide concrete and supportive ways for integrity to be operationalized from a practical classroom perspective.

Faculties and departments bear the primary responsibility for planning and delivering academic programs. Various roles, mechanisms, teaching and learning functions, and governance elements interact at these levels to promote academic integrity. From faculty-level deans to department heads and others in leadership positions, down through the various academics, TAs, and departmental administrators and secretaries, students will interact with the individuals within these meso-level units most often during their academic journeys. Therefore, it is important that the leadership of these units not only share aspirational messages about the importance of integrity, but also provide concrete and supportive ways for integrity to be operationalized from a practical classroom perspective.
At this particular level, passive, proactive, and disciplinary approaches to academic integrity must be differentiated. All these approaches may be needed and must be carefully balanced to ensure that no particular one supersedes the others. One example of a passive approach to academicintegrity would be to ensure that course syllabi contain a statement on academic integrity, with links to relevant institutional policies and procedures. Having faculty and departmental websites include links to academic integrity policies and supports is another example of the passive approach to academic integrity. All too often, however, these approaches are regarded as all that is needed for providing students with the required information to take responsibility for their actions. Although that may be true to some extent, passive approaches in and of themselves are insufficient to actually support student learning. I cannot emphasize this enough. Having a statement about academic integrity in the course syllabus and having links to a website do not absolve instructors, TAs, department heads, or anyone else of providing proactive, ongoing, and interactive support to students.

Although that may be true to some extent, passive approaches in and of themselves are insufficient to actually support student learning. I cannot emphasize this enough. Having a statement about academic integrity in the course syllabus and having links to a website do not absolve instructors, TAs, department heads, or anyone else of providing proactive, ongoing, and interactive support to students.
Proactive support includes explicit training offered at regular intervals (e.g., every academic year) for faculty, staff, and students. A commitment to providing proactive support can be an opportunity to partner with other units on campus, such as the library or AIO, and to invite guest facilitators to offer interactive workshops. It can also be an opportunity for in-house experts to showcase the research or teaching innovations that they have been working on. At the University of Calgary, we have had great success with inviting experts from the privacy of information office to facilitate workshops about the types of information that can and cannot be shared under privacy laws when dealing with cases of academic integrity violations. Previously, there was a shocking variance in the ways in which information was shared after violations had occurred and a case had been brought forward. By providing regular training from the information privacy office, we were able to build both individual and collective knowledge that led to better processes and fairer treatment of everyone involved.

In the disciplinary process, ensuring clear communications about what to do, when to do it, and whom to involve is an excellent starting point. In addition, it is key to have processes and expectations not only documented, but also readily available. Professors, TAs, staff, and students all need to know what to expect when a violation occurs. The process needs to be written out in plain language, with each step explained in detail, and to be easy to locate (especially for those who are new to the faculty or department). Department members should be able to immediately find information about what to do in case of a breach, without having to dig around or ask someone else where to find it. Ideally, this information also should be actively shared regularly (e.g., once per semester) at department meetings, as a reminder about what to do and where to look for information at the moment it is needed. Faculty-level and departmental guidelines and processes need to align with institutional-level policies and procedures so that the entire organization is working in a systematic and consistent manner to address academic integrity.

Nonacademic Units

Nonacademic Units
There are numerous nonacademic units on campus that support academic integrity. These include but are not limited to the academic support center, English-language center, libraries, and teaching and learning services (Nicosia, 2019). This list is by no means exhaustive. Next, I elaborate on a few common nonacademic units that support integrity.

There are numerous nonacademic units on campus that support academic integrity. These include but are not limited to the academic support center, English-language center, libraries, and teaching and learning services (Nicosia, 2019). This list is by no means exhaustive. Next, I elaborate on a few common nonacademic units that support integrity.
The Library

The Library
The library can act as a hub where all campus stakeholders can feel safe asking questions. Despite that, the library as a unit on campus, and librarians as a group of professionals have been overlooked in academic integrity literature (Drinan & Gallant, 2008). Librarians have a unique role to play in upholding and promoting academic integrity, as they can act as a centralized resource with the ability to reach out to faculty, students, and other campus stakeholders (Auer & Krupar, 2001; Oliphant, 2002; Wood, 2004). Librarians, however, can do far more than teach people how to cite and reference (Nicosia, 2019; Wood, 2004); they can be proactive champions of academic integrity. They also serve as a bridge between faculty and students, as well as between students and other support units on campus, such as the writing center (Wood, 2004), as well as beyond campus into the greater community, such as connecting with primary and secondary schools and public libraries (Wrenn & Kohl, 2012).

Despite that, the library as a unit on campus, and librarians as a group of professionals have been overlooked in academic integrity literature (Drinan & Gallant, 2008). Librarians have a unique role to play in upholding and promoting academic integrity, as they can act as a centralized resource with the ability to reach out to faculty, students, and other campus stakeholders (Auer & Krupar, 2001; Oliphant, 2002; Wood, 2004). Librarians, however, can do far more than teach people how to cite and reference (Nicosia, 2019; Wood, 2004); they can be proactive champions of academic integrity. They also serve as a bridge between faculty and students, as well as between students and other support units on campus, such as the writing center (Wood, 2004), as well as beyond campus into the greater community, such as connecting with primary and secondary schools and public libraries (Wrenn & Kohl, 2012).
The library can offer a welcome reception for incoming students and new faculty, provide tours during orientation, and provide ongoing support throughout the academic year (Chen & Van Ullen, 2011). One particularly responsive library provides a “podcast virtual library tour” (Chen & Van Ullen, 2011, p. 209). Libraries create spaces in which learning happens in a judgement-free environment.

One particularly responsive library provides a “podcast virtual library tour” (Chen & Van Ullen, 2011, p. 209). Libraries create spaces in which learning happens in a judgement-free environment.
Librarians are not only subject matter experts in information sciences; academic librarians can also be assigned to specific discipline areas. When assigned to a specific discipline, librarians can familiarize themselves with not only the literature in that field, but also the particular academic integrity issues that affect that discipline (Shifter Caravello, 2007). Librarians are arguably the unsung heroes of integrity on many college campuses.

Academic Integrity Office and Honor Code Staff

Academic Integrity Office and Honor Code Staff
Institutions that are privileged enough to have a centralized academic integrity office (AIO) must recognize that they have a distinct advantage over schools that take a decentralized approach, which can lead toinconsistent messaging or processes. Even so, there is no standard job description for those who work in AIOs (Eerkes, 2010). Job responsibilities might include providing informal support and education, advising faculty and decision-makers, managing educational programs, and even coordinating hearings (Eerkes, 2010). Schools with a traditional or modified honor code system embedded into the school culture have been shown to have an advantage over non–honor code schools (McCabe et al., 2012; Roberts & Hai-Jew, 2009). As McCabe et al. (2012) point out, those who have experienced an honor code firsthand are more likely to be proponents of that system. Those who work to support the honor code become key role models on campus for students and other stakeholders.

Schools with a traditional or modified honor code system embedded into the school culture have been shown to have an advantage over non–honor code schools (McCabe et al., 2012; Roberts & Hai-Jew, 2009). As McCabe et al. (2012) point out, those who have experienced an honor code firsthand are more likely to be proponents of that system. Those who work to support the honor code become key role models on campus for students and other stakeholders.
The honor code system is somewhat unique to the United States, but a school can have an honorcultureeven if it does not have an explicit honor code (McCabe et al., 2012). Conversely, an honor code that is not supported by an institutional culture of honor ultimately will not be effective (McCabe et al., 2012). A centralized AIO can play a key role in supporting the development and advancement of institutional academic integrity culture.

Student Affairs

Student Affairs
Student affairs is a vital area of the learning organization that supports academic integrity (Bertram Gallant, 2008; Eerkes, 2010). Student affairs units are organized differently at each institution and can include a variety of subunits within them, including student judicial affairs, student conduct, academic support, tutoring, writing centers, and student advising. At some schools, the AIO can be housed within student affairs. Rather than dwelling on the different possible structures of student affairs within a given learning organization, it may be more useful to look at the function of this meso-level area of the institution. With respect to academic integrity, the primary objective of student affairs is to “preserve … the integrity of our scholarship so that the activities of the college or university can unfold as intended” (Eerkes, 2010, p. 101).

Teaching and Learning Centers

Teaching and Learning Centers
The role of the campus teaching and learning center is becoming increasingly important on campuses, due in part to the shifting conversation around academic integrity to recognize the role that faculty members play in not only reporting breaches of integrity after they have happened, but preventing them in the first place. Teaching and learning centers canprovide faculty members with professional opportunities to learn how to design better assessments and understand how pedagogy facilitates academic integrity. Teaching and learning centers serve to help faculty become proactive, rather than reactive, when it comes to academic integrity.

Student Wellness Centers

Student Wellness Centers
Wellness centers on campus play a vital role in supporting students’ physical, emotional, and mental well-being. Academic integrity professionals understand the links between academic integrity and mental health. When students are unsure if they are citing and referencing properly, their anxiety can escalate due to the fear of being accused of plagiarism (Ashworth, Bannister, & Thorne, 1997). Students can also experience extreme stress levels as they navigate the student judicial processes. There is more work to be done on many campuses to create links between proactive approaches to academic integrity and positive health, but suffice to say that the student wellness center is often a silent but necessary partner in academic integrity matters.

THE MACRO LEVEL: THE INSTITUTION OR ORGANIZATION

THE MACRO LEVEL: THE INSTITUTION OR ORGANIZATION
The role of the institution has changed considerably over the past half-century. Until the mid–twentieth century, universities and colleges actedin loco parentis, standing in for parents (Allmendinger, 1973; Bertram Gallant, 2008; Eerkes, 2010). This parental system included close supervision over such aspects of student life as residence, meals, recreation and social activities, character, and orderly behavior (Allmendinger, 1973). Although the erosion of thein loco parentisfunction of the university began in the mid-1800s (Allmendinger, 1973), it was not until a century later, during the social upheaval of the 1960s and 1970s, that court decisions ended the quasi-parental role of institutions (Eerkes, 2010). What remained were written policies, procedures, and supporting documents that articulated the expectations of student conduct, but these documents often have an embedded focus on rule compliance and behavior control (Bertram Gallant, 2008; Eerkes, 2010). It has only been since the turn of the twenty-first century that teaching and learning approaches to academic integrity have emerged as a counterapproach to rule compliance. In this section, I address these institutional-level systems and approaches that include aspects of governance that apply to all students (and sometimes other members of the campus community), regardless of the academic discipline.

The role of the institution has changed considerably over the past half-century. Until the mid–twentieth century, universities and colleges acted
in loco parentis
, standing in for parents (Allmendinger, 1973; Bertram Gallant, 2008; Eerkes, 2010). This parental system included close supervision over such aspects of student life as residence, meals, recreation and social activities, character, and orderly behavior (Allmendinger, 1973). Although the erosion of the
in loco parentis
function of the university began in the mid-1800s (Allmendinger, 1973), it was not until a century later, during the social upheaval of the 1960s and 1970s, that court decisions ended the quasi-parental role of institutions (Eerkes, 2010). What remained were written policies, procedures, and supporting documents that articulated the expectations of student conduct, but these documents often have an embedded focus on rule compliance and behavior control (Bertram Gallant, 2008; Eerkes, 2010). It has only been since the turn of the twenty-first century that teaching and learning approaches to academic integrity have emerged as a counterapproach to rule compliance. In this section, I address these institutional-level systems and approaches that include aspects of governance that apply to all students (and sometimes other members of the campus community), regardless of the academic discipline.
Policies and Procedures

Policies and Procedures
Many schools struggle with the tension between encouraging students to do well and punishing them when they either fail academically or fail to conduct themselves in acceptable ways, as outlined in the institutional policy documents. As Bertram Gallant (2018) points out, however, there is a difference between failure and fraud. The former can happen even when individuals make honest attempts to do their best work, whereas the latter has an element of intentionality and preplanning. There is a need to recognize the difference between failure and fraud in student behavior. Many institutional policies and procedures start with an implicit assumption of fraud. Policy approaches that take punitive approach rather than an educational one remain common (Stoesz et al., 2019).

As Bertram Gallant (2018) points out, however, there is a difference between failure and fraud. The former can happen even when individuals make honest attempts to do their best work, whereas the latter has an element of intentionality and preplanning. There is a need to recognize the difference between failure and fraud in student behavior. Many institutional policies and procedures start with an implicit assumption of fraud. Policy approaches that take punitive approach rather than an educational one remain common (Stoesz et al., 2019).
Tracey Bretag and colleagues identified five core elements of exemplary academic integrity policy, based on their analysis of policy documents from thirty-nine Australian universities (Bretag et al., 2011a, 2011b). These exemplary core elements have been nicely summarized by the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency of Australia (TEQSA, 2017, p. 10):

Tracey Bretag and colleagues identified five core elements of exemplary academic integrity policy, based on their analysis of policy documents from thirty-nine Australian universities (Bretag et al., 2011a, 2011b). These exemplary core elements have been nicely summarized by the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency of Australia (TEQSA, 2017, p. 10):
Access:The policy is easy to locate and read and is concise and comprehensible.

Access:
The policy is easy to locate and read and is concise and comprehensible.
Approach:There is a statement of purpose with an educative focus up front and throughout the policy.

Approach:
There is a statement of purpose with an educative focus up front and throughout the policy.
Responsibility:The policy details responsibilities for all stakeholders, including students, teachers, professional staff, and senior managers.

Responsibility:
The policy details responsibilities for all stakeholders, including students, teachers, professional staff, and senior managers.
Detail:The policy provides extensive but not excessive description of breaches, outcomes, and processes.

Detail:
The policy provides extensive but not excessive description of breaches, outcomes, and processes.
Support:The policy points to proactive and embedded systems to enable implementation of the policy.

Support:
The policy points to proactive and embedded systems to enable implementation of the policy.
These elements of exemplary policies provide a useful guideline for institutions when updating academic integrity policies and procedures. Just as the shift from thein loco parentisfunction of the university took many decades to occur, so too might it take a long time for policy to evolve. It is not unreasonable to expect that policy shifts toward more pedagogical approaches may continue to evolve throughout the remainder of the century and even beyond. It will be up to those working in the postsecondary sector to carry that work forward in the coming years.

In this section, I have examined several key individual roles that exist primarily within the institution (at the meso and macro levels). I will look at key stakeholders who are connected to the institution but whoseinvolvement is not part of the day-to-day operations of the organization, such as parents, in the section later in this chapter that addresses the macro level.
