involvement is not part of the day-to-day operations of the organization, such as parents, in the section later in this chapter that addresses the macro level.
THE MEGA LEVEL: THE COMMUNITY

THE MEGA LEVEL: THE COMMUNITY
The mega level is important because “there is a communal interest in the propriety of the university’s regulation” (Frenken, 2013, p. 128). In other words, even though postsecondary institutions may have the right to self-govern in matters of academic integrity, external stakeholders are interested in knowing not only that the institution engages in self-governance on such matters, but also how it goes about it. The various stakeholders who are primarily situated outside the institution are too numerous to name, so I will limit my discussion to one that is of particular importance: parents and families.

The mega level is important because “there is a communal interest in the propriety of the university’s regulation” (Frenken, 2013, p. 128). In other words, even though postsecondary institutions may have the right to self-govern in matters of academic integrity, external stakeholders are interested in knowing not only that the institution engages in self-governance on such matters, but also how it goes about it. The various stakeholders who are primarily situated outside the institution are too numerous to name, so I will limit my discussion to one that is of particular importance: parents and families.
The Role of Parents and Families

The Role of Parents and Families
Don McCabe and his colleagues (2012) have aptly pointed out that parental interest in academic integrity has been limited and adversarial. Parents and families are heavily invested in their children’s success (Sarita, 2015). In some cases, parents have been known to go to great lengths to ensure that their children are admitted to particular schools, as evidenced by the U.S. college admissions scandal dubbed “Operation Varsity Blues,” which made headlines around the world in 2019 (Golden & Burke, 2019; Miller & Bromwich, 2019). There have been other, less sensational, cases of parents being so invested in their children’s success that they have engaged in unethical behavior, such as completing academic work for on behalf of their children or enabling cheating (Eaton & Dressler, 2019; Lathrop & Foss, 2005). In addition to active parental interference, there is ample research to show that parental pressure can be so oppressive that some students feel must take any action necessary to achieve a high academic standing, even if that means plagiarizing or cheating (Sarita, 2015).

Don McCabe and his colleagues (2012) have aptly pointed out that parental interest in academic integrity has been limited and adversarial. Parents and families are heavily invested in their children’s success (Sarita, 2015). In some cases, parents have been known to go to great lengths to ensure that their children are admitted to particular schools, as evidenced by the U.S. college admissions scandal dubbed “Operation Varsity Blues,” which made headlines around the world in 2019 (Golden & Burke, 2019; Miller & Bromwich, 2019). There have been other, less sensational, cases of parents being so invested in their children’s success that they have engaged in unethical behavior, such as completing academic work for on behalf of their children or enabling cheating (Eaton & Dressler, 2019; Lathrop & Foss, 2005). In addition to active parental interference, there is ample research to show that parental pressure can be so oppressive that some students feel must take any action necessary to achieve a high academic standing, even if that means plagiarizing or cheating (Sarita, 2015).
Parents tend to get involved with the institution directly only when there is an alleged or actual academic integrity violation involving their own children (McCabe et al., 2012). Typically, parents have been less invested in helping institutions build a culture of integrity than they are in protecting their own children, even if it means fighting the institution when their children have been found responsible for a violation (McCabe et al., 2012). Administrators suddenly become concerned about irate parents going to news media or posting their opinions on social media, in addition to threats of filing court cases against the university.

Parents tend to get involved with the institution directly only when there is an alleged or actual academic integrity violation involving their own children (McCabe et al., 2012). Typically, parents have been less invested in helping institutions build a culture of integrity than they are in protecting their own children, even if it means fighting the institution when their children have been found responsible for a violation (McCabe et al., 2012). Administrators suddenly become concerned about irate parents going to news media or posting their opinions on social media, in addition to threats of filing court cases against the university.
Such parents have come to be known as “helicopter parents,” hovering over their children as they exude constant anxiety and worry about them (Miller & Bromwich, 2019). Parental anxiety has escalated further in recent years, creating the phenomenon of “snowplow parents,” who “are more like … machines chugging ahead, clearing obstacles in their child’s path to success, so they don’t have to encounter failure, frustration or lost opportunities” (Miller & Bromwich, 2019, n.p.). Snowplow parents send university administrators running for cover, particularly if there is a threat of legal action. Administrators can take some comfort in the fact that most judges dismiss academic misconduct cases because it has long been established that universities have the right to manage student conduct matters internally (Eerkes, 2010). It is relatively rare that judges, at least in the United States and Canada, have not ruled in favor of the institution, provided that procedural fairness is evident (Eerkes, 2010; Hannah, 1998; Kelleher, 2016, McCabe et al., 2012). But that does not stop some parents from trying.

Such parents have come to be known as “helicopter parents,” hovering over their children as they exude constant anxiety and worry about them (Miller & Bromwich, 2019). Parental anxiety has escalated further in recent years, creating the phenomenon of “snowplow parents,” who “are more like … machines chugging ahead, clearing obstacles in their child’s path to success, so they don’t have to encounter failure, frustration or lost opportunities” (Miller & Bromwich, 2019, n.p.). Snowplow parents send university administrators running for cover, particularly if there is a threat of legal action. Administrators can take some comfort in the fact that most judges dismiss academic misconduct cases because it has long been established that universities have the right to manage student conduct matters internally (Eerkes, 2010). It is relatively rare that judges, at least in the United States and Canada, have not ruled in favor of the institution, provided that procedural fairness is evident (Eerkes, 2010; Hannah, 1998; Kelleher, 2016, McCabe et al., 2012). But that does not stop some parents from trying.
There are more productive ways for parents to take a stand on academic integrity matters, many of which can happen even before a violation has occurred. Instead of acting as snowplows, they can be partners in their children’s learning. Parents can have open and supportive conversations with their children about how to make ethical decisions, how to self-advocate when students need extra learning support, and how to recognize when students have to work on building particular skills (e.g., time management) that will serve them well during their studies and later in life, as well as during their student years. A key question to ask is: how can we engage parents as partners, rather than as protesters, in matters relating to academic integrity? Actively seeking ways to engage parents productively can be one way that an institution can help this external stakeholder group become integrity allies with it. As with educators, parents play a key role in acting as role models of ethical behavior.

There are many more macro-level stakeholders that merit further consideration. The connection between institutions and ministries of education or higher education quality assurance bodies, for example, is one that has yet to be explored in depth in the literature.

A NETWORKED APPROACH TO ACADEMIC INTEGRITY

A NETWORKED APPROACH TO ACADEMIC INTEGRITY
Creating a culture of engagement cannot happen if individual practitioners are working in isolation (Kenny, Watson, & Desmarais, 2016). For too long, the work of student affairs professionals in particular has been disassociated from the work of faculty (Bertram Gallant, 2008). Students benefit when academics partner with others on campus, such as studentaffairs professionals and librarians, to promote and uphold integrity (Duff, Rogers, & Harris, 2006; Kuh et al., 1995). Professors, librarians, or student advocates cannot be effective so long as they are working as individual actors, without the support of the larger structures in which they work.

Creating a culture of engagement cannot happen if individual practitioners are working in isolation (Kenny, Watson, & Desmarais, 2016). For too long, the work of student affairs professionals in particular has been disassociated from the work of faculty (Bertram Gallant, 2008). Students benefit when academics partner with others on campus, such as student
affairs professionals and librarians, to promote and uphold integrity (Duff, Rogers, & Harris, 2006; Kuh et al., 1995). Professors, librarians, or student advocates cannot be effective so long as they are working as individual actors, without the support of the larger structures in which they work.
Informal and formal support networks can help individuals at the micro level, but they can also link the micro, meso, macro, and mega levels. What Hutchings, Huber, and Ciccone (2011) say about the scholarship of teaching and learning applies very well to academic integrity initiatives on campuses: the “lines of cause and effect.… are not immediate and direct, many institutions point to more web-like, multidirectional, cascading connections” (p. 39). Developing personal and informal networks of support is essential for supporting academic integrity. Conversations about organizational change, as well as developing one’s own professional practice, often happen behind the scenes, in informal contexts and personal networks where colleagues trust each other (Roxå& Mårtensson, 2009, 2012; Verwood & Poole, 2016). The importance of having individual conversations with students, colleagues, and community stakeholders cannot be overemphasized. Formal networks, such as those established by professional associations, and regional and international communities that support academic integrity offer important ways for individuals to connect across disciplines (meso level), institutions (macro level) and beyond (mega level).

Importance of Ongoing Development and Training

Importance of Ongoing Development and Training
Campus stakeholders can develop capacity and competence with regard to upholding the principles of academic integrity in a productive way (Colella-Sandercock & Alahmadi, 2015; Griffith, 2013). Such training will not be effective if it is offered or taken only once. The notion of a one-time workshop at which one can acquire all the skills, knowledge, and dispositions to understand and support academic integrity is a myth. For example, training in appropriate paraphrasing requires continued practice before students build competence and confidence with this skill.

Campus stakeholders can develop capacity and competence with regard to upholding the principles of academic integrity in a productive way (Colella-Sandercock & Alahmadi, 2015; Griffith, 2013). Such training will not be effective if it is offered or taken only once. The notion of a one-time workshop at which one can acquire all the skills, knowledge, and dispositions to understand and support academic integrity is a myth. For example, training in appropriate paraphrasing requires continued practice before students build competence and confidence with this skill.
Individual training is often offered at the meso level (Roxå& Mårtensson, 2012) because of discipline-specific interests and expectations with regard to how academic work is undertaken in a particular field. For example, academic integrity training for faculty members in the English department would (and probably should) differ from that offered in the chemical engineering department. Although policies may exist at an institutional level, pedagogy is implemented at the departmental and individual instructor levels. Academic integrity training for those in teaching roles needs to address both institutional and disciplinary interests. When it comes toacademic integrity training, there is no such thing as “set it and forget it.” Just as ethical decision-making requires us to make judgments about how we are going to act every single day, learning about ethics and integrity is an ongoing process.

academic integrity training, there is no such thing as “set it and forget it.” Just as ethical decision-making requires us to make judgments about how we are going to act every single day, learning about ethics and integrity is an ongoing process.
Learning how to act ethically starts long before students ever reach the postsecondary level. There is an urgent need to set the expectations for academic integrity early in students’ learning. To do so, the preservice ethics training that teachers receive must include explicit instruction on how to support academic integrity in the K–12 classroom. It is not enough to say that children should start learning about academic integrity in elementary, middle, or high school. For that to happen, those who teach those children must learn how to support them, and that starts with teacher education.

CONCLUSIONS

CONCLUSIONS
Students do not learn in isolation; they are connected to learning and development through their peers, professors and other members of the learning community. Academic integrity stakeholders are interconnected across levels, and job functions. The work of the student affairs professional must be connected to the faculty, which must be connected to the librarians, and most of all, connected to the students.

Academic integrity stakeholders are interconnected across levels, and job functions. The work of the student affairs professional must be connected to the faculty, which must be connected to the librarians, and most of all, connected to the students.

5

5
Evaluation and Assessment

Evaluation and Assessment
This is not a chapter about how to create a “plagiarism-proof assignment”—no such thing exists. It is futile to try to outsmart students when it comes to plagiarism, because as fast as technology changes, so too do the ways in which students can cheat and plagiarize (Whiteman & Gordon, 2001). Tricia Bertram Gallant has challenged us to reframe the question “How do we stop students from cheating?” to “how do we ensure students are learning?” (2008, p. 6). To riff on Bertram Gallant’s challenge to reframe unproductive questions, I suggest that when it comes to assessment design, perhaps the question for educators is not: how do we outsmart students when we design tests and assessments? Instead, we should ask: how do we engage students as partners in ethical learning? Starting with the intention of engaging in ethical teaching and learning shifts the assessment conversation substantially.

This is not a chapter about how to create a “plagiarism-proof assignment”—no such thing exists. It is futile to try to outsmart students when it comes to plagiarism, because as fast as technology changes, so too do the ways in which students can cheat and plagiarize (Whiteman & Gordon, 2001). Tricia Bertram Gallant has challenged us to reframe the question “How do we stop students from cheating?” to “how do we ensure students are learning?” (2008, p. 6). To riff on Bertram Gallant’s challenge to reframe unproductive questions, I suggest that when it comes to assessment design, perhaps the question for educators is not: how do we outsmart students when we design tests and assessments? Instead, we should ask: how do we engage students as partners in ethical learning? Starting with the intention of engaging in ethical teaching and learning shifts the assessment conversation substantially.
In this chapter, I discuss evaluation and assessment through the lens of academic integrity. There are assessment design strategies that can minimize academic misconduct and simultaneously promote effective learning (Morris, 2016). Assessment design that promotes student-centered approaches to effective learning also promotes integrity. I explore some of these strategies in this chapter. In keeping with the theme of this book, I touch upon tough topics such as academic freedom, recycling of assignments and exams, the role of formative assessment in upholding academic integrity, and creating opportunities for students to take risks while they learn.

There are assessment design strategies that can minimize academic misconduct and simultaneously promote effective learning (Morris, 2016). Assessment design that promotes student-centered approaches to effective learning also promotes integrity. I explore some of these strategies in this chapter. In keeping with the theme of this book, I touch upon tough topics such as academic freedom, recycling of assignments and exams, the role of formative assessment in upholding academic integrity, and creating opportunities for students to take risks while they learn.
ASSESSING WITH INTEGRITY

ASSESSING WITH INTEGRITY
It is utterly unethical for an instructor say things like “None of you will pass the exam that you are about to take” or “Only one of you will get an A on your paper for this course,” or even “I do not need to provide assessment criteria because I am the professor.” Yet phrases such as these continue to be spoken in classrooms around the world. If we accept the idea that cultivating ethical conduct among students requires a multistakeholder approach, then we cannot talk about academic integrity without addressing instructional integrity, and specifically ethical assessment of student learning.

It is utterly unethical for an instructor say things like “None of you will pass the exam that you are about to take” or “Only one of you will get an A on your paper for this course,” or even “I do not need to provide assessment criteria because I am the professor.” Yet phrases such as these continue to be spoken in classrooms around the world. If we accept the idea that cultivating ethical conduct among students requires a multistakeholder approach, then we cannot talk about academic integrity without addressing instructional integrity, and specifically ethical assessment of student learning.
Concepts such as procedural fairness and natural justice are discussed at length in the literature about addressing student breaches of integrity. A strong body of literature about fair assessment of student learning also exists (Ragupathi & Lee, 2020; Scott et al., 2014; Suskie, 2000; Tierney, 2011). There remains a need to amplify the conversation around ethical assessment of student learning that has been ongoing for decades (McCabe & Pavela, 1997).

Concepts such as procedural fairness and natural justice are discussed at length in the literature about addressing student breaches of integrity. A strong body of literature about fair assessment of student learning also exists (Ragupathi & Lee, 2020; Scott et al., 2014; Suskie, 2000; Tierney, 2011). There remains a need to amplify the conversation around ethical assessment of student learning that has been ongoing for decades (McCabe & Pavela, 1997).
The ways in which instructors assess students is inherently values-laden. The philosophical approaches to student assessment are contentious and even politicized (Scott et al., 2014). Instructor interpretations about what counts as fair grading varies wildly (Tierney et al., 2011). I will refrain from extending this discussion into the domain of standardized testing; although that topic is worthy of debate among those who are concerned about equitable and fair student assessment (Scott et al., 2014), it is beyond the scope of this book.

Just Say No to Recycling Assignments and Exams

Just Say No to Recycling Assignments and Exams
This may seem like common sense to avoid recycling old assessments, but numerous faculty today still insist on reusing old assignments, term paper topics, quizzes, and final exams. Changing assessments a minimum of once per term has been found to promote academic integrity among students (Christensen Hughes, 2017). There is a fundamentally unjust double standard if institutions prohibit students from submitting previous work for academic credit, labeling it self-plagiarism, and then turn a blind eye to professors who do effectively the same thing when they recycle previous assignments and tests. When instructors fail to take the time to revise their assessments, even a little bit, for their current cohort of students, they may be sending an implicit message that they do not care enough about their current students to take the time to develop meaningful, fresh, and new—or even updated—assignments. Recycling old assignments and quizzes can send a strong message to students that professorsdo not care about them. If students perceive that instructors do not care about them, there is a higher likelihood that they will plagiarize or cheat (Christensen Hughes, 2017; Rezanejad & Rezaei, 2013).

This may seem like common sense to avoid recycling old assessments, but numerous faculty today still insist on reusing old assignments, term paper topics, quizzes, and final exams. Changing assessments a minimum of once per term has been found to promote academic integrity among students (Christensen Hughes, 2017). There is a fundamentally unjust double standard if institutions prohibit students from submitting previous work for academic credit, labeling it self-plagiarism, and then turn a blind eye to professors who do effectively the same thing when they recycle previous assignments and tests. When instructors fail to take the time to revise their assessments, even a little bit, for their current cohort of students, they may be sending an implicit message that they do not care enough about their current students to take the time to develop meaningful, fresh, and new—or even updated—assignments. Recycling old assignments and quizzes can send a strong message to students that professors
do not care about them. If students perceive that instructors do not care about them, there is a higher likelihood that they will plagiarize or cheat (Christensen Hughes, 2017; Rezanejad & Rezaei, 2013).
Communicate Clear Assessment Criteria

Communicate Clear Assessment Criteria
One factor that contributes to student plagiarism is unclear assessment criteria (Broeckelman-Post, 2008; Curtis & Vardanega 2016; Stappenbelt, 2012; Sterngold, 2004). There may have been a time when professors’ knowledge and position of authority allowed them to rely solely on their own experience and opinions to assess students, but such teacher-centric approaches have been challenged for decades. It is no longer acceptable (or ethical) for professors to fail to provide clear assessment criteria or the opportunity for students to ask for clarification.

One factor that contributes to student plagiarism is unclear assessment criteria (Broeckelman-Post, 2008; Curtis & Vardanega 2016; Stappenbelt, 2012; Sterngold, 2004). There may have been a time when professors’ knowledge and position of authority allowed them to rely solely on their own experience and opinions to assess students, but such teacher-centric approaches have been challenged for decades. It is no longer acceptable (or ethical) for professors to fail to provide clear assessment criteria or the opportunity for students to ask for clarification.
Ensuring that all parties understand assessment criteria is a shared responsibility.

Ensuring that all parties understand assessment criteria is a shared responsibility.
It is up to instructors to provide fair and clear assessment criteria. In turn, students are responsible for ensuring that they understand the criteria and for seeking clarification if they are confused. Tools such as rubrics can help students understand what is expected of them (Curtis & Vardanega, 2016; Ragupathi & Lee, 2020). There are various types of rubrics, and although their use has been contested, they can work well when they are employed thoughtfully, with the intention of supporting and promoting students’ learning (Ragupathi & Lee, 2020).

It is up to instructors to provide fair and clear assessment criteria. In turn, students are responsible for ensuring that they understand the criteria and for seeking clarification if they are confused. Tools such as rubrics can help students understand what is expected of them (Curtis & Vardanega, 2016; Ragupathi & Lee, 2020). There are various types of rubrics, and although their use has been contested, they can work well when they are employed thoughtfully, with the intention of supporting and promoting students’ learning (Ragupathi & Lee, 2020).
Students have also reported that they get confused when teachers have different expectations for citing and referencing (Adam, 2016). One professor could be a stickler for following a specific style guide, and another might be oblivious to the details and have the opinion that if the source is cited at all, that is good enough. Although this variance in instructional approaches to strictness in citing and referencing might not be ideal (or even ethical), it remains the current reality of higher education in many countries. It could be argued that individual variances among instructors in terms of how work is graded could indicate systemic injustice for students trying to learn what is expected of them. From a student’s perspective, it can look like the rules change with each professor encountered. Short of a fundamental shift, the tenets of academic freedom allow individual professors to assess students as they deem appropriate (Frenken, 2013). This disparity in education is unlikely to change any time soon. In the absence of systemic change, what instructors can do is to provide clear assessment criteria to their students, with specific detail about what they expect. Sharing insights into why a professor has developed particular assessment criteria can be even more helpful to students. For example,even if they do not necessarily agree with a professor’s nitpickiness, knowing why certain approaches are implemented can help students accept what is expected of them for that particular course.

Assume Assessments Are Being Shared

Assume Assessments Are Being Shared
A few years ago, Dr. Julia Christensen Hughes visited our campus to talk about academic integrity. In a campuswide address, Christensen Hughes told academic staff to expect that if they have given an assignment or exam once, to assume that students have shared it and most likely have shared it online. You could see the faces of the faculty members drop as she went on to explain that when educators do not change their assignments and simply recycle them every year, it sends a message that instructors do not care about their teaching or students’ learning. She urged the faculty to look at it from the students’ perspective: when professors communicate, even inadvertently, that they do not care about teaching or learning, students are the ones who feel cheated (Christensen Hughes, 2017). It is naive to expect that the test or assignment that you have previously designed is not available to students in some format.

In a campuswide address, Christensen Hughes told academic staff to expect that if they have given an assignment or exam once, to assume that students have shared it and most likely have shared it online. You could see the faces of the faculty members drop as she went on to explain that when educators do not change their assignments and simply recycle them every year, it sends a message that instructors do not care about their teaching or students’ learning. She urged the faculty to look at it from the students’ perspective: when professors communicate, even inadvertently, that they do not care about teaching or learning, students are the ones who feel cheated (Christensen Hughes, 2017). It is naive to expect that the test or assignment that you have previously designed is not available to students in some format.
We live in a sharing culture (Blum, 2009). There is no point bemoaning that fact. It could be considered hypocritical for professors to complain about students sharing assignments and files in one breath, and in the next breath post slides in class that contain unattributed photos that someone else has taken. (Sharing slide decks with unattributed photos, graphics, and other visuals is common among educators.) Professors must ensure that they model integrity by giving attribution to others for content they use in their teaching materials.

Professors must ensure that they model integrity by giving attribution to others for content they use in their teaching materials.
Avoid Premade Text Banks

Avoid Premade Text Banks
In addition to sharing assignments, it is just as easy to share tests and quizzes. Educators are naive to believe claims that “instructor-only” course packs, which often include premade test banks, are not easily accessible to students. There are online businesses that specialize in the sale of academic tests, marketing them as “study guides” to students, when the exact same product is marketed to educators as “secure test banks.” There have been cases where sizable groups of students have accessed test questions online prior to an exam, resulting in numerous students being found responsible for academic misconduct (Jaschik, 2018; Slark, 2020a, 2020b). The bottom line for teachers is this: if a resource is available to educators, it is available to students too.

Lowering the Stakes

Lowering the Stakes
High-stakes assessments are those in which much is riding on achieving success in a single instance. An example would be a final essay worth 50 percent or more of the course grade. Research has shown that students are more likely to cheat in high-stakes assessments. Shifting to lower-stakes assessment can decrease incidents of plagiarism (Macdonald & Carroll, 2006; Morris, 2016); however, this must be balanced with the total number of assignments. Having 100 small assessments, each worth 1 percent of the final course grade, or 50 assessments, each worth 2 percent, is likely not going to reduce stress for anyone. Lowering the stakes works only if the overall number of combined assessments (including tests, papers, in-class writing, and any other learning tasks) are reasonable and manageable for both students and educators.

Incorporating Reflection

Incorporating Reflection
When learning is viewed as aprocessrather than an endproduct, students gain a deeper sense of accomplishment with the outcome of their work (Hodgkinson et al., 2016). Incorporating reflection as an element of assessment can help students focus on the learning process (Eaton, Guglielmin, & Otoo, 2017). Focusing on learning as a process, rather than as an end product, can help to keep the focus on learning as an ongoing and lifelong journey.

rather than an end

Incorporating reflection as an element of assessment can help students focus on the learning process (Eaton, Guglielmin, & Otoo, 2017). Focusing on learning as a process, rather than as an end product, can help to keep the focus on learning as an ongoing and lifelong journey.
Growing Ideas Ethically

Growing Ideas Ethically
Educators must create opportunities for students to germinate and incubate their ideas, and then allow them to grow academically and emotionally within safe learning environments. If students constantly operate under the fear that they will be accused of plagiarism in some form or another, they may not take risks as they are attempting to master the knowledge and skills required of them.

Educators must create opportunities for students to germinate and incubate their ideas, and then allow them to grow academically and emotionally within safe learning environments. If students constantly operate under the fear that they will be accused of plagiarism in some form or another, they may not take risks as they are attempting to master the knowledge and skills required of them.
Formative Feedback

Formative Feedback
It is important to differentiate between the summative assessment of a particular task or project and formative assessment of the learning process. Much can be done to incorporate formative assessment during the learning process before the final work is submitted (Black & Wiliam, 2009;Macdonald & Carroll, 2006; Morris, 2016; Morrissette, 2011). Teach Citing, Referencing, and Research Skills in Meaningful Ways

Teach Citing, Referencing, and Research Skills in Meaningful Ways
There are many manuals about how to teach the technical and mechanical aspects of citing and referencing. Such approaches show students what to do and how to do it, but often omit why it is important to do so. The focus of academic integrity education is often deficit-based: avoid plagiarism or avoid behaviors or actions that could result in allegations of academic misconduct. This deficit-based thinking starts with fear and emphasizes fear-based approaches that can ultimately make citing and referencing a miserable task rather than a journey of discovery.

There are many manuals about how to teach the technical and mechanical aspects of citing and referencing. Such approaches show students what to do and how to do it, but often omit why it is important to do so. The focus of academic integrity education is often deficit-based: avoid plagiarism or avoid behaviors or actions that could result in allegations of academic misconduct. This deficit-based thinking starts with fear and emphasizes fear-based approaches that can ultimately make citing and referencing a miserable task rather than a journey of discovery.
A strengths-based approach to teaching academic integrity may be more productive, interesting, and engaging. In a brilliant article, Hendricks and Quinn propose teaching referencing as a means to develop “epistemological empowerment” (2000, p. 447). After analyzing qualitative data that they collected through interviews with six first-year English as a Second Language (ESL) students, they found that the participants in their study often focused on referencing as a means to avoid plagiarism rather than to build knowledge. In other words, citing and referencing are often seen as a technical activity rather than a way of developing epistemicagency (Elgin, 2013). As a result of their study, Hendricks and Quinn (2000) urge educators to move beyond the superficial and technical aspects of citing and referencing and show students how to connect the dots between citing and referencing and knowledge building. An example of this is Dr. Mairi Cowan, a history professor at the University of Toronto, who sends her students on a “footnote treasure hunt” (Cowan, 2019) to help them understand how and why footnotes leave important clues about original sources.

In a brilliant article, Hendricks and Quinn propose teaching referencing as a means to develop “epistemological empowerment” (2000, p. 447). After analyzing qualitative data that they collected through interviews with six first-year English as a Second Language (ESL) students, they found that the participants in their study often focused on referencing as a means to avoid plagiarism rather than to build knowledge. In other words, citing and referencing are often seen as a technical activity rather than a way of developing epistemic
agency (Elgin, 2013). As a result of their study, Hendricks and Quinn (2000) urge educators to move beyond the superficial and technical aspects of citing and referencing and show students how to connect the dots between citing and referencing and knowledge building. An example of this is Dr. Mairi Cowan, a history professor at the University of Toronto, who sends her students on a “footnote treasure hunt” (Cowan, 2019) to help them understand how and why footnotes leave important clues about original sources.
It is also worth talking with students about how citing and referencing are not necessarily intellectually agnostic acts. As Amy Robillard has pointed out, “Most writers know on some level that citations aren’t simply matters of rationality and logic. Citations reveal a great deal about personal allegiances. We cite the people we cite because wefeelcertain things toward them” (2006, p. 261, emphasis in original). For students to get to the point where they feel something about the source material that they are citing, they must interact with it in a meaningful way that goes beyond the technical aspects of citation or fear-based reasons for doing so. To do that, we must find meaningful, creative ways of teaching students why citing and referencing are important, starting from a strengths-based position rather than deficit thinking.

Sample Activity: Inquiry into Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs

Sample Activity: Inquiry into Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs
I teach mainly graduate students, and I am adamant that graduate students consult original sources whenever possible. Our library offers students an extraordinary array of resources. If a student cannot access a source easily, they can get through interlibrary loan or document delivery services. Students do not always have adequate opportunity to learn how to use the library. Introductory orientations are insufficient. Students need opportunities to learn how to use their institutional library in ways that are meaningful, intentional, and discipline-specific.

I teach mainly graduate students, and I am adamant that graduate students consult original sources whenever possible. Our library offers students an extraordinary array of resources. If a student cannot access a source easily, they can get through interlibrary loan or document delivery services. Students do not always have adequate opportunity to learn how to use the library. Introductory orientations are insufficient. Students need opportunities to learn how to use their institutional library in ways that are meaningful, intentional, and discipline-specific.
Here is an example of an inquiry activity that I conducted with a group of master’s of education students some years ago (Eaton, 2012) to teach library use, as well as the importance of consulting original source material. I based it on the hierarchy of needs popularized by the American psychologist Abraham Maslow. I used resources readily available in our library for students to consult. It started with a question to the class: “Where did Maslow’s pyramid come from?”

Here is an example of an inquiry activity that I conducted with a group of master’s of education students some years ago (Eaton, 2012) to teach library use, as well as the importance of consulting original source material. I based it on the hierarchy of needs popularized by the American psychologist Abraham Maslow. I used resources readily available in our library for students to consult. It started with a question to the class: “Where did Maslow’s pyramid come from?”
Some students thought that this was a trick question. Others thought that it was too easy. We started by brainstorming some possible answers. Everything from aliens to Egyptian pyramids came up during our pre-activity brainstorming. We had a few good laughs, and then I sent thestudents on their quest to answer the question that I had posed to them, telling them everything that they needed to find the answer could be found in our university library. I told them that they could work individually, in pairs, or in groups, but they only had one day to complete the inquiry, and we would be talking about their results in class the following day. And off they went to find the answer to the question.

Some students thought that this was a trick question. Others thought that it was too easy. We started by brainstorming some possible answers. Everything from aliens to Egyptian pyramids came up during our pre-activity brainstorming. We had a few good laughs, and then I sent the
students on their quest to answer the question that I had posed to them, telling them everything that they needed to find the answer could be found in our university library. I told them that they could work individually, in pairs, or in groups, but they only had one day to complete the inquiry, and we would be talking about their results in class the following day. And off they went to find the answer to the question.
They found Maslow’s 1943 article, “A Theory of Human Motivation,” which our library has available in digital form. Then they had to go into the stacks to find Maslow’s 1954 book,Motivation and Personality,which was available only in hard copy. They also found a number of other works, which we discussed as a group in class the next day.

They found Maslow’s 1943 article, “A Theory of Human Motivation,” which our library has available in digital form. Then they had to go into the stacks to find Maslow’s 1954 book,
Motivation and Personality,
which was available only in hard copy. They also found a number of other works, which we discussed as a group in class the next day.
The students discovered that the pyramid does not exist anywhere in Maslow’s original work. Nowhere. While the original ideas may be Maslow’s, the pyramid is not. Someone, somewhere along the way, adapted his original theory into the pyramid graphic. No one knows who first adapted the work into a pyramid. The pyramid is someone else’s interpretation of Maslow’s original work, and it has become an iconic representation of his ideas. The iconic pyramid of what has become known as “Maslow’s hierarchy of needs” is at best an interpretation or a riff on the original work.

The students discovered that the pyramid does not exist anywhere in Maslow’s original work. Nowhere. While the original ideas may be Maslow’s, the pyramid is not. Someone, somewhere along the way, adapted his original theory into the pyramid graphic. No one knows who first adapted the work into a pyramid. The pyramid is someone else’s interpretation of Maslow’s original work, and it has become an iconic representation of his ideas. The iconic pyramid of what has become known as “Maslow’s hierarchy of needs” is at best an interpretation or a riff on the original work
.
Through their library inquiry, the students found what Maslow actually says about the hierarchy of needs: “if I may assign arbitrary figures for the sake of illustration, it is as if the average citizen is satisfied perhaps 85% in his physiological needs, 70% in his safety needs, 50% in his love needs, 40% in his self-esteem needs and 10% in his self-actualization needs” (Maslow, 1943, pp. 388–389). So even if wewereto draw a diagram to represent Maslow’s hierarchy, the physiological needs would need to represent a much bigger piece of the pyramid.

So even if we
were
to draw a diagram to represent Maslow’s hierarchy, the physiological needs would need to represent a much bigger piece of the pyramid.
The students’ reactions to this inquiry varied from puzzled to surprised to horrified. All of them had seen the pyramid at some point in their studies. It is ubiquitous in textbooks and online. None of them had ever thought to question its origins. As a class, we documented these discoveries from the inquiry, which I have written about on my blog (Eaton, 2012):

The students’ reactions to this inquiry varied from puzzled to surprised to horrified. All of them had seen the pyramid at some point in their studies. It is ubiquitous in textbooks and online. None of them had ever thought to question its origins. As a class, we documented these discoveries from the inquiry, which I have written about on my blog (Eaton, 2012):
1. Original works are adapted by others. Some purists argue that mashups are an aberration; that they defile the original work. People have been modifying and adapting original works for centuries.

1. Original works are adapted by others
. Some purists argue that mashups are an aberration; that they defile the original work. People have been modifying and adapting original works for centuries.
2. Find the original sources whenever possible.In today’s world, it is easier than ever to find original source documents. Libraries have digitized versions of primary sources going back for decades. It is important for students and researchers to learn to “drill down” and find the original sources of information. If Maslow’s original article from 1943 has been digitized and is accessible through the local library, it is worth the effort to try to find the original source for your own research. It may be easier than you think to access it.

2. Find the original sources whenever possible.
In today’s world, it is easier than ever to find original source documents. Libraries have digitized versions of primary sources going back for decades. It is important for students and researchers to learn to “drill down” and find the original sources of information. If Maslow’s original article from 1943 has been digitized and is accessible through the local library, it is worth the effort to try to find the original source for your own research. It may be easier than you think to access it.
3. Don’t believe everything you see on the Internet.The pyramid figure that has come to represent Maslow’s work appears all over the Internet. Yet, it never appears anywhere in his original work. There is value in learning to discriminate between original research and what is presented on the Internet as “truth.”

3. Don’t believe everything you see on the Internet.
The pyramid figure that has come to represent Maslow’s work appears all over the Internet. Yet, it never appears anywhere in his original work. There is value in learning to discriminate between original research and what is presented on the Internet as “truth.”
4. Check others’ citations. Maslow’s pyramid has been cited in both academic and popular articles as originating from both his 1943 article and his 1954 book. Yet, the pyramid appears in neither original source. It is important for researchers, scholars, and students to (respectfully) check other authors’ citations. Do not take it for granted that simply because a reference appears in a bibliography, that the citation is correct.

4. Check others’ citations
. Maslow’s pyramid has been cited in both academic and popular articles as originating from both his 1943 article and his 1954 book. Yet, the pyramid appears in neither original source. It is important for researchers, scholars, and students to (respectfully) check other authors’ citations. Do not take it for granted that simply because a reference appears in a bibliography, that the citation is correct.
5. Learn to “drill deep” in your research.Often, we take it for granted that others’ research is “the real deal.” Part of our professional practice means that we allow our curiosity to drive our search for knowledge. Learning to “drill deep” means that you take on the challenge of finding out for yourself, learning to analyze and think critically, rather than relying on what others say.

5. Learn to “drill deep” in your research.
Often, we take it for granted that others’ research is “the real deal.” Part of our professional practice means that we allow our curiosity to drive our search for knowledge. Learning to “drill deep” means that you take on the challenge of finding out for yourself, learning to analyze and think critically, rather than relying on what others say.
As I reflect on this inquiry, I also see the value in a “rapid response” kind of activity. It is important for students to know that they can find original sources quickly and with relative ease. At first, some students felt that having to go to the library in person and search through the stacks was inconvenient, although they later admitted that the value of finding the original source was worth the trip to the library.

As I reflect on this inquiry, I also see the value in a “rapid response” kind of activity. It is important for students to know that they can find original sources quickly and with relative ease. At first, some students felt that having to go to the library in person and search through the stacks was inconvenient, although they later admitted that the value of finding the original source was worth the trip to the library.
At the beginning of this chapter, I posed another question: how do we engage students as partners in ethical learning? Inquiry activities such as this one not only engage students, but empower them. This particular group of students learned the value of consulting primary sources in a unique and meaningful way. Some of them had a visceral response to what they found. None of them ever complained after that about my unrelenting insistence on finding original sources whenever possible. Since that time, the myth of Maslow’s pyramid has been challenged more widely, so this activity may not work with today’s students. (But if you think it would, you are welcome to use this activity with your own students.) The key is to find meaningful, relevant, and provocative activities that show them the value of citing and referencing beyond technical minutiae.

I will add that I only ever used this activity once. That group of students went on to tell other students, as well as professors and people beyond their “school circle,” about what they learned. A couple of them told me that they even challenged a professor in a subsequent course who talked about “Maslow’s pyramid” in class. Although it was never my intention for students to publicly challenge another professor, it worked out in the end, as the students were able to show what they learned as a result of our inquiry. The other professor was unaware that the pyramid was not Maslow’soriginal work and was gracious and humble enough to allow the students to talk about what they had learned. (The same professor later vowed never to mention the pyramid again in class.)

The other professor was unaware that the pyramid was not Maslow’s
original work and was gracious and humble enough to allow the students to talk about what they had learned. (The same professor later vowed never to mention the pyramid again in class.)
The ripple effect of this inquiry meant that I never used it a second time, as it lost its novelty. The students were so excited and affected by what they had learned that by the following year, many of the incoming students already knew that Maslow’s pyramid was “a hoax.” I will be the first one to admit that I have yet to come up with an inquiry with as much of an impact as that one had, but I continue to revise my assessments every year so that they are fresh and new in courses where I have the autonomy to do so. In courses that I am assigned to teach that have a standardized format and the assignments are preset, I instead engage colleagues in ongoing conversations about how and why instructional integrity is crucial, including having new assessments at least once a year. I am not always successful at convincing course coordinators that assessments need to be changed regularly, but that does not stop me from having the conversation.

In courses that I am assigned to teach that have a standardized format and the assignments are preset, I instead engage colleagues in ongoing conversations about how and why instructional integrity is crucial, including having new assessments at least once a year. I am not always successful at convincing course coordinators that assessments need to be changed regularly, but that does not stop me from having the conversation.
Let me add here that since conducting that inquiry activity, I learned that the pyramid attributed to Maslow was actually appropriated by him from the Siksika people, who are part of the Blackfoot Confederacy in Canada (Blood & Heavy Head, 2011). There is now ample evidence to show that the notion of self-actualization did not originate with Maslow but was merely popularized by him after he spent time with the Blackfoot people. The irony of these multiple appropriations of knowledge without attribution should not be lost on us.

ONLINE AND REMOTE LEARNING

ONLINE AND REMOTE LEARNING
It is a myth that there is more plagiarism in online and distance learning courses. In 2020, the world underwent unprecedented changes to learning due to the COVID-19 crisis. Institutions across the world moved their classes from face-to-face to a remote format in a matter of days. As a result, conversations and concerns about academic integrity in online and remote learning bubbled to the surface. Here, I explain the historical context regarding online learning and academic misconduct and then reflect on the COVID-19 crisis.

It is a myth that there is more plagiarism in online and distance learning courses. In 2020, the world underwent unprecedented changes to learning due to the COVID-19 crisis. Institutions across the world moved their classes from face-to-face to a remote format in a matter of days. As a result, conversations and concerns about academic integrity in online and remote learning bubbled to the surface. Here, I explain the historical context regarding online learning and academic misconduct and then reflect on the COVID-19 crisis.
There are many myths and misperceptions about academic misconduct in online learning, and among them is the often-erroneous perception or opinion that there is more cheating of all kinds in online courses (Harris et al., 2019; Harton, Aladia, & Gordon, 2019; Miller & Young-Jones, 2012). There is evidence to suggest that once someone has actually taken or taught an online course, their perceptions about how easy it is to cheat inan e-learning environment diminishes (Kennedy et al., 2000). In other words, there are indications suggesting that those who think cheating and plagiarism happen more frequently in e-learning courses are those who have never experienced teaching and learning in an online environment themselves.

There are many myths and misperceptions about academic misconduct in online learning, and among them is the often-erroneous perception or opinion that there is more cheating of all kinds in online courses (Harris et al., 2019; Harton, Aladia, & Gordon, 2019; Miller & Young-Jones, 2012). There is evidence to suggest that once someone has actually taken or taught an online course, their perceptions about how easy it is to cheat in
an e-learning environment diminishes (Kennedy et al., 2000). In other words, there are indications suggesting that those who think cheating and plagiarism happen more frequently in e-learning courses are those who have never experienced teaching and learning in an online environment themselves.
This could be exacerbated by the fact that many people, including faculty, continue to dispute the legitimacy of online and distance learning in the first place. Skeptics of online learning continue to challenge the idea that meaningful learning can occur in online contexts, a point which proponents of online learning continually work to refute (Hurst et al., 2013; Miller & Young-Jones, 2012). For those who stand against online learning, it is easy to see how claims of increased cheating would be tempting to make. There are some parallels with this line of argumentation with those who are proponents of segregationist approaches to learning who claimed that Black students cheated more than White students (Educational Fund of the Citizens’ Councils, 1956). Their assumption was that Black students cheated morebecausethey were Black, without considering contextual or societal factors such as low socioeconomic status or academic disadvantage. Similar prejudices are found today against international students, those for whom English is a second language and those who study online. For some nontraditional students, e-learning has offered them an opportunity to improve their academic standing and qualifications while working full time (Bacow et al., 2012). For students living in rural and remote areas, online courses provide these students with access to learning that otherwise would not be available to them (Gereluk et al., 2020). Although this is not the case for all students who learn online, there are a portion who are less privileged (socioeconomically and otherwise) than their peers who take traditional face-to-face courses. In some cases, anti-online-learning proponents fail to care about equity and access for those who face barriers to traditional learning.

The COVID-19 pandemic forced a rapid rethink of teaching and learning. Many institutions turned to online and remote-learning options quickly. Educators and policymakers moved away from opinion-based arguments about cheating in online courses, and instead turned to empirical research for answers. For more than two decades before the coronavirus crisis hit, academics and educators were emphasizing that overall, there is little to no evidence to support the notion that there is more cheating in online and remote learning courses than in traditional face-to-face courses (Fyock & Sutphin, 1995; Heberling, 2002; Watson & Sottile, 2010). Some studies have found there actually islessacademic misconduct in online and remote courses classes than in traditional face-to-face courses (Bretag et al., 2018, 2019; Davis et al., 2009; Hart & Morgan, 2010; Stuber-McEwen, Wiseley, & Hoggatt, 2009). The COVID-19 pandemic forced a rapid rethink of teaching and learning. Many institutions turned to online and remote-learning options quickly. Educators and policymakers moved away from opinion-based arguments about cheating in online courses, and instead turned to empirical research for answers. For more than two decades before the coronavirus crisis hit, academics and educators were emphasizing that overall, there is little to no evidence to support the notion that there is more cheating in online and remote learning courses than in traditional face-to-face courses (Fyock & Sutphin, 1995; Heberling, 2002; Watson & Sottile, 2010). Some studies have found there actually is
less
academic misconduct in online and remote courses classes than in traditional face-to-face courses (Bretag et al., 2018, 2019; Davis et al., 2009; Hart & Morgan, 2010; Stuber-McEwen, Wiseley, & Hoggatt, 2009). Some examples of comparative empirical
studies comparing students in face-to-face versus online courses include the following:
- A study of students in online and traditional registered nurse to baccalaureate nursing (RN-BSN) programs. The study participants included online (n= 330) versus face-to-face nursing students (n= 44). Respondents in both groups were predominantly White, female, and married. Age was found to be a stronger determinant of cheating behaviors, with younger students being more likely to engage in academic misconduct. Among both groups, cheating behaviors among those enrolled in traditional face-to-face programs were reported at statistically significant higher rates than among their online counterparts (Hart & Morgan, 2010).

- A study at a midsize Christian university in the United States with undergraduate students (N= 225) enrolled in on-campus (n= 87) and online (n= 138) courses. Students in traditional face-to-face classes were significantlymorelikely to commit acts of academic misconduct, including plagiarism (Stuber-McEwen et al., 2009).

- A survey of students (N= 459) at an Australia university, with a long history of distance education programs. The survey was completed by internal (on campus) students (n= 210) and distance learners (n= 248). Overall, more on-campus students reported engaging in cheating behaviors than those enrolled in distance education programs. One noteworthy result was that 78 percent of internal students self-reported to have engaged in cheating behaviors at least once, whereas only 35 percent of their distance education peers self-reported similar behaviors. The average age of the distance education students was 35.8 years, compared with an average age of 22.4 years of the on-campus students, suggesting a relationship between the maturity of students and cheating behavior (Kidwell & Kent, 2008).

The average age of the distance education students was 35.8 years, compared with an average age of 22.4 years of the on-campus students, suggesting a relationship between the maturity of students and cheating behavior (Kidwell & Kent, 2008).
Having said this, there is a difference between emergency remote learning and online learning. In the studies mentioned here, there was an assumption that students had some choice in whether they took their classes online or face-to-face, which was not the case during the rapid shift to remote learning caused by the coronavirus crisis. Many educators who moved to remote learning were inexperienced at teaching in online environments. As a result, they may not have assessed students in ways appropriate to online environments (e.g., timed and unproctored online tests with questions from a previously used test bank). Finally, students themselves were learning under stressful conditions, including what for many was a new way of learning. Stress has been identified as one of the factors that put students at risk of cheating. Increases in cheating behaviors thatreportedly occurred during the pandemic may not occur under normal online learning circumstances. There is no doubt that the changes to education as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic will have long-lasting effects. In turn, this could result in educators reconsidering how assessment plays a role in academic integrity.

THE CONNECTION BETWEEN ASSESSMENT, INTEGRITY, AND ENGAGEMENT

THE CONNECTION BETWEEN ASSESSMENT, INTEGRITY, AND ENGAGEMENT
Assessment strategies that promote academic integrity also promote a learner-centered approach. There may be more academic misconduct, including plagiarism, in courses where instructors have a teacher-centric transmissionist approach to teaching and assessment (Sutherland-Smith, 2008). Educational approaches that instead promote transformational approaches to teaching (Sutherland-Smith, 2008; Morris, 2016) that are more student-focused have the double benefit of promoting learning and academic integrity simultaneously.

Assessment strategies that promote academic integrity also promote a learner-centered approach. There may be more academic misconduct, including plagiarism, in courses where instructors have a teacher-centric transmissionist approach to teaching and assessment (Sutherland-Smith, 2008). Educational approaches that instead promote transformational approaches to teaching (Sutherland-Smith, 2008; Morris, 2016) that are more student-focused have the double benefit of promoting learning and academic integrity simultaneously.
Learner-centered approaches are linked, in turn, to improved student engagement (Morris, 2016). In an era where institutions systematically monitor and report on student engagement using tools such as the National Survey of Student Engagement (NSSE), it is worth engaging in conversations with individual instructors, as well as program planners, curriculum developers, and administrators, about how to make the links between academic integrity and student engagement more visible.

CONCLUSION

CONCLUSION
I cannot overstress the importance of ethical assessment of student learning. This involves the design and implementation of meaningful and relevant assessments, the inclusion of formative assessment at every level, regular revision of assessments, rejection of premade test banks, and recycling of previous assessments. Engaging students as partners in their own learning is a key aspect of ethical teaching and learning. Advocating for ethical assessment is an ongoing aspect of our professional practice as educators, and one that we must continue to emphasize whenever we have the opportunity.

Advocating for ethical assessment is an ongoing aspect of our professional practice as educators, and one that we must continue to emphasize whenever we have the opportunity.

Self-Plagiarism

Self-Plagiarism
Self-plagiarism is one of the least understood aspects of plagiarism, in both the educational and publication contexts. There are those who believe (vehemently) that there is no such thing as self-plagiarism. Scholars have argued that the term “self-plagiarism” itself is an oxymoron (Broome, 2004) or a misnomer (Thurman et al., 2016), or at least a mislabeling of what has come to be regarded as unethical writing and publication practices (Thurman et al., 2016). Some dissenters argue that one’s ideas and words are one’s own, and that if plagiarism is defined as some kind of theft, then one cannot steal from oneself. That argument fails to consider that there are some circumstances in which onecansteal from oneself, such as insurance fraud and embezzlement (Hexham, 2005). We need to be clear that when we talk about self-plagiarism, we are not talking about stealing from oneself, but rather deceiving those who give us credit for our work. In this chapter, I address this poorly understood phenomenon, focusing on how educators can help students focus on demonstrating their learning as they progress through various academic courses.

There are those who believe (vehemently) that there is no such thing as self-plagiarism. Scholars have argued that the term “self-plagiarism” itself is an oxymoron (Broome, 2004) or a misnomer (Thurman et al., 2016), or at least a mislabeling of what has come to be regarded as unethical writing and publication practices (Thurman et al., 2016). Some dissenters argue that one’s ideas and words are one’s own, and that if plagiarism is defined as some kind of theft, then one cannot steal from oneself. That argument fails to consider that there are some circumstances in which one
can
steal from oneself, such as insurance fraud and embezzlement (Hexham, 2005). We need to be clear that when we talk about self-plagiarism, we are not talking about stealing from oneself, but rather deceiving those who give us credit for our work. In this chapter, I address this poorly understood phenomenon, focusing on how educators can help students focus on demonstrating their learning as they progress through various academic courses.
After witnessing some heated and unrelenting debate between professors who had opposing views on how self-plagiarism should be viewed and addressed among graduate students, a colleague and I undertook an inquiry into how self-plagiarism was defined and understood in our discipline of social sciences (Eaton & Crossman, 2018). We wanted to put an end to the acrimony by presenting an evidence-based argument, or at the very least, by engaging in a discussion of evidence from scholarly sources.In this chapter, I expand on that work, offering further discussion about how to tackle this topic in higher education contexts.

After witnessing some heated and unrelenting debate between professors who had opposing views on how self-plagiarism should be viewed and addressed among graduate students, a colleague and I undertook an inquiry into how self-plagiarism was defined and understood in our discipline of social sciences (Eaton & Crossman, 2018). We wanted to put an end to the acrimony by presenting an evidence-based argument, or at the very least, by engaging in a discussion of evidence from scholarly sources.
In this chapter, I expand on that work, offering further discussion about how to tackle this topic in higher education contexts.
Of course, the irony is not lost on me that critics could claim that I am recycling previously published work on the very topic that I am exploring in this chapter. Let me clarify that I am notreplicatingprevious work; I am expanding on it. (That is one of the ways to avoid self-plagiarism, by the way.) I have also endeavored to model what good referencing and citation can look like as you expand on previous work.

SELF-PLAGIARISM IN ACADEMIC PUBLISHING

SELF-PLAGIARISM IN ACADEMIC PUBLISHING
Discussing self-plagiarism in academic publishing is relevant because the ideas that have been adopted in scholarly circles have spilled over into the classroom, creating even more confusion and vitriolic debate. In general, there is little guidance available on how to understand and prevent self-plagiarism among students and novice researchers (Eaton & Crossman, 2018). However, in the study I conducted with my colleague, Dr. Katherine (Katie) Crossman, we found thousands of entries in the scholarly literature, dating as far back as the 1960s.

Discussing self-plagiarism in academic publishing is relevant because the ideas that have been adopted in scholarly circles have spilled over into the classroom, creating even more confusion and vitriolic debate. In general, there is little guidance available on how to understand and prevent self-plagiarism among students and novice researchers (Eaton & Crossman, 2018). However, in the study I conducted with my colleague, Dr. Katherine (Katie) Crossman, we found thousands of entries in the scholarly literature, dating as far back as the 1960s.
Self-plagiarism is also referred to as “duplicate,” “dual,” or “redundant” publication (Baggs, 2008; Kassirer & Angell, 1995; Langdon-Neuner, 2008; Roig, 2005, 2008), but these terms apply mainly to advanced scholars who publish their work in more than one journal. In academic circles, a standard of ethical publication practice has developed, saying that an author is allowed to receive credit for her or his workonce. Julia Cowell (2017) points out that although “authors feel ownership of their own work, publication ethics dictate that manuscripts are original and duplication of previously published work is not allowed” (p. 7). In other words, don’t double-dip. Of course, it is not as simple as that, but that is the basic premise.

Self-plagiarism is also referred to as “duplicate,” “dual,” or “redundant” publication (Baggs, 2008; Kassirer & Angell, 1995; Langdon-Neuner, 2008; Roig, 2005, 2008), but these terms apply mainly to advanced scholars who publish their work in more than one journal. In academic circles, a standard of ethical publication practice has developed, saying that an author is allowed to receive credit for her or his work
once
. Julia Cowell (2017) points out that although “authors feel ownership of their own work, publication ethics dictate that manuscripts are original and duplication of previously published work is not allowed” (p. 7). In other words, don’t double-dip. Of course, it is not as simple as that, but that is the basic premise.
A brief statement on copyright is relevant there. Although copyright is related to plagiarism, the two should not be confused. Authors could be violating the copyright agreements that they have made with publishers if they republish their work elsewhere. Although open-access journals are becoming more prevalent, many journals are still owned and operated by commercial publishers who require authors to agree to transfer copyright to them as part of the publication process. In such cases, the authors then forfeit their right to reproduce the published work, either in part or in whole, depending on the terms of the agreement, even when the ideas, words, and results are their own. A good number of scholars are eager to sign publication agreements with journals prior to their work being released, only to become resentful postpublication because they realizethat they have forfeited their freedom to reproduce their work as they please. This is when ideology and reality collide.

In such cases, the authors then forfeit their right to reproduce the published work, either in part or in whole, depending on the terms of the agreement, even when the ideas, words, and results are their own. A good number of scholars are eager to sign publication agreements with journals prior to their work being released, only to become resentful postpublication because they realize
that they have forfeited their freedom to reproduce their work as they please. This is when ideology and reality collide.
A deep discussion of the ideological aspects of copyright is beyond the scope of this book, but suffice it to say that it is a reality of academic publishing that remains contentious and ongoing. When it comes to self-plagiarism, authors are at risk of violating commercial publishing contracts they may have made if they reproduce their work without determining the details of how to do so according to the terms of those agreements.

A deep discussion of the ideological aspects of copyright is beyond the scope of this book, but suffice it to say that it is a reality of academic publishing that remains contentious and ongoing. When it comes to self-plagiarism, authors are at risk of violating commercial publishing contracts they may have made if they reproduce their work without determining the details of how to do so according to the terms of those agreements.
One reason why this topic has become so prominent in academic publishing could be due to the “publish or perish” culture of higher education (Brochard, 2004; Moosa, 2018; Noè& Batten, 2006). Within such a culture, there is an erroneous assumption that the number of one’s publications is an indication of the quality of one’s scholarship. One journal editor talks about scholars who try to game the system, as if “being published were a sports competition in which the number of medals obtained indicates the level of excellence” (Brochard, 2004, p. 1857). Brochard (2004) asserts that “quality, which requires integrity, is far more fundamental to science than quantity” (p. 1858). It is easy for someone who has permanent employment or tenure to make such a declaration. The reality is that for individuals with precarious employment or those who are at the start of their careers, their experiences exist in opposition to such ideals. In academia, it is essential for researchers to demonstrate that they are capable of producing publications as a means of demonstrating their worth. (I say this as a description of the system, not an endorsement of it.) The need to demonstrate one’s publication productivity is due in part to metrics or key performance indicators that are increasingly applied to institutions by the governments that fund them, or other bodies who rank institutions. Such ranking results in conclusions, however accurate or erroneous, that some institutions are of higher or lesser caliber than others.

The reality is that for individuals with precarious employment or those who are at the start of their careers, their experiences exist in opposition to such ideals. In academia, it is essential for researchers to demonstrate that they are capable of producing publications as a means of demonstrating their worth. (I say this as a description of the system, not an endorsement of it.) The need to demonstrate one’s publication productivity is due in part to metrics or key performance indicators that are increasingly applied to institutions by the governments that fund them, or other bodies who rank institutions. Such ranking results in conclusions, however accurate or erroneous, that some institutions are of higher or lesser caliber than others.
One common metric of institutional success is the number of scientific publications published by academic staff in a given year. So the “publish or perish” culture is propagated by systemic approaches about what counts as success. In turn, this affects institutional reputation and funding. At the individual level, the number of publications listed on a scholar’s curriculum vitae can affect the likelihood of getting hired or promoted, as well as being considered suitable for tenure or worthy of research grants (Moosa, 2018).

One common metric of institutional success is the number of scientific publications published by academic staff in a given year. So the “publish or perish” culture is propagated by systemic approaches about what counts as success. In turn, this affects institutional reputation and funding. At the individual level, the number of publications listed on a scholar’s curriculum vitae can affect the likelihood of getting hired or promoted, as well as being considered suitable for tenure or worthy of research grants (Moosa, 2018).
On a personal note, I spent many years as a contingent, part-time faculty member (also known as “adjuncts,” “sessionals,” or “lecturers,” depending on the institution). During those years, I would teach as many courses as I was offered, supplementing my income by teaching additional noncredit continuing education classes, working as a research assistant, and doing independent freelance and consulting work. It was a patchwork career thatlasted more than twenty years. More than one pragmatic mentor commented to me that if I aspired to a full-time role in academia, I would be wise to increase the number of publications under my belt. By the time I was hired into a full-time faculty position, I had published six articles in peer-reviewed journals, along with a number of book chapters, peer-reviewed conference proceedings, and a variety of other non-peer-reviewed publications. One colleague confided in me that the number of publications I had listed on my curriculum vitae at the time I was hired was really “a minimum” to be considered for a full-time faculty job. Whether that person was correct could be debated, but it is worth considering that such viewpoints remain pervasive in academia.
