“Salami Slicing”

“Salami Slicing”
As Dr. Crossman and I undertook our study into self-plagiarism, we found a related phenomenon known as “salami slicing” (Eaton & Crossman, 2018). It is also called “fragmented” and “piecemeal” publication (Baggs, 2008; Kassirer & Angell, 1995; Langdon-Neuner, 2008; Roig, 2005, 2008). It refers to the practice of breaking a data set into multiple chunks and then publishing separate articles on each smaller data set (Hoit, 2007; Kassirer & Angell, 1995; Roig, 2005). The phenomenon started to be vigorously discussed in scholarly circles in the 1980s (Broad, 1981), and it remains contentious today. Some assert that the way in which we do research has changed, and today there may be circumstances in which publishing multiple articles from the same study could be acceptable (Baggs, 2008; Owen, 2004). Others disagree, contending that it is still preferable to avoid this practice (Hoit, 2007; Fonseca, 2013).

As Dr. Crossman and I undertook our study into self-plagiarism, we found a related phenomenon known as “salami slicing” (Eaton & Crossman, 2018). It is also called “fragmented” and “piecemeal” publication (Baggs, 2008; Kassirer & Angell, 1995; Langdon-Neuner, 2008; Roig, 2005, 2008). It refers to the practice of breaking a data set into multiple chunks and then publishing separate articles on each smaller data set (Hoit, 2007; Kassirer & Angell, 1995; Roig, 2005). The phenomenon started to be vigorously discussed in scholarly circles in the 1980s (Broad, 1981), and it remains contentious today. Some assert that the way in which we do research has changed, and today there may be circumstances in which publishing multiple articles from the same study could be acceptable (Baggs, 2008; Owen, 2004). Others disagree, contending that it is still preferable to avoid this practice (Hoit, 2007; Fonseca, 2013).
The idea of not reproducing one’s own work in academic publications can be tricky when researchers write more than one paper from the same data set. If researchers report on smaller chunks of their results in different papers, they are caught in an ethical loop in which they are required to state their methods in each paper they write; but in doing so, they can be accused of self-plagiarism (Thurman et al., 2016). This can be exacerbated if journal editors use text-matching software to screen submitted manuscripts. The software can identify exact text matches in a matter of moments, alerting editors to work that has been replicated, either by lifting it from others or from one’s own previous work. This can result in an immediate and nonnegotiable rejection of the manuscript. Even though we ask educators to engage in a critical analysis of originality reports generated by text-matching software, we know that they do not always do that, and neither do journal editors who have such software at their disposal.

The software can identify exact text matches in a matter of moments, alerting editors to work that has been replicated, either by lifting it from others or from one’s own previous work. This can result in an immediate and nonnegotiable rejection of the manuscript. Even though we ask educators to engage in a critical analysis of originality reports generated by text-matching software, we know that they do not always do that, and neither do journal editors who have such software at their disposal.
In some cases, scholars are encouraged by their supervisors and administrators, to get as many articles as possible out of a single study. This mandate can be directly at odds with what journal editors and publishers would like to see the opposite happen. These tensions seem to be increasing and point to larger systemic issues that the individual academic cannot solve alone.

In some cases, scholars are encouraged by their supervisors and administrators, to get as many articles as possible out of a single study. This mandate can be directly at odds with what journal editors and publishers would like to see the opposite happen. These tensions seem to be increasing and point to larger systemic issues that the individual academic cannot solve alone.
Over a decade ago, Bretag and Mahmud (2009) called for “agreement and guidelines which clearly differentiate between legitimate textual re-use and inappropriate textual re-use … ‘self-plagiarism’ ” (p. 194). Despite the call for clarity and guidelines for publishers and academic authors, there still seems to be more debate than agreement around the topic in academic publishing communities. So far as I have been able to determine, although individual journals or publishers may state their expectations, the academic publishing community as a whole continues to struggle with what is ethical and why when it comes to re-presenting one’s own work.

SELF-PLAGIARISM IN STUDENT WORK

SELF-PLAGIARISM IN STUDENT WORK
As we undertook our inquiry into self-plagiarism, it became obvious to us that the topic had been thoroughly discussed in literature relating to academic publishing, even if a good chunk of that discussion came in the form of editorials and letters to the editor, with less empirical research on the topic than we had anticipated (Eaton & Crossman, 2018). Vigorous debate about the topic remains within the realm of scientific and scholarly publishing.

As we undertook our inquiry into self-plagiarism, it became obvious to us that the topic had been thoroughly discussed in literature relating to academic publishing, even if a good chunk of that discussion came in the form of editorials and letters to the editor, with less empirical research on the topic than we had anticipated (Eaton & Crossman, 2018). Vigorous debate about the topic remains within the realm of scientific and scholarly publishing.
In addition to research literature, we examined institutional academic misconduct regulations and policy documents. Having said that, the institutional regulations contained a clear definition: self-plagiarism occurred when a student submitted the same work to more than one course for course credit without the knowledge or permission of both instructors (Eaton & Crossman, 2018). We realized that this neat and tidy definition might work in cases where an undergraduate student submitted the same paper to two different professors in different courses, without changing the content at all. There was an implicit value assumption in the academic regulations that could be interpreted such that students were responsible for demonstrating their learning in new ways with each course they took. When students submit the same paper for more than one course without the knowledge of their professors, they are not demonstrating that they have learned anything new.

In addition to research literature, we examined institutional academic misconduct regulations and policy documents. Having said that, the institutional regulations contained a clear definition: self-plagiarism occurred when a student submitted the same work to more than one course for course credit without the knowledge or permission of both instructors (Eaton & Crossman, 2018). We realized that this neat and tidy definition might work in cases where an undergraduate student submitted the same paper to two different professors in different courses, without changing the content at all. There was an implicit value assumption in the academic regulations that could be interpreted such that students were responsible for demonstrating their learning in new ways with each course they took. When students submit the same paper for more than one course without the knowledge of their professors, they are not demonstrating that they have learned anything new.
Policy development, interpretation, implementation, and analysis constitute values-laden and subjective work (Ozga, 1999). When it comes to how self-plagiarism in particular is articulated and addressed in institutionalpolicy, subjectivity and values assumptions are deeply embedded. There can be an unstated assumption that students who submit the same work for more than one course may be lazy, uninterested in the subject matter, or deceitful. This assumption is rarely, if ever, articulated explicitly in institutional policy documents, but the implication can be ingrained, even if it is subtle.

Teaching and Learning Perspectives

Teaching and Learning Perspectives
The underlying values assumptions in academic misconduct policy can be especially problematic if teaching and learning support, in terms of how to help students understand what is expected and how to act ethically, is not provided. In terms of self-plagiarism, even when we found specific references to it in institutional policy, we uncovered little supporting documentation that taught students how to reference, incorporate, or adapt their own work in ethical ways. Institutional policies relating to self-plagiarism do little to help students and educators understand how students can scaffold learning from one course to the next, while still maintaining academic integrity standards.

In terms of self-plagiarism, even when we found specific references to it in institutional policy, we uncovered little supporting documentation that taught students how to reference, incorporate, or adapt their own work in ethical ways. Institutional policies relating to self-plagiarism do little to help students and educators understand how students can scaffold learning from one course to the next, while still maintaining academic integrity standards.
Similarly, I have heard students complain that if professors in different courses require them to do assignments that are basically the same in both courses, then why not submit the same paper for both courses? This question is a critique about how courses and programs are organized and monitored. It also speaks to the possible lack of communication between professors about the subject matter that they are covering and the kinds of assignments that they give to students. Students can feel frustrated when they take courses where the overlap is so obvious that they do not feel they are learning anything new. This can be exacerbated when the courses are required, and students do not have the option of dropping the course or changing courses if they want to meet certain program requirements. We know that when students feel an assignment is pointless, they are more likely to cheat (McCabe, 1992). What could be more pointless than having to do essentially the same assignment for two different courses?

This can be exacerbated when the courses are required, and students do not have the option of dropping the course or changing courses if they want to meet certain program requirements. We know that when students feel an assignment is pointless, they are more likely to cheat (McCabe, 1992). What could be more pointless than having to do essentially the same assignment for two different courses?
Although there may be values-based assumptions embedded in policy, there are also values-based assumptions about teaching and learning. Students should be able to expect that they will learn new things and be challenged in new ways with each course they take. This means that there must be communication between instructors who teach similar courses, and also between those who manage programs and those who teach them, in order to ensure the learning objectives for each course might be related, but not exactly the same. Further, there should not be so much overlap between the content of courses that it causes students to feel frustrated ordisengaged. Students need practical coaching on how to scaffold their learning from one course to the next without fear that they will be accused of self-plagiarism. It is important that institutional policies are supported with pragmatic teaching and learning resources that focus on students’ learning in productive and positive ways.

Teaching the Art of Acknowledgment

Teaching the Art of Acknowledgment
One simple strategy that educators can use with undergraduate students is to teach them how to include a brief acknowledgment at the end of their papers to show how they are scaffolding learning from previous courses. Often, it is not until graduate school, when students are preparing their theses, that they are introduced to the practice of writing acknowledgments. Even then, writing acknowledgments is often an afterthought—something dashed off quickly at the end of a project, without much guidance about how to do it. For some, it is an exercise in anxiety (Wiley, 2020).

One simple strategy that educators can use with undergraduate students is to teach them how to include a brief acknowledgment at the end of their papers to show how they are scaffolding learning from previous courses. Often, it is not until graduate school, when students are preparing their theses, that they are introduced to the practice of writing acknowledgments. Even then, writing acknowledgments is often an afterthought—something dashed off quickly at the end of a project, without much guidance about how to do it. For some, it is an exercise in anxiety (Wiley, 2020).
There is no reason why we cannot enculturate students much earlier in their schooling (in their undergraduate program, or even in secondary school) in the practices of acknowledging those who have had a strong and positive influence on their learning. This does not have to be elaborate or belabored. Instead, it can be straightforward and simple. For example: “I would like to thank Professor Baker, who taught me English 201: Overview of American Literature. I have scaffolded what I learned from her course into this paper on Thoreau’s poetry.” In this way, the student is not only avoiding self-plagiarism, he or she is demonstrating metacognitive awareness of the learning process, as well as showing appreciation to a professor who had a strong and positive influence on this person.

Graduate Education

Graduate Education
Even when institutional policies address the notion of self-plagiarism, the focus is often on not resubmitting work done in one course for another course without the knowledge or permission of the professors. Such clear policies can work well in undergraduate education, but less so in graduate education, where learning can include coursework, but it also involves a great deal of more independent or loosely guided learning. In situations like this, the lines between self-plagiarism and scaffolding one’s own learning become less clear. Many of the inquiries that I receive about self-plagiarism are from graduate students who are fearful of being accused of or found responsible for self-plagiarism if they reuse previous material in their final research report (e.g., a capstone paper, thesis, or dissertation).This material could have been generated in any number of contexts, including but not limited to the following:

Such clear policies can work well in undergraduate education, but less so in graduate education, where learning can include coursework, but it also involves a great deal of more independent or loosely guided learning. In situations like this, the lines between self-plagiarism and scaffolding one’s own learning become less clear. Many of the inquiries that I receive about self-plagiarism are from graduate students who are fearful of being accused of or found responsible for self-plagiarism if they reuse previous material in their final research report (e.g., a capstone paper, thesis, or dissertation).
This material could have been generated in any number of contexts, including but not limited to the following:
- Course papers

- Research proposals

- Candidacy or comprehensive exam papers

- Graduate symposia or colloquia

Course papers
Research proposals
Candidacy or comprehensive exam papers
Graduate symposia or colloquia
What I typically tell graduate students and their supervisors is that if there is evidence of learning, then it is doubtful that there is self-plagiarism. I say “doubtful” because under certain circumstances, there could be self-plagiarism, but the first line of questioning should be, as Tricia Bertram Gallant (2008) has guided us: is there evidence of learning? If there is, then keep the focus there and encourage deepening and broadening of that learning.

Considerations for the Manuscript-Based Thesis

Considerations for the Manuscript-Based Thesis
The topic of self-plagiarism is particularly relevant to graduate students undertaking a manuscript-based thesis or dissertation. It is also called “PhD by publication” (Brien, 2008; Draper, 2019; Freeman, 2018; O’Keeffe, 2020), “publication-based thesis (PBT)” (Sharmini et al., 2015, p. 89), or “thesis by publication (TBP)” (Merga, 2015, p. 291). This approach to graduate research requires the student to either publish, or at least submit for publication, chapters or sections of a thesis prior to defending it, preferably in peer-reviewed journals.

The topic of self-plagiarism is particularly relevant to graduate students undertaking a manuscript-based thesis or dissertation. It is also called “PhD by publication” (Brien, 2008; Draper, 2019; Freeman, 2018; O’Keeffe, 2020), “publication-based thesis (PBT)” (Sharmini et al., 2015, p. 89), or “thesis by publication (TBP)” (Merga, 2015, p. 291). This approach to graduate research requires the student to either publish, or at least submit for publication, chapters or sections of a thesis prior to defending it, preferably in peer-reviewed journals.
Although this style of thesis has been common in some European countries for decades, particularly in the science and medical fields, it has begun to gain popularity in other countries in recent decades, concomitant with the rise of performance-based research metrics (Brien, 2008; Draper, 2019; Freeman, 2018; O’Keeffe, 2020). Although degree qualifications frameworks and standards exist in many countries about the requirements needed to earn a graduate degree, there remains a lack of clarity and consistency across institutions about what is expected in a manuscript-based thesis (Brien, 2018; Merga, 2015).

Although this style of thesis has been common in some European countries for decades, particularly in the science and medical fields, it has begun to gain popularity in other countries in recent decades, concomitant with the rise of performance-based research metrics (Brien, 2008; Draper, 2019; Freeman, 2018; O’Keeffe, 2020). Although degree qualifications frameworks and standards exist in many countries about the requirements needed to earn a graduate degree, there remains a lack of clarity and consistency across institutions about what is expected in a manuscript-based thesis (Brien, 2018; Merga, 2015).
A manuscript-based thesis can provide benefits to emerging scholars because it allows them to establish a publication record and a reputation in their chosen field (Brien, 2008; Freeman, 2018). There is also considerable emphasis placed on students publishing their work in “well-regarded, peer-reviewed journals” (Merga, 2015, p. 291). It has been suggested that examiners regard a thesis more highly if sections of it have been published in highly reputable journals prior to the student’s defense (Merga, 2015;Sharmini et al., 2015). As such, it has not been lost on scholars that this approach to thesis-writing introduces novice scholars into the “publish or perish” culture even earlier in their careers (Brien, 2008), embedding them early into the neoliberal higher educational system in which they aspire to work (O’Keeffe, 2020).

A manuscript-based thesis can provide benefits to emerging scholars because it allows them to establish a publication record and a reputation in their chosen field (Brien, 2008; Freeman, 2018). There is also considerable emphasis placed on students publishing their work in “well-regarded, peer-reviewed journals” (Merga, 2015, p. 291). It has been suggested that examiners regard a thesis more highly if sections of it have been published in highly reputable journals prior to the student’s defense (Merga, 2015;
Sharmini et al., 2015). As such, it has not been lost on scholars that this approach to thesis-writing introduces novice scholars into the “publish or perish” culture even earlier in their careers (Brien, 2008), embedding them early into the neoliberal higher educational system in which they aspire to work (O’Keeffe, 2020).
There is scant guidance available for students, supervisors, or graduate examiners about how to handle self-plagiarism in a manuscript-based thesis. Brien (2008) has pointed out that some Australian universities “accept previously published work (including works that are not academic or scholarly)” (p. 8) as contributions toward the fulfillment of a degree. It is reasonable to expect that that practice is not limited to Australia, or if it is, then it will not be for much longer. There has also been discussion in the literature about how to evaluate an individual graduate student’s work when the publications are coauthored with others, and in some cases, a team of others (Shamini, 2015). It can be difficult, if not impossible, to understand where the individual student’s contributions begin and end because in some cases, the entire project was a collaborative effort from a particular research team or lab. This presents complexities for supervisors, examiners, and others who advise students on matters relating to writing, plagiarism, and academic integrity in general.

Brien (2008) has pointed out that some Australian universities “accept previously published work (including works that are not academic or scholarly)” (p. 8) as contributions toward the fulfillment of a degree. It is reasonable to expect that that practice is not limited to Australia, or if it is, then it will not be for much longer. There has also been discussion in the literature about how to evaluate an individual graduate student’s work when the publications are coauthored with others, and in some cases, a team of others (Shamini, 2015). It can be difficult, if not impossible, to understand where the individual student’s contributions begin and end because in some cases, the entire project was a collaborative effort from a particular research team or lab. This presents complexities for supervisors, examiners, and others who advise students on matters relating to writing, plagiarism, and academic integrity in general.
As yet, there are no clear guidelines for manuscript-based theses, as there are for undergraduate course papers, in defining what counts as self-plagiarism. For that reason, it is advisable for students and their supervisors to engage in ongoing and open conversations about what is acceptable and what is not. Not only is it important to have conversations, but it is also important to have the expectations written so that in the case of a dispute, the parties involved have a record of what was agreed upon.

CONCLUSIONS

CONCLUSIONS
Although there may be commonalities in how self-plagiarism is understood in publishing and educational contexts insofar as double-dipping can be considered unethical, it is important for educators and administrators not to conflate the conventions of academic publishing with those of higher education. Fundamentally, students in higher education are there to learn. The process of learning is neither simple nor linear. It is imperative for educators to offer students an opportunity to scaffold their learning in an environment that is free from the fear of being punished or accused of self-plagiarism. It is equally important for educators not to pass along to students systemic injustices that exist in the academic publishing and performance-ranking worlds. If anything, it is incumbent upon those who work in higher education to improve the system from within, in orderto ensure that it is just and fair for the students first and foremost, but also for the next generation of scholars and educators.

It is equally important for educators not to pass along to students systemic injustices that exist in the academic publishing and performance-ranking worlds. to ensure that it is just and fair for the students first and foremost, but also for the next generation of scholars and educators.

Academic File Sharing: Sharing Is Caring, and Other Myths

Academic File Sharing: Sharing Is Caring, and Other Myths
File sharing, also called “file swapping” (Rogerson, 2014), is not new, but it has changed since the dawn of the Internet. It is one of the student behaviors that most aggravates educators, policymakers, and academic integrity scholars. This chapter is divided into three main sections. I begin by exploring some of the conceptual underpinnings of file sharing through the lens of communications theory, and then I discuss how and why students share files, and I finally conclude with a discussion of what we, as educators, scholars, and policymakers, can do about file sharing in ways that focus on ethical student learning.

File sharing, also called “file swapping” (Rogerson, 2014), is not new, but it has changed since the dawn of the Internet. It is one of the student behaviors that most aggravates educators, policymakers, and academic integrity scholars. This chapter is divided into three main sections. I begin by exploring some of the conceptual underpinnings of file sharing through the lens of communications theory, and then I discuss how and why students share files, and I finally conclude with a discussion of what we, as educators, scholars, and policymakers, can do about file sharing in ways that focus on ethical student learning.
UNDERSTANDING COMMUNICATION SYSTEMS

UNDERSTANDING COMMUNICATION SYSTEMS
There are many ways that students, as well as teachers, share content. Today, the majority of sharing happens with digital files, so I address this topic from that perspective. There are a variety of reasons why students share files. Some want to see what an example of excellent work looks like so they can imitate it. Others will plagiarize or copy test answers. Some share their own work with others because they feel obligated to do so. There is no single reason why students share academic work. We can draw from classic and modern communication theory and models to understand how academic file-sharing works (Doyle, 2016; Fawkes & Gregory, 2001; Rubin & Windahl, 1986).

There are many ways that students, as well as teachers, share content. Today, the majority of sharing happens with digital files, so I address this topic from that perspective. There are a variety of reasons why students share files. Some want to see what an example of excellent work looks like so they can imitate it. Others will plagiarize or copy test answers. Some share their own work with others because they feel obligated to do so. There is no single reason why students share academic work. We can draw from classic and modern communication theory and models to understand how academic file-sharing works (Doyle, 2016; Fawkes & Gregory, 2001; Rubin & Windahl, 1986).
Although the practice of students sharing academic work on a small individual scale has likely existed for hundreds of years, the first documented evidence we have of intentional systematic sharing among groups of students can be traced to the twentieth century. This was likely facilitated and amplified by technologies such as the photocopier (O’Connell, 2016), followed by the Internet (Kleinrock, 2019; Morrison, 2009), which were developed in that century. In turn, this led to the massive, web-based file sharing that perplexes and frustrates twenty-first-century educators. Looking at the issue from another perspective, one of the most famous early file-sharing sites, Napster, began operating in 1999 (Cenite et al., 2009; Harris, 2019). Therefore, the majority of today’s students have never known a worldwithoutfile sharing. Although there are still students born before 1999 who take classes today, it is not a matter so much of when individuals were born as the sharing culture in which they were raised (Blum, 2009). It also means there is not a professor working today who could reasonably claim to be unaware of the existence of file sharing.

file sharing. It also means there is not a professor working today who could reasonably claim to be unaware of the existence of file sharing.
Around the same time as the original iteration of Napster developed, online communities designed specifically for the sharing of academic work and peer help began to emerge (McCollum, 1996; Vassileva, 1997; Vassileva & Deters, 2001; Vassileva et al., 2004; Wang & Vassileva, 2004). Originally designed as altruistic closed communities “to assist learners as they engage in problem-solving activities” (Vassileva & Deters, 2001, p. 1), they have evolved into a large, commercial industry. Unlike the original iteration of Napster, which was shut down in 2001 for copyright infringement, academic file-sharing sites have proliferated.

Models of Communication Systems

Models of Communication Systems
There are many models of communications systems. I have kept my treatment of this subject brief and simplified here, to provide just enough of an overview of how some of these systems apply to student file sharing (Doyle, 2016; Fawkes & Gregory, 2001). These systems are broadly classified as being transmissionist in nature (e.g., one-to-one or one-to-many) or networked communities (e.g., many-to-many). I briefly explain each system and then elaborate further in the next section with more examples.

There are many models of communications systems. I have kept my treatment of this subject brief and simplified here, to provide just enough of an overview of how some of these systems apply to student file sharing (Doyle, 2016; Fawkes & Gregory, 2001). These systems are broadly classified as being transmissionist in nature (e.g., one-to-one or one-to-many) or networked communities (e.g., many-to-many). I briefly explain each system and then elaborate further in the next section with more examples.
- One-to-one:This is the simplest communication system, in which one person communicates directly with another. The communication starts at a single point of origin and ends at another.

- One-to-many:In this system, one person communicates with many others. The communication starts at a single point of origin, but it is broadcast to numerous others.

- Many-to-many (networked):Unlike the transmissionist models described in this list, in many-to-many communication, individuals exchange ideas and share content, including academic work, on a network. In a networked environment, individuals can be both transmitters and receivers of information. Users can further extend this sharing beyond a particular network by sharing content to other networks. Many-to-many networks might be moderated or unmoderated, and users might be known to one another or be anonymous.

One-to-one:
This is the simplest communication system, in which one person communicates directly with another. The communication starts at a single point of origin and ends at another.
One-to-many:
In this system, one person communicates with many others. The communication starts at a single point of origin, but it is broadcast to numerous others.
Many-to-many (networked):
Unlike the transmissionist models described in this list, in many-to-many communication, individuals exchange ideas and share content, including academic work, on a network. In a networked environment, individuals can be both transmitters and receivers of information. Users can further extend this sharing beyond a particular network by sharing content to other networks. Many-to-many networks might be moderated or unmoderated, and users might be known to one another or be anonymous.
For the purposes of academic file sharing, we can consider two types of networked communities: open and closed. An example of a closed network would be a course housed within a learning management system (LMS) that is accessible only to students who have paid to take the course, along with their instructors and the various technical and administrative actors who work behind the scenes to support the course. Typically, such closed networked environments are subject to intensive institutional oversight and activities may be bound by institutional policies and procedures. Not only are users known to one another, their activities can be (and often are) closely monitored.

For the purposes of academic file sharing, we can consider two types of networked communities: open and closed. An example of a closed network would be a course housed within a learning management system (LMS) that is accessible only to students who have paid to take the course, along with their instructors and the various technical and administrative actors who work behind the scenes to support the course. Typically, such closed networked environments are subject to intensive institutional oversight and activities may be bound by institutional policies and procedures. Not only are users known to one another, their activities can be (and often are) closely monitored.
In an open many-to-many network, such as commercial academic file-sharing sites, there can be a massive number of points of origin and many receivers. These networks are populated by heterogenous and autonomous users who act as individual agents (Wang & Vassileva, 2004, p. 1). Users in open, many-to-many networking environments are more likely to be anonymous and operate outside the boundaries of an educational institution. In fact, they may purposefully circumvent institutional supports in favor of engaging in an anonymous online community, where they feel free to operate outside the confines of institutional regulations.

TYPES OF FILE SHARING

TYPES OF FILE SHARING
Now that I have addressed some of the basic models of communication systems, I discuss the complexities of how, when, and why people engage in academic file sharing. Depending on the context, some types of file sharing are considered more acceptable than others; therefore, I offer concrete examples of how academic content is shared, highlighting some possible ethical complexities.

Now that I have addressed some of the basic models of communication systems, I discuss the complexities of how, when, and why people engage in academic file sharing. Depending on the context, some types of file sharing are considered more acceptable than others; therefore, I offer concrete examples of how academic content is shared, highlighting some possible ethical complexities.
Student-to-Student Sharing (One-to-One)

Student-to-Student Sharing (One-to-One)
One student taking notes for a peer who is absent from class due to illness and then passing those notes along to the classmate is a classic andbenevolent example of one-to-one content sharing. Note taking for a friend is an act that many of us have engaged in during our schooling. Most people would agree that a student taking notes for a peer who is ill is not only acceptable, but commendable.

One student taking notes for a peer who is absent from class due to illness and then passing those notes along to the classmate is a classic and
benevolent example of one-to-one content sharing. Note taking for a friend is an act that many of us have engaged in during our schooling. Most people would agree that a student taking notes for a peer who is ill is not only acceptable, but commendable.
A second and more deceptive example would be a student e-mailing a copy of her paper from a course she took two years ago to another student taking the same course today, so that the latter can make minor modifications, such as substituting their own name and course information for that of the person who actually wrote the paper, and then submitting it as their own academic work. In terms of academic misconduct, this would be considered plagiarism at many schools, with both parties being responsible to some degree. Passing along one’s own work so that someone else can pass it off as their own is problematic. This type of situation becomes more complex if the person supplying the work has already graduated, because most educational institutions lack any kind of policy to deal with alumni who enable academic misconduct unless the act is very egregious, such as having plagiarized a thesis. From these scenarios, one can see how academic content-sharing can be viewed as altruistic in certain situations but unethical in others.

Instructor-Initiated File Sharing (One-to-Many)

Instructor-Initiated File Sharing (One-to-Many)
An altruistic example of one-to-many academic content sharing would be a teacher sharing work from a previous student with those they teach in subsequent semesters. Ethical instructors would ask students for their permission before sharing their work with others. There are various possible scenarios that might play out when an instructor decides to share one student’s work with other students. One of these is when a teacher redacts identifying information from the student paper or asks the student to provide a deidentified copy for sharing purposes. Other times, they share the work intact, complete with the student’s identifying information. In some cases, instructors share examples of papers from any student who has given permission, regardless of the grade of the paper. More common, though, is an instructor sharing the work as an exemplar of excellence.

An altruistic example of one-to-many academic content sharing would be a teacher sharing work from a previous student with those they teach in subsequent semesters. Ethical instructors would ask students for their permission before sharing their work with others. There are various possible scenarios that might play out when an instructor decides to share one student’s work with other students. One of these is when a teacher redacts identifying information from the student paper or asks the student to provide a deidentified copy for sharing purposes. Other times, they share the work intact, complete with the student’s identifying information. In some cases, instructors share examples of papers from any student who has given permission, regardless of the grade of the paper. More common, though, is an instructor sharing the work as an exemplar of excellence.
Provided that a student has consented to their work being used as a model and understands how and with whom it will be shared, then this type of sharing is not unethical, in theory. This method of sharing starts from a position of trust. The students trust the instructor to share their work with others according to the terms agreed upon. In turn, the teacher trusts the next cohort of students to use the shared academic work in an ethical way. The teacher might also assume that since they graded the first paper and will also grade subsequent papers, the chances of plagiarism aretheoretically slim to none, as the original source material has been distributed by the individual who is in charge of grading the incoming papers.

theoretically slim to none, as the original source material has been distributed by the individual who is in charge of grading the incoming papers.
There is an assumption that instructor-initiated file sharing occurs in a closed system, in which all participants act ethically. If you were to ask many faculty members who engage in this practice if they were enabling inappropriate file sharing, they might balk at the idea, citing their attitude of care and generosity and sharing with consent. Moreover, they might see this as being responsive to students’ requests and an effective pedagogical practice. They might argue that sharing examples of past work can provide students with a concrete example of what excellence looks like. Combined with a rubric or other clearly defined assessment criteria, students can have a better idea of what is expected of them. All of this sounds good—in theory.

There is an assumption that instructor-initiated file sharing occurs in a closed system, in which all participants act ethically. If you were to ask many faculty members who engage in this practice if they were enabling inappropriate file sharing, they might balk at the idea, citing their attitude of care and generosity and sharing with consent. Moreover, they might see this as being responsive to students’ requests and an effective pedagogical practice. They might argue that sharing examples of past work can provide students with a concrete example of what excellence looks like. Combined with a rubric or other clearly defined assessment criteria, students can have a better idea of what is expected of them. All of this sounds good—in theory.
The problem, of course, is that files can be shared beyond the instructor’s own circle of influence. For example, if a student’s paper is later posted to a website designed for many-to-many sharing (e.g., a commercial file-sharing site), it can then be sold to a buyer anywhere in the world unbeknownst to either the original creator or the instructor, then a clear breach of integrity has occurred. The reality is that it might be difficult to prove who broke the trust.

The problem, of course, is that files can be shared beyond the instructor’s own circle of influence. For example, if a student’s paper is later posted to a website designed for many-to-many sharing (e.g., a commercial file-sharing site), it can then be sold to a buyer anywhere in the world unbeknownst to either the original creator or the instructor, then a clear breach of integrity has occurred. The reality is that it might be difficult to prove who broke the trust.
Instructors may be dismayed at the thought of such extended sharing, claiming that it exceeds the boundaries of consent; however, the reality is that once a student’s academic work has been shared in any kind of digital format, it cannot be unshared. Neither instructors nor students can control how digital files are passed from one person or organization to the next. Many sharing communities operate on the basis of trust (Wang & Vassileva, 2004), but it is naive to think that such trust cannot be broken.

Instructor-Enabled Peer-to-Peer File Sharing (Many-to-Many)

Instructor-Enabled Peer-to-Peer File Sharing (Many-to-Many)
In addition to instructors distributing academic work from past students as a model for current students, instructors might facilitate file sharing among members of the same class. Examples of such a model for academic sharing include online forums and discussion boards, such as those that might be self-contained within an LMS. An asynchronous discussion board might be moderated by the course instructor, and students post copies of their own academic work, such as draft papers for peer review or final papers, projects, or posters as part of a digital end-of-term showcase.

In addition to instructors distributing academic work from past students as a model for current students, instructors might facilitate file sharing among members of the same class. Examples of such a model for academic sharing include online forums and discussion boards, such as those that might be self-contained within an LMS. An asynchronous discussion board might be moderated by the course instructor, and students post copies of their own academic work, such as draft papers for peer review or final papers, projects, or posters as part of a digital end-of-term showcase.
Students have expressed apprehension or objections about posting their own work to discussion boards or sharing it in class, for fear that their classmates might resubmit the work as their own to another professor(Fitzgerald, 2007; Robillard & Howard, 2008). Yet we continue to ask students to do this in the name of formative feedback and collaborative learning (Wiliam, 2018).

Students have expressed apprehension or objections about posting their own work to discussion boards or sharing it in class, for fear that their classmates might resubmit the work as their own to another professor
(Fitzgerald, 2007; Robillard & Howard, 2008). Yet we continue to ask students to do this in the name of formative feedback and collaborative learning (Wiliam, 2018).
Some instructors not only encourage in-class file sharing, they practically insist upon it, in the name of peer formative feedback. When peer assessment through file sharing is endorsed by course coordinators or administrators, instructors might feel obliged to use this feedback method even if they feel uneasy about it. There can be subtle elements of instructional coercion when an academic leader encourages junior staff members or those with precarious employment to engage in assessment that may have an unethical aspect to it. Today, I refuse to engage in peer-to-peer file sharing as formative assessment, but I was not always in a position to do so, as I spent many years as a part-time contract academic staff. So I can appreciate that some teachers may not be able to negotiate if they have precarious employment. When possible, I encourage educators to start conversations aboutethicalassessment of student work. If teachers are going to impose individual summative assessments of student work, then it isunethicalto oblige students to share their work with anyone but their teacher if they do not wish to do so, even under the guise of formative assessment.

I used to instruct my own students to engage in this type of formative peer assessment, but I stopped once I realized that not only do students appropriate their peers’ work, they might also find themselves caught up in the commercial file-sharing cartels that incentivize students to share any academic content at all, even if it is not theirs to share.

Student-Controlled, Closed-Group Sharing (Many-to-Many)

Student-Controlled, Closed-Group Sharing (Many-to-Many)
Although the notion of a truly “closed” group is a misnomer when it comes to content sharing, there are private collections of term papers or other academic work held and shared by groups of students for use by other members of that group. This typically happens when students taking classes at the same institution share materials from particular courses that they are taking, such as class notes, instructional slide decks, lecture materials, assessment tasks, copies of exams, and exam answers (Rogerson & Basanta, 2016). Some materials might also be shared beyond the closed group with other students taking similar courses elsewhere, but the primary purpose of closed-group sharing is to benefit those in one’s own social circle.

Although the notion of a truly “closed” group is a misnomer when it comes to content sharing, there are private collections of term papers or other academic work held and shared by groups of students for use by other members of that group. This typically happens when students taking classes at the same institution share materials from particular courses that they are taking, such as class notes, instructional slide decks, lecture materials, assessment tasks, copies of exams, and exam answers (Rogerson & Basanta, 2016). Some materials might also be shared beyond the closed group with other students taking similar courses elsewhere, but the primary purpose of closed-group sharing is to benefit those in one’s own social circle.
The practice of storing and sharing academic work among students allegedly began within fraternities (Goodman, 1971; McCabe, 1992, McCabe, Butterfield, & Treviño, 2012; Harris et al., 2019; Pincus & Schmelkin, 2003;Thornton, 1977), leading to the emergence of the term “frat files.” Although catchy, this label is misleading because other closed groups (e.g., sororities, student clubs, or informal groups) engage in the same practice. Although membership in a Greek society has been identified as a risk factor that may contribute to student cheating (McCabe, 1992, McCabe et al., 2012), it is important to acknowledge that not all student organizations, clubs, or societies engage in or endorse the practice of providing copies of academic work to their members. Once again, moral binaries are not helpful when trying to puzzle through complex behaviors.

These files have also been dubbed “crib files” (Brunvand, 1988, n.p.); “depositories of old term papers” (Associated Press, 1972, p. G5), “test files” (Pincus & Schmelkin, 2003, p. 204), or “examination files” (Wright & Kelly, 1974, p. 34). The lack of consistency in nomenclature has made it difficult for academic integrity scholars to trace the history of student-operated, closed-group file sharing, but we know that the practice started during a time when such papers and texts existed only in hard-copy versions, often stored in boxes housed in a common location that members of the group could access easily but outsiders could not. More common today are digital files distributed via shared online folders or drives.

G5), “test files” (Pincus & Schmelkin, 2003, p. 204), or “examination files” (Wright & Kelly, 1974, p. 34). The lack of consistency in nomenclature has made it difficult for academic integrity scholars to trace the history of student-operated, closed-group file sharing, but we know that the practice started during a time when such papers and texts existed only in hard-copy versions, often stored in boxes housed in a common location that members of the group could access easily but outsiders could not. More common today are digital files distributed via shared online folders or drives.
In addition to shared online folders, students share files or communicate about course content via social networking platforms, which are continuously evolving (Varghese, 2011). The social networking sites of today will one day become extinct, in the same way that MySpace has faded from use (Varghese, 2011). Social media services do not exist in perpetuity and typically have a life cycle that goes through phases of introduction, growth, maturity, and subsequent decline (Varghese, 2011). The social platforms that students use today are not necessarily the ones that they will use in the future. The use of social networking platforms varies among different people, who demonstrate preferences for different services depending on factors such as age, socioeconomic status, goals, and personal preferences (Bolton et al., 2013). Social media activity has been broadly classified into two categories: contributing and consuming (Bolton et al., 2013; Schlosser, 2005; Shao, 2009). These transactional binaries have been contested by those who assert that there is a sense of reciprocity in online communities, in which users are willing to give, take, and interact with other members of the group (Cenite et al., 2009).

Open Free Sharing (Many-to-Many)

Open Free Sharing (Many-to-Many)
There are so many permutations of open sharing on the Internet that it is practically impossible to name them all. Some of them are truly open and publicly available; for example, students can turn to Yahoo Answersand Reddit for homework solutions (Wolverton, 2016). Although user names are required to interact on some of these platforms, the systems operate on such a massive scale that they are effectively open sites rather than communities.

There are so many permutations of open sharing on the Internet that it is practically impossible to name them all. Some of them are truly open and publicly available; for example, students can turn to Yahoo Answers
and Reddit for homework solutions (Wolverton, 2016). Although user names are required to interact on some of these platforms, the systems operate on such a massive scale that they are effectively open sites rather than communities.
Other open-sharing sites contain thousands of articles, books, and other academic and scientific writings. Such sites have been started as an act of resistance against academic publishers and are maintained by those ideologically opposed to paywalls that act as a barrier to accessing knowledge. Users download content that they might not be able to access without paying a fee otherwise. In some cases, users might lack the financial means for or be ideologically opposed to paying a fee for the content. Although users might download content from these sites for the purposes of copying or plagiarizing the material, these sites are nevertheless part of a larger, systemic, open-sharing movement for academic content with ethically complex motivations.

Commercial File-Sharing Industry (Many-to-Many)

Commercial File-Sharing Industry (Many-to-Many)
Commercial content-sharing enterprises exist primarily for the purposes of generating profit, even though they “operate under the guise of information repositories, student support communities and assistance centers tempting contributors and users to recycle and repurpose materials through exchange arrangements” (Rogerson & Basanta, 2016, p. 273). The nature of the communications and exchanges is transactional and intentional. Users might get paid to upload content, and they also pay for the privilege of downloading it. In some scenarios, users are able to upload more files than they download in order to avoid paying fees. One possible scenario would be that a student uploads two documents to “unlock” the privilege of downloading one. In this way, commercial enterprises can quickly amass high volumes of academic content, which they can then sell in perpetuity. Although the cost to the user for one download might be relatively small, these online businesses are scaled up to serve a nearly limitless customer base. Unlike academic publishers, who might charge a high price for a single high-quality textbook to a limited number of students, commercial content-sharing enterprises charge a small fee for a single product, but their customer base is massive, and they exert little to no quality control over the content. They resell the same content over and over again, indiscriminately, to anyone willing to pay for it.

Commercial content-sharing enterprises exist primarily for the purposes of generating profit, even though they “operate under the guise of information repositories, student support communities and assistance centers tempting contributors and users to recycle and repurpose materials through exchange arrangements” (Rogerson & Basanta, 2016, p. 273). The nature of the communications and exchanges is transactional and intentional. Users might get paid to upload content, and they also pay for the privilege of downloading it. In some scenarios, users are able to upload more files than they download in order to avoid paying fees. One possible scenario would be that a student uploads two documents to “unlock” the privilege of downloading one. In this way, commercial enterprises can quickly amass high volumes of academic content, which they can then sell in perpetuity. Although the cost to the user for one download might be relatively small, these online businesses are scaled up to serve a nearly limitless customer base. Unlike academic publishers, who might charge a high price for a single high-quality textbook to a limited number of students, commercial content-sharing enterprises charge a small fee for a single product, but their customer base is massive, and they exert little to no quality control over the content. They resell the same content over and over again, indiscriminately, to anyone willing to pay for it.
Although some of these services market themselves as help-based services, there is evidence that some of their practices are implemented for the specific purpose of ensuring users evade detection. InChapter 3, I discussed the type of plagiarism in which an individual runs an original source thatexists in a format that is not easily copied through optical character recognition (OCR) to make it copyable. Commercial file-sharing sites use this practice in reverse—they take files that have been uploaded and then purposely convert them into a format such as JPEG or GIF (Rogerson, 2014). The purpose of doing so is to make the files less detectable by text-matching software, as well as by educators. When students download the files, they simply use software to convert the file back into a readable format so they can cut and paste some or all of the content into their own assignments. In doing so, the metaproperties of the document would show that it was created by the student, not someone else, which can make detection difficult. If a student simply cut and pasted their own name and student ID number onto a paper originally written by someone else, the metadata might reveal this.

UNDERSTANDING FILE-SHARING BEHAVIOR

UNDERSTANDING FILE-SHARING BEHAVIOR
The reasons why students engage in file-sharing behaviors might be more complex than they appear at first glance. Motivations can range from the benevolent intention to help others, to desperation of needing content of any kind to hand in by a deadline, to a consciousness of resistance against perceived systemic injustices that exist in higher education broadly, or a desire to make money. Online-sharing sites are easy to access and use. Perceived benefits include time saving and high potential for grade improvement with low risk of being caught (Rogerson & Basanta, 2016).

Sharing, Caring, and Coercion

Sharing, Caring, and Coercion
We teach children from a young age that sharing is a desirable behavior. Parenting books often contain explicit content, even entire chapters, on how to teach your child to share. One popular parenting book says:

We teach children from a young age that sharing is a desirable behavior. Parenting books often contain explicit content, even entire chapters, on how to teach your child to share. One popular parenting book says:
Willingness to share represents a big step in your child’s development. Any action that looks like sharing—handing a toy to another, offering a bite of food—should be praised with delight as a step forward. You are helping build lifelong values of friendship, generosity and nonattachment. Begin to build your child’s habit of sharing by calling immediate attention to each behavior in that direction. Be alert to rewardapproximatesuccesses, for progress in this area tends to occur in small steps. (Blanchard et al., 2009, p. 62, emphasis in original)

Parenting books discuss at length about how positively reinforcing sharing behavior among young children takes time and repeated effort. We begin to condition children from about the time they can walk that sharing is not only desirable, it is morally praiseworthy.

Parenting books discuss at length about how positively reinforcing sharing behavior among young children takes time and repeated effort. We begin to condition children from about the time they can walk that sharing is not only desirable, it is morally praiseworthy.
Psychologists have linked sharing and giving behaviors with the development of a child’s self-concept as being a helpful, generous, and good person (Grusec & Redler, 1980). Helping behaviors among children are indicative of prosocial behavior and psychosocial competence (Grusec & Redler, 1980; Tyler & Varma, 1988). These behaviors are also associated with positive self-worth, optimism, and interpersonal trust (Tyler & Varma, 1988). We teach children from a young age that sharing is caring.

Psychologists have linked sharing and giving behaviors with the development of a child’s self-concept as being a helpful, generous, and good person (Grusec & Redler, 1980). Helping behaviors among children are indicative of prosocial behavior and psychosocial competence (Grusec & Redler, 1980; Tyler & Varma, 1988). These behaviors are also associated with positive self-worth, optimism, and interpersonal trust (Tyler & Varma, 1988). We teach children from a young age that sharing is caring.
When children go to school, teachers reinforce the “sharing is caring” message. Books on classroom behavior and discipline echo the same themes as parenting books, such as that “good sharing” (Boynton, 2005, p. 113) is important. The trick is knowing the difference between “good” and “bad” sharing. This idea of good and bad sharing may help young children to understand that it is acceptable to share their own toys, but not to share something that is not theirs. The problem is that the notion of good and bad sharing can serve to reinforce the moral binaries that we are trying to avoid when it comes to understanding academic integrity breaches later in life.

When children go to school, teachers reinforce the “sharing is caring” message. Books on classroom behavior and discipline echo the same themes as parenting books, such as that “good sharing” (Boynton, 2005, p. 113) is important. The trick is knowing the difference between “good” and “bad” sharing. This idea of good and bad sharing may help young children to understand that it is acceptable to share their own toys, but not to share something that is not theirs. The problem is that the notion of good and bad sharing can serve to reinforce the moral binaries that we are trying to avoid when it comes to understanding academic integrity breaches later in life.
When it comes to academic conduct, there may be an underlying assumption that sharing one’s own work with others is an act of generosity; however, doing so can be an act of misconduct in cases where individuals share others’ work without their knowledge or permission. In such cases, both the student who shared the work and the one who misused it can be found to have committed misconduct, depending on the school’s definition of what constitutes collusion. So even an act intended as generosity can be considered misconduct. The lines between what is and is not acceptable in terms of student sharing have become blurred, particularly since the dawn of the Internet (Blum, 2009; Blum, 2016; Chibry & Kurz, 2019; Rogerson & Basanta, 2016). It might be easy to teach a small child that it is acceptable to share her own toys, but not someone else’s, because those items are tangible. When the items are intangible, such as music files, memes, or academic work, what is “mine” has come to mean “what I have access to.”

Gifting Systems

Gifting Systems
The notion of gifting goes back to ancient times. One of the best-known authors on the topic was Marcel Mauss, whose original French essays on the topic have been translated into English several times and remain relevant today. Mauss (2002) elaborates on the social practices of gifting in detail. In the twenty-first century, digital gifting has become common. Grandmothers send e-transfers at birthdays and holidays, and e-gift cards for books, coffee, and other items are given daily around the world. Intoday’s world, gifts do not need to be tangible to be exchanged or enjoyed. Of key interest for this chapter is the notion of social conventions around gifting that include obligations to reciprocate or repay in some form. Giesler and colleagues (Giesler, 2006; Giesler & Pohlmann, 2003) apply Mauss’s anthropological theories to file sharing by exploring the online-sharing community of Napster through the lens of gifting culture, identifying reciprocity as a behavioral norm in online-sharing communities.

The Influence of Coercion

The Influence of Coercion
For sharing repositories to be populated with student work that other students can then refer to, or harvest, for their own purposes, the database must be populated with authentic examples of student work. Students are expected to populate the files so that others can then use them later. Academic file-sharing communities are often presented as being free or low cost, but as Rogerson and Basanta (2016) have pointed out, they are not free of obligation. Users might feel directly pressured or subtly coerced into contributing, depending on the type of community.

Students are expected to populate the files so that others can then use them later. Users might feel directly pressured or subtly coerced into contributing, depending on the type of community.
Although some students may be willing participants in this complicit behavior, others may find themselves caught in the uncomfortable position of wanting to fit in with their peer group but not wanting to surrender their own academic work to do so. This may be particularly true for closed-group sharing among students in which there is a social expectation to contribute to the group in order to fit in, maintain membership, or be considered a generous member of the group. Peer pressure can be extraordinary in peer-sharing groups, especially when users are known to one another and motivated to maintain their social connection to the group. In one study, students that were surveyed reported that they themselves are not cheating if they help others cheat, suggesting that peer pressure to help friends is strong (McCabe, 1992).

In one study, students that were surveyed reported that they themselves are not cheating if they help others cheat, suggesting that peer pressure to help friends is strong (McCabe, 1992).
Similarly, instructors can be complicit agents in coercing students to share their work. Instructors are in a position of authority and power over students. When they require or encourage students to share their work with one another, they are using their position of power to oblige students to comply with the request. We have already addressed that students might not feel comfortable sharing their work with peers in class (Fitzgerald, 2007; Robillard & Howard, 2008). Students may feel they have no choice but to comply, or else they risk punitive consequences, such as a lower grade or being regarded as uncooperative by their teacher. The power relationships between teachers and students cannot be ignored when it comes to peer-to-peer academic file sharing being couched as a course requirement.

File Sharing as an Act of Resistance

File Sharing as an Act of Resistance
When students believe their course assessments are unfair or that their instructors do not care about them, they may engage in academic cheating behaviors (Christensen Hughes, 2017; Genereux & MacLeod, 1995; McCabe, 1992). It is reasonable to assume that if students hold such beliefs, that engaging in file sharing as an act of resistance against an educational system, or even an instructor, that they perceive as unjust.

When students believe their course assessments are unfair or that their instructors do not care about them, they may engage in academic cheating behaviors (Christensen Hughes, 2017; Genereux & MacLeod, 1995; McCabe, 1992). It is reasonable to assume that if students hold such beliefs, that engaging in file sharing as an act of resistance against an educational system, or even an instructor, that they perceive as unjust.
Power and authority are key concepts when considering academic file sharing as an act of resistance. Even before the Internet was available to the average consumer, scholars pointed out that individuals’ engagements with mass media can be politicized, and “social, political, and cultural institutions stress the value of being well-informed and politically active” (Rubin & Windahl, 1986, p. 189). Academic file sharing of pirated scientific and scholarly articles is arguably the most politicized form; it has been called a conscious act of civil disobedience in academia (James, 2020).

Even before the Internet was available to the average consumer, scholars pointed out that individuals’ engagements with mass media can be politicized, and “social, political, and cultural institutions stress the value of being well-informed and politically active” (Rubin & Windahl, 1986, p. 189). Academic file sharing of pirated scientific and scholarly articles is arguably the most politicized form; it has been called a conscious act of civil disobedience in academia (James, 2020).
The topic of paywalls in academic publishing is hotly debated among professors and students alike; however, file sharing is not limited to students. Content-sharing sites similar to those aimed at students are available to academics and researchers as well. The open-access platform Sci-Hub, for example, offered more than 50 million scientific journal articles in a free, downloadable format (Fyfe et al., 2017). Although the specific motives for downloading articles may differ among users, some scholars do it as an act of resistance against profit-hungry journal publishers and a system that they perceive as unfair.

Academic file sharing can be positioned within the theoretical framework of emancipatory pedagogy, which includes key concepts of critical reflection on the power structures inherent in society and realizing that one can take action to transcend injustice (Freire, 2018). Emancipatory pedagogy is also dialogue and the exchange of ideas and knowledge as a means to develop one’s comprehension about knowledge itself. If we look at academic file sharing through the lens of emancipation, it is arguably among the most wide-scale acts of resistance and knowledge liberation in the twenty-first century.

Commodified Sharing: File Sharing as an Act of Academic Capitalism

Commodified Sharing: File Sharing as an Act of Academic Capitalism
Notions of academic file sharing as benevolent gifting, and or even an emancipatory act, become corrupted in commodified versions of file sharing, for which the primary purpose is not altruism, or even resistance, but rather profit. In such cases, students may be led to believe that they are entering an altruistic sharing community, only to find themselves entangledin a system in which they become exploited. Students pay fees to download files that they believe will help them. In other cases, students have the opportunity to avoid paying for downloads by uploading multiple files in exchange for downloading one. In other instances, companies might pay students a nominal fee for their uploads. Students may think the companies are there to help them, but the primary business function of these predatory companies is to generate profit.

In other cases, students have the opportunity to avoid paying for downloads by uploading multiple files in exchange for downloading one. In other instances, companies might pay students a nominal fee for their uploads. Students may think the companies are there to help them, but the primary business function of these predatory companies is to generate profit.
Academic file-sharing companies are insistent upon having their sites populated by as many academic files as possible. This has led to instances where companies have explicitly urged students to log into their institution’s LMS for the purposes of indiscriminately harvesting material from all their past and present courses and then uploading those materials to file-sharing sites. They might do this in order to unlock the privilege of downloading fewer files in return, or in exchange for a nominal fee. The motivations for uploading files to file-sharing sites can be complex; they are not always nefarious. I have heard of cases where financially disadvantaged students upload files to earn a few bucks that they desperately need to buy a meal.

The motivations for uploading files to file-sharing sites can be complex; they are not always nefarious. I have heard of cases where financially disadvantaged students upload files to earn a few bucks that they desperately need to buy a meal.
From the consumer side of the equation, students have no opportunity as consumers to thoroughly review a file before they download it. Students often have little idea about the quality of the file that they are buying. Transactions are made on the premise ofcaveat emptor—buyer beware. User agreements might also be obscured, appearing on screen in a small and/or light gray font that is difficult to read, for example. Once a student has purchased a file, the critical reflection inherent in emancipatory approaches as discussed here can be absent if the purpose of the download is simply to manipulate the identifying information on the file in order to turn in someone else’s academic work as one’s own, with no intellectual engagement at all.

INSTITUTIONAL AND EDUCATOR RESPONSES TO FILE SHARING

INSTITUTIONAL AND EDUCATOR RESPONSES TO FILE SHARING
There has been little research done on how institutions address file sharing from a policy perspective. We can draw from existing research to see that the postsecondary policy responses to both file sharing and contract cheating are vague at best (Stoesz et al., 2019). One reason for this is because file sharing is not necessarily considered to constitute misconduct. If the user merely uses the material as a study guide for learning purposes, that would not be considered unethical. However, if the student uses that material to gain an unfair advantage (e.g., plagiarism or contract cheating), that clearly is misconduct.

How to Determine If File Sharing Has Occurred

How to Determine If File Sharing Has Occurred
From an assessment perspective, educators need to be alert to the possibility of unethical file sharing. They also need to know how to detect if unethical file sharing has occurred (Rogerson, 2014; Rogerson & Basanta, 2016). Rogerson (2014) noted that “file swapping site usage was identified through the inclusion of inappropriate and irrelevant material, bibliographic ‘mashups’ where academic journal and book information was blended into a single reference, and cross matching identified by Turnitin where students relied on the same file swapping source” (Rogerson, 2014, p. 3). Detection can be time consuming and rely on educators having both the experience and the motivation to determine if the work is the result of the student’s own genuine effort (Rogerson & Basanta, 2016).

From an assessment perspective, educators need to be alert to the possibility of unethical file sharing. They also need to know how to detect if unethical file sharing has occurred (Rogerson, 2014; Rogerson & Basanta, 2016). Rogerson (2014) noted that “file swapping site usage was identified through the inclusion of inappropriate and irrelevant material, bibliographic ‘mashups’ where academic journal and book information was blended into a single reference, and cross matching identified by Turnitin where students relied on the same file swapping source” (Rogerson, 2014, p. 3). Detection can be time consuming and rely on educators having both the experience and the motivation to determine if the work is the result of the student’s own genuine effort (Rogerson & Basanta, 2016).
Educating the Educators

Educating the Educators
There is an urgent need for educators to understand that file sharing not only happens, but that it is also prolific. Two colleagues of mine at the University of Calgary, Prof. Nancy Chibry and Dr. Ebba Kurz, offer an educational development workshop for fellow faculty and teaching assistants on what file sharing is and how it works (Chibry & Kurz, 2019; University of Calgary, 2019). They focus on commercial providers and the predatory nature of their business models. Participants often find themselves agog as they log into global commercial file-sharing sites themselves and find material from courses that they teach posted there.

Avoiding Morally Superior Responses

Avoiding Morally Superior Responses
When Prof. Chibry and Dr. Kurz identify that a work from a particular student has been shared, they call in that student for an interview in which they show them the work posted online and proceed to engage in a candid conversation about the repercussions, which can vary depending on the case. They also discuss possible reputational risks to students in terms of future prospective employers who might conduct an Internet search as part of the hiring process. Employers who sniff out unethical or inappropriate conduct among prospective job candidates might move to another applicant without ever informing these candidates that they were disqualified based on their online-sharing behavior. Conversations such as these underscore the need to engage students in reflective, critical dialogue about the consequences of their Internet behavior and ethical decision-making, while avoiding finger wagging.

They also discuss possible reputational risks to students in terms of future prospective employers who might conduct an Internet search as part of the hiring process. Employers who sniff out unethical or inappropriate conduct among prospective job candidates might move to another applicant without ever informing these candidates that they were disqualified based on their online-sharing behavior. Conversations such as these underscore the need to engage students in reflective, critical dialogue about the consequences of their Internet behavior and ethical decision-making, while avoiding finger wagging.
Conversely, professors who claim that their own students would never engage in file sharing exhibit a different kind of moral superiority—one inwhich they position themselves and their own students as being better than the “unethical other.” A more helpful approach would be to consider oneself and one’s students as members of the larger institutional community, in which all stakeholders share the responsibility for academic integrity education and holding one another to ethical standards of conduct. Academic file sharing is a problem that extends beyond the walls of any single instructor’s physical or virtual classroom, and it is incumbent upon us as members of the educational community to understand that teaching and learning ethically are both individual and collective responsibilities.
