Teaching Students to Protect Their Own Work

Teaching Students to Protect Their Own Work
Part of the educational process around file sharing is not only raising awareness among educators and teaching assistants (TAs), but educating students about how to protect their own work. Students may find themselves under tremendous peer pressure or instructor expectation to share their work, even if they do not want to. Some practical strategies for students who feel they have no choice but to share their work include:

Part of the educational process around file sharing is not only raising awareness among educators and teaching assistants (TAs), but educating students about how to protect their own work. Students may find themselves under tremendous peer pressure or instructor expectation to share their work, even if they do not want to. Some practical strategies for students who feel they have no choice but to share their work include:
- Share incomplete work:Share only a small section of a draft work instead of an entire paper.

- Share one-to-one instead of one-to-many:Although sharing a file with only one person at a time does not guarantee that it will not be subsequently misused, it may reduce the rate at which it is distributed. If peer sharing is a forced requirement in a course, sharing via e-mail is better than sharing on a discussion board.

- Express concerns when appropriate:Some instructors may be unaware of the illicit academic file sharing or may deny that it could happen in their own classes. In cases where students feel that they can trust the instructor to listen to them without punitive repercussions, expressing concerns to the instructor might be helpful. Proposing alternatives to posting academic work in a many-to-many format (e.g., one-to-one e-mail) might allow a concerned student to negotiate a compromise.

- Redact and resave portions of the work:Graying out portions of the work and then saving it in a format that is not easily copied might also help.

Share incomplete work:
Share only a small section of a draft work instead of an entire paper.
Share one-to-one instead of one-to-many:
Although sharing a file with only one person at a time does not guarantee that it will not be subsequently misused, it may reduce the rate at which it is distributed. If peer sharing is a forced requirement in a course, sharing via e-mail is better than sharing on a discussion board.
Express concerns when appropriate:
Some instructors may be unaware of the illicit academic file sharing or may deny that it could happen in their own classes. In cases where students feel that they can trust the instructor to listen to them without punitive repercussions, expressing concerns to the instructor might be helpful. Proposing alternatives to posting academic work in a many-to-many format (e.g., one-to-one e-mail) might allow a concerned student to negotiate a compromise.
Redact and resave portions of the work:
Graying out portions of the work and then saving it in a format that is not easily copied might also help.
None of these tactics are likely to prevent unethical peer file sharing entirely, but they might help students to become more aware of the value of their own work, not only as an intellectual product, but as one that could be commodified and exploited by others.

None of these tactics are likely to prevent unethical peer file sharing entirely, but they might help students to become more aware of the value of their own work, not only as an intellectual product, but as one that could be commodified and exploited by others.
Copyright

Copyright
Copyright violations are part of the collateral damage of file sharing. Although in many jurisdictions, students own the copyright of their academic work, they do not necessarily have the right to share other types of files, such as instructor-developed course resources, such as slide decks and handouts, or materials developed by academic departments, such as exams that are used across a number of sections of the same course. Some file-sharing services actively promote the sharing of copyrighted materials (Rogerson, 2014). I have seen examples of materials for which others (e.g., the instructor) hold the copyright, and a commercial enterprise then superimposes its own copyright notice over the material, making it appear as if the company, not the creator, owns the copyright, which is not only deceptive but also illegal in many jurisdictions.

CONCLUSIONS

CONCLUSIONS
File sharing can occur in a variety of ways: one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many. The motivations for it are complex, ranging from benevolent gifting, coerced sharing, a political act of resistance, to a means of earning some cash. File sharing is rampant across academia. Any professor who uses Sci-Hub or other academic file-sharing sites to avoid paying for academic content (which, to be fair, is probably most of us) should think twice before wagging a finger with moral superiority at students who download course-based content from the Internet. However, even if themotivediffers, theactof downloading prohibited content does not. I would argue that most professors cannot claim the moral high ground when it comes to academic file sharing, so they should avoid demonizing students who do the same. Further, it is imperative for educators who endorse or insist upon in-class content sharing as part of the learning process to consider how they contribute to the mixed messages sent to students about file sharing in academic contexts. Inchapter 8, I explore the realm of contract cheating, which shares some characteristics with file sharing, but with one key difference: educators rarely consider term-paper mills as an acceptable form of academic interaction.

Contract Cheating: Outsourced Academic Work

Contract Cheating: Outsourced Academic Work
Contract cheating happens when students engage a third party to complete academic work on their behalf (Clarke & Lancaster, 2006; QAA, 2017). The term “contract cheating” was coined by two researchers in the United Kingdom in 2006, Robert Clarke and Thomas Lancaster, whose early work focused on computer science students buying assignments from a website called Rent-a-Coder (Clarke & Lancaster, 2006, p. 1). Readers might be more familiar with the terms “essay mill” or “paper mill,” but these do not cover all types of outsourced academic work. As a result, “contract cheating” has been used as a broad umbrella term encompassing a “cluster of practices” (Bretag et al., 2019, p. 1838) that include but are not limited to essay mills, homework completion services, dissertation writing services, substitute examination takers, and imposters for online courses. Researchers have proposed that when we talk about completing work, we are talking about when a “third party makes a contribution to the work of the student, such that there is reasonable doubt as to whose work the assessment represents” (Draper & Newton, p. 2017, p. 1).

Contract cheating happens when students engage a third party to complete academic work on their behalf (Clarke & Lancaster, 2006; QAA, 2017). The term “contract cheating” was coined by two researchers in the United Kingdom in 2006, Robert Clarke and Thomas Lancaster, whose early work focused on computer science students buying assignments from a website called Rent-a-Coder (Clarke & Lancaster, 2006, p. 1). Readers might be more familiar with the terms “essay mill” or “paper mill,” but these do not cover all types of outsourced academic work. As a result, “contract cheating” has been used as a broad umbrella term encompassing a “cluster of practices” (Bretag et al., 2019, p. 1838) that include but are not limited to essay mills, homework completion services, dissertation writing services, substitute examination takers, and imposters for online courses. Researchers have proposed that when we talk about completing work, we are talking about when a “third party makes a contribution to the work of the student, such that there is reasonable doubt as to whose work the assessment represents” (Draper & Newton, p. 2017, p. 1).
One might wonder why a book on plagiarism contains a chapter on contract cheating. If traditional (if contested) definitions of plagiarism imply some kind of theft or appropriation of another’s work without the original creator’s knowledge or permission, then would it not stand to reason thatbuyingacademic work would be a kind of antithesis to that, especially ifthe creators are paid for their services and are aware that their created work was being sold to, and used by, someone else? The problem is more complicated than that, but it centers around the single premise of deception. When students submit academic work that they did not complete themselves, and they know full well that they did not do the work, they are engaging in a kind of premeditated deception that experts have called “morally reprehensible” (Bertram Gallant, 2016, n.p.). It is a deliberate form of cheating that violates the expectation of institutions, as well as individual educators, that students are doing their own work. Some have explicitly argued for outsourced academic work to be considered plagiarism (Rothschild, 2011; Sivasubramaniam et al., 2016), although others have pointed out that it might be more accurately aligned with fraud (Draper & Newton, 2017; Foltýnek & Králíková, 2018; Newton & Lang, 2016). Either way, a book tackling tough topics in academic integrity would be incomplete without a discussion of contract cheating, as it is an issue of growing and urgent importance in education.

When students submit academic work that they did not complete themselves, and they know full well that they did not do the work, they are engaging in a kind of premeditated deception that experts have called “morally reprehensible” (Bertram Gallant, 2016, n.p.). It is a deliberate form of cheating that violates the expectation of institutions, as well as individual educators, that students are doing their own work. Some have explicitly argued for outsourced academic work to be considered plagiarism (Rothschild, 2011; Sivasubramaniam et al., 2016), although others have pointed out that it might be more accurately aligned with fraud (Draper & Newton, 2017; Folt
ý
nek & Kr
á
l
í
kov
á
, 2018; Newton & Lang, 2016). Either way, a book tackling tough topics in academic integrity would be incomplete without a discussion of contract cheating, as it is an issue of growing and urgent importance in education.
In the sections that follow, I discuss small-scale contract cheating first, looking at those who are likely closest to the student, the enablers. Then I discuss the individuals who complete academic work in exchange for a fee. Following that, I address the commercial contract cheating industry as a whole, exploring how it started and has evolved throughout the twentieth and twenty-first centuries.

A CHEATER BY ANY OTHER NAME: ENABLERS AND SUPPLIERS

A CHEATER BY ANY OTHER NAME: ENABLERS AND SUPPLIERS
Although early reports used words such as “ghostwriter,” experts now advocate against using that term, which can normalize the practice of hiring someone else to complete academic work on behalf of a student. Normalization often has the effect of making one of the most egregious forms of academic misconduct seem acceptable (Bertram Gallant, 2016). Although ghostwriters have existed in the literary and publishing worlds for centuries, the main difference between professional writers and students is that the main objective of being a student is (or at least should be) tolearn. When students bypass learning and go straight for the grade or the credential, they are effectively corrupting the learning process. By extension, this calls into question the validity of the credentials they receive, which are intended to serve as confirmation of successful completion of learning. The concept of “successful completion” carries with it the assumption that the student has earned a credential honestly. When students have someone else complete the work on their behalf, they are not only trying to circumvent the system, but subvert it. For that reason, theword “ghostwriter” should be reserved for those who work as legitimate professional writers, not those who help students cheat.

There are two broad classifications of those who do academic work on behalf of others. There are those who are personally close to the student, who believe that they are helping by doing the work for the student. We call these people “enablers” (Eaton & Dressler, 2019). They include parents, family, partners, friends, and so on. Then there are those involved in the commercial contract cheating industry, which can then be further subdivided into individual freelancers and large corporate entities (Newton & Lang, 2016). I propose that we call the organizations and individuals who provide academic work to others for money as “suppliers,” to emphasize the transactional nature of the relationship. It is important to recognize that when students engage in contract cheating, “education is viewed as a product to be bought, sold or traded rather than an intrinsically motivated, effortful and potentially transformative individual process” (Bretag et al., 2018, p. 3). The term “supplier” is also used in legal contexts to refer to those who sell tangible and intangible goods (Law Insider, n.d.). I discuss each of these groups in the section that follows.

Enablers

Enablers
When my colleague, Roswita Dressler, and I were working on a contract cheating study, we borrowed the term “enabler” from psychology (APA, n.d.), to refer to individuals who are motivated to help students out of love or loyalty and who can, in their efforts to help, end up contributing to academically harmful behavior (Eaton & Dressler, 2019). Enablers often think that they are helping students, and although they may have good intentions, their interventions often cross the fine line between helping and doing the student’s work for them (Eaton & Dressler, 2019). People who fall into this category generally do not accept money to do the student’s work, but instead do it for free out of a sense of loyalty, duty, or love (Bretag et al., 2018; Clarke & Lancaster, 2006; Lancaster & Clarke, 2016; Owings & Nelson, 2014). Enablers can include parents, caregivers, partners, friends, personal tutors, and classmates, among others (Bretag et al., 2018; Harper et al., 2018; Lancaster & Clarke, 2016). The result is a violation of the implicit expectation that students do their own work, effectively breaking the unspoken learning contract between students, instructors, and the institution issuing the credential.

When my colleague, Roswita Dressler, and I were working on a contract cheating study, we borrowed the term “enabler” from psychology (APA, n.d.), to refer to individuals who are motivated to help students out of love or loyalty and who can, in their efforts to help, end up contributing to academically harmful behavior (Eaton & Dressler, 2019). Enablers often think that they are helping students, and although they may have good intentions, their interventions often cross the fine line between helping and doing the student’s work for them (Eaton & Dressler, 2019). People who fall into this category generally do not accept money to do the student’s work, but instead do it for free out of a sense of loyalty, duty, or love (Bretag et al., 2018; Clarke & Lancaster, 2006; Lancaster & Clarke, 2016; Owings & Nelson, 2014). Enablers can include parents, caregivers, partners, friends, personal tutors, and classmates, among others (Bretag et al., 2018; Harper et al., 2018; Lancaster & Clarke, 2016). The result is a violation of the implicit expectation that students do their own work, effectively breaking the unspoken learning contract between students, instructors, and the institution issuing the credential.
In a survey of over 14,000 students across eight universities in Australia, Tracey Bretag and her colleagues found that receiving help from an enabler to be among the most common type of unauthorized assistance (Bretag et al., 2018). Students will most often turn to a current classmateor a former student of the course, followed by turning to friends and family members for assistance (Bretag et al., 2018). There is a comfort level with students approaching someone whom they know to ask for help. I want to be clear that it is perfectly acceptable for students to ask for help if they are struggling, but there is a difference between helping students tolearnand helping them tocheat. Enablers may not be able to recognize when they have crossed the line between helping and cheating. In fact, this may be more of a fuzzy gray zone. It can be helpful to keep in mind that the moment that the student is no longer learning, what may be happening could be considered cheating instead. It is wise to be aware that if learning has been taken out of the equation, cheating may be inserted in its place.

Parents as Enablers

Parents as Enablers
There have been cases where enablers have gone so far as to interfere with a student’s academic work without that person’s knowledge or consent. One of the most scandalous examples was the U.S. college admissions scandal dubbed “Operation Varsity Blues,” which involved parents and family members conspiring with college admissions counselors and others to ensure that their children received admission offers from particular colleges. In some cases, the children were allegedly unaware of what their families had done to try and assure their admission to a selected school (Golden & Burke, 2019).

There have been cases where enablers have gone so far as to interfere with a student’s academic work without that person’s knowledge or consent. One of the most scandalous examples was the U.S. college admissions scandal dubbed “Operation Varsity Blues,” which involved parents and family members conspiring with college admissions counselors and others to ensure that their children received admission offers from particular colleges. In some cases, the children were allegedly unaware of what their families had done to try and assure their admission to a selected school (Golden & Burke, 2019).
The parents involved in Operation Varsity Blues are an example of “snowplow parents” (Miller & Bromwich, 2019), discussed inChapter 4. When it comes to conspiring to help students cheat, there could just as easily also be “snowplow partners”—the spouses, boyfriends, girlfriends, or other people related to students, who plow ahead with ensuring that the students’ academic work is completed and submitted no matter what. “Snowplow parents” or “snowplow partners” can enable cheating either by completing the academic work themselves or by passing it on to a supplier and handling the transaction on behalf of a student.

Suppliers

Suppliers
The commercial contract cheating industry is comprised of both large corporate entities and the individuals who work for them. A supplier can work directly with a student (direct supplier) or they can provide services to an organization that acts as a kind of broker or agent, which then sells their products to the student (indirect supplier).

The commercial contract cheating industry is comprised of both large corporate entities and the individuals who work for them. A supplier can work directly with a student (direct supplier) or they can provide services to an organization that acts as a kind of broker or agent, which then sells their products to the student (indirect supplier).
Individual Suppliers

Individual Suppliers
Individuals can be either direct or indirect suppliers of contract cheating services. Individuals who supply services directly to students operate mainly as freelancers. Online buy-sell-trade marketplaces can connect customers with suppliers (Newton & Lang, 2016), as can personal networks. Individuals can also supply indirectly to students by working for a commercial essay mill or other contract cheating service or company. In such cases, individual suppliers either bid on gigs or are given assignments by the agency (Newton & Lang, 2016). An individual can be both a direct and an indirect supplier.

Individuals can be either direct or indirect suppliers of contract cheating services. Individuals who supply services directly to students operate mainly as freelancers. Online buy-sell-trade marketplaces can connect customers with suppliers (Newton & Lang, 2016), as can personal networks. Individuals can also supply indirectly to students by working for a commercial essay mill or other contract cheating service or company. In such cases, individual suppliers either bid on gigs or are given assignments by the agency (Newton & Lang, 2016). An individual can be both a direct and an indirect supplier.
There are more and more accounts of individuals who have disclosed their role as suppliers to the commercial contract cheating industry. Some have offered first-person accounts of working as suppliers for the industry (Martin, 1972; Gray, 1977; Tomar, 2013). Others have shared their stories with a reporter or researcher who has told their story on their behalf (BBC, 2018; BBC News, 2019; DiRisio, 2019; Sutherland, 2019). In one early account, Martin (1972) (writing under a pseudonym) discusses the flourishing term paper industry operating mainly on the Eastern Seaboard of the United States in the 1970s. He gives elaborate details of his experiences of working in this industry, noting how he worked his way up by being a supplier to “three of the major Boston term paper companies” and later becoming “president of the fourth” (Martin, 1972, p. 69).

In one early account, Martin (1972) (writing under a pseudonym) discusses the flourishing term paper industry operating mainly on the Eastern Seaboard of the United States in the 1970s. He gives elaborate details of his experiences of working in this industry, noting how he worked his way up by being a supplier to “three of the major Boston term paper companies” and later becoming “president of the fourth” (Martin, 1972, p. 69).
Interestingly, Martin notes that prior to entering into the term paper industry, “he was a teaching associate at ‘one of America’s best universities’ ” (p. 69). This supports the idea that some underemployed college professors contribute to the contract cheating industry by acting as suppliers for it. This idea has been explored by popular news media (Turner, 2017), although more research still must be done to uncover more information. There is, however, strong evidence suggesting that many individual contract cheating suppliers are highly qualified. One study reported that 90 percent of individual suppliers to the contract cheating industry have master’s degrees or higher (Sivasubramaniam, 2016).

One study reported that 90 percent of individual suppliers to the contract cheating industry have master’s degrees or higher (Sivasubramaniam, 2016).
Although there is no single profile of an individual supplier, reports suggest that they range from those who work in academic sweatshops in Africa (BBC News, 2019; Simons, 2019; Sutherland, 2019) and other non-Western nations (Sivasubramaniam, 2016) to middle-class Americans and Canadians (Martin, 1972; Tomar, 2013; DiRisio, 2019). One individual supplier was described as a “clean-cut, unassuming 20-something-year-old” (DiRisio, 2019). Just as we need to be cautious about engaging in racialized stereotypes about students who engage in academic misconduct, we also need to be cautious about stereotyping contract cheating suppliers.

ORIGINS OF THE COMMERCIAL ACADEMIC BLACK MARKET

ORIGINS OF THE COMMERCIAL ACADEMIC BLACK MARKET
Individuals completing academic work on behalf of other individuals have been documented as a kind of clandestine freelance business since the 1700s (Mallon, 1989). Although such individual suppliers still operate by offering their services in online marketplaces or other buy-sell-trade websites, scholars have documented that a large-scale commercial industry actually began to develop around the mid-twentieth century. No one knows exactly where or how the industry began, but the most documented evidence comes from the United States. One scholar suggests that the democratization and increase of postsecondary education in the 1960s and 1970s brought with it a simultaneous increase in cheating (Bertram Gallant, 2008). Pivotal events from that time that remain etched in the collective memory of the American people, such as the Vietnam War and Watergate, occurred concurrently with news reports of wide-scale cheating at American colleges (Bertram Gallant, 2008; Mallon, 1989). Mallon makes a specific connection between the rise of the term paper industry and “that time of ethical confusion known as the Nixon administration” (1989, p. 93).

No one knows exactly where or how the industry began, but the most documented evidence comes from the United States. One scholar suggests that the democratization and increase of postsecondary education in the 1960s and 1970s brought with it a simultaneous increase in cheating (Bertram Gallant, 2008). Pivotal events from that time that remain etched in the collective memory of the American people, such as the Vietnam War and Watergate, occurred concurrently with news reports of wide-scale cheating at American colleges (Bertram Gallant, 2008; Mallon, 1989). Mallon makes a specific connection between the rise of the term paper industry and “that time of ethical confusion known as the Nixon administration” (1989, p. 93).
By all this, I am not suggesting that contract cheating began in the United States. Social upheaval was occurring in many countries around the world during that same time. Instead, I am suggesting that scholars have established a correlative link between the social upheaval that was occurring around the world and the moral shift of the 1960s and 1970s, and the emergence of contract cheating as a large-scale commercial industry.

By all this, I am not suggesting that contract cheating began in the United States. Social upheaval was occurring in many countries around the world during that same time. Instead, I am suggesting that scholars have established a correlative link between the social upheaval that was occurring around the world and the moral shift of the 1960s and 1970s, and the emergence of contract cheating as a large-scale commercial industry.
By the mid-1970s, the academic black market was declared to be “big business” (Hammer, 1976). Thomas Mallon (1989) writes in detail about the agencies that flourished in the 1970s in the United States by selling hard copies of essays on particular topics. He outlines that they worked by having “thousands and thousands of these essays on file—on Malthus and Plato and Rousseau and Homer and the Russian Revolution. They solicited college kids in ads placed in the back of underground magazines” (Mallon, 1989, pp. 89–90). Mainstream magazines such asRolling Stonealso featured such ads, with one service claiming to have more than 14,000 papers on file, with a toll-free hotline that had been offering “ ‘Research Assistance’ (‘since 1970’)” (Mallon, 1989, p. 90).

He outlines that they worked by having “thousands and thousands of these essays on file—on Malthus and Plato and Rousseau and Homer and the Russian Revolution. Rolling Stone
also featured such ads, with one service claiming to have more than 14,000 papers on file, with a toll-free hotline that had been offering “ ‘Research Assistance’ (‘since 1970’)” (Mallon, 1989, p. 90).
Mallon (1989) describes the 1970s essay mill system and payment schemes in meticulous detail, explaining that company catalogs offering term papers on various topics were designed to look like college admissions catalogs, “with a picture of young men and women gaily passing under a Gothic arch at some generic alma mater” (p. 90). The catalogs were not free, Mallon notes. A basic catalog would cost about one dollar and would “arrive by UPS with the firm’s Chicago address, but not its name onthe envelope” (p. 90). Here was evidence of the clandestine marketing systems these companies had in place half a century ago.

the envelope” (p. 90). Here was evidence of the clandestine marketing systems these companies had in place half a century ago.
One such service was Authors’ Research Services (ARS), which noted that all orders were confidential and “all 16,000 and more papers in the catalogue have been written by ARS’s ‘staff of professional writers, each writer a specialist in one or more academic areas’ ” (Mallon, 1989, p. 90). The ads for today’s contract cheating companies, which operate almost exclusively online, echo these claims of the 1970s in almost perfect synch.

Mallon’s account of the burgeoning essay mill essay of the 1970s is fascinating for academic integrity scholars to peruse. Others have pointed out that it was not only prewritten papers that were available in the 1970s, but also bespoke academic work of any kind, including graduate theses (Gray, 1977). These documented facts should serve as a wake-up call for educators and administrators who refuse to believe that such an industry exists or claim that if it does, that students attheirinstitution would neverdreamof using these services. I regularly encounter academics and administrators who make such dismissive claims. Meanwhile, the industry continues to thrive at an exponential rate, as it has been doing since the early 1970s.

GOING DIGITAL: EMERGENCE OF THE ONLINE CHEATING CARTELS

GOING DIGITAL: EMERGENCE OF THE ONLINE CHEATING CARTELS
On June 8, 1997, a headline on the front page of theNew York Timesread, “On the Internet, Term Papers Are Hot Items.” The article, by Peter Applebome, started with a captivating hook: “When Bill Clinton vowed that every 12-year-old in America would be able to log into the Internet, he probably did not have in mind logging on to the Evil House of Cheat or Cheater.com to download term papers on ‘Hamlet’, Crazy Horse, or Mayan architecture” (Applebome, 1997, p. 1). Although theNew York Timeshad been reporting about contract cheating for a couple of decades by that point, the Internet changed the industry dramatically, bringing with it many new opportunities, among them the development of contract cheating as a global online business, which the BBC estimated in 2019 to be worth more than a billion U.S. dollars (BBC News, 2019).

Writing for theWashington Post, Arlene Levinson made an astute discovery. She found that one of the early domain names registered towww.1sttermpaper.com, a contract cheating company in the United States, was registered to Ward Warren (Levinson, 2001). The name matched that of a man who allegedly became “a self-made millionaire at 23” (Shepherd, 1973, p. 172) by launching Termpapers Unlimited Inc. with his brother in the early 1970s. Although the reporter was unable to confirm if the name of the person who owned the domain was the same man, it would be a remarkable coincidence if it were not.

You can tell by the size of our library that we have had tens of thousands of happy satisfied customers.” Scrolling down to the bottom of the page, one can see that the final FAQ on the page asks: “How can I tell when the report was written?” A methodical cataloguing system is explained, noting that papers written after the year 1970 were indicated as “files with the number 1 to 100,000.” This would seem to point to the existence of a well-established company that just happened to have operated in the same state as Termpapers Unlimited decades earlier. Currently,
www.1sttermpaper.com
is no longer operational. From what we know about the contract cheating industry, however, it would not be surprising if the same parent company were operating today under a different website domain.
Professors and scholars have been writing about Internet-based contract cheating for decades (Oliphant, 2002; Scanlon, 2002; Whiteman & Gordon, 2001), but deeper investigations to understand how the industry operates did not start gaining momentum until the term “contract cheating” was coined by Clarke and Lancaster (2006). Media scandals in Australia (McNeilage & Visentin, 2014; Visentin, 2015) and the United Kingdom(Yorke, 2017) have resulted in large-scale, coordinated efforts not only to understand the corporate cheating cartels, but to combat them.

Contract Cheating Industry: Business Models and Operations

Contract Cheating Industry: Business Models and Operations
Because the contract cheating industry has always existed on the margins, with companies being privately rather than publicly held and many of them operating online, its size and scope remain elusive. The early business models from the 1970s, in which a parent company had subsidiary offices in various locations, are still common. The difference is that the business operations are now mainly Internet based. Parent companies operate multiple online storefronts (sometimes dozens or hundreds), customizing their marketing on the various websites to the particular market segments they wish to target.

Because the contract cheating industry has always existed on the margins, with companies being privately rather than publicly held and many of them operating online, its size and scope remain elusive. The early business models from the 1970s, in which a parent company had subsidiary offices in various locations, are still common. The difference is that the business operations are now mainly Internet based. Parent companies operate multiple online storefronts (sometimes dozens or hundreds), customizing their marketing on the various websites to the particular market segments they wish to target.
While conducting a study on contract cheating, Roswita Dressler and I observed that a company might offer a site for American customers through one online storefront operating under a.com Uniform Resource Locator (URL) and have a mirror site, complete with maple leaves, targeted at Canadian customers and operating under a .ca URL (Eaton & Dressler, 2019). The companies would even localize the marketing language used on the website to make it seem as though the company were local, using phrases such as “sixth grade” on its American site but “grade six” on its Canadian site (Eaton & Dressler, 2019). I suppose it only stands to reason that these online cheating cartels would localize their marketing to just about any country in the world, since they also offered services in multiple languages (Eaton & Dressler, 2019).

The companies would even localize the marketing language used on the website to make it seem as though the company were local, using phrases such as “sixth grade” on its American site but “grade six” on its Canadian site (Eaton & Dressler, 2019). I suppose it only stands to reason that these online cheating cartels would localize their marketing to just about any country in the world, since they also offered services in multiple languages (Eaton & Dressler, 2019).
It is common for students to place orders online when purchasing contract cheating services and products from commercial providers. Companies will often have an online portal through which the workflow and transactions are managed. In some models, a contractor is assigned to the job moments after it is submitted. Another business model includes an online auction, in which students upload a copy of their assignment and contractors bid on the job (Newton & Lang, 2016). Assignments are turned around quickly, with the average delivery time being about five days, though about a quarter of the orders are completed within twenty-four hours (Newton & Lang, 2016).

Companies market their services aggressively, targeting students through online ads and on social media (Fellner, 2020). Companies also infiltrate campuses directly, hiring students to distribute flyers and post ads on bulletin boards. Some companies have been known to sponsor student parties, offering groups up to thousands of dollars and paying forparty supplies and services (e.g., DJs, bartenders, and alcohol), on the condition that students give out swag or hang banners advertising the services of the contract cheating companies (Young, 2020).

Legal Aspects of Contract Cheating

Legal Aspects of Contract Cheating
Unlike plagiarism and other forms of academic cheating that are dealt with at the institutional level, the introduction of external third parties, particularly those that operate on a commercial level, have propagated questions such as, “Is this legal?” among many people, both on and off college campuses. Legal action against term paper mills started in the early 1970s in the United States, not long after the industry began to flourish (McCormick & Whaley, 2014; Newton & Lang, 2016).

Unlike plagiarism and other forms of academic cheating that are dealt with at the institutional level, the introduction of external third parties, particularly those that operate on a commercial level, have propagated questions such as, “Is this legal?” among many people, both on and off college campuses. Legal action against term paper mills started in the early 1970s in the United States, not long after the industry began to flourish (McCormick & Whaley, 2014; Newton & Lang, 2016).
On October 20, 1972, theNew York Timeswas one of the first newspapers to report on the courts ordering a contract cheating business to close. The brief but detailed article explains how the New York State Supreme Court ordered the closure of “a group of ghost writers who sold term papers, essays and theses for advanced degrees to college students” (p. 84), based on a case brought forward by the attorney general. The article goes on to note that the service “operated from an office on 15 East 40th Street” between October and December 1971. What is fascinating about this article is a statement by the attorney general’s office that “the action was aimed [at] the term-paper sellers rather than the student customers because the students were given immunity to testify in the case” (p. 84). Educators, scholars, and students in the twenty-first century advocate for the same approach of going after the companies, which have now grown into multimillion-dollar conglomerates, operating mainly online, but serving millions of students in a variety of countries.

The article goes on to note that the service “operated from an office on 15 East 40th Street” between October and December 1971. Educators, scholars, and students in the twenty-first century advocate for the same approach of going after the companies, which have now grown into multimillion-dollar conglomerates, operating mainly online, but serving millions of students in a variety of countries.
Another critical point of the 1972New York Timesaccount can be found in the final line of the article, which states, “The defendant companies were Termpapers, Inc., and three subsidiaries” (p. 84). This shows the business model of a parent company operating with multiple subsidiaries, which dates back decades. This model continues to be evident today, though it thrives principally as an online industry.

Contract cheating is currently illegal in several U.S. states, but not all of them. The research center at the Florida State University College of Law (n.d.) has maintained an excellent website with information about statutes and legislative information about the contract cheating industry in the United States. In New Zealand, a law was introduced in 2011 making it illegal to advertise or provide cheating services to students (Draper & Newton, 2017; Newton & Lang, 2016). In Canada, three arrests were made for exam impersonation at universities between 2012 and 2019 (Eaton,2020), though formal legislation has yet to be brought forward in any Canadian province or territory. However, other countries have been actively working to establish legislation that would make contact cheating illegal (Awdry & Newton, 2019; Draper & Newton, 2017; Newton & Lang, 2016). For example, in late 2019, the Australian government (2019) brought forward draft legislation that would “make it an offence to provide or advertise academic cheating services” (p. 1). The bill proposed to punish suppliers with up to two years of imprisonment and fines of up to 105,000 Australian dollars, reports John Ross (2019) ofTimes Higher Education. This converts to about $62,220 U.S. dollars. It is not unreasonable to expect that over the next couple of decades, more countries around the world will begin to enact legislation to make contract cheating illegal.

Understanding the Student Side of Contract Cheating

Understanding the Student Side of Contract Cheating
It has been difficult for researchers to ascertain exactly how many students engage in contract cheating. In one study of 698 student respondents from across nine postsecondary institutions, Scanlon and Neumann (2002) found that “6.0% of participants indicated that they bought papers online sometimes, whereas only 2.3% specified they did so often or very frequently” (p. 380). In a large meta-analysis of 1,378 data sets, Curtis and Clare (2017) found that an aggregate of 3.5 percent of students engaged in contract cheating, although they noted some variance in their samples. Other estimates have ranged from one in seven students, or about 14 percent (Newton, 2018), to 22 percent (Hosney & Fatima, 2014). There also appears to be a consensus among researchers that if a student buys academic work once, that person is at a significant risk of becoming a repeat offender (Curtis & Claire, 2017; Scanlon & Newman, 2002).

Risks to Students: Blackmail and Academic Sanctions

Risks to Students: Blackmail and Academic Sanctions
In 2018, the BBC aired an exposéon the student experience of contract cheating. The first interviewee, a clean-cut young graduate, explains how he worked as a supplier to the industry. The second interviewee, whose face is never revealed, shares his story of using a contract cheating service. The latter explained that his laptop was stolen during a weekend trip to London. The laptop contained three essays that he had not backed up, one of which was due three days later. The student explains he “went into panic mode” and decided to pay for an essay because he had been denied an extension to the due date of his assignment. The student explained how he ordered and paid for his assignment through an online service, and goes on to state that a couple of days after receiving his essay, he began to receivee-mails from the company demanding more money, with threats that if he did not pay, that the essay would be posted online (which meant that it could be found by text-matching software used by the university, and hence the student might be exposed as a fraud). The demands for more money increased. The student reported that he eventually paid an extra 400 British pounds, but the company sent the essay directly to the university anyway, reporting the student for using their services. He was immediately called in by the administration for academic misconduct.

The demands for more money increased. The student reported that he eventually paid an extra 400 British pounds, but the company sent the essay directly to the university anyway, reporting the student for using their services. He was immediately called in by the administration for academic misconduct.
Other reports of students being blackmailed for using contract cheating companies began to surface not long after this story aired (O’Brien, 2019; Ross, 2018). In early 2020, research on contract cheating companies blackmailing their “customers” emerged, debunking the myth that this was simply an urban legend (Yorke, Sefcik, & Veeran-Colton, 2020). Blackmail from contract cheating companies poses a real threat to students financially, psychologically, and academically, and for the most part, students are unaware of these risks (Yorke et al., 2020).

PREVENTION

PREVENTION
In this section, I offer some strategies for prevention, but I do so with a caveat. Preventative measures are not a guarantee. It can be difficult to prevent cheating that results from a well-intentioned “snowplow enabler” who insists on doing the work on the student’s behalf or helping them so much that it becomes unclear who actually did the work. Nevertheless, educators can take some steps to keep the focus on students’ learning to help prevent contract cheating (Baird & Clare, 2017; Clare et al., 2017; Harper et al., 2020; Newton & Lang, 2016).

In this section, I offer some strategies for prevention, but I do so with a caveat. Preventative measures are not a guarantee. It can be difficult to prevent cheating that results from a well-intentioned “snowplow enabler” who insists on doing the work on the student’s behalf or helping them so much that it becomes unclear who actually did the work. Nevertheless, educators can take some steps to keep the focus on students’ learning to help prevent contract cheating (Baird & Clare, 2017; Clare et al., 2017; Harper et al., 2020; Newton & Lang, 2016).
Have Open Conversations with Students about Contract Cheating

Have Open Conversations with Students about Contract Cheating
Let students know that you are aware that contract cheating exists. Some faculty remain oblivious to the existence of the contract cheating industry. When I talk with my students openly about contract cheating, some of them are surprised that I know about it. Explain that when students outsource their work, they are not learning. I tell my students, “You are here to learn, and I am here to help you do that. If you are not learning, I am not doing my job. So, if you find yourself in a position where you are tempted to make a decision you might regret later, come and talk to me first. We’ll figure it out together.” By doing this, I am communicating to my students that I care about them, first and foremost. It is important to putthe students first and the submission of assignments second. I also tell my students that I am trained in how to identify signs of contract cheating in student work. Although I am not perfect at this, the idea that a professor is alert to particular signs of contract cheating is enough to raise a red flag for students. Making students aware that there are systems in place to detect contract cheating can be an effective prevention strategy (Baird & Clare, 2017), but it is also important to keep the focus on learning, rather than on “Gotcha!” (Howard, 2001).

Make Learning the Focus, not Grades

Make Learning the Focus, not Grades
How educators place their focus on learning will vary depending on the constraints placed upon them by the systems in which they work. Some examples include reviewing draft work, engaging in class and individual discussion about the work, extending deadlines if students find themselves in overwhelming or exceptional circumstances, and engaging in time management and assignment-planning activities. Give students every opportunity to learn before you give them a summative grade.

Give students every opportunity to learn before you give them a summative grade.
Avoid Recycling Assignments

Avoid Recycling Assignments
Although I discussed this in detail inChapter 5, on evaluation and assessment, it is worth stressing again. Contract cheating has been identified as being more prevalent in courses where there is ample opportunity to outsource the assignment (Baird & Claire, 2017). Recycling assignments semester after semester and year after year is tantamount to inviting students to engage in file sharing, contract cheating, and plagiarism.

Focus on Assignments That Are Relevant to Students’ Own Lives

Focus on Assignments That Are Relevant to Students’ Own Lives
Instead of assigning an essay on the plot ofHamlet,why not ask students to find some aspect ofHamletthat resonates with them personally and connect it to their local community. For example, a focus on Hamlet’s madness could lead to an exploration of mental health in young men, leading to an inquiry about what supports a modern-day Hamlet could have accessed on campus or in the local city to help him. (Of course, accessing such supports might have changed the entire outcome of the play, and that is a different discussion.) The objective is to go from the general to the specific. There are already many essays about Hamlet and mental illness, but by extending the inquiry to a local context, with specificreferences to resources and upcoming events on the students’ own campus that address mental health, the likelihood of an outsourced product from a contract cheating supplier that is specific to the assignment goals may be diminished.

Assess Students in a Variety of Ways

Assess Students in a Variety of Ways
Although there is debate about whether the straight-up essay assigned as homework is among the easiest to outsource (Harper et al., 2020), there is evidence that certain types of assignments are outsourced more often, with the boring old essay near the top of the list. Assessing students in a variety of ways not only helps to prevent contract cheating, it is also an aspect of effective pedagogy. When we acknowledge this, we can begin to think creatively about how to assess students in more diverse ways, such as oral exams, practice-based exams, and creative work (Harper et al., 2020), as well as case studies in which the criteria or variables for the case change (Baird & Clare, 2017). There are myriad ways to assess students in creative and engaging ways that keep the focus on learning. Brainstorming new assessment ideas, experimenting with various assessment types and then reflecting on how well they worked can provide educators with an opportunity to develop professionally as they uphold academic integrity. Not only that, but the class is likely to be more interesting for students, too.

Detection

Detection
In this section, I offer evidence-informed strategies about how educators can identify a case of contract cheating in student work.

In this section, I offer evidence-informed strategies about how educators can identify a case of contract cheating in student work.
Provide Training to Educators

Provide Training to Educators
Providing professors and teaching assistants (TAs) with practical, hands-on training about how to identify contract cheating is an effective way to help them detect it (Claire et al., 2017; Dawson & Sutherland-Smith, 2018a, 2018b). Training opportunities for educators on how to identify contract cheating remain limited or even nonexistent in many jurisdictions. This is certainly a topic worthy of consideration for professional development days, teachers’ conventions, and graduate TA workshops.

Training opportunities for educators on how to identify contract cheating remain limited or even nonexistent in many jurisdictions. This is certainly a topic worthy of consideration for professional development days, teachers’ conventions, and graduate TA workshops.
In the absence of training, simple and practical tools may help educators interested in learning more. Although such tools are not a substitute for hands-on training, they can serve as a starting point and help thosewho do not have access to professional development that is focused on contract cheating. A number of practical tools are freely available on the Internet to help teachers become aware of how to detect contract cheating and what to do when they suspect or discover a case (Bretag & Harper, n.d.; Eaton, 2018, 2019; International Center for Academic Integrity, 2016; University of California San Diego, n.d.; University of New South Wales, n.d.).

Be Alert to Signs of Contract Cheating

Be Alert to Signs of Contract Cheating
Some telltale signs that an assignment has been outsourced include:

Some telltale signs that an assignment has been outsourced include:
- The contents of the assignment do not match the instructions. If the submission differs from the assigned topic, there could be cause for concern regarding a possible violation of academic integrity.

- The writing is vague and imprecise. Commercial contract cheating suppliers need to work quickly, so the product can end up overly generalized and vague (Tomar, 2013).

- The writing and analysis do not match the student’s skill level. A first-year undergraduate student is unlikely to be able to write about advanced theories, for example. If the work is more advanced than what the student should be capable of given her or his level, it could signal that someone else completed the work.

- The metadata does not match. In Microsoft Word, this means looking under the Properties tab to see if the name of the writer matches the name of the person who submitted the assignment. A mismatch of metadata is not absolute proof that the assignment has been completed by someone else (because students can share computers), but it can be at least a yellow flag when considered in conjunction with additional evidence.

- There are bizarre referencing and citations. If the student has referenced obscure or out-of-print books that are not available at the institutional library, this might be cause for concern. Similarly, if the student has referenced other kinds of sources that would not be reasonably available to him or her, this might also signal cause for concern.

These are not the only signs of contract cheating, and neither should any of them be considered proof that an assignment was completed by someone else. But these are examples of things that can alert an educator that there might be reasons to dig deeper to see if the work was outsourced.

Discovery Interview

Discovery Interview
One of the most successful strategies that educators can use to determine if contract cheating has occurred is to conduct an interview with the student (Baird & Clare, 2017; Bretag, 2017; QAA, 2017). Adiscovery interviewis a one-to-one conversation with a student to determine if contract cheating has occurred. Colleagues at Bow Valley College in Canada developed an internal resource for their teaching staff to help them learn how to conduct such an interview. They gave me permission to adapt and share the resource, which is available for free on the Internet as a one-page, open-access download (Eaton, 2019). Here are some of the key highlights:

Colleagues at Bow Valley College in Canada developed an internal resource for their teaching staff to help them learn how to conduct such an interview. They gave me permission to adapt and share the resource, which is available for free on the Internet as a one-page, open-access download (Eaton, 2019). Here are some of the key highlights:
- Take a neutral stance.Avoid accusing the student. Instead, start with an exploratory intention. Try to work with the student to figure out what happened.

- Avoid showing anger.A discovery interview is not a trial. It is about understanding how the student went about getting the assignment completed.

- Allow the student the opportunity to explain themself.Engage the student in an open conversation. The point of the interview is to discover what happened. To do that, the student must be given an opportunity to talk.

- Document what happened.Write down what questions you asked, as well as how the student responded. This can be useful if further investigation is required. Let the student know that you will be taking notes.

Take a neutral stance.
Avoid accusing the student. Instead, start with an exploratory intention. Try to work with the student to figure out what happened.
Avoid showing anger.
A discovery interview is not a trial. It is about understanding how the student went about getting the assignment completed.
Allow the student the opportunity to explain themself.
Engage the student in an open conversation. The point of the interview is to discover what happened. To do that, the student must be given an opportunity to talk.
Document what happened.
Write down what questions you asked, as well as how the student responded. This can be useful if further investigation is required. Let the student know that you will be taking notes.
Some common questions and conversation probes to guide a discovery interview include the following:

Some common questions and conversation probes to guide a discovery interview include the following:
- Tell me how you went about completing this assignment.

- What resources did you consult to complete your work? Why did you choose those resources?

- In your work, you mention these advanced terms/concepts. Could you explain to me in your own words what these mean to you?

- Tell me about your conclusion. How did you arrive at that conclusion?

- Is there anything else that you’d like to tell me?

Using an approach such as this, it should become evident whether students have completed their own work, gotten extra help, outsourced it, or struggled terribly with the concepts involved.

Take Steps to Validate Students’ Identities

Take Steps to Validate Students’ Identities
News reports of imposters taking college entrance exams on behalf of students in the United States have been reported by the media as far back as the mid-1960s (Tolchin, 1965), and exam impersonation continues to be a problem today (Harper et al., 2020; Theophille & King, 2019). In addition, exam impersonators have been arrested and charged with fraud in some jurisdictions (Meager, 2016; Prisiajny & Lai, 2015). Identity verification tools are becoming more common for in-person exams. Such tools require that students present a valid government photo ID before going into the exam hall. A proctor runs the ID through a scanner to determine if it is real or fake, and then, a visual check of the photo ID to match it to the student’s face can be conducted. Such checks may not prevent all exam impersonation, but they can act as a deterrent.

News reports of imposters taking college entrance exams on behalf of students in the United States have been reported by the media as far back as the mid-1960s (Tolchin, 1965), and exam impersonation continues to be a problem today (Harper et al., 2020; Theophille & King, 2019). In addition, exam impersonators have been arrested and charged with fraud in some jurisdictions (Meager, 2016; Prisiajny & Lai, 2015). Identity verification tools are becoming more common for in-person exams. Such tools require that students present a valid government photo ID before going into the exam hall. A proctor runs the ID through a scanner to determine if it is real or fake, and then, a visual check of the photo ID to match it to the student’s face can be conducted. Such checks may not prevent all exam impersonation, but they can act as a deterrent.
As more courses move to online and remote formats, the question of how to validate students’ identities becomes more urgent. E-proctoring services are becoming more prevalent, and the topic of e-assessment has become a point of interest among educators and researchers. The TeSLA Project, funded by the European Commission, is an example of a large-scale, multicountry initiative to advance e-assessment of student work, including facial recognition, voice recognition, keystroke patterns, and plagiarism detection, among other tools (Baró-Soléet al., 2018; Edwards et al., 2019; TeSLA, 2020). There are questions related to data security and privacy that are beyond the scope of this book, but suffice it to say that identity verification is becoming simultaneously more commonplace and more sophisticated. In terms of the prevention of plagiarism and other forms of academic misconduct, it is likely that identity verification will become a more prevalent topic of discussion, particularly in higher education, where class size continues to grow and online and remote learning programs proliferate.

CONCLUSION

CONCLUSION
Students engage in contract cheating for a variety of reasons and in a number of ways, from working with an enabler with good intentions to falling prey to large-scale, commercial cheating cartels designed to separate students from their money while absolving themselves of any of the associated risks of academic misconduct. But the bottom line is that when a third party intervenes, a student’s learning is not only interrupted, it is disrupted. As education becomes increasingly more corporatized and commodified, so too does academic cheating (Bretag et al., 2018).

9
Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion

Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion
In this chapter, I tackle some of the most complex and polarizing aspects of academic misconduct: diversity, equity, and inclusion. Many terms and labels are used to refer to those students who do not fit into the primarily White, English-speaking, high-achieving dominant class. I address some of the most contentious debates happening with regard to plagiarism in higher education: international students, students for whom English is an Additional Language (EAL), and other racialized minorities. I also discuss students with learning disabilities, which is not so much a topic of vigorous debate as it is marginalized or practically absent from broader discussions about academic integrity. As Henry et al. (2017) point out, “Despite many efforts, which most often amount to no more than well-worded mission statements and cosmetic changes, inequality, indifference, and reliance on outmoded conservative traditions characterize the modern neoliberal university” (p. 300). Addressing systemic inequities about how particular groups of students are treated with regard to academic integrity is important and necessary.

In this chapter, I tackle some of the most complex and polarizing aspects of academic misconduct: diversity, equity, and inclusion. Many terms and labels are used to refer to those students who do not fit into the primarily White, English-speaking, high-achieving dominant class. I address some of the most contentious debates happening with regard to plagiarism in higher education: international students, students for whom English is an Additional Language (EAL), and other racialized minorities. I also discuss students with learning disabilities, which is not so much a topic of vigorous debate as it is marginalized or practically absent from broader discussions about academic integrity. As Henry et al. (2017) point out, “Despite many efforts, which most often amount to no more than well-worded mission statements and cosmetic changes, inequality, indifference, and reliance on outmoded conservative traditions characterize the modern neoliberal university” (p. 300). Addressing systemic inequities about how particular groups of students are treated with regard to academic integrity is important and necessary.
I began this book by situating myself within the work, as discussed in the preface. When we start from a place of critical reflexivity about our own identities, we acknowledge our subjectivity and biases, as well as our intersubjective relationships with others (Walshaw, 2011). Although I have expertise in academic integrity and plagiarism, I am not an expert in diversity, equity, and inclusion. I am a White woman scholar whose primary employment has been at North American universities. I have discussedelsewhere that I grew up poor and was instructed from an early age at home to believe that education was emancipatory, a path to a better life (Eaton, 2020). I have also had the privilege of living and studying abroad in a foreign language. Having said that, my heritage is British and my native language is English, both of which situate me within the Eurocentric, dominant culture that permeates Western educational institutions. Although I consider myself an advocate and an ally, I can make no claims of being subjected to systemic injustice based on race, language, or academic ability.

Having said that, my heritage is British and my native language is English, both of which situate me within the Eurocentric, dominant culture that permeates Western educational institutions. Although I consider myself an advocate and an ally, I can make no claims of being subjected to systemic injustice based on race, language, or academic ability.
For those who engage in academic integrity scholarship, advocacy, education, and administration, it is incumbent upon us to understand who we are in relation to those with whom we interact. Not all experiences are equal, especially when it comes to academic integrity and breaches of it. Understanding our individual positionality in relation to others, as well as in relation to the larger systems in which we work, can help us to engage in more thoughtful conversations about the values of academic integrity (International Center for Academic Integrity, 2014) and how we enact them, both individually and collectively.

BIAS AND RACIAL PROFILING

BIAS AND RACIAL PROFILING
Plagiarism among so-called international students has long been a subject of debate (Haitch, 2016) that is embedded within a wider dialogue about the commodification and neoliberalization of higher education in general (Saltmarsh, 2005). Although the broader topic of neoliberalization is relevant, it has already been covered at length in the literature (e.g., Apple, 2004; Hébert & Abdi, 2013; Olssen & Peters, 2005). Therefore, in this discussion, I maintain a tighter focus on academic integrity and plagiarism, as these have implications for individual educators, case managers, and others whose work directly deals with alleged or actual academic misconduct. This chapter is also aimed at readers in educational contexts where the dominant language is English (e.g., the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and New Zealand, among others). For readers working in other language contexts, what I discuss here may be transferrable, as the research that informs this chapter has been conducted in countries where English as a Foreign Language (EFL) is taught (Amiri & Razmjoo, 2016; Sabbaghan, 2010).

Plagiarism among so-called international students has long been a subject of debate (Haitch, 2016) that is embedded within a wider dialogue about the commodification and neoliberalization of higher education in general (Saltmarsh, 2005). Although the broader topic of neoliberalization is relevant, it has already been covered at length in the literature (e.g., Apple, 2004; H
é
bert & Abdi, 2013; Olssen & Peters, 2005). Therefore, in this discussion, I maintain a tighter focus on academic integrity and plagiarism, as these have implications for individual educators, case managers, and others whose work directly deals with alleged or actual academic misconduct. This chapter is also aimed at readers in educational contexts where the dominant language is English (e.g., the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and New Zealand, among others). For readers working in other language contexts, what I discuss here may be transferrable, as the research that informs this chapter has been conducted in countries where English as a Foreign Language (EFL) is taught (Amiri & Razmjoo, 2016; Sabbaghan, 2010).
There has been much discussion on North American campuses and beyond about plagiarism among students from particular countries. It is not only important, but essential, for members of academic communities to puzzle through the complexities and understand the issue from a variety of perspectives. There is a risk of implicit bias, if not outright racism,when we talk about international students and academic misconduct (Bexley & Vu, 2015; Bretag, 2019; Leask, 2006; Openo, 2019; Rennie et al., 2018). It is important to resist the temptation to demonize people as being predisposed to plagiarize simply because of where they come from.

There has been much discussion on North American campuses and beyond about plagiarism among students from particular countries. It is not only important, but essential, for members of academic communities to puzzle through the complexities and understand the issue from a variety of perspectives. There is a risk of implicit bias, if not outright racism,
when we talk about international students and academic misconduct (Bexley & Vu, 2015; Bretag, 2019; Leask, 2006; Openo, 2019; Rennie et al., 2018). It is important to resist the temptation to demonize people as being predisposed to plagiarize simply because of where they come from.
The term “international students” is used pejoratively in discourse about plagiarism (and other forms of academic and nonacademic misconduct). There is no consensus, globally or domestically, on how to define “international students.” It is a broad term that has been misused. In some jurisdictions, there are specific classifications applied to those students who require a visa to study in a local context (and often pay exorbitantly higher tuition than domestic students). When used in this way, the term “international student” includes those who may be native English speakers from countries with similar educational structures and systems (Eaton & Burns, 2018). For example, a Canadian student who speaks English as a first language and has a European background studying in the United States is an international student. Similarly, an American student who speaks English as a first language studying in Canada would also be an international student.

The term “international students” is used pejoratively in discourse about plagiarism (and other forms of academic and nonacademic misconduct). There is no consensus, globally or domestically, on how to define “international students.” It is a broad term that has been misused. In some jurisdictions, there are specific classifications applied to those students who require a visa to study in a local context (and often pay exorbitantly higher tuition than domestic students). When used in this way, the term “international student” includes those who may be native English speakers from countries with similar educational structures and systems (Eaton & Burns, 2018). For example, a Canadian student who speaks English as a first language and has a European background studying in the United States is an international student. Similarly, an American student who speaks English as a first language studying in Canada would also be an international student.
The terms “international student” (Amsberry, 2010; Badke, 2002; Marsden, Carroll, & Neill, 2005) and “overseas visa student” (Marsden, Carroll, & Neill, 2005, p. 1) may be used in vague, ill-defined, and pejorative ways when discussing academic misconduct. In some cases, these terms have become a euphemism to refer to students who are not White and whose first language is not English. The euphemism can also extend to students who come from countries where English is an official language of instruction, but where the dominant culture is anything other than European, such as Hong Kong and Singapore.

The terms “international student” (Amsberry, 2010; Badke, 2002; Marsden, Carroll, & Neill, 2005) and “overseas visa student” (Marsden, Carroll, & Neill, 2005, p. 1) may be used in vague, ill-defined, and pejorative ways when discussing academic misconduct. In some cases, these terms have become a euphemism to refer to students who are not White and whose first language is not English. The euphemism can also extend to students who come from countries where English is an official language of instruction, but where the dominant culture is anything other than European, such as Hong Kong and Singapore.
One scholar with deep expertise in the area of internationalization in higher education notes that “students from ‘other cultures’ are frequently highlighted as being perpetrators of this crime against the academic community of enlightened Western scholars” (Leask, 2006, p. 183). This quotation captures the attitudes of a subset of those who work in higher education contexts who truly believe that they (the White, English-speaking, dominant class) are the enlightened, and all others are not only culturally inferior and academically deficient, but also culpable of misconduct because they come from a different background; in their eyes, such people are classified as “undesirable others” (Saltmarsh, 2005, p. 1). This attitude only exacerbates the ethical and moral binaries that have often characterized opinions on, and approaches to addressing, plagiarism (Bertram Gallant, 2008; Valentine, 2006).

One scholar with deep expertise in the area of internationalization in higher education notes that “students from ‘other cultures’ are frequently highlighted as being perpetrators of this crime against the academic community of enlightened Western scholars” (Leask, 2006, p. 183). This quotation captures the attitudes of a subset of those who work in higher education contexts who truly believe that they (the White, English-speaking, dominant class) are the enlightened, and all others are not only culturally inferior and academically deficient, but also culpable of misconduct because they come from a different background; in their eyes, such people are classified as “undesirable others” (Saltmarsh, 2005, p. 1). This attitude only exacerbates the ethical and moral binaries that have often characterized opinions on, and approaches to addressing, plagiarism (Bertram Gallant, 2008; Valentine, 2006).
Just as there are stereotypes and assumptions about international students, so too are there assumptions about domestic students. We must be careful not to talk about students studying in culturally heterogeneousenvironments as if they were a homogeneous group. For example, researchers have talked about Australian students (Ehrich et al., 2016; Marsden et al., 2005), Canadian students (Austin et al., 2006; Marquez-Perez, 2000), and even American students (McCabe, 1992) as if these groups were culturally and linguistically homogenous, which is not the case at all. Domestic students include thousands of people from ethnically and linguistically diverse backgrounds (Bexley & Vu, 2015; Eaton & Burns, 2018). Bexley and Vu point out that “the university is no longer an enclave for a small group of Anglo-Saxon elites brought up in ‘good families’ and having attended ‘good schools’ ” (2015, n.p.).

Just as there are stereotypes and assumptions about international students, so too are there assumptions about domestic students. We must be careful not to talk about students studying in culturally heterogeneous
environments as if they were a homogeneous group. For example, researchers have talked about Australian students (Ehrich et al., 2016; Marsden et al., 2005), Canadian students (Austin et al., 2006; Marquez-Perez, 2000), and even American students (McCabe, 1992) as if these groups were culturally and linguistically homogenous, which is not the case at all. Domestic students include thousands of people from ethnically and linguistically diverse backgrounds (Bexley & Vu, 2015; Eaton & Burns, 2018). Bexley and Vu point out that “the university is no longer an enclave for a small group of Anglo-Saxon elites brought up in ‘good families’ and having attended ‘good schools’ ” (2015, n.p.).
We should also be cautious about comparative studies that aim to identify cheating differences between students from two or more different countries or geocultural regions, particularly if one or more of the areas studied have student bodies who are linguistically and culturally diverse, such as the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom (see Marquez-Perez, 2000), or, even more broadly, Asia (Greenblatt, 2009). Some studies have compared students from a “mono-culture” (Mansouri & Arber, 2017), with students studying in countries with culturally diverse populations (Chapman & Lupton, 2004; Diekhoff et al., 1999; Labeff, Shinohara, & Yasukawa, 1999). In some cases, researchers have not addressed cultural heterogeneity at all, not realizing that their results are like comparing apples to all the fruit in the basket.

We should also be cautious about comparative studies that aim to identify cheating differences between students from two or more different countries or geocultural regions, particularly if one or more of the areas studied have student bodies who are linguistically and culturally diverse, such as the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom (see Marquez-Perez, 2000), or, even more broadly, Asia (Greenblatt, 2009). Some studies have compared students from a “mono-culture” (Mansouri & Arber, 2017), with students studying in countries with culturally diverse populations (Chapman & Lupton, 2004; Diekhoff et al., 1999; Labeff, Shinohara, & Yasukawa, 1999). In some cases, researchers have not addressed cultural heterogeneity at all, not realizing that their results are like comparing apples to all the fruit in the basket.
These studies can have an underlying value assumption—namely, that students who study in one country are somehow more ethical or morally superior to students from another. There are so many systemic factors that must be taken into consideration that “culture,” or the country where students are working, simply cannot tell the whole story. Comparative studies that fail to address linguistic and cultural diversity can further propagate racialized approaches to academic misconduct that detract from a focus on helping students learn.
