There are so many systemic factors that must be taken into consideration that “culture,” or the country where students are working, simply cannot tell the whole story. Comparative studies that fail to address linguistic and cultural diversity can further propagate racialized approaches to academic misconduct that detract from a focus on helping students learn.
CULTURE, VALUES, AND MYTHS

CULTURE, VALUES, AND MYTHS
There has been ample discussion of culture in the academic integrity literature (e.g., Amsberry, 2010; Liu, 2005; Phan, 2006; Saltmarsh, 2005). There has been an almost pathological focus on comparing students from collectivist versus individualist cultures using Hofstede’s (1984, 2001) cultural dimensions. In particular, there has been particular emphasis on comparing students from Confucian heritage countries with those from more individualist Western nations (Chien, 2014; Ehrich et al., 2016; Sowden, 2005). There has been a corresponding lack of consideration of the critiques of Hofstede’s models, which include criticism of hismethodological simplicity (Jones, 2007); the assumption that culture can be equated with nations (Baskerville, 2003); reductionist interpretations of culture that are overly linear and ultimately promote binary approaches to cultural understanding (Hampden-Turner & Trompenaars, 1997), and an overall lack of criticality about the complexities of the definitions and understandings of what culture is (Baskerville, 2003; Hampden-Turner & Trompenaars, 1997; Jones, 2007). Hampden-Turner and Trompenaars (1997) explicitly object to the position that a culture can be either individualist or collectivist, instead proposing that culture cannot be understood as “a series of straight lines” (p. 150).

There has been ample discussion of culture in the academic integrity literature (e.g., Amsberry, 2010; Liu, 2005; Phan, 2006; Saltmarsh, 2005). There has been an almost pathological focus on comparing students from collectivist versus individualist cultures using Hofstede’s (1984, 2001) cultural dimensions. In particular, there has been particular emphasis on comparing students from Confucian heritage countries with those from more individualist Western nations (Chien, 2014; Ehrich et al., 2016; Sowden, 2005). There has been a corresponding lack of consideration of the critiques of Hofstede’s models, which include criticism of his
methodological simplicity (Jones, 2007); the assumption that culture can be equated with nations (Baskerville, 2003); reductionist interpretations of culture that are overly linear and ultimately promote binary approaches to cultural understanding (Hampden-Turner & Trompenaars, 1997), and an overall lack of criticality about the complexities of the definitions and understandings of what culture is (Baskerville, 2003; Hampden-Turner & Trompenaars, 1997; Jones, 2007). Hampden-Turner and Trompenaars (1997) explicitly object to the position that a culture can be either individualist or collectivist, instead proposing that culture cannot be understood as “a series of straight lines” (p. 150).
These very same critiques against binary approaches to understanding culture parallel the ethical dichotomies that academic integrity experts highlight as problematic when addressing academic misconduct. The world cannot simply be divided into “individualist versus collectivist” or “cheaters and noncheaters.” Individuals are infinitely more complex than these simplistic classifications. For these reasons, I implore educators and administrators to reject the notion that students from any particular country might plagiarize or cheat more often than any other. Such assertions are not only unhelpful, they propagate systemic racism against particular groups. It is more important to keep the focus on learning for all students, rather than try to explain plagiarism as a function of culture.

A Problem of Acculturation, not Culture

A Problem of Acculturation, not Culture
Another problem with much of the academic misconduct research is that it often deals with self-reported data or perceptions. A different picture emerges when we turn our attention to studies that investigate actual cases. In a study of 158 undergraduate students, Martin, Rao, and Sloan (2011) found that student acculturation, not ethnicity, was a stronger predictor of plagiarizing behavior. The researchers screened student participants’ research papers using Turnitin and found that 61 percent of them showed plagiarism. The researchers then used surveys to determine demographic differences and dimensions of acculturation. Results showed that students of Asian heritage didnotplagiarize more than other students. There were, however, differences among students from a variety of backgrounds who identified as being more acculturated with American educational norms. Martin and colleagues (2011) discussed the possibility that students who are less acculturated are potentially more alienated and may have a poorer understanding of the educational expectations and norms of the local culture in which they are studying. This points toacculturationto educational norms and expectations, rather than heritage, language, or culture, as being risk factors.

The Need for Academic Integrity Education: Tutorials, Workshops, and Ongoing Learning

The Need for Academic Integrity Education: Tutorials, Workshops, and Ongoing Learning
Academic integrity tutorials and ongoing education can help students better integrate into their learning environments. Integration is understood to be “a two-sided process and as the capacity of people to live together with full respect for the dignity of each individual, the common good, pluralism and diversity, non-violence and solidarity, as well as their ability to participate in social, cultural, economic and political life” (Council of Europe, 2008, p. 11). The Council of Europe (2008) notes that immigrants in a country should, like all other citizens, abide by the laws and values of the host country. The same idea can be applied to students studying in a foreign host country: they must abide by the policies and educational expectations of their host institution and host country. The problem is that often no one tells incoming students—regardless of whether they are domestic or international—what the rules are. Students are expected to understand the values of academic integrity and how to enact them from the moment they step onto campus. The expectation that students should already know the academic expectations and institutional policies relating to academic integrity is a broader example of a systemic injustice, not only toward particular groups of students, but all students.

Academic integrity tutorials and ongoing education can help students better integrate into their learning environments. Integration is understood to be “a two-sided process and as the capacity of people to live together with full respect for the dignity of each individual, the common good, pluralism and diversity, non-violence and solidarity, as well as their ability to participate in social, cultural, economic and political life” (Council of Europe, 2008, p. 11). The Council of Europe (2008) notes that immigrants in a country should, like all other citizens, abide by the laws and values of the host country. The same idea can be applied to students studying in a foreign host country: they must abide by the policies and educational expectations of their host institution and host country. The problem is that often no one tells incoming students—regardless of whether they are domestic or international—what the rules are. Students are expected to understand the values of academic integrity and how to enact them from the moment they step onto campus. The expectation that students should already know the academic expectations and institutional policies relating to academic integrity is a broader example of a systemic injustice, not only toward particular groups of students, but all students.
Several studies have identified academic acculturation as being a strong predictor of plagiarism and other kinds of academic misconduct (Hurst et al., 2013; Sowden, 2005; Thompson et al., 2017). Research addressing the effects of direct instruction on academic integrity in the form of tutorials, workshops, and ongoing education has shown that both domestic students and those from other countries consistently have a better understanding of the values of academic integrity and institutional expectations about how to enact those values as a result of having direct academic integrity education (Benson et al., 2019; Chen & Van Ullen, 2011; Stoesz & Yudintseva, 2018; Stoesz & Los, 2019; Thompson et al., 2017).

Research addressing the effects of direct instruction on academic integrity in the form of tutorials, workshops, and ongoing education has shown that both domestic students and those from other countries consistently have a better understanding of the values of academic integrity and institutional expectations about how to enact those values as a result of having direct academic integrity education (Benson et al., 2019; Chen & Van Ullen, 2011; Stoesz & Yudintseva, 2018; Stoesz & Los, 2019; Thompson et al., 2017).
Academic integrity tutorials must go beyond indoctrination if they are to focus on inclusivity, dignity, and respect for persons. Many mandatory academic integrity tutorials follow a transmissionist model of education (Sutherland-Smith, 2008), in which students receive information but do not actively engage in learning. Some academic integrity tutorials are set up as automated, asynchronous e-learning modules that involve no human-to-human interaction whatsoever. That is because the goal of many tutorials is primarily to ensure that students who are found responsible for academic misconduct cannot use the excuse that they did not know what was expected of them or did not know the rules. In these cases, the primary goal of these tutorials is rooted in academic misconduct case management and policy, with the goal of student learning taking a back seat.For academic integrity education to be learner-focused, it is important to keep the notion of a two-sided process in mind. Students need opportunities to reflect, engage in dialogue, ask questions, and practice new skills in a safe environment focused on learning.

Overrepresentation of Racialized Minorities in Student Conduct Cases

Overrepresentation of Racialized Minorities in Student Conduct Cases
“Overrepresentation” is a term borrowed from criminal justice to refer to the excessive number of a particular group who are incarcerated, compared to their number or percentage in the overall population (Campbell & Wellman, 2020). When we use this term to talk about student conduct, we are talking about learners from a particular segment of the student body who are reported for misconduct more often than would be warranted given their representation in the general student population. There is a growing body of evidence showing that racialized minorities are overrepresented in academic misconduct cases, including plagiarism (Bertram Gallant, Binkin, & Donohue, 2015; Bretag, 2019; Christensen Hughes, 2010; Openo, 2019). This includes students from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, as well as students of color (Christensen Hughes, 2010). In other words, it could be that racialized minorities do not necessarily cheat or plagiarize more, but they are reported for it more often, found responsible of misconduct more often, and subsequently punished more harshly than White students. It is erroneous to assume that the composition of the groupreportedfor academic misconduct accurately represents the group whocommittedmisconduct. Because faculty members are reluctant to report plagiarism or other forms of misconduct for a variety of reasons (Flint, Clegg, & Macdonald, 2006; Jendrek, 1989; McCabe, 1993), there is likely a significant difference between reporting rates and the actual incidence of plagiarism and other forms of misconduct.

Racial and ethnic profiling are concerns in the criminal justice system (Boylan, 2011), as well as in student judicial affairs (Armour, 2016; Fabelo et al., 2011; Freeman, 2007). Research findings on students’ nonacademic misconduct can inform how we understand bias in the identification and management of academic integrity violations. One report from Texas found that once other variables had been accounted for, African American students were 31 percent more likely to be subjected to disciplinary action for misconduct than their Latinx or White peers (Fabelo et al., 2011, p. x). The same study showed that White students were less likely to be suspended or expelled from school for misconduct, and girls were less likely to be removed than boys (Fabelo et al., 2011). White girls were more likely to be forgiven or punished less harshly than any other group. No comparablestudies have been done for academic integrity violations, to the best of my knowledge. It is worth asking ourselves: who gets punished and who is most easily forgiven when breaches of academic integrity occur?

One report from Texas found that once other variables had been accounted for, African American students were 31 percent more likely to be subjected to disciplinary action for misconduct than their Latinx or White peers (Fabelo et al., 2011, p. x). The same study showed that White students were less likely to be suspended or expelled from school for misconduct, and girls were less likely to be removed than boys (Fabelo et al., 2011). White girls were more likely to be forgiven or punished less harshly than any other group. No comparable
studies have been done for academic integrity violations, to the best of my knowledge. It is worth asking ourselves: who gets punished and who is most easily forgiven when breaches of academic integrity occur?
Educational institutions often pay little attention to the possibility of racial or ethnic profiling in academic misconduct reporting (Christensen Hughes, 2010). In other words, when schools collect data about who plagiarizes or cheats, they often do not pay attention to whether particular student groups are represented more than others. Similarly, we fail to consider bias in reporting practices that might result in students from particular groups being identified as having committed more misconduct than others. There is an urgent need to address the issue of implicit bias in academic misconduct reporting and case management.

CONSIDERATIONS FOR DECOLONIZING AND INDIGENIZING ACADEMIC INTEGRITY

CONSIDERATIONS FOR DECOLONIZING AND INDIGENIZING ACADEMIC INTEGRITY
Considerations about decolonization and Indigenization have been all but absent from the academic integrity discourse, even though Indigenous work on academic integrity is starting to develop (e.g., Maracle, 2020). There is an urgent need to engage Indigenous peoples in conversations about academic integrity, not because Indigenous students are any more prone to breaches of misconduct than any other students, but because those from settler backgrounds have much to learn about Indigenous ways of knowing and being that could benefit all students.

Considerations about decolonization and Indigenization have been all but absent from the academic integrity discourse, even though Indigenous work on academic integrity is starting to develop (e.g., Maracle, 2020). There is an urgent need to engage Indigenous peoples in conversations about academic integrity, not because Indigenous students are any more prone to breaches of misconduct than any other students, but because those from settler backgrounds have much to learn about Indigenous ways of knowing and being that could benefit all students.
My colleague, Dr. Dustin Louie, an Indigenous scholar from “the Nadleh Whut’en and Nee Tahi Buhn First Nations of northern British Columbia,” Canada, points to the decolonizing practice of negotiating, which emphasizes “relationship building and connected futures instead of competing interests” (Louie et al., 2017, pp. 24, 47). Not surprisingly, research on academic integrity has shown that misconduct is less likely to happen when students believe that their teachers care about them (Christensen Hughes, 2017). Relationship building, not only with students, but with all stakeholders within and beyond our educational institutions, is fundamental to promoting academic integrity.

My colleague, Dr. Dustin Louie, an Indigenous scholar from “the Nadleh Whut’en and Nee Tahi Buhn First Nations of northern British Columbia,” Canada, points to the decolonizing practice of negotiating, which emphasizes “relationship building and connected futures instead of competing interests” (Louie et al., 2017, pp. 24, 47). Not surprisingly, research on academic integrity has shown that misconduct is less likely to happen when students believe that their teachers care about them (Christensen Hughes, 2017). Relationship building, not only with students, but with all stakeholders within and beyond our educational institutions, is fundamental to promoting academic integrity.
Dr. Louie’s approach to teaching and learning also involves incorporating the Indigenous concept of “witnessing” into his classes (Louie, 2019, 2020). He has described how he takes time to explain to his students what witnessing is from an Indigenous perspective, including a responsibility that the witness becomes a keeper of that knowledge and is expected to remember and be able to recall the knowledge at a later time. Witnessing is a responsibility requiring attentiveness, care, respect, and trust (Louie, 2019, 2020)—values that are also characterized as beingfundamental to academic integrity (International Center for Academic Integrity, 2014).

fundamental to academic integrity (International Center for Academic Integrity, 2014).
There are other interesting parallels between witnessing as an Indigenous approach to learning and Western interpretations of integrity. For example, drawing on the work of Jane Hindeman (2002), plagiarism scholar Amy Robillard (2006) describes citation as an act of witnessing, elaborating that it is an intentional practice of understanding, acknowledging, and honoring source material. The connections between Western understanding of academic integrity and Indigenous ways of knowing, however, remain underdeveloped and deserve more intentional consideration.

Further questions to consider on this topic include the following:

Further questions to consider on this topic include the following:
- How do Indigenous ways of knowing and being embody what we think of as “academic integrity” (e.g., attribution of sources or those who came before us)?

- How can we think critically about disrupting established ways of sharing knowledge in a way that is more inclusive of Indigenous perspectives, approaches, and values?

- How do our established ways of knowledge transmission (i.e., writing, citing, and referencing) privilege certain ways of knowing while devaluing others?

- Are there aspects of decolonization that we need to think about when it comes to academic misconduct/learning/teaching/assessing?

- Are there aspects of academic misconduct and social justice that we need to think about in terms of better supporting Indigenous students?

- What questions do we need to be asking?

- What conversations should we be having that we are not already having?

ETHICAL CITATION OF AN ACT OF SOCIAL JUSTICE

ETHICAL CITATION OF AN ACT OF SOCIAL JUSTICE
Embedded within Indigenous knowledge systems are long-standing practices of how to attribute knowledge to those who came before us. Indigenous authors have noted that Western citing and referencing practices lack sufficient consideration for how to ethically represent Indigenous knowledge (Justice, 2018; Younging, 2018). Similarly, feminist and ethnic studies scholars have called for deeper consideration of how citing and referencing practices are embedded within patriarchal, Eurocentric ontologies and epistemologies (Ahmed, 2013; Tuck et al., 2015). There is a social justice aspect to how we cite and reference. When it comes to Indigenousknowledge in particular, many referencing and style guides remain silent on the topic of how to properly give attribution in ways that are respectful to Indigenous populations (Younging, 2018). Younging’s (2018) guide to writing by and about Indigenous peoples addresses questions relating to style and process. It provides useful and instructive insights into topics such as seeking wisdom and advice from elders, collaborating respectfully with Indigenous peoples, and respecting oral traditions.

Embedded within Indigenous knowledge systems are long-standing practices of how to attribute knowledge to those who came before us. Indigenous authors have noted that Western citing and referencing practices lack sufficient consideration for how to ethically represent Indigenous knowledge (Justice, 2018; Younging, 2018). Similarly, feminist and ethnic studies scholars have called for deeper consideration of how citing and referencing practices are embedded within patriarchal, Eurocentric ontologies and epistemologies (Ahmed, 2013; Tuck et al., 2015). There is a social justice aspect to how we cite and reference. When it comes to Indigenous
knowledge in particular, many referencing and style guides remain silent on the topic of how to properly give attribution in ways that are respectful to Indigenous populations (Younging, 2018). Younging’s (2018) guide to writing by and about Indigenous peoples addresses questions relating to style and process. It provides useful and instructive insights into topics such as seeking wisdom and advice from elders, collaborating respectfully with Indigenous peoples, and respecting oral traditions.
Since many disciplines still require the use of style guides from major organizations, at this point, Younging’s guide serves as a companion to, rather than a replacement for, the style guides that are typically required by academic departments or faculties. As a result, more and more librarians are beginning to supplement official reference manuals with libguides that specifically address Native American and Indigenous studies, including how to respectfully give attribution to elders and knowledge keepers (e.g., University of Massachusetts Amherst, 2019; University of British Columbia, 2020; University of Saskatchewan, 2019).

LEARNING DISABILITIES

LEARNING DISABILITIES
Another area where there is a disgraceful lack of substantial research is around the relationship of learning disabilities to academic misconduct. If we look to the literature on nonacademic misconduct with this focus, we may find some insights. Fabelo et al. (2011) found that nearly three-quarters of students who qualified for special education services in Texas were suspended or expelled at least once for nonacademic misconduct. Those classified as having “emotional disturbances” (Fabelo et al., 2011, p. xi) were among the most likely to be suspended or expelled. This again points to systemic injustices against those who do not fit into a stereotypical mold of what students should do, how they should perform, and who they should be. When students do not conform, for whatever reason, it seems there is a tendency to immediately shift the focus away from learning and toward punishing.

Another area where there is a disgraceful lack of substantial research is around the relationship of learning disabilities to academic misconduct. If we look to the literature on nonacademic misconduct with this focus, we may find some insights. Fabelo et al. (2011) found that nearly three-quarters of students who qualified for special education services in Texas were suspended or expelled at least once for nonacademic misconduct. Those classified as having “emotional disturbances” (Fabelo et al., 2011, p. xi) were among the most likely to be suspended or expelled. This again points to systemic injustices against those who do not fit into a stereotypical mold of what students should do, how they should perform, and who they should be. When students do not conform, for whatever reason, it seems there is a tendency to immediately shift the focus away from learning and toward punishing.
There has been very little large-scale research about how students with learning disabilities in higher education fare when it comes to plagiarism and cheating; however, some smaller studies provide useful information. In one mixed-methods study comparing thirty-one undergraduate students with dyslexia with thirty-one without dyslexia (aged eighteen to forty-nine years), Kinder and Elander (2011) reported that those with dyslexia had lower confidence in writing and found it more difficult. Students with dyslexia also scored lower than their peers without dyslexia in understanding authorship and knowledge about how to avoid plagiarism. The students’ responses about the possible links between dyslexia and plagiarismwere mixed, but the researchers concluded that students with dyslexia might be at a higher risk of engaging in accidental or unintentional plagiarism. The researchers advocated for more intentional intensive writing intervention support and academic skills development for postsecondary students with dyslexia.

Students with dyslexia also scored lower than their peers without dyslexia in understanding authorship and knowledge about how to avoid plagiarism. The students’ responses about the possible links between dyslexia and plagiarism
were mixed, but the researchers concluded that students with dyslexia might be at a higher risk of engaging in accidental or unintentional plagiarism. The researchers advocated for more intentional intensive writing intervention support and academic skills development for postsecondary students with dyslexia.
Kinder and Elander (2011) offer only one example of the link between learning disabilities and plagiarism. Many students have undiagnosed learning disabilities, which may have important implications for student learning, accessing learning support, and being at risk of being accused of plagiarism or other forms of academic misconduct. Research on the latter is lacking, and establishing the link between learning disabilities and academic misconduct could have important implications for educators and students.

CONCLUSION

CONCLUSION
There is ample evidence to suggest systemic bias against non-White students for whom English is an additional language when reporting and sanctioning breaches of academic integrity, and plagiarism in particular. Indigenous students and those with learning accessibility needs may be marginalized to the extent that they are effectively ignored when it comes to talking about academic integrity. Higher education, on the whole, has done a poor job of applying principles of equity, diversity, and inclusion to academic integrity. Educators benefit from taking a humble stance on academic integrity, in which we aim to understand our students rather than punish them (Leask, 2006). As educators, it is incumbent upon us to reject the notion that “we are justified in demanding that students adapt and ultimately conform to our culturally determined ways of teaching” (Leask, 2006, pp. 193–194). Instead, we must expand our repertoire of teaching strategies continually and actively reject the idea that one way of teaching is effective for all students (Leask, 2006).

Indigenous students and those with learning accessibility needs may be marginalized to the extent that they are effectively ignored when it comes to talking about academic integrity. Higher education, on the whole, has done a poor job of applying principles of equity, diversity, and inclusion to academic integrity. Educators benefit from taking a humble stance on academic integrity, in which we aim to understand our students rather than punish them (Leask, 2006). As educators, it is incumbent upon us to reject the notion that “we are justified in demanding that students adapt and ultimately conform to our culturally determined ways of teaching” (Leask, 2006, pp. 193–194). Instead, we must expand our repertoire of teaching strategies continually and actively reject the idea that one way of teaching is effective for all students (Leask, 2006).
A fundamental concept in equity, diversity, and inclusion is that of individual human dignity (Council of Europe, 2008). Every student, regardless of cultural heritage, native language, or academic ability, deserves to be treated with dignity. The International Center for Academic Integrity (International Center for Academic Integrity, 2014) has articulated six fundamental values of academic integrity: courage, fairness, honesty, respect, responsibility, and trust. Although dignity could be assumed to be embedded within all of these, perhaps future iterations of the fundamental values could include dignity as an explicitly articulated value in order to better align with our current understanding of human rights, diversity, equity, and inclusion.

A fundamental concept in equity, diversity, and inclusion is that of individual human dignity (Council of Europe, 2008). Every student, regardless of cultural heritage, native language, or academic ability, deserves to be treated with dignity. The International Center for Academic Integrity (International Center for Academic Integrity, 2014) has articulated six fundamental values of academic integrity: courage, fairness, honesty, respect, responsibility, and trust. Although dignity could be assumed to be embedded within all of these, perhaps future iterations of the fundamental values could include dignity as an explicitly articulated value in order to better align with our current understanding of human rights, diversity, equity, and inclusion.
I close this chapter with a call to action for more dialogue, more research, and a stronger focus on human dignity in all matters related to equity, diversity, and inclusion as they relate to academic integrity. As we engage more deeply in this work, it will be important to include stakeholders from the affected groups in our dialogue and research. To approach these complex topics ethically, we must be inclusive and intentional when it comes to whom we invite to take part in our research teams, policy development meetings, and program design meetings. Academic integrity advocates must also advocate for equity, diversity, and inclusion, as these concepts are fundamental to twenty-first-century educational ethics.

Recognizing, Reporting, and Resolving Plagiarism

Recognizing, Reporting, and Resolving Plagiarism
It is better to prevent plagiarism, but if that has failed and a case has been identified, then case management follows. There is more than one way to detect and address plagiarism, particularly in student writing. When possible, the focus should still be on the process of learning, not simply the end product. It is important to balance institutional interests of having consistent and credible policies, systems, and structures in place to ensure fair and equitable treatment of students across various disciplines over time, with the need for individualized approaches that consider each student as a human being who continues to learn and develop throughout schooling, and even throughout life. When it comes to how to deal with academic misconduct, and plagiarism in particular, the tensions among institutional, faculty-level, departmental, and individual positions are ubiquitous across higher education. Although tensions can be useful for creating opportunities for ongoing dialogue, communication, and education, they add complexity to an already challenging situation.

There is more than one way to detect and address plagiarism, particularly in student writing. When possible, the focus should still be on the process of learning, not simply the end product. It is important to balance institutional interests of having consistent and credible policies, systems, and structures in place to ensure fair and equitable treatment of students across various disciplines over time, with the need for individualized approaches that consider each student as a human being who continues to learn and develop throughout schooling, and even throughout life. When it comes to how to deal with academic misconduct, and plagiarism in particular, the tensions among institutional, faculty-level, departmental, and individual positions are ubiquitous across higher education. Although tensions can be useful for creating opportunities for ongoing dialogue, communication, and education, they add complexity to an already challenging situation.
Others before me have covered the topics of detection, management, and reporting thoroughly and thoughtfully (Carroll, 2007, 2016; Carroll & Appleton, 2005; Sutherland-Smith, 2008), so I keep my treatment of these topics brief. I offer pragmatic advice that may be especially helpful for teaching assistants (TAs) and other early-career educators. What I add to the extant literature is an amplified discussion of several invisible aspectsof dealing with plagiarism and other types of academic misconduct—namely, the tensions between policy and practice, as well as the emotional labor involved with detection and case management. I conclude by contemplating how to improve upon what currently happens, including a call for more systematic training and an examination of alternative ways to address breaches of academic integrity, such as restorative practices.

MAINTAING AN EDUCATOR’S MINDSET

MAINTAING AN EDUCATOR’S MINDSET
As educators, we are often situated within departments, which are nested within faculties that comprise the larger learning organization. Educators might appear to work in insolation but are in fact part of a larger system, which exists, at least in part, to teach and provide learning opportunities. Identifying and dealing with plagiarism and other forms of academic misconduct are related to institutional mandates of upholding quality assurance in education, but we cannot disentangle misconduct from the teaching and learning contexts in which it happens.

As educators, we are often situated within departments, which are nested within faculties that comprise the larger learning organization. Educators might appear to work in insolation but are in fact part of a larger system, which exists, at least in part, to teach and provide learning opportunities. Identifying and dealing with plagiarism and other forms of academic misconduct are related to institutional mandates of upholding quality assurance in education, but we cannot disentangle misconduct from the teaching and learning contexts in which it happens.
Many educators espouse the notion of a growth mindset (Claro et al., 2016; Dweck, 2008, 2015, 2016) or the belief behind the growth mindset is that “intelligence is not fixed and can be developed” (Claro et al., 2016, p. 8864). Carol Dweck, a leading scholar in this area, defines it this way:

Many educators espouse the notion of a growth mindset (Claro et al., 2016; Dweck, 2008, 2015, 2016) or the belief behind the growth mindset is that “intelligence is not fixed and can be developed” (Claro et al., 2016, p. 8864). Carol Dweck, a leading scholar in this area, defines it this way:
Individuals who believe their talents can be developed (through hard work, good strategies, and input from others) have a growth mindset. They tend to achieve more than those with a more fixed mindset (those who believe their talents are innate gifts). This is because they worry less about looking smart and they put more energy into learning. (Dweck, 2016, p. 2)

Individuals who believe their talents can be developed (through hard work, good strategies, and input from others) have a growth mindset. They tend to achieve more than those with a more fixed mindset (those who believe their talents are innate gifts). This is because they worry less about looking smart and they put more energy into learning. (Dweck, 2016, p. 2)
Many educators find this approach to be a positive and productive way to approach learning. They will carefully invest time and energy in learning how to cultivate a growth mindset in their learners and promote this approach in their classrooms, only to throw the entire belief system out the window when they encounter a case of plagiarism or other academic misconduct.

Many educators find this approach to be a positive and productive way to approach learning. They will carefully invest time and energy in learning how to cultivate a growth mindset in their learners and promote this approach in their classrooms, only to throw the entire belief system out the window when they encounter a case of plagiarism or other academic misconduct.
There have been a number of studies about faculty perceptions of plagiarism and responses to it (Flint et al., 2006; Jendrek, 1989; Hu, 2010), but there has been less research examining educators’ emotional and psychological responses to plagiarism. The reality is that educators react in emotional ways when they suspect or confirm a case of student plagiarism. It can be confusing, frustrating, and disappointing to realize that a student has plagiarized. Finding a case of plagiarism need not disrupt the belief systems that have guided an educator’s entire professional practice. If you are an educator who subscribes to the notion of the growth mindset, it can be helpful to keep that at the forefront of your mind as you find yourselfconfronted with the complexities of plagiarism or other breaches of integrity.

If you are an educator who subscribes to the notion of the growth mindset, it can be helpful to keep that at the forefront of your mind as you find yourself
confronted with the complexities of plagiarism or other breaches of integrity.
It is crucial to avoid a mindset of “Gotcha!” (Price, 2002; Whiteman & Gordon, 2001), also known as being the “plagiarism police” (Carroll, 2007; Howard, 2002; Levin, 2006) or pursuing a witch hunt (Levin 2003; Carroll, 2007). It is imperative for educators who suspect or can prove plagiarism to resist a knee-jerk reaction to judge students as being morally corrupt or guilty. It is problematic if we trade our identity as an educator for that of an enforcer, discarding all the aspirational elements of teaching and learning that brought us to the profession in the first place. Do not bypass due process and proceed directly to judgment. Instead, focus on understandingwhathappened,howit happened, andwhyit happened before jumping to conclusions. Keep your growth mindset even when you find yourself in ethically challenging situations.

Checking Our Biases

Checking Our Biases
We often ask our students to engage their critical thinking skills, and it is incumbent upon us, as educators, administrators, and support staff, to lead by example and do the same. This starts with being aware of the cognitive biases that we bring to our work, and then take steps to mitigate them. When students plagiarize, professors and others can see this as a blatant disregard for educational expectations and norms and assume that all plagiarism is deliberate, even if that is not the case (Adam, Anderson, & Spronken-Smith, 2017; Blum, 2016). Academics can be susceptible to a number of biases when it comes to academic misconduct:

We often ask our students to engage their critical thinking skills, and it is incumbent upon us, as educators, administrators, and support staff, to lead by example and do the same. This starts with being aware of the cognitive biases that we bring to our work, and then take steps to mitigate them. When students plagiarize, professors and others can see this as a blatant disregard for educational expectations and norms and assume that all plagiarism is deliberate, even if that is not the case (Adam, Anderson, & Spronken-Smith, 2017; Blum, 2016). Academics can be susceptible to a number of biases when it comes to academic misconduct:
Confirmation Bias

Confirmation Bias
This is the tendency for people, including trained scientists, to look more favorably at evidence that confirms their already established point of view (Mynatt, Doherty, & Tweney, 1977). Confirmation bias could lead someone to insist that students who plagiarize do so intentionally, or because they are lazy. Although this may be true in some cases, there is ample research to support that this is not the norm.

This is the tendency for people, including trained scientists, to look more favorably at evidence that confirms their already established point of view (Mynatt, Doherty, & Tweney, 1977). Confirmation bias could lead someone to insist that students who plagiarize do so intentionally, or because they are lazy. Although this may be true in some cases, there is ample research to support that this is not the norm.
Anchoring Bias

Anchoring Bias
Anchoring bias, also called “focalism,” occurs when someone relies heavily on an initial piece of information to make a judgment, a decision, or a conclusion that may be inaccurate (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). Forexample, a professor could erroneously conclude that students who plagiarize do so intentionally, based on an institutional report about academic misconduct that presents information about plagiarism cases and how they were dealt with. Institutional reports can provide important information to understand patterns of how academic misconduct is reported and how cases are dealt with through official institutional channels, but they often omit important information. For example, they do not summarize research findings showing that a high percentage of academic misconduct cases, including plagiarism, are not officially reported (Coren, 2011; Jendrek, 1989; Thomas, 2017); and that faculty members tend to bypass formal policies and guidelines in favor of dealing with plagiarism directly with students (Flint, Clegg, & Macdonald, 2006; McCabe, 1993). Even though institutional reports may present accurate information about the cases handled through official channels, they may still be incomplete in terms of presenting accurate information about actual rates of incidence or reasons why plagiarism has occurred.

For example, they do not summarize research findings showing that a high percentage of academic misconduct cases, including plagiarism, are not officially reported (Coren, 2011; Jendrek, 1989; Thomas, 2017); and that faculty members tend to bypass formal policies and guidelines in favor of dealing with plagiarism directly with students (Flint, Clegg, & Macdonald, 2006; McCabe, 1993). Even though institutional reports may present accurate information about the cases handled through official channels, they may still be incomplete in terms of presenting accurate information about actual rates of incidence or reasons why plagiarism has occurred.
Self-Serving Bias

Self-Serving Bias
Self-serving bias can lead people to conclude that when good things happen, it is because they did things correctly and they are responsible for their own success (internal attribution), but bad things happen as the result of external factors (external attribution) (Bradley, 1978). With regard to plagiarism, self-serving bias could lead a professor to conclude that a student plagiarized because she or he was lazy or deceitful, without taking into account whether the professor provided clear expectations about how to cite references, or where to seek additional guidance. Further, self-serving bias can lead professors to absolve themselves of any responsibility for students’ plagiarism, despite ample evidence showing that explicit instruction can help students understand the expectations for how to undertake the assignment (Belter & Du Pré, 2009; Moniz, Fine, & Bliss, 2008).

Bias Blind Spot

Bias Blind Spot
The bias blind spot phenomenon suggests that individuals see biases as applying to others but not to themselves (Pronin, Lin, & Ross, 2002). In the case of plagiarism, it could lead someone to think that his or her conclusions about why students plagiarize are unbiased and objective, whereas other people’s ideas are flawed.

The bias blind spot phenomenon suggests that individuals see biases as applying to others but not to themselves (Pronin, Lin, & Ross, 2002). In the case of plagiarism, it could lead someone to think that his or her conclusions about why students plagiarize are unbiased and objective, whereas other people’s ideas are flawed.
It is imperative that those of us who work in education check our biases and refrain from generalizing about why students plagiarize, and even more important to check our assumption that all plagiarism is deliberate.This applies even when we are frustrated or exasperated because we must, as higher education professionals, lead by example and base our understanding on evidence, rather than basing our assumptions on emotional responses or opinions. Now that we have focused on keeping an educator’s mindset and checking our biases, we are better prepared to move into a discussion about identifying and managing a case of plagiarism.

RECOGNIZING PLAGIARISM

RECOGNIZING PLAGIARISM
The process of identifying plagiarism is often called “detection,” but this term is problematic because it conjures up notions of the teacher as a detective, which brings with it connotations of policing student work. In turn, this propagates the kind of moral binaries and adversarial relationships between students and teachers that we need to avoid. The words that we use to talk about academic integrity and its breaches matter enormously. For this reason, I prefer “identify” or “recognize” instead of “detect,” to avoid subtle underlying connotations of “Gotcha!” or assumptions of guilt. Identifying and recognizing are more neutral terms can facilitate a growth mindset, rather than a punitive one.

The process of identifying plagiarism is often called “detection,” but this term is problematic because it conjures up notions of the teacher as a detective, which brings with it connotations of policing student work. In turn, this propagates the kind of moral binaries and adversarial relationships between students and teachers that we need to avoid. The words that we use to talk about academic integrity and its breaches matter enormously. For this reason, I prefer “identify” or “recognize” instead of “detect,” to avoid subtle underlying connotations of “Gotcha!” or assumptions of guilt. Identifying and recognizing are more neutral terms can facilitate a growth mindset, rather than a punitive one.
There are two main ways that a potential case of plagiarism can be identified: by humans and by software. I say “potential case” because identifying plagiarism is a process rather than a singular moment, and it involves careful analysis, not jumping to a conclusion (Carroll, 2007). In this section, I explore several common methods used by educators to recognize plagiarism in student work. I use the term “educator” here inclusively to refer to professors, TAs, librarians, and others who might engage with students and their academic work.

I say “potential case” because identifying plagiarism is a process rather than a singular moment, and it involves careful analysis, not jumping to a conclusion (Carroll, 2007). I use the term “educator” here inclusively to refer to professors, TAs, librarians, and others who might engage with students and their academic work.
Educator Identification of Plagiarism

Educator Identification of Plagiarism
Identifying plagiarism often begins with a hunch or a suspicion that something is not right. When an educator asks if the work that they are reviewing was really created by the person who submitted it, this can be the first sign that something is not right (Carroll, 2007). Educators should trust their instincts and use the hunch as an awareness tool to determine if a deeper investigation is warranted. If something does not seem right with a student’s work, do not ignore it or make assumptions about what happened. Trust that as the educator, you are the person who is most likely to be able to identify if academic misconduct has happened, because you are the person most closely connected to the student and the course content (Frenken, 2013). Here are some telltale signs to help you recognize plagiarism in student work:

Identifying plagiarism often begins with a hunch or a suspicion that something is not right. When an educator asks if the work that they are reviewing was really created by the person who submitted it, this can be the first sign that something is not right (Carroll, 2007). Educators should trust their instincts and use the hunch as an awareness tool to determine if a deeper investigation is warranted. If something does not seem right with a student’s work, do not ignore it or make assumptions about what happened. Trust that as the educator, you are the person who is most likely to be able to identify if academic misconduct has happened, because you are the person most closely connected to the student and the course content (Frenken, 2013). Here are some telltale signs to help you recognize plagiarism in student work:
- Abrupt changes in tone or style:Whether it is prose, design, music, art, or computer code, sudden shifts in tone or style can signal that different individuals were involved in the creation of the work (Carroll, 2007: Davis, Drinan, & Bertram Gallant, 2009). If parts of the work are poorly written, especially the introduction and conclusion, and the rest is flawless, it could be that the student did not write the majority of the work (Carroll, 2007).

- Changes in font type or color:If the font changes abruptly in a paper, it can signal that that portion of the work might have been lifted from somewhere else (Carroll, 2007).

- Obscure vocabulary or jargon:The use of specialized professional or technical jargon that the student might not reasonably be expected to know can be a sign of plagiarism (Carroll, 2007), as can the use of archaic words that have fallen out of use.

- Citing and referencing errors and mixed bibliographic styles:It is quite common for students to copy citations directly from the source material and paste them into their work (Carroll, 2007). I encourage approaching this particular sign with some caution, as sometimes students who lack confidence in or knowledge of citing and referencing trust that whoever wrote or signed off on the source material likely knew the rules better than them. This can be an indicator that the student’s intentions were honorable, but their skills or confidence need more work.

If parts of the work are poorly written, especially the introduction and conclusion, and the rest is flawless, it could be that the student did not write the majority of the work (Carroll, 2007).

If the font changes abruptly in a paper, it can signal that that portion of the work might have been lifted from somewhere else (Carroll, 2007).
Obscure vocabulary or jargon:
The use of specialized professional or technical jargon that the student might not reasonably be expected to know can be a sign of plagiarism (Carroll, 2007), as can the use of archaic words that have fallen out of use.
Citing and referencing errors and mixed bibliographic styles:
It is quite common for students to copy citations directly from the source material and paste them into their work (Carroll, 2007). I encourage approaching this particular sign with some caution, as sometimes students who lack confidence in or knowledge of citing and referencing trust that whoever wrote or signed off on the source material likely knew the rules better than them. This can be an indicator that the student’s intentions were honorable, but their skills or confidence need more work.
These are just a few ways that educators can recognize plagiarism in students’ work, but this list is by no means exhaustive. Recognizing and then confirming plagiarism in student work can involve careful analysis on the part of the educator.

Text-Matching Software

Text-Matching Software
Text-matching software goes by a variety of other names, including “plagiarism detection,” “antiplagiarism,” or “plagiarism prevention” software. But these other names are misleading. Let me be perfectly clear: these products do not detectplagiarism—rather, they identify instances where a portion of one text has an exact match to another piece of text. An exact match of a portion of text merely alerts an educator that there may be cause to dig deeper and possibly initiate an investigation. Do not conflate text matching with a guilty verdict of plagiarism without further analysis.

Text-matching software goes by a variety of other names, including “plagiarism detection,” “antiplagiarism,” or “plagiarism prevention” software. But these other names are misleading. Let me be perfectly clear: these products do not detect
plagiarism—
rather, they identify instances where a portion of one text has an exact match to another piece of text. An exact match of a portion of text merely alerts an educator that there may be cause to dig deeper and possibly initiate an investigation. Do not conflate text matching with a guilty verdict of plagiarism without further analysis.
There are a variety of commercially available text-matching software available, as well as noncommercial software created by computer scientists and engineers (European Network for Academic Integrity, 2019).Commercially available products are not used uniformly across all countries and jurisdictions. Although this software has become almost ubiquitous in Australia and the United Kingdom, its use is more limited in countries such as Canada (Eaton et al., 2020), among others. It is likely that as time goes on, the use of technology will become more prevalent in the assessment and oversight of student work, including text matching and identity verification.

UNDERSTANDING THE ROLE OF POLICY

UNDERSTANDING THE ROLE OF POLICY
The question of what comes after an educator suspects or identifies a case of plagiarism can get a little tricky. Often, there are differences between what should happen and what actually happens after a suspected case of academic misconduct is reported. To understand why, we turn our attention to the role of policy in handling violations of academic integrity. Policy drives institutional procedures, processes, and expectations for identifying, reporting, and resolving cases. Policy provides the overall framework that drives the processes undertaken at the institutional (macro), departmental (meso), and individual (micro) levels (seeChapter 4for more information about the levels). So in order to understand why and how cases are reported and then managed, it is imperative to understand the role of policy.

The question of what comes after an educator suspects or identifies a case of plagiarism can get a little tricky. Often, there are differences between what should happen and what actually happens after a suspected case of academic misconduct is reported. To understand why, we turn our attention to the role of policy in handling violations of academic integrity. Policy drives institutional procedures, processes, and expectations for identifying, reporting, and resolving cases. Policy provides the overall framework that drives the processes undertaken at the institutional (macro), departmental (meso), and individual (micro) levels (see
Chapter 4
for more information about the levels). So in order to understand why and how cases are reported and then managed, it is imperative to understand the role of policy.
Formal policies and procedures for dealing with plagiarism exist at many postsecondary institutions, but it would be folly to assume that the regulatory bodies for higher education quality assurance in every country in the world require that institutions have such formalized policies. In fact, formal policies for addressing plagiarism in higher education have yet to be fully developed in many countries. Along the same lines, there are some countries where policy guidance might exist, but it is not readily available to either instructors or students.

Formal policies and procedures for dealing with plagiarism exist at many postsecondary institutions, but it would be folly to assume that the regulatory bodies for higher education quality assurance in every country in the world require that institutions have such formalized policies. In fact, formal policies for addressing plagiarism in higher education have yet to be fully developed in many countries. Along the same lines, there are some countries where policy guidance might exist, but it is not readily available to either instructors or students.
Due to the closed nature of education and politics generally in some countries, it is not possible to explore the nature of how academic misconduct is handled there. Even naming specific countries where academic misconduct policies are nonexistent or difficult to find could potentially jeopardize individuals who might be working toward advancing academic or research misconduct management in those countries, so I intentionally refrain from doing so. Suffice to say that there are no universally accepted policy approaches about how to detect or manage a case of plagiarism, and some institutions, as well as some countries, are more progressive than others in their approach to academic misconduct case management.

Due to the closed nature of education and politics generally in some countries, it is not possible to explore the nature of how academic misconduct is handled there. Even naming specific countries where academic misconduct policies are nonexistent or difficult to find could potentially jeopardize individuals who might be working toward advancing academic or research misconduct management in those countries, so I intentionally refrain from doing so. Suffice to say that there are no universally accepted policy approaches about how to detect or manage a case of plagiarism, and some institutions, as well as some countries, are more progressive than others in their approach to academic misconduct case management.
Even in countries where student conduct policies are established in accordance with the principles of natural justice and fair process, inconsistencies abound. InChapter 2, as well as in my previous research, I havediscussed that there are no universally agreed-upon definitions of plagiarism in higher education (Eaton, 2017b). Similarly, there is little consensus about how to define contract cheating or other forms of academic misconduct (Stoesz et al., 2019). These inconsistencies at higher policy levels can have a ripple effect, as faculty members and students who move from one institution to another throughout their schooling and employment can be regulated by different policies and definitions along the way. It should come as no surprise that faculty members react in an “idiosyncratic fashion” (Jendrek, 1989, p. 401) when responding to alleged or actual academic misconduct.

Elements of Exemplary Academic Integrity Policy

Elements of Exemplary Academic Integrity Policy
Tracey Bretag and her colleagues studied the academic integrity policies of thirty-nine universities in Australia, and as a result of that work, they developed a set of five core principles for exemplary policy (Bretag et al., 2011a, 2011b):

Tracey Bretag and her colleagues studied the academic integrity policies of thirty-nine universities in Australia, and as a result of that work, they developed a set of five core principles for exemplary policy (Bretag et al., 2011a, 2011b):
1. Access:The policy must be easy to find and easy to understand.

1. Approach:Academic integrity policy starts with a clear statement of intent, preferably taking an educative rather than a punitive stance.

1. Responsibility:The responsibilities for various stakeholders are clearly stated, including senior leaders, academic staff, professional and support staff, and students.

1. Detail:An excellent policy includes detailed descriptions rather than vague gestures. The level of detail should be “extensive but not excessive” (Bretag et al., 2011b, p. 7).

1. Support:Systems must be in place to enact and implement policy. This includes but is not limited to clear procedures, resources, training, and proactive measures to educate students.

Access:
The policy must be easy to find and easy to understand.
Approach:
Academic integrity policy starts with a clear statement of intent, preferably taking an educative rather than a punitive stance.
Responsibility:
The responsibilities for various stakeholders are clearly stated, including senior leaders, academic staff, professional and support staff, and students.
Detail:
An excellent policy includes detailed descriptions rather than vague gestures. The level of detail should be “extensive but not excessive” (Bretag et al., 2011b, p. 7).
Support:
Systems must be in place to enact and implement policy. This includes but is not limited to clear procedures, resources, training, and proactive measures to educate students.
Academic integrity policies and procedures also need to be revisited and updated on a regular basis. In an ideal scenario, the next date for revision should be publicly noted in the current documents, with the relevant stakeholders held responsible for ensuring that the policies are reviewed and revised on schedule. Relevant stakeholders include not only senior-level administrators but also student representatives because ultimately, the implementation of the policy directly affects students.

The Academic Integrity Policy Myth

The Academic Integrity Policy Myth
In formal institutional policies and procedures, as well as informal guidelines, detection, reporting, investigation, and case management areoften presented as an orderly sequence of actions that results in a student being found responsible or not. If the student is found to have committed plagiarism, one or more possible sanctions can be applied. Sanctions can be either instructive, such as mandatory remedial academic integrity education; or punitive, such as a grade reduction, suspension, or expulsion (Eerkes, 2010). Some institutions include a combination of instructive and punitive sanctions, which can be applied in different ways depending on the particular details of a case.

Almost every experienced administrator can explain the institution’s policies and procedures as a series of “if-then” statements, such as the following:

Almost every experienced administrator can explain the institution’s policies and procedures as a series of “if-then” statements, such as the following:
- If the professor suspects plagiarism, then it is their responsibility to gather the evidence and report it to the academic conduct office/department head, associate dean, or some other internal third party designated to have more authority than the professor in the academic misconduct reporting process,in accordance with the institutional policy.

- If the designated party determines that academic misconduct has occurred, then it determines the sanction and proceeds to inform the student of the decision,in accordance with the institutional policy.

- If the student disagrees with the sanction, then they have the right to appeal,in accordance with the institutional policy.

If the professor suspects plagiarism, then it is their responsibility to gather the evidence and report it to the academic conduct office/department head, associate dean, or some other internal third party designated to have more authority than the professor in the academic misconduct reporting process,
in accordance with the institutional policy
.

in accordance with the institutional policy
.
If the student disagrees with the sanction, then they have the right to appeal,
in accordance with the institutional policy
.
Although the process does not play out precisely this way at every postsecondary institution, the common denominator is “in accordance with the institutional policy.” Policies and procedures are established as part of a regulatory framework to govern and manage breaches of academic misconduct. Policies and procedures articulate a clear, systematic process that usually involves a neatly defined set of sequential steps.

Although the process does not play out precisely this way at every postsecondary institution, the common denominator is “in accordance with the institutional policy.” Policies and procedures are established as part of a regulatory framework to govern and manage breaches of academic misconduct. Policies and procedures articulate a clear, systematic process that usually involves a neatly defined set of sequential steps.
However, what actually happens when a professor suspects or provides evidence of plagiarism (or some other violation of academic integrity) perhaps could be more accurately illustrated as a spaghetti diagram, with squiggly lines and arrows veering off in a number of different directions. For more than half a century, researchers have shown time and time again that the majority of faculty do not follow established institutional policies. As far back as the mid-1960s, Bowers’s academic misconduct surveys of students, faculty, and administrators across the United States showed that only a small fraction of students who commit misconduct are caught and subsequently sanctioned (Bowers, 1964, 1966). However, what actually happens when a professor suspects or provides evidence of plagiarism (or some other violation of academic integrity) perhaps could be more accurately illustrated as a spaghetti diagram, with squiggly lines and arrows veering off in a number of different directions. For more than half a century, researchers have shown time and time again that the majority of faculty do not follow established institutional policies. As far back as the mid-1960s, Bowers’s academic misconduct surveys of students, faculty, and administrators across the United States showed that only a small fraction of students who commit misconduct are caught and subsequently sanctioned (Bowers, 1964, 1966). In every decade since, subsequent studies have corroborated these findings:
1970s:In a survey of 108 faculty members at DePauw University, Indiana, Wright and Kelly (1974) found that 65 percent of faculty membersreported confronting students directly, but only 15 percent reported a case of plagiarism to an administrator.

1980s:In a survey of 80 faculty members at Arizona State University, 65 percent of the respondents reported catching students engaging in some form of academic cheating, but only 21 percent of them reported it to the administration (Singhal, 1982). Two years later, a survey of 164 faculty members at a large public university in the United States showed that 39 percent of the respondents would report the incident to the administration, 34 percent would lower the student’s grade after discussing the incident with the student, and 26 percent would give the student a warning (Nuss, 1984). At the end of the decade, Jendrek (1989) reported that 60 percent of 337 faculty members of a midwestern American public university reported having witnessed academic cheating, and only 33 percent of those faculty reported it to their department chair and 8 percent ignored the incident entirely.

1990s:A survey administered across 16 colleges and universities across the United States, resulting in 789 usable faculty responses, revealed that the decision of whether to report an incident depends on the particular case. Moreover, only 43 percent of faculty who identified a case of academic misconduct reported it to the institutional authorities (McCabe, 1993), with a more likely response being to bypass institutional expectations in favor of dealing with incidents on an individual basis with the student directly.

2000s:In an institutional case study of a large public university in the United States, 72 faculty members disclosed that they had suspected 460 incidents of misconduct among undergraduate students, and 110 suspected cases of misconduct among graduate students. On average, respondents suspected an average of eight occurrences of unethical behavior within the previous year. A total of 46 percent of respondents reported addressing the issues through informal counseling, with only 12 out of 72 respondents (about 16 percent) indicating that they had reported students (Nadelson, 2007).

The overall response rate was 24.2 percent. Although exact numbers of respondents at each institution was not disclosed, the overall results showed that faculty were much more likely to speak to the student directly than to report the incident.

The consistency in the results across more than five decades of research shows a clear pattern: the majority of faculty members prefer to deal with misconduct directly with their own students rather than reporting it formally, and they will often bypass formal institutional policies and procedures, regardless of how exemplary they think they are. As a result, pleas from administrators for faculty to “use the process” (Reed, 2020, n.p.) are likely to be ignored.

COMMON BARRIERS TO REPORTING

COMMON BARRIERS TO REPORTING
There are a number of barriers to reporting academic misconduct, and it is important to anticipate and mitigate them before you find yourself faced with a case. Several barriers to reporting have been comprehensively covered by others, such as the time and effort that it takes to prepare the evidence (Coalter, Lim, & Wanorie, 2008; McCabe, 1993; Pickard, 2006; Taylor, Usick, & Paterson, 2004); fear of confrontations with administrators (Flint et al., 2006; Paterson et al., 2003); and threats to job security (Crossman, 2019). In the section that follows, I expand on the already rich dialogue about the barriers to reporting by exploring some of the persistent ones that remain particularly tough.

There are a number of barriers to reporting academic misconduct, and it is important to anticipate and mitigate them before you find yourself faced with a case. Several barriers to reporting have been comprehensively covered by others, such as the time and effort that it takes to prepare the evidence (Coalter, Lim, & Wanorie, 2008; McCabe, 1993; Pickard, 2006; Taylor, Usick, & Paterson, 2004); fear of confrontations with administrators (Flint et al., 2006; Paterson et al., 2003); and threats to job security (Crossman, 2019). In the section that follows, I expand on the already rich dialogue about the barriers to reporting by exploring some of the persistent ones that remain particularly tough.
Lack of Knowledge about Reporting Expectations and Procedures

Lack of Knowledge about Reporting Expectations and Procedures
Just as students can lack knowledge about what is expected of them in terms of preventing plagiarism, faculty can lack an understanding about what is expected of them when they suspect or identify a case. Not knowing the institutional procedures is a key reason that faculty do not report plagiarism or other forms of misconduct (Eaton, 2017a; Maramark & Maline, 1993). Just as institutions have some responsibility for ensuring that students understand what is expected of them, they bear some responsibility for ensuring that faculty understand their expectations. It is not enough for administrators to wave a printout of a policy around at a department meeting and demand that faculty members follow it. Acculturation for academic integrity is just as important for faculty members and TAs as for students. Academic integrity needs to be part of onboarding and ongoing training to ensure that the staff and faculty share a clear idea of what is expected of them (Singhal, 1982). Then, as with students, atleast they cannot blame “the system” and claim that no one ever explained what was expected of them.

Ideological Objections

Ideological Objections
Even when educators know what their institution expects of them, they might not follow the policy or procedures for a variety of reasons, including ideological objections, which can result in teaching staff becoming conscientious objectors to the policy and the institutionally imposed reporting expectations. Next, I explore some reasons why faculty choose to circumvent formal policies. I highlight the importance of procedural fairness in academic misconduct case management (Heafitz King, 2012) and address the role that administrative law and judicial approaches play in case management (Kelleher, 2016). I also explore the idea that by the time a case of plagiarism has been clearly identified, institutions are likely to abandon pedagogical approaches in favor of policy enactment, which can result in ideological objections to reporting.

Belief That Plagiarism/Academic Misconduct Is a Matter of Pedagogy, not Policy

Belief That Plagiarism/Academic Misconduct Is a Matter of Pedagogy, not Policy
Many faculty consider that it is both their right and their responsibility to address plagiarism directly with their students rather than reporting it formally (Jendrek, 1989; Taylor et al., 2004). When it comes to addressing academic misconduct, individual faculty members often prefer to see themselves as independent actors rather than as being situated within a department that is itself nested within a larger system. A sense of instructional independence can be tied, at least in part, to notions of academic freedom that uphold the “freedom of the teacher to profess, publish, and criticize without fear of repercussion resulting from conflict with administration and governing bodies” (Frenken, 2013, p. 146).

Many faculty consider that it is both their right and their responsibility to address plagiarism directly with their students rather than reporting it formally (Jendrek, 1989; Taylor et al., 2004). When it comes to addressing academic misconduct, individual faculty members often prefer to see themselves as independent actors rather than as being situated within a department that is itself nested within a larger system. A sense of instructional independence can be tied, at least in part, to notions of academic freedom that uphold the “freedom of the teacher to profess, publish, and criticize without fear of repercussion resulting from conflict with administration and governing bodies” (Frenken, 2013, p. 146).
One of the tenets of academic freedom is that professors have an expertise in academic matters, and this expertise is relevant to the assessment of student work. However, academic freedom with regard to teaching often focuses heavily on “front end” teaching activities (Frenken, 2013, p. 147), such as curriculum development and content delivery, without sufficient direction about how these are tied to the evaluation of student work, which often requires disciplinary expertise in order to make a fair assessment of student learning. The result is that “evaluation is a murky academic zone” (Frenken, 2013, p. 147) when it comes to academic freedom. Frenken also points out that assessment is considered a pedagogical activity until the moment when a breach of academicintegrity has been identified, at which point it is then often regarded as an administrative matter.

Frenken also points out that assessment is considered a pedagogical activity until the moment when a breach of academic
integrity has been identified, at which point it is then often regarded as an administrative matter.
Reporting a suspected or actual case results in the matter being turned over to an administrator, whose role is to ensure that university policy is followed and sanctions are applied consistently. The justification for this is to ensure procedural fairness, which helps to ensure that decisions regarding academic misconduct sanctioning are less likely to be challenged, or if they are challenged, appeals are less likely to be heard. If procedural fairness and due process are not followed, that could violate students’ human rights (Carroll & Appleton, 2005; Macdonald & Carroll, 2006). It is easy to see how in this pivotal moment, when pedagogical assessment becomes an administrative matter, the focus shifts away from student learning, with more attention being paid to institutional risk management.

Reporting a suspected or actual case results in the matter being turned over to an administrator, whose role is to ensure that university policy is followed and sanctions are applied consistently. The justification for this is to ensure procedural fairness, which helps to ensure that decisions regarding academic misconduct sanctioning are less likely to be challenged, or if they are challenged, appeals are less likely to be heard. If procedural fairness and due process are not followed, that could violate students’ human rights (Carroll & Appleton, 2005; Macdonald & Carroll, 2006). It is easy to see how in this pivotal moment, when pedagogical assessment becomes an administrative matter, the focus shifts away from student learning, with more attention being paid to institutional risk management.
This shift in focus away from student learning and toward institutional risk management is a watershed moment. At the moment when a professor formally reports plagiarism (or any other breach of integrity), they might effectively forfeit any further rights to engage in pedagogical assessment of a student’s learning, their relationship with the student and their knowledge of the student’s overall circumstances become irrelevant, and they are effectively excluded from further discussion of the matter (Frenken, 2013). The role that faculty members “play in the disciplinary process is often limited to flagging suspected plagiarism, consulting with administration on the suspected plagiarism, and perhaps appearing before a disciplinary committee to repeat their grounds for suspecting plagiarism” (Frenken, 2013, p. 126). Even if a professor wishes to advocate for leniency, such pleas are often dismissed in the name of procedural fairness. After reporting a breach of integrity, “the professor can only act as a witness for the administration, that is, on behalf of the administration” (p. 143).

The role that faculty members “play in the disciplinary process is often limited to flagging suspected plagiarism, consulting with administration on the suspected plagiarism, and perhaps appearing before a disciplinary committee to repeat their grounds for suspecting plagiarism” (Frenken, 2013, p. 126). Even if a professor wishes to advocate for leniency, such pleas are often dismissed in the name of procedural fairness. After reporting a breach of integrity, “the professor can only act as a witness for the administration, that is, on behalf of the administration” (p. 143).
I hasten to add here that this notion of being a witness differs fundamentally from the one discussed inChapter 9, on equity, diversity, and inclusion. The repositioning of a faculty member from educator to witness on behalf of the administration is an implicit shift that occurs in an unspoken way, and without the consent of the educator. Many educators could remain unaware that they have been moved into the role of witness; they just know that something feels wrong. This form of witnessing has nothing to do with relationship building, equity, diversity, or inclusion; rather, it is a form of tacit coercion to which many educators object, although they may find themselves powerless to change it.
