Some have argued that plagiarism, in particular, straddles administration and academics, and that excluding professors entirely from case management could violate their academic freedom (Frenken, 2013). On those grounds alone, faculty should be involved in some way in decisions relating to plagiarism and academic cheating among their own students. Thishas been confirmed by research in which 789 faculty respondents from 16 U.S. schools were surveyed, and “96% of the faculty” from non–honor code schools felt that they should be involved in the process of dealing with academic misconduct. Furthermore, 81 percent of faculty respondents from honor code schools felt that they should be involved in the handling of cheating incidents, with 15 percent indicating that “students should have sole responsibility for the process” (McCabe, 1993, p. 655). The idea that students should handle academic misconduct cases among their peers is an approach taken in some U.S. schools, but that is generally not the process in other parts of the world. Nevertheless, the idea that faculty want to be part of discussions and decisions that affect their own students when it comes to plagiarism and cheating must not be ignored.

It could be that there are more conscientious objectors at institutions with a strong culture of academic freedom supported by an established faculty union, as opposed to schools where teachers are not unionized and one’s job security can be linked, either directly or indirectly, to conforming to administrative policies and procedures. Having said that, the relationship between academic freedom and individual instructors’ beliefs about reporting and managing plagiarism have yet to be fully explored through systematic research.

Having said that, the relationship between academic freedom and individual instructors’ beliefs about reporting and managing plagiarism have yet to be fully explored through systematic research.
It is easy to see why faculty members would object to being excised from discussions about how to resolve academic misconduct cases, as well as any expectation, or even implication, that they will forfeit their ability to advocate for their own students. It is no wonder that so many faculty circumvent official policies and procedures or refuse to report cases. Academic integrity policies are designed, at least in part, to mitigate the risk of lawsuits or appeals end up exacerbating adversarial relationships between the administration and the academics.

Objections to How Policy Is Implemented

Objections to How Policy Is Implemented
In addition to being excluded from decisions relating to case resolution, many faculty members object to how institutional policy is implemented, or perhaps more accurately stated, how theyperceivepolicy is applied (Bruton & Childers, 2015; Taylor et al., 2004). Some faculty lack confidence that their administration will apply institutional policy consistently and fairly (Flint et al., 2006; McCabe, 1993; Paterson et al., 2003; Taylor et al., 2004). What faculty members may see or hear in hallway conversations can make it seem as though some students are sanctioned in overly harsh ways, whereas others get away with just a warning for the same act. This can generate frustration, even if these observations are only partially informed because the full details of cases, including the resolutions, are often notdisclosed to faculty members on the grounds of protecting student privacy. If faculty members perceive that sanctions are either too lenient (Flint et al., 2006; MacLeod & Eaton, 2020; McCabe, 1993) or too harsh (Taylor et al., 2004), they can lose confidence in their administration and the university system as a whole. In turn, this can lead to heightened aversion to official policies and increased avoidance of established procedures for reporting.

Challenges to One’s Professional Identity

Challenges to One’s Professional Identity
In professions where ethical conduct is fundamental to the role, one’s identity can become indistinguishable from one’s work. Ethicists and educators alike promote the idea that academic integrity in the classroom and ethical professional conduct, as well as ethical conduct more broadly, are linked (e.g., Christensen Hughes & Bertram Gallant, 2016; Guerrero-Dib et al., 2020; Harding et al., 2004). Educators do not necessarily want to assume the function of a police officer (Sutherland-Smith, 2008). This positioning of educator as enforcer can be antithetical to the educational objectives of creating safe learning spaces, where failure is seen as a learning opportunity rather than a punishable act. As such, some professors openly renounce any expectation that they report their students for misconduct, on the grounds that patrolling plagiarism, or any other breach of integrity, is fundamentally at odds with their role as caring and supportive educators.

The Emotional Labor of Detecting, Reporting, and Managing Cases

The Emotional Labor of Detecting, Reporting, and Managing Cases
The term “emotional labor” is the often-invisible effort required to “manage a wide range of feeling” (Hochschild, 2012, p. 8) associated with a particular job. When managing multiple and sometimes conflicting feelings, we are often also called on to suppress them in order to perform the task before us and maintain an outward appearance of professionalism or calm (Hochschild, 2012). The everyday intensity of the emotional labor that teachers, student affairs professionals, and administrators do as part of their daily job can escalate quickly when a case of plagiarism or other academic misconduct occurs. These issues have been discussed in the academic integrity literature, though often without using the term “emotional labor” to explicitly address all the internal and invisible labor required to detect, report, and manage academic misconduct.

When managing multiple and sometimes conflicting feelings, we are often also called on to suppress them in order to perform the task before us and maintain an outward appearance of professionalism or calm (Hochschild, 2012). The everyday intensity of the emotional labor that teachers, student affairs professionals, and administrators do as part of their daily job can escalate quickly when a case of plagiarism or other academic misconduct occurs. These issues have been discussed in the academic integrity literature, though often without using the term “emotional labor” to explicitly address all the internal and invisible labor required to detect, report, and manage academic misconduct.
Emotional labor has risks. “The worker can become estranged or alienated from an aspect of self … that isusedto do the work” (Hochschild, 2012, p. 20, emphasis in original). A person can become disengaged, jaded, or just simply burned out. Many readers no doubt have experience working with colleagues or administrators who are emotionally disengaged, unsympathetic,or indifferent, sometimes to the point of being callous. When it comes to academic misconduct, it can happen that the burned-out administrator might respond to an emotionally emphatic educator with what appears to be stubborn insensitivity or lack of interest. The emotional labor of dealing with academic misconduct can take its toll on people in different ways, some of which may depend on their role.

These are not exhaustive lists, but rather examples intended to highlight common emotional responses. Each person’s emotional response will be unique and individual, and may even vary depending on the case. The role that emotional labor plays in recognizing, reporting, and resolving breaches of academic integrity has been addressed to some extent in the research, but there is more work to be done if we want to fully understand the mental health impact on all stakeholders involved in the process.

Student Reporting of Plagiarism

Student Reporting of Plagiarism
Although I have focused mainly on faculty responses to misconduct, I would be remiss if I did not briefly address what responsibility, if any, students bear in reporting plagiarism. There can be drastic differences in expectations of students at schools with traditional honor codes, where reporting can be considered an obligation, as opposed to other educational contexts. The research has shown that by and large, students do not feel that it is their responsibility to report their peers who engage in academic misconduct, including plagiarism (Mahmud, Bretag, & Foltýnek, 2019; Nuss, 1984; Wright & Kelly, 1974).

Although I have focused mainly on faculty responses to misconduct, I would be remiss if I did not briefly address what responsibility, if any, students bear in reporting plagiarism. There can be drastic differences in expectations of students at schools with traditional honor codes, where reporting can be considered an obligation, as opposed to other educational contexts. The research has shown that by and large, students do not feel that it is their responsibility to report their peers who engage in academic misconduct, including plagiarism (Mahmud, Bretag, & Folt
ý
nek, 2019; Nuss, 1984; Wright & Kelly, 1974).
Students’ reluctance to out their peers begins early in life. Elementary and secondary students, for example, are reluctant to disclose information about any kind of misconduct to teachers or parents due to fear of their friends being punished, as well as fear of retribution from the offender or others in the class, such as getting beaten up after school (Boynton, 2005). These fears are instilled from an early age, and expecting students to change their perceptions and behaviors as they transition from secondary to postsecondary institutions may be naive. By that point, the fears may have become ingrained and the reluctant behavior has been reinforced for many years, perhaps even the majority of the students’ lifetime.

HOW TO IMPROVE THE PROCESS: EXPLORING THE ART OF THE POSSIBLE

HOW TO IMPROVE THE PROCESS: EXPLORING THE ART OF THE POSSIBLE
In this chapter, I have explored some fundamental, systemic flaws in the reporting and resolution process concerning plagiarism that have existed for decades. I have explored how deep tensions between pedagogy and policy lead to outright rejection of expectations to follow institutional policy and procedure, and how existing systems can exacerbate adversarial relationships between academics and university administrators. All this could lead to a sense of despair about how plagiarism and other breaches of academic integrity could be addressed in ways that are productive and fair, ensuring that justice prevails. There are no easy answers to systemicinequities, but there are possibilities that we can explore to fundamentally shift the conversation in a more positive direction.

Educational Development for Upholding Academic Integrity

Educational Development for Upholding Academic Integrity
Academic integrity training for prevention, identification, and case management is lacking during training for those who aspire to a career teaching in primary or secondary school. The situation is worse in higher education, where faculty might receive little or no training or even informal mentoring during their graduate training or early career (Serviss, 2016). It is not until most faculty are faced with a case of academic misconduct that they try to figure out what the next steps might be.

Academic integrity training for prevention, identification, and case management is lacking during training for those who aspire to a career teaching in primary or secondary school. The situation is worse in higher education, where faculty might receive little or no training or even informal mentoring during their graduate training or early career (Serviss, 2016). It is not until most faculty are faced with a case of academic misconduct that they try to figure out what the next steps might be.
Academic integrity education should not be limited to students; it should include training for academics and administrators, as well as TAs. There is ample evidence showing that when educators engage in professional development for academic integrity, they show a better understanding of, and appreciation for, institutional policies. They are likely to better understand what is expected of them and how to identify and handle academic misconduct cases (Cameron, 2019; Dawson & Sutherland-Smith, 2018; Singhal, 1982). Training can also help to establish organizational cultural norms, designed to foster a more collaborative, less adversarial approach to reporting and case management.

Academic integrity education should not be limited to students; it should include training for academics and administrators, as well as TAs. There is ample evidence showing that when educators engage in professional development for academic integrity, they show a better understanding of, and appreciation for, institutional policies. They are likely to better understand what is expected of them and how to identify and handle academic misconduct cases (Cameron, 2019; Dawson & Sutherland-Smith, 2018; Singhal, 1982). Training can also help to establish organizational cultural norms, designed to foster a more collaborative, less adversarial approach to reporting and case management.
It has already been established that transmissionist models of instruction have limited usefulness when it comes to promoting academic integrity (Sutherland-Smith, 2008). It is important for institutional leaders to implement academic integrity training not as part of a managerialist approach to the oversight of knowledge workers, but rather as intellectual engagement with academics and other members of the university community. Training cannot be simply about indoctrinating people about how to follow administrative processes that might be fundamentally flawed. Instead, educational development opportunities must create meaningful opportunities for dialogue and the open exchange of ideas. The tensions that exist between ethical teaching and learning, policy enactment, academic freedom, student advocacy, and institutional risk management must not only be acknowledged, but explored and discussed by various stakeholders.

Preservice Teacher Training

Preservice Teacher Training
Although this book is focused on higher education, I would be remiss if I did not comment on the need for increased academic integrity training in preservice teacher education. A common complaint among professors is that first-year students come to campus ill prepared in terms ofunderstanding what is expected of them when it comes to upholding academic integrity. This means that students need to be acculturated earlier, but part of the problem is that primary and secondary teachers often do not receive training in promoting academic integrity during their teacher education programs (Bens, 2010; Eaton, 2017a; Mammen & Meyiwa, 2013). This has created a “chicken and egg” situation, in which educators at every level end up deficient in terms of training and professional development.

Although this book is focused on higher education, I would be remiss if I did not comment on the need for increased academic integrity training in preservice teacher education. A common complaint among professors is that first-year students come to campus ill prepared in terms of
understanding what is expected of them when it comes to upholding academic integrity. This means that students need to be acculturated earlier, but part of the problem is that primary and secondary teachers often do not receive training in promoting academic integrity during their teacher education programs (Bens, 2010; Eaton, 2017a; Mammen & Meyiwa, 2013). This has created a “chicken and egg” situation, in which educators at every level end up deficient in terms of training and professional development.
I contend that teacher education is the starting point, meaning that academic integrity training actually can start in higher education. Professors teach their students, including those in preservice teacher education programs. In turn, licensed teachers go on to teach children in primary and secondary school, so learners become acculturated to the idea of academic integrity from an early age. But until academic integrity education is systematically and intentionally incorporated into preservice teacher education, the finger-pointing will likely continue.

Alternative Approaches: Restorative Justice

Alternative Approaches: Restorative Justice
Since the turn of the millennium, interest has been growing about how to use restorative practices to address academic conduct issues, as an alternative to traditional policy grounded in administrative law (Armour, 2016; Johnson, 2018; Kara & MacAlister, 2010, McCabe, Butterfield, & Treviño, 2012). Advocates have called for restorative practices to be considered for both nonacademic misconduct (e.g., bullying) (Armour, 2016) and breaches of academic integrity (Johnson, 2018; Kara & MacAlister, 2010; McCabe, Butterfield, & Treviño, 2012; Sopcak, 2019, 2020).

ñ

ñ
o, 2012; Sopcak, 2019, 2020).
Sometimes complex cases of academic misconduct can involvenonacademicmisconduct at the same time, such as when fellow students are bullied into giving their assignments to someone else for the purposes of copying them or instructors are threatened with violence or job loss if they report academic misconduct. Newer approaches, such as restorative practices, are emerging to challenge long-standing methods of addressing misconduct. Whenever established approaches are challenged, we have an opportunity to tackle the tough topic of if and how new ways of doing things can and should be considered.

CONCLUSIONS

CONCLUSIONS
Individual members of the academic community come and go from institutions over time. Even though some may stay for many years, or even decades, ultimately the institution generally outlives the individuals who become part of it. The tensions that exist between institutional andindividual objectives can actually be useful in helping to maintain a balance between punitive and pedagogical approaches to dealing with plagiarism, which is important in a learning organization because “without differences of opinion, there can be no debate about important issues or synthesis of learning” (Kling, 2009, n.p.). Because plagiarism is an important issue in education, it is incumbent upon those in positions of authority to create opportunities for open dialogue as individual stakeholders build and synthesize their knowledge of how to handle breaches of integrity.

Individual members of the academic community come and go from institutions over time. Even though some may stay for many years, or even decades, ultimately the institution generally outlives the individuals who become part of it. The tensions that exist between institutional and
individual objectives can actually be useful in helping to maintain a balance between punitive and pedagogical approaches to dealing with plagiarism, which is important in a learning organization because “without differences of opinion, there can be no debate about important issues or synthesis of learning” (Kling, 2009, n.p.). Because plagiarism is an important issue in education, it is incumbent upon those in positions of authority to create opportunities for open dialogue as individual stakeholders build and synthesize their knowledge of how to handle breaches of integrity.
I conclude this chapter by acknowledging a need to balance pedagogical approaches with case management. Finding ways to keep the focus on learning throughout the process may engage individual academics, administrators, and students in more productive approaches, with more positive outcomes. If establishing multistakeholder approaches to upholding academic integrity is the goal, then every effort should be made to reduce or eliminate adversarial relationships or the pitting of academics against the administration. Instead, keeping the focus first and foremost on student learning and development can help to ensure that responses to breaches of integrity are approached equitably and fairly.

Plagiarism by Professors and Researchers

Plagiarism by Professors and Researchers
It would be remiss of me to write a book on tackling plagiarism as a tough topic in higher education without addressing academic and research misconduct by those who are not students. This includes but is not limited to professors, researchers, research chairs, postdoctoral fellows, and administrators. In this chapter, I will use the terms “professors,” “faculty,” and “researchers” inclusively, to mean all those who engage in research and knowledge dissemination in higher education who are not students. This is for simplicity, but also because the concepts of ethical and professional conduct are relevant to a wide range of individuals within learning organizations (Bruhn et al., 2002). There is a solid body of literature about faculty perceptions of student plagiarism (Coren, 2011; Halupa & Bolliger, 2013; Hu, 2010; Jendrek, 1989; MacLeod, 2014; Zivcakova et al., 2012), but very little about faculty attitudes about plagiarism among their peers. Some scholars have urged us to consider the disconnect between the obsession with student plagiarism and misconduct and the apparent dismissal of the same transgressions when the responsible party is a faculty member (Bertram Gallant, 2008; Callahan, 1982). Plagiarism by professors is viewed as more egregious than when students do it, with misappropriation of student work being among the most heinous of offenses (Becker, 2019).

This includes but is not limited to professors, researchers, research chairs, postdoctoral fellows, and administrators. In this chapter, I will use the terms “professors,” “faculty,” and “researchers” inclusively, to mean all those who engage in research and knowledge dissemination in higher education who are not students. This is for simplicity, but also because the concepts of ethical and professional conduct are relevant to a wide range of individuals within learning organizations (Bruhn et al., 2002). There is a solid body of literature about faculty perceptions of student plagiarism (Coren, 2011; Halupa & Bolliger, 2013; Hu, 2010; Jendrek, 1989; MacLeod, 2014; Zivcakova et al., 2012), but very little about faculty attitudes about plagiarism among their peers. Some scholars have urged us to consider the disconnect between the obsession with student plagiarism and misconduct and the apparent dismissal of the same transgressions when the responsible party is a faculty member (Bertram Gallant, 2008; Callahan, 1982). Plagiarism by professors is viewed as more egregious than when students do it, with misappropriation of student work being among the most heinous of offenses (Becker, 2019).
REVISITING THE 4M FRAMEWORK

REVISITING THE 4M FRAMEWORK
There is an underlying and often unquestioned assumption that by the time people have graduated from a program in higher education, they should know better than to plagiarize and also know how to avoid doing so. Another assumption is that the university is a community of scholars, with professors engaging in creative and innovative work on a daily basis (Erickson et al., 2020; Frenken, 2013). Universities may be communities of scholarship, but that does not mean they are immune to plagiarism or other breaches of integrity outside the student body. Just as it is impossible to predict every possible type of student misconduct, the same is true of faculty, administrators, and researchers. Thus, for the purposes of this chapter, I focus mostly on plagiarism, though I situate it within a broader conversation about academic and research misconduct.

There is an underlying and often unquestioned assumption that by the time people have graduated from a program in higher education, they should know better than to plagiarize and also know how to avoid doing so. Another assumption is that the university is a community of scholars, with professors engaging in creative and innovative work on a daily basis (Erickson et al., 2020; Frenken, 2013). Universities may be communities of scholarship, but that does not mean they are immune to plagiarism or other breaches of integrity outside the student body. Just as it is impossible to predict every possible type of student misconduct, the same is true of faculty, administrators, and researchers. Thus, for the purposes of this chapter, I focus mostly on plagiarism, though I situate it within a broader conversation about academic and research misconduct.
There are various complexities that arise when faculty and researchers plagiarize. We can use the 4M Framework discussed earlier in this book to guide an exploration of this topic (seeChapter 4). The 4M Framework provides a structure for us to examine this issue from different levels: micro (individual), meso (departmental), macro (institutional), and mega (the broader community). One of the key differences between student and professorial plagiarism is the level of impact. When a student plagiarizes, it rarely affects anyone in the broader community (mega level), but when a professor plagiarizes or engages in other forms of research or academic malpractice in the dissemination of their findings, it can affect the broader scientific and scholarly communities, as well as society at large. So unlike students, professors and researchers are accountable to the wider community for their actions. This could be one reason why the activities of organizations such as the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) and Retraction Watch play a key role in providing accountability at the mega level.

One of the key differences between student and professorial plagiarism is the level of impact. When a student plagiarizes, it rarely affects anyone in the broader community (mega level), but when a professor plagiarizes or engages in other forms of research or academic malpractice in the dissemination of their findings, it can affect the broader scientific and scholarly communities, as well as society at large. So unlike students, professors and researchers are accountable to the wider community for their actions. This could be one reason why the activities of organizations such as the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) and Retraction Watch play a key role in providing accountability at the mega level.
THE TRANSITION FROM STUDENT TO FACULTY

THE TRANSITION FROM STUDENT TO FACULTY
The transition from student to faculty is often slow. It can start with a part-time role as a teaching assistant (TA) or research assistant and meander from there in a variety of directions that might include a role as a postdoctoral scholar, part-time contingent academic (e.g., adjunct status), or other non-tenure-track role, or the coveted full-time tenure-track position. In other words, an acculturation process is expected to occur within the postsecondary system, such that by the time a person obtains a full-time job, they have become fully socialized into the expectations of academia (Rosch & Reich, 1996). One’s professional identity is developed duringpostsecondary education and continues through the early career years (Austin et al., 2005; Rosch & Reich, 1996).

The transition from student to faculty is often slow. It can start with a part-time role as a teaching assistant (TA) or research assistant and meander from there in a variety of directions that might include a role as a postdoctoral scholar, part-time contingent academic (e.g., adjunct status), or other non-tenure-track role, or the coveted full-time tenure-track position. In other words, an acculturation process is expected to occur within the postsecondary system, such that by the time a person obtains a full-time job, they have become fully socialized into the expectations of academia (Rosch & Reich, 1996). One’s professional identity is developed during
postsecondary education and continues through the early career years (Austin et al., 2005; Rosch & Reich, 1996).
The development of the academic identity may be an individual journey, but it is not a solitary endeavor. It is situated within the particular institutions in which one works, as well as within the broader postsecondary context. One’s professional identity is influenced in part by mentors, colleagues, superiors, and others within the institution (Rosch & Reich, 1996), as well as beyond it. This acculturation can, and often does, occur at more than one institution. As an individual moves from one institution to another to complete more advanced degrees, and then goes on to get a job at a school or gigs at multiple institutions (Kezar et al., 2019), the acculturation process happens at an interinstitutional level, hovering in the boundary between the macro and mega levels of higher education.

The development of the academic identity may be an individual journey, but it is not a solitary endeavor. It is situated within the particular institutions in which one works, as well as within the broader postsecondary context. One’s professional identity is influenced in part by mentors, colleagues, superiors, and others within the institution (Rosch & Reich, 1996), as well as beyond it. This acculturation can, and often does, occur at more than one institution. As an individual moves from one institution to another to complete more advanced degrees, and then goes on to get a job at a school or gigs at multiple institutions (Kezar et al., 2019), the acculturation process happens at an interinstitutional level, hovering in the boundary between the macro and mega levels of higher education.
There is evidence suggesting that academic integrity increases in importance as people move up through the ranks of academia. First-year students are more likely to engage in academic misconduct of all kinds, including plagiarism (Bertram Gallant, Binkin, & Donohue, 2015). As students mature, both in terms of progressing through their academic programs and as they age, the likelihood of cheating at school tends to decrease, with mature students being less likely to engage in academic misconduct than their younger classmates (Harris et al., 2019; Hart & Morgan, 2010; Kidwell & Kent, 2008). This is not to suggest that people “age out” of cheating behaviors. There will always be a small percentage of individuals who misbehave no matter their circumstances or career stage. The reasons why there may be less plagiarism and other kinds of misconduct among older students are inconclusive. It could be that mature students have more self-awareness and confidence to ask for help if they need it, or that as students move through the educational system, they develop better research and self-regulation skills or become more aware of what is expected of them. It is likely to be some combination of these or other factors.

There is evidence suggesting that academic integrity increases in importance as people move up through the ranks of academia. First-year students are more likely to engage in academic misconduct of all kinds, including plagiarism (Bertram Gallant, Binkin, & Donohue, 2015). As students mature, both in terms of progressing through their academic programs and as they age, the likelihood of cheating at school tends to decrease, with mature students being less likely to engage in academic misconduct than their younger classmates (Harris et al., 2019; Hart & Morgan, 2010; Kidwell & Kent, 2008). This is not to suggest that people “age out” of cheating behaviors. There will always be a small percentage of individuals who misbehave no matter their circumstances or career stage. The reasons why there may be less plagiarism and other kinds of misconduct among older students are inconclusive. It could be that mature students have more self-awareness and confidence to ask for help if they need it, or that as students move through the educational system, they develop better research and self-regulation skills or become more aware of what is expected of them. It is likely to be some combination of these or other factors.
Research by a pharmacy professor, Dr. Zubin Austin, and colleagues at the University of Toronto showed that academic integrity and professional ethics can develop over time (Austin et al., 2005, 2006). In one study, the authors surveyed seventy-eight senior-level students and forty-one pharmacy educators. The results showed that more than 90 percent of students and educators admitted to one or more acts of academically dishonest behavior during their schooling. Furthermore,100 percentof the pharmacy educators admitted to passing around old exams and lab books to other students when they were in school, and 95 percent of students admitted to the same. Similarly, 92 percent of educators and 83 percent of students admitted to falsifying or fabricating lab data during their training (Austin et al., 2005). Copying and pasting information directly from theweb without citing it was also noted as being a cheating behavior that students engaged in. These numbers seem shocking given the high levels of trust that the public places in pharmacists.

web without citing it was also noted as being a cheating behavior that students engaged in. These numbers seem shocking given the high levels of trust that the public places in pharmacists.
What is particularly interesting, though, is that the faculty group rated cheating behaviors much more seriously than the students did. Students seemed to be more ambivalent about the seriousness of cheating, whereas the professors considered it more egregious. Even though the professors self-reported that they had engaged in cheating and plagiarism when they were students themselves, by the time they became educators, they found such behavior not only more serious, but more offensive. The authors suggested that there may be a developmental aspect to academic integrity, speculating that “professional morality” (Austin et al., 2005, p. 154) may be something that one develops throughout education. Austin and his colleagues (2005, 2006) were quick to point out that even if this theory holds true, it does not mean that we should excuse or ignore academic misconduct among students. In fact, addressing it could contribute to students’ ethical development.

The bottom line here is that the moral and ethical expectations of faculty members and other employees of the academy are more demanding and rigorous than those of students. Faculty and higher education professionals are expected to have been fully enculturated to the ethical values and moral principles that underpin the daily decisions about how they go about their work. There is also an implicit, if erroneous, assumption that faculty members and other university staff possess the skills to enact academic and research integrity. There is a third assumption: that professors and educational professionals serve as role models for those whom they teach or advise.

EXPECTATIONS FOR ETHICAL CONDUCT AMONG FACULTY

EXPECTATIONS FOR ETHICAL CONDUCT AMONG FACULTY
Many institutions have codes of conduct by which faculty and other employees of the institution are expected to abide. These statements outline the expectations for behavioral norms within the institution. Behavioral norms for those working in a given profession reflect the collective understanding of those who work within it (Braxton & Bayer, 1999). By definition, professions self-regulate by means of systematic and required training, specialized knowledge, and collegial discipline that includes expectations for ethical conduct within the profession (Bruhn et al., 2002; Reader, 1966). One of the characteristics of professionals is that they self-monitor and self-police so as to avoid having regulations imposed upon them by external bodies such as governments (Bruhn et al., 2002). Within higher education, norms “specify the prescribed and proscribed patternsof behavior in the performance of research, service and teaching roles” and are “variants of professional ethics” (Braxton & Bayer, 1999, p. 3). In other words, behaviors and actions in higher education, and education more broadly, are deeply rooted in an expectation of ethical conduct. Norms are also the foundation of professional self-regulation (Braxton & Bayer, 1999, p. 4).

Professions such as engineering, medicine, nursing, and K–12 teaching have associations to which members must belong and remain in good standing in order to work in their field. These external bodies work to ensure quality within the profession itself. There is no such professional body to directly oversee the quality of work done by academics (Bruhn et al., 2002; Callahan, 1982). Some professors, such as those who work in engineering, social work, or nursing, might also be members of a professional or accreditation body that sets expectations for those who teach in the profession. For the most part, institutions will neither interfere nor engage with external professional codes of conduct, except perhaps to indicate that professors who teach in those disciplines are expected to adhere to the standards of their profession (Euben & Lee, 2005). Those professors whose work does not oblige them to be a member in good standing of an external professional association may be subject to less ethical scrutiny of their work, unless a particular behavior is flagged, of course.

For the most part, institutions will neither interfere nor engage with external professional codes of conduct, except perhaps to indicate that professors who teach in those disciplines are expected to adhere to the standards of their profession (Euben & Lee, 2005). Those professors whose work does not oblige them to be a member in good standing of an external professional association may be subject to less ethical scrutiny of their work, unless a particular behavior is flagged, of course.
Since the beginning of universities, there has been a deeply rooted assumption that the subject matter expertise of faculty members equates, or at least contributes to, quality assurance in the teaching, research, and supervision of graduate students. The associations to which professors belong have traditionally been characterized by scholarly or intellectual activities rather than regulatory ones. Each association might produce a journal that shares new research from the field and would typically meet annually by hosting a conference for its members. These scholarly associations focus on the intellectual activity of members, with little consideration given to their ethical conduct other than to assume that if a scholar is acting unethically, then that fact will surface in their scholarship. Attempts to regulate academia in the same way as other professions have consistently failed (Bruhn et al., 2002). The notion that scholarly societies would concern themselves withappliedethics, scrutinizing the actions and behaviors of their members on a regular basis in order for them to retain their membership in the society, has been rejected by scholars, even though that is exactly what happens among doctors, engineers, and other professionals. Other bodies, such as the American Association of University Professors (AAUP), address the unjust or inappropriate behavior of institutions in dealing with individual members, but they “[do] not get involved in isolated instances of misconduct on the part of individual faculty members” (Bruhn et al., 2002, p. 463).

Limitations of Current Ethics Training

Limitations of Current Ethics Training
There is much less ethical training provided in academia than in industry (Kezar & Sam, 2011). In many countries, professors and others whose research involves interacting with humans or animals are encouraged or required to take research ethics training (Australian Government, 2018; CIHR, NSERC & SSHRC, 2018; Israel, 2016; National Research Council, 2014). Research ethics training focuses narrowly on the ethical treatment of human and animal research subjects. It generally does not address other ethical questions related to research, such as plagiarism.

There is much less ethical training provided in academia than in industry (Kezar & Sam, 2011). In many countries, professors and others whose research involves interacting with humans or animals are encouraged or required to take research ethics training (Australian Government, 2018; CIHR, NSERC & SSHRC, 2018; Israel, 2016; National Research Council, 2014). Research ethics training focuses narrowly on the ethical treatment of human and animal research subjects. It generally does not address other ethical questions related to research, such as plagiarism.
Even though the notion of research ethics has existed for centuries (Faden & Beauchamp, 1986), it was not until the Helsinki Declaration of 1964 that research ethics began to be formalized. The Helsinki Declaration was developed after the Nuremberg trials revealed the devastating atrocities of Nazi medical experimentation during World War II (Israel, 2016; Thomas & Petit, 2017; World Medical Association, 2018). The Helsinki Declaration details the expectations for human participants in medical research. It has undergone several revisions since it was first developed, and it remains the foundation of medical ethics today.

Even though the notion of research ethics has existed for centuries (Faden & Beauchamp, 1986), it was not until the Helsinki Declaration of 1964 that research ethics began to be formalized. The Helsinki Declaration was developed after the Nuremberg trials revealed the devastating atrocities of Nazi medical experimentation during World War II (Israel, 2016; Thomas & Petit, 2017; World Medical Association, 2018). The Helsinki Declaration details the expectations for human participants in medical research. It has undergone several revisions since it was first developed, and it remains the foundation of medical ethics today.
In the decades following the Helsinki Declaration, research ethics began to develop more formally, and later they expanded beyond medical research to all scientific and scholarly disciplines involving the use of humans or animals for research. Today, research ethics training is often overseen by institutional research ethics boards (REBs), which are also responsible for reviewing applications from researchers who intend to undertake research with human or animal subjects to ensure that they proceed in an ethical way.

In the decades following the Helsinki Declaration, research ethics began to develop more formally, and later they expanded beyond medical research to all scientific and scholarly disciplines involving the use of humans or animals for research. Today, research ethics training is often overseen by institutional research ethics boards (REBs), which are also responsible for reviewing applications from researchers who intend to undertake research with human or animal subjects to ensure that they proceed in an ethical way.
There is no question that researchers need formal and informal training to understand the fundamental concepts of ethical research conduct, such as informed consent, minimizing harm, and respect for persons (Israel, 2016). Some have criticized the activities and approach of institutional REBs, noting an almost pathological focus on regulatory compliance that is linked to research funding (Israel, 2016). This focus on compliance has created adversarial relationships between researchers and their institutional REBs (Israel, 2016). In some ways, these adversarial relationships between professors and their institutional REBs parallel the adversarial relationships between students and their professors, as well as between academics and the administration, when it comes to academic integrity policy and procedures.

In some ways, these adversarial relationships between professors and their institutional REBs parallel the adversarial relationships between students and their professors, as well as between academics and the administration, when it comes to academic integrity policy and procedures.
The relevance of the discussion about research ethics training to plagiarism and academic integrity is that although many current research ethics training programs mention the importance of the dissemination of researchresults, issues relating to publication ethics, plagiarism, and general research integrity remain neglected. There are few opportunities for emerging or established researchers to undergo training on plagiarism prevention and publication ethics. The writing centers that provide services to students already operate at or over maximum capacity just trying to serve students. And many professors would be too embarrassed to visit them to ask for help anyway. Just as there is a need to provide ongoing and continuous support to students to develop their understanding of academic integrity, there is also a need for institutions to provide ongoing and systematic training for their faculty about plagiarism prevention and ethical publication of research.

Some would argue that the peer review process involved in scientific and scholarly publishing provides a rigorous examination of academic research activities and is designed to provide quality assurance oversight of academic work. That may have been true at one time, but today, the questions of academic publishing are infinitely more complex than they used to be. COPE is an international organization founded in 1997 to address issues of research misconduct and publication ethics (COPE, 2020). This committee provides guidance to journal editors and publishers on matters relating to scholarly and scientific publishing, including plagiarism and self-plagiarism.

Similarly, the Center for Scientific Integrity, based in the United States, states on its website that its purpose is “to promote transparency and integrity in science and scientific publishing, and to disseminate best practices and increase efficiency in science” (Retraction Watch, 2020). The center maintains a database of scientific and scholarly papers that have been retracted for any variety of reasons and regularly publishes news about retracted papers via the Retraction Watch website (Retraction Watch, 2020). Currently, Retraction Watch had over 11,000 items in its database (Retraction Watch, 2020).

Journal editors continue to plead for authors to consider questions of plagiarism and research integrity on almost a daily basis. More recently, journal editors have noted the encroachment of the contract cheating industry into academic publishing, discussing how journal editors need to be alert to manuscripts that have been written by paper mills (Byrne & Christopher, 2020). It would seem that the rate of faculty misconduct when it comes to plagiarism, self-plagiarism, data fabrication and falsification, and other research misconduct is increasing at least as much as student academic misconduct, if not more. There is, however, currently little empirical data available on the rate of faculty plagiarism or other forms of scientific misconduct.

External organizations and publications provide some oversight at the broader community (mega) level, but individual cases of plagiarism areaddressed at the institutional (macro) level. We can begin to see some of the tensions that exist between the macro and mega levels when it comes to academic and research misconduct among faculty.

INSTITUTIONAL RESPONSES AND RESPSONSIBILITIES

INSTITUTIONAL RESPONSES AND RESPSONSIBILITIES
When a faculty member or another member of the institutional community plagiarizes or engages in some other form of academic or research misconduct, the institution is negatively affected. Public confidence in the institution can erode as a result of faculty misconduct (Sutherland-Smith, 2008). In this section, I explore reactive responses from institutions to a case of faculty misconduct, and then I discuss possible proactive steps that an institution can take to mitigate risks and further establish a culture of integrity.

When a faculty member or another member of the institutional community plagiarizes or engages in some other form of academic or research misconduct, the institution is negatively affected. Public confidence in the institution can erode as a result of faculty misconduct (Sutherland-Smith, 2008). In this section, I explore reactive responses from institutions to a case of faculty misconduct, and then I discuss possible proactive steps that an institution can take to mitigate risks and further establish a culture of integrity.
Addressing a Case of Plagiarism or Other Academic Misconduct by Professors and Researchers

Addressing a Case of Plagiarism or Other Academic Misconduct by Professors and Researchers
There are a range of institutional responses to plagiarism and other unethical conduct by professors and researchers. In some cases, institutions attempt to cover up cases of faculty plagiarism to mitigate harm to the institutional reputation (Hexham, 2004; Gillis, 2011). Others have illustrated how institutions have disavowed professors and researchers when a case of plagiarism has been exposed (Seltzer, 2018). There have been other cases where it has been announced to the media that a faculty member or administrator found responsible for plagiarism or research misconduct has stepped down from her or his role, and it remains unclear if that was done voluntarily or as a result of discussions with the administration. If a professor plays an administrative role, such as that of dean, they might lose that leadership role but remain on staff as a professor (Gillis, 2011).

If a professor plays an administrative role, such as that of dean, they might lose that leadership role but remain on staff as a professor (Gillis, 2011).
The fundamental values of integrity that have been widely adopted include courage, fairness, honesty, respect, responsibility, and trust (ICAI, 2014). It is incumbent upon institutions to enact these values, just as it is upon individuals. This applies not only to processes and procedures, but also to how the institution deals with misconduct in terms of internal and external communications.

Policy, Procedures, and Process

Policy, Procedures, and Process
In some cases, institutions have extensive policies, procedures, and guidelines for student conduct, but scant guidance for professors and otheremployees (Euben & Lee, 2005). One of the first things that an institution can do is ensure parity in terms of policies for students and those for faculty and employees. Institutions have tended to shy away from defining types of misconduct for professors, opting instead for broad, general statements (Euben & Lee, 2005). This can create a double standard, in which students are held to exacting requirements but professors are not. Policy documents need to clearly outline the expectations for ethical academic and research conduct among professors in clear and accessible language.

In some cases, institutions have extensive policies, procedures, and guidelines for student conduct, but scant guidance for professors and other
employees (Euben & Lee, 2005). One of the first things that an institution can do is ensure parity in terms of policies for students and those for faculty and employees. Institutions have tended to shy away from defining types of misconduct for professors, opting instead for broad, general statements (Euben & Lee, 2005). This can create a double standard, in which students are held to exacting requirements but professors are not. Policy documents need to clearly outline the expectations for ethical academic and research conduct among professors in clear and accessible language.
The same classifications and definitions for academic misconduct that apply to students can be adapted for faculty. For example, if students are forbidden to use contract cheating services, it must be prohibited for professors as well. I am not suggesting that institutions adopt a particular stance to academic misconduct in terms of severity; rather, I am arguing that the general approach to academic rigor that is applied to students, as articulated in institutional policy documents, should also be expected of faculty and documented in ways that ensure parity.

For example, if students are forbidden to use contract cheating services, it must be prohibited for professors as well. I am not suggesting that institutions adopt a particular stance to academic misconduct in terms of severity; rather, I am arguing that the general approach to academic rigor that is applied to students, as articulated in institutional policy documents, should also be expected of faculty and documented in ways that ensure parity.
In addition to formal policies, institutions must establish safe and effective procedures so that misconduct can be reported and then addressed. Research has shown that when someone reports a faculty member for plagiarism, the whistleblower can be turned away by those who are in a position to help, and the situation is even worse for graduate students who report (Becker, 2019). The policies and procedures need to be easily accessible to everyone in the institution, which includes being searchable on the institutional website.

Investigations: Due Process and Procedural Fairness

Investigations: Due Process and Procedural Fairness
Just as students have the right to due process and procedural fairness in a misconduct investigation, so should faculty and researchers. One key difference is that professors and researchers are employees; however, industry approaches to employee discipline may not work well in higher education (Euben & Lee, 2005). In industry, the model of progressive discipline, in which increasingly harsher sanctions are imposed with each recurring offense, is almost ubiquitous, but this approach is less common in academia (Euben & Lee, 2005). One reason for this is that faculty members and researchers are expected to know how to behave because they have spent years becoming acculturated to academic life.

Just as students have the right to due process and procedural fairness in a misconduct investigation, so should faculty and researchers. One key difference is that professors and researchers are employees; however, industry approaches to employee discipline may not work well in higher education (Euben & Lee, 2005). In industry, the model of progressive discipline, in which increasingly harsher sanctions are imposed with each recurring offense, is almost ubiquitous, but this approach is less common in academia (Euben & Lee, 2005). One reason for this is that faculty members and researchers are expected to know how to behave because they have spent years becoming acculturated to academic life.
In many jurisdictions, individuals have the right to privacy, and the case would likely be addressed through an internal investigation, just as student misconduct is, unless the misconduct were egregious enough to be criminal in nature. If criminal activity is apparent, then law enforcement might be involved. For example, in some jurisdictions, it is considered an act offraud to buy academic work from term paper mills or contract cheating services, regardless of who the customer is. It is a given that students are not the only ones using these services; so are some professors who are desperate to increase the number of journal articles they publish in a given year (Byrne & Christopher, 2020). If the nature of the research misconduct presents a risk to the public in some way, the right to personal privacy might be weighed against safety considerations.

Communications

Communications
If institutions are cautious about how or whether they share information on student academic misconduct, they can be even more reluctant to publicize details about faculty transgressions. The communications aspect of faculty misconduct is more complicated than it is with students. Many institutional communications plans inadequately address how to address high-profile cases of research misconduct. There can be no cookie-cutter way to respond to cases because each one is unique, but having an overall communications strategy would be helpful. Responses from institutional representatives that are platitudes or hollow bureaucratic postulations that are carefully crafted to protect the institution and reveal nothing are not helpful. Instead, taking the time to come up with straightforward, fact-based communications that do not violate privacy laws and show a genuine respect for the process and the need to uphold scientific and scholarly integrity can go a lot further in upholding public trust. It takes courage for an institution to admit when something has gone wrong, but that is precisely one of the values that can be invoked during a public relations crisis.

Hiring Practices

Hiring Practices
It is no secret that fewer and fewer permanent, full-time jobs are available in higher education. Because of the shortage of secure, full-time academic employment opportunities, the requirements to become a successful job applicant are increasingly demanding. Doctorates are a minimum requirement for most full-time academic positions today, as is having a solid track record of publication. Yet many universities have no formalized mechanisms to verify the credentials of applicants to academic positions. Fake degrees, fraudulent credentials, and phony transcripts have been a problem in both society and academia for some time (Attewell & Domina, 2011; Ekpu, 2019; Lee, 2005). Empirical data available about the extent of fake credentials among professors or higher education professionals is extremely limited; however, there is ample evidence to show that we should be concerned (CBC, 2017; Ekpu, 2019; Onyango, 2019). Although manyregistrars’ offices will check the credential documents of prospective students applying to particular programs, not all human resources offices perform parallel checks of applicants to academic positions. At a minimum, institutions need rigorous and systematic processes to verify the credentials of applicants for academic positions.

It is no secret that fewer and fewer permanent, full-time jobs are available in higher education. Because of the shortage of secure, full-time academic employment opportunities, the requirements to become a successful job applicant are increasingly demanding. Doctorates are a minimum requirement for most full-time academic positions today, as is having a solid track record of publication. Yet many universities have no formalized mechanisms to verify the credentials of applicants to academic positions. Fake degrees, fraudulent credentials, and phony transcripts have been a problem in both society and academia for some time (Attewell & Domina, 2011; Ekpu, 2019; Lee, 2005). Empirical data available about the extent of fake credentials among professors or higher education professionals is extremely limited; however, there is ample evidence to show that we should be concerned (CBC, 2017; Ekpu, 2019; Onyango, 2019). Although many
registrars’ offices will check the credential documents of prospective students applying to particular programs, not all human resources offices perform parallel checks of applicants to academic positions. At a minimum, institutions need rigorous and systematic processes to verify the credentials of applicants for academic positions.
Although some institutions conduct background checks on applicants, they mainly focus on determining whether they have a criminal record (Bentahar, 2020). There are few systematic mechanisms in place to check an applicant’s ethical misconduct if it was not criminal. In the absence of formal systems, informal mechanisms can be implemented. For example, once candidates’ credentials have been verified, incorporating into the job interview questions about academic and research integrity should be a standard practice. These might include asking philosophical or hypothetical questions, because reporting and investigating breaches of integrity become part of one’s job in higher education. In addition, asking practical questions about a candidate’s experience with academic or research misconduct is not out of line. Of course, a hiring committee should never ask for the identifying information of any individuals involved, but getting a sense of a candidate’s attitudes and experience can be helpful in determining if they will be a good fit for the role generally.

FACULTY MISCONDUCT AS A RESEARCH AREA

FACULTY MISCONDUCT AS A RESEARCH AREA
The topic of faculty misconduct has been addressed at some length in the literature; however, the discussions, much like this book chapter, have been scholarly but avoid the inclusion of primary research data. There are reasons for this. First, engaging in discussions about the topic is a valuable activity in and of itself. Another reason for the lack of research on this topic could be that it is a risky realm for an individual to research, particularly if a study focuses on one’s home institution. Institutions do not always take kindly to professors who undertake research that might damage the reputation of the institution. This type of research focus is sometimes called “backyard research” and happens when researchers notice something at their own institution and begin an inquiry to learn more.

The topic of faculty misconduct has been addressed at some length in the literature; however, the discussions, much like this book chapter, have been scholarly but avoid the inclusion of primary research data. There are reasons for this. First, engaging in discussions about the topic is a valuable activity in and of itself. Another reason for the lack of research on this topic could be that it is a risky realm for an individual to research, particularly if a study focuses on one’s home institution. Institutions do not always take kindly to professors who undertake research that might damage the reputation of the institution. This type of research focus is sometimes called “backyard research” and happens when researchers notice something at their own institution and begin an inquiry to learn more.
Although not related to plagiarism, the case of Dr. Derek Pyne, a full-time associate professor in Canada who learned that colleagues in his department were publishing in predatory or deceptive journals, is noteworthy. Pyne (2017) published his findings in a peer-reviewed, scholarly journal. According to a report from the Canadian Association of University Teachers (CAUT, 2019), Pyne was required by his university to undergo a psychological evaluation. He obliged. The psychologist who conducted the evaluation “indicated there was no evidence to support a diagnosis ofmental illness” (CAUT, 2019, p. 14). Nevertheless, Pyne was suspended without pay. The report goes on to comment that the university stated in formal documents that it was “committed to academic freedom and the independent research activities of its faculty” (p. 14), and that the suspension was unrelated to Pyne’s research. Rather, a statement released by the university president indicated that “the discipline imposed is related to matters, which I am unable to comment on due to both employment and privacy law” (CAUT, 2019, p. 14). Pyne was allowed to return to work later the same year.

Although not related to plagiarism, the case of Dr. Derek Pyne, a full-time associate professor in Canada who learned that colleagues in his department were publishing in predatory or deceptive journals, is noteworthy. Pyne (2017) published his findings in a peer-reviewed, scholarly journal. According to a report from the Canadian Association of University Teachers (CAUT, 2019), Pyne was required by his university to undergo a psychological evaluation. He obliged. The psychologist who conducted the evaluation “indicated there was no evidence to support a diagnosis of
mental illness” (CAUT, 2019, p. 14). Nevertheless, Pyne was suspended without pay. The report goes on to comment that the university stated in formal documents that it was “committed to academic freedom and the independent research activities of its faculty” (p. 14), and that the suspension was unrelated to Pyne’s research. Rather, a statement released by the university president indicated that “the discipline imposed is related to matters, which I am unable to comment on due to both employment and privacy law” (CAUT, 2019, p. 14). Pyne was allowed to return to work later the same year.
Individual professors may have academic freedom in matters relating to research, which also grants them the right to “criticize the institution” and be free from “institutional censorship” (CAUT, 2019, p. 16). However, this case illustrates that matters can quickly get complicated for an individual researcher who decides to publish research about fellow colleagues.

Individual professors may have academic freedom in matters relating to research, which also grants them the right to “criticize the institution” and be free from “institutional censorship” (CAUT, 2019, p. 16). However, this case illustrates that matters can quickly get complicated for an individual researcher who decides to publish research about fellow colleagues.
In academic integrity research, there can be deep value in undertaking an institutional self-study (Bertram Gallant & Drinan, 2008), but there also can be real risks to individual faculty members who undertake such research. Institutional self-studies about controversial topics such as academic integrity or misconduct among professors present less risk to the researcher when they are endorsed by the university administration. But it takes a courageous administration to allow institutional self-studies to be undertaken in earnest, without interfering with the research process or insisting that the results be whitewashed or censored.

In academic integrity research, there can be deep value in undertaking an institutional self-study (Bertram Gallant & Drinan, 2008), but there also can be real risks to individual faculty members who undertake such research. Institutional self-studies about controversial topics such as academic integrity or misconduct among professors present less risk to the researcher when they are endorsed by the university administration. But it takes a courageous administration to allow institutional self-studies to be undertaken in earnest, without interfering with the research process or insisting that the results be whitewashed or censored.
For those interested in pursuing ethical conduct of professors as a research area, it may be more strategic for the individual researcher to avoid conducting inquiries into one’s own institution as a starting point, but instead examine thephenomenonof faculty misconduct more broadly. This approach has already brought deep value to an understudied area (Braxton & Bayer, 1999; Bruhn et al., 2002; Kelley & Chang, 2007). I am not suggesting that there isnota need to investigate faculty misconduct, because there certainly is. I am suggesting, however, that this area is potentially risky for an individual researcher to undertake alone, particularly if the topic under study is one’s own institution.

CONCLUSION

CONCLUSION
A career in higher academia brings with itnoblesse oblige(Bruhn, 2002); the obligation of acting honorably, nobly, and generously toward others. When professors, administrators, or researchers plagiarize others’ work or engage in some other form of misconduct, they are violating the expected norms of the academy and of society. Just as proactive approaches to academic integrity are possible for students, so they are for institutions.Embedding integrity into hiring and training practices is a good place to start. Institutional self-study and self-monitoring are activities that require ongoing institutional commitment and support. Addressing academic and research transgressions with integrity requires courageous leadership. All of these are possible, but the tone must be set at the most senior levels of the administration in order for policies, procedures, and processes to be implemented systematically and fairly.

A career in higher academia brings with it
noblesse oblige
(Bruhn, 2002); the obligation of acting honorably, nobly, and generously toward others. When professors, administrators, or researchers plagiarize others’ work or engage in some other form of misconduct, they are violating the expected norms of the academy and of society. Just as proactive approaches to academic integrity are possible for students, so they are for institutions.
Embedding integrity into hiring and training practices is a good place to start. Institutional self-study and self-monitoring are activities that require ongoing institutional commitment and support. Addressing academic and research transgressions with integrity requires courageous leadership. All of these are possible, but the tone must be set at the most senior levels of the administration in order for policies, procedures, and processes to be implemented systematically and fairly.

Conclusion: Contemplating the Future of Plagiarism

Conclusion: Contemplating the Future of Plagiarism
In this concluding chapter, I contemplate what the future of plagiarism could look like as we advance further into the twenty-first century. I highlight key points from various chapters to show how our notions of plagiarism and academic integrity underwent dramatic changes in the twentieth and early twenty-first century. I synthesize ideas from previous chapters to stimulate a discussion of what might await us through the remainder of this century and beyond, and the challenges that we might be called upon to address as learning, writing, attribution, and knowledge sharing continue to evolve. I offer calls to action and topics for future research to further develop the field of academic integrity as an area of inquiry, education, and policy.

HISTORY IN THE MAKING

HISTORY IN THE MAKING
InChapter 1, I offered a brief history of plagiarism, paying particular attention to how the Internet influenced writing since the mid-1990s. During the later stages of writing this book, in February 2020, Larry Tesler, dubbed the “inventor of copy-and-paste computer functions” (Schudel, 2020), passed away. His obituary in theWashington Postsays the following: “For his best-known innovation, Tesler adapted an age-old practice ofschoolchildren—cutting out pictures and pasting them in scrapbooks—to computers. At first, he thought the term ‘cut-and-paste’ would apply strictly to design and visual images” (Schudel, 2020). But it is clear that “cut-and-paste” did not just apply to images. It went on to include text; and in fact the act of cutting and pasting changed how people write, cite—and plagiarize.

In
Chapter 1
, I offered a brief history of plagiarism, paying particular attention to how the Internet influenced writing since the mid-1990s. During the later stages of writing this book, in February 2020, Larry Tesler, dubbed the “inventor of copy-and-paste computer functions” (Schudel, 2020), passed away. His obituary in the
Washington Post
says the following: “For his best-known innovation, Tesler adapted an age-old practice of
schoolchildren—cutting out pictures and pasting them in scrapbooks—to computers. At first, he thought the term ‘cut-and-paste’ would apply strictly to design and visual images” (Schudel, 2020). But it is clear that “cut-and-paste” did not just apply to images. It went on to include text; and in fact the act of cutting and pasting changed how people write, cite—and plagiarize.
Less than two months after Tesler’s passing, Microsoft announced its “Rewrite” feature in Word (Eaton, 2020; Zhang, 2020). The new feature uses machine learning to suggest better ways to rewrite entire sentences. People in the tech world were calling it a “game changer” from the moment Rewrite was unveiled (Ellis, 2020, n.p.). At the time of its release in April 2020, the feature was available only in English. I expect that will change quickly, and as the feature becomes more widely available, it will challenge educators and administrators to rethink notions of individual authorship, plagiarism, and learning. I can imagine a scenario in which a person could use Tesler’s cut-and-paste feature to insert someone else’s content into Word, then use the rewrite function to have the software change each sentence in the paper, such that the end result might be better written than the original.

I expect that will change quickly, and as the feature becomes more widely available, it will challenge educators and administrators to rethink notions of individual authorship, plagiarism, and learning. InChapter 2, I offered an updated way to define plagiarism that includes nontext-based disciplines. In terms of our current thinking, we have yet to wrap our collective minds around the ways in which machine learning could (and likely will) challenge us to redefine plagiarism. In the case of the scenario I described previously, the resulting rewritten paper would not be original work, but that might not be recognized by text-matching software or a human educator. What will we, as educators, do when students submit a paper that is neither original work, nor plagiarized (at least according to our current definitions of plagiarism)? How much actual learning or writing development will happen when students use this new feature? Could it be that human and machine interactions in writing become so intertwined as to become indistinguishable? If so, does the notion of plagiarism itself become extinct? These are likely just a few of the philosophical and pedagogical questions that educators will have to contend with as machine learning becomes more integrated with our day-to-day lives. We can say one thing for certain: history is always in the making.

In the same chapter, I contended that computer scientists, more than scholars from any other discipline, have challenged previous definitions of plagiarism that focused almost exclusively on prose and ideas. They have prompted the rest of academia to consider how plagiarism can be manifested in computer code. In turn, that led to a further expansion of how we understand plagiarism in other nontext-based disciplines, such as music, design, art, and data. Computer scientists also shifted our thinking about term paper mills as businesses that buy and sell essays, renaming it to“contract cheating,” a practice from which almost no discipline is exempt. I suspect that as we move further into the twenty-first century, scientists and engineers will continue to challenge our current understandings of plagiarism. In particular, those with expertise in machine learning, artificial intelligence, and cybersecurity will be drawn into the conversation in new and essential ways.

The role that artificial intelligence and machine learning play in education is a hot topic. At the beginning of the second decade of the twenty-first century, a number of news items challenged us to think about how artificial intelligence and machine learning affect learning, writing, and publishing (Mindzak, 2020; Robitzski, 2020; Young, 2020). Jeffrey Young (2020, n.p.) asks, “Are algorithmically-generated term papers the next big challenge to academic integrity?” The answer is probably yes—or, at the very least, papers written by algorithms are likely to count among the next big challenges. A few weeks later, Michael Mindzak (2020) posed the question: “What happens when a machine can write as well as an academic?” The answer has yet to be determined, but the question is worthy of attention.

I anticipate that defining plagiarism will become even more impossible as technology becomes more intertwined with our lives. Scholars have also begun to contemplate what changes in technology mean for academic integrity. The unethical use of paraphrasing and translation software and online tools among students has been explored by some scholars (e.g., Carmichael & Weiss, 2019; Mundt & Groves, 2016; Prentice & Kinden, 2019; Rogerson & McCarthy, 2017), although the research in this area has yet to mature. Forbidding students from using such tools is about as useless as banning cell phones from the class. It would be a losing battle that would only propagate moralistic dichotomies, positioning those who use emergent technologies as bad and those who adhere to using only approved technological tools as good. Ultimately, we will need to find ways to use technology ethically in learning contexts, even when the tools are not on some institutional list of approved learning technologies.

Ultimately, we will need to find ways to use technology ethically in learning contexts, even when the tools are not on some institutional list of approved learning technologies.
Having lists of approved technologies is probably worse than having lists of approved books for libraries and school curricula. The implication is that if technologies or books are not on the “approved list,” then they are effectively banned, even if that is not stated explicitly. Censoring learning tools and materials might not make sense when we are talking about ethics in educational contexts. Educators, policymakers, and researchers will need to figure out how to incorporate technologies such as paraphrasing software, machine translation, and other emerging technologies in ethical ways.

One thing is clear: the realm of plagiarism no longer belongs only to the humanists. (I say this as someone with undergraduate and graduate degrees in literature.) There has been a long-standing division, in bothscholarship and practice, between those who study plagiarism from a purely compositional or literary perspective, and those from other disciplines with an interest in and commitment to helping students learn in ethical ways (Howard, 2000a). Intellectual elitism has no place in academic integrity research, advocacy, or practice. Now, more than ever, there is an urgent need for conversations about plagiarism and academic integrity to include academics, scholars, advocates, and leaders from every department on campus. This is because academic integrity, as well as its breaches, have become fundamentally more complex in the twenty-first century, and this is likely to be amplified in the future.

COMPLEXITY AND CHAOS

COMPLEXITY AND CHAOS
One of the characteristics of academic integrity research and plagiarism scholarship, particularly in the twentieth century (which I addressed inChapter 3), was the need to consider both individual and contextual factors (Bertram Gallant, 2008; Bretag, 2016; Leask, 2006; McCabe & Treviño, 1997; McCabe et al., 2002). This was an attempt, in part, to move away from moralistic dichotomies that position those who cheat as evil and those who do not as good. The introduction of contextual factors has challenged us to move beyond ethical binaries and consider that even when good people find themselves in challenging situations, they might make unwise decisions for any variety of reasons.
