Chapter 3
), was the need to consider both individual and contextual factors (Bertram Gallant, 2008; Bretag, 2016; Leask, 2006; McCabe & Trevi
ñ
o, 1997; McCabe et al., 2002). This was an attempt, in part, to move away from moralistic dichotomies that position those who cheat as evil and those who do not as good. The introduction of contextual factors has challenged us to move beyond ethical binaries and consider that even when good people find themselves in challenging situations, they might make unwise decisions for any variety of reasons.
As we progress into the twenty-first century, it is time to consider the next major shift in academic integrity research. I contend that such a shift necessitates moving from consideringcontextto consideringcomplexity. I am not proposing that we throw away our understanding of the individual and contextual factors that influence academic integrity. Just as twentieth-century scholars suggested that we consider contextual factors in addition to individual ones, I am proposing instead that we layer onto what we already know. Complexity is a consideration for academic integrityin addition toindividual and contextual factors.

InChapter 4, I discussed the need for a multistakeholder approach to academic integrity. I used the 4M Framework as a model to identify the various stakeholders and understand how they fit into various levels of a learning system—namely, micro (individual), meso (departmental), macro (institutional), and mega (societal) levels (Eaton et al., 2019; Friberg 2016; Kalu et al., 2018; Kenny et al., 2016; Poole & Simmons, 2013; Simmons, 2016; Williams et al., 2013). This model appears straightforward at first glance; however, as we begin to consider the ways in which all stakeholders interact simultaneously within and between the different levels, it is easy to imagine chaos. Chaos itself has become characteristic of learning,leadership, and change at both the organizational and societal levels in the twenty-first century (Burnes, 2005, Stacey et al., 2000; Wheatley, 2006). If we take a multistakeholder approach to plagiarism using the 4M Framework as a point of departure, we can see that we still have much work to do in terms of understanding how individuals within the system interact between one another and within the system itself.

External stakeholders, those at the macro level that exist outside the confines of our campuses, are likely to continue to push the boundaries of how we understand academic integrity. External actors, particularly commercial entities such as file-sharing companies and contract-cheating companies, will continue to put stress on the higher education system and academic integrity in particular.

Complexity Theory

Complexity Theory
An in-depth explanation of complexity theory is beyond the scope of this book. Instead, I offer key highlights, with references to original works for further follow-up. Complexity theory grew out of general systems theory of the 1960s (Grobman, 2005; von Bertalanffy, 1968). Systems theory grew out of the natural sciences and was used to explain how complex biological systems survive, adapt, and evolve (Grobman, 2005; von Bertalanffy, 1968). Complex systems are dynamic, nonlinear, and at times unpredictable in nature (Burnes, 2005). Systems that are too stable can wither and die; on the other hand, if they are too overwhelmed by change, they can collapse (Burnes, 2005). Systems that flourish are those that can adapt to change and thrive “on the edge of chaos” (Stacey et al., 2000, p. 106). Chaos has become a key topic discussed among complexity theorists and social change activists (Burnes, 2005, Stacey et al., 2000; Wheatley, 2006), although it has yet to be addressed in depth by those who study plagiarism or academic ethics.

Complex systems are dynamic, nonlinear, and at times unpredictable in nature (Burnes, 2005). Systems that are too stable can wither and die; on the other hand, if they are too overwhelmed by change, they can collapse (Burnes, 2005). Systems that flourish are those that can adapt to change and thrive “on the edge of chaos” (Stacey et al., 2000, p. 106). Chaos has become a key topic discussed among complexity theorists and social change activists (Burnes, 2005, Stacey et al., 2000; Wheatley, 2006), although it has yet to be addressed in depth by those who study plagiarism or academic ethics.
For academic integrity scholars and practitioners, the timing of the development of complexity theory is worth noting. InChapter 4, I discussed how universities and colleges actedin loco parentis(standing in for parents) until the mid-twentieth century (Allmendinger, 1973; Bertram Gallant, 2008; Eerkes, 2010). Then, during the social unrest of the 1960s and 1970s, court decisions effectively overturned the in loco parentis function of postsecondary institutions (Eerkes, 2010). These decisions resulted in subtle but permanent ideological and operational shifts in how postsecondary institutions addressed student conduct.

These decisions resulted in subtle but permanent ideological and operational shifts in how postsecondary institutions addressed student conduct.
Systems theory began to mature right around the time that thein loco parentisfunction of universities was being challenged in the courts in the United States. Although the developments may seem unrelated orcoincidental, both emerged during a time of significant social unrest and societal shifts that were happening during the mid-twentieth century.

These systems-level changes were also reflected in teaching and learning. InChapter 2, I discussed how positivist notions about defining plagiarism as a set number of words that emerged in the 1960s were almost immediately challenged and rejected by scholars (Howard, 2000b). Even so, these reductionist notions continue to persist, as do the tensions between those who seek absolute definitions of plagiarism and those who have developed a tolerance for ambiguity and chaos. Twenty-first-century educators, higher education professionals, administrators and academic integrity advocates must continue to cultivate an understanding that complexity and chaos are part of the learning systems in which we work, and in which our students learn.

THE IMPACT OF OPEN EDUCATION AND OPEN SCIENCE

THE IMPACT OF OPEN EDUCATION AND OPEN SCIENCE
InChapter 5, I examined how assessment design and evaluation play a role in student plagiarism. Over the past several years, the open learning movement has gained momentum (Cronin, 2020; Farrow, 2016; O’Byrne et al., 2014). In terms of academic integrity and plagiarism, open education advocates promote the use of open access, open educational resources, and Creative Commons licensing of work for open sharing. This brings with it new ideas about how creative works can not only be used, but reused, recycled, repurposed, and remixed. These advances point to future directions for academic integrity researchers to investigate as the field of assessment continues to evolve.

In
Chapter 5
, I examined how assessment design and evaluation play a role in student plagiarism. Over the past several years, the open learning movement has gained momentum (Cronin, 2020; Farrow, 2016; O’Byrne et al., 2014). In terms of academic integrity and plagiarism, open education advocates promote the use of open access, open educational resources, and Creative Commons licensing of work for open sharing. This brings with it new ideas about how creative works can not only be used, but reused, recycled, repurposed, and remixed. These advances point to future directions for academic integrity researchers to investigate as the field of assessment continues to evolve.
The moral foundation of the open education movement is human rights and the recognition that education should be free and open to all (Farrow, 2016). These are exciting changes in teaching and learning, rooted in a belief that access to education is a democratic right. Open learning could represent the next big paradigm shift in education, but paradigm shifts come with growing pains. Educators have already acknowledged that the “the move to digitized, online and freely accessible learning resources brings profound ethical challenges” (Farrow, 2016, p. 93).

The moral foundation of the open education movement is human rights and the recognition that education should be free and open to all (Farrow, 2016). These are exciting changes in teaching and learning, rooted in a belief that access to education is a democratic right. Open learning could represent the next big paradigm shift in education, but paradigm shifts come with growing pains. Educators have already acknowledged that the “the move to digitized, online and freely accessible learning resources brings profound ethical challenges” (Farrow, 2016, p. 93).
The controversy surrounding the creative reuse of others’ work is an example of how chaos and complexity will continue to challenge our notions of academic integrity, authorship, ownership, intellectual property, and attribution. To say that there are tensions between the notion of students producing their own individual, original work and the individual and collaborative creative use of content is an understatement. There is the possibility of a paradigm collision between the almost-pathological value that educators, institutions, and society at large have placed on individualauthorship, and open and collaborative work, where knowledge advancement is a community effort, often with many individuals working independently and yet in a connected way in efforts to understand things in new ways.

I concluded my writing of this book as the COVID-19 crisis swept across the world. The move to remote learning was abrupt, bringing with it challenges to academic integrity relating specifically to learning in online environments. It also brought with it a global response among scientists to engage in open science to accelerate the development of a vaccine (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, 2020; Zastrow, 2020). This brought an unprecedented commitment to collective knowledge building. As a result, publishers and journals have been engaging in open access in ways previously unknown, and online-sharing platforms allowing scientists to track the spread of the disease, share data, and model possible outcomes proliferated within a matter of weeks (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, 2020). The pandemic also brought with it rapid publication of scientific papers—a number of which were retracted in short order (Retraction Watch, 2020).

I concluded my writing of this book as the COVID-19 crisis swept across the world. The move to remote learning was abrupt, bringing with it challenges to academic integrity relating specifically to learning in online environments. It also brought with it a global response among scientists to engage in open science to accelerate the development of a vaccine (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, 2020; Zastrow, 2020). This brought an unprecedented commitment to collective knowledge building. As a result, publishers and journals have been engaging in open access in ways previously unknown, and online-sharing platforms allowing scientists to track the spread of the disease, share data, and model possible outcomes proliferated within a matter of weeks (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, 2020). The pandemic also brought with it rapid publication of scientific papers—a number of which were retracted in short order (Retraction Watch, 2020).
We do not yet know the long-term impact of the pandemic on teaching, learning, or science. It is possible that the pandemic might accelerate a paradigm shift toward open science and open learning. Educators, scientists, and members of the public will still expect and trust that work produced as part of the open education and open science movements is reliable, valid, credible, and ethically trustworthy. Conversations about what that means for academic and research integrity will no doubt continue in the coming years. Changes to institutional policies, procedures, and practices, which traditionally happen at a crawl, may become stale or difficult to apply in ways that make sense ethically in a world that moves faster than the process of revising institutional policy takes.

Conversations about what that means for academic and research integrity will no doubt continue in the coming years. Changes to institutional policies, procedures, and practices, which traditionally happen at a crawl, may become stale or difficult to apply in ways that make sense ethically in a world that moves faster than the process of revising institutional policy takes.
As I reflect on the process of writing this book, it occurs to me that the researchers who catalyzed the academic integrity movement, particularly Don McCabe and Tracey Bretag, offered us many possibilities for research and advocacy. Educators and advocates now ought to think about what it means to work in a post-McCabe, post-Bretag, postpandemic world. We are undertaking the task of thinking about what teaching and learning ethically mean as we move forward in the twenty-first century; this will no doubt be shaped in ways that we cannot yet anticipate.

TACKLING THE COMPLEXITIES OF SELF-PLAGIARISM

TACKLING THE COMPLEXITIES OF SELF-PLAGIARISM
InChapter 6, I delved into some of the complexities of self-plagiarism, highlighting particular problems for graduate students and researchers.Just as technology brings complications, I can see the potential for technology to solve problems relating to academic misconduct. For example, I wonder how the use of open scientific and data repositories could help to solve the issue of self-plagiarism. If researchers post their “Methods” section in an online and open access data archive for their project, in theory they could simply include a link to the online archive rather than stating their methods over and over in various conference presentations and publications. Having projects archived in a central place online, and then using that archive as a digital space to point to instead of duplicating the same writings, could be an exciting possibility. Of course, that would mean that universities, conference organizers, and scientific publishers would have to accept the validity of a link to an online archive of the project in lieu of a particular section that is currently expected as part of a project write-up. What this might mean for the future of blind peer review has yet to be learned. The mental and philosophical shift about what does and does not need to be included in every academic paper is probably more difficult than the technical shift itself. Data repositories already exist. The academic publishing industry, as well as academics themselves, need to catch up.

CONTEMPLATING THE COMMODIFICATION OF MISCONDUCT

CONTEMPLATING THE COMMODIFICATION OF MISCONDUCT
As we consider the impact of technology on writing and learning, there are other aspects of technology that may come to the foreground, highlighting how plagiarism and other forms of academic misconduct are part of a larger conversation around academic corruption. InChapter 7, I explored how file sharing has become ubiquitous across education, but its commodification presents particular problems in terms of students being exploited. As I conclude this work, I am cognizant of an increasing number of companies that are combining file sharing with tutoring. More and more companies whose ethical motives remain debated are striving to establish partnerships with postsecondary institutions and academic publishers. I suspect that as we move further into the twenty-first century, the situation of third-party vendors striving for legitimacy as so-called academic partners is going to become only more complicated. At present, file-sharing and online tutoring companies are considered by some to be more scourge than solution, and their future role in higher education remains unclear.

InChapter 8, I discussed the practice of contract cheating, noting that although some have positioned the practice as a form of plagiarism, others have argued that it fits better under the umbrella of fraud. This presents an indication that the lines between plagiarism and fraud may be blurring. This is a complexity that we should pay attention to. In the contract-cheatingworld, there are already indications that the use of cryptocurrency as a means to engage in online academic outsourcing is expanding (Bailey, 2019; Kaaru, 2019). At this point in time, the role that cryptocurrency plays in academic misconduct is so far off the radar of most academics and administrators that it does not even register; or if they are aware of the possibility, it might seem like a science fiction story set in some distant future that is too far from our current reality to give it much credence. I contend that instead of dismissing these early indicators of possible evolutions in academic misconduct, it is imperative for educators to identify emergent trends so early-response systems can be developed.

Educators and advocates in some countries are well aware of the impact that contract cheating has on education, whereas others still struggle even to get their administrators to pay attention, let alone admit that it is a problem. InChapter 8, I touched upon the history and legal aspects of contract cheating. The year 2022 marks the fiftieth anniversary of the first documented cases of legal action against the early term paper mills in the United States, which happened along the Eastern Seaboard in 1972 (McCormick & Whaley, 2014; Newton & Lang, 2016). Educators, students, and advocates around the world will have a golden opportunity—literally, to mark the golden anniversary of these first legal cases—through global events, such as (but not limited to) the International Day of Action against Contract Cheating, to raise awareness and campaign for stronger responses against this predatory industry, whose main focus is not to help students, but to exploit them.

ADVANCING ACADEMIC INTEGRITY AS A SOCIAL JUSTICE ISSUE

ADVANCING ACADEMIC INTEGRITY AS A SOCIAL JUSTICE ISSUE
InChapter 9, I addressed the topics of equity, diversity, and inclusion as they apply to academic integrity. By and large, questions relating to social justice in academic misconduct reporting and case management have yet to be fully explored. Most institutions do not pay adequate attention to the possibility of implicit bias in academic misconduct reporting that can lead to overrepresentation of racialized minorities, particularly foreign-born students for whom English is an Additional Language (EAL). Even if institutions document reporting statistics, few if any pay attention to the numbers of international and EAL students who are reported and subsequently found responsible for such behavior. I suspect that the reason for this, even among well-intentioned administrators, is concern that if such data were collected, it could easily (and erroneously) be construed as individuals from a particular group cheating more, rather than them potentially being singled out more often. There is a need for more awareness and action toensure that reporting practices and case management are equitable in terms of diverse student populations.

Decolonization and Indigenization of Academic Integrity

Decolonization and Indigenization of Academic Integrity
Another area for further development of academic integrity from a social justice perspective is decolonization and Indigenization. Many educators of settler European heritage remain unaware of Indigenous ways of knowing, teaching, and learning. Embedded within Indigenous knowledge systems are long-standing practices of how to attribute knowledge to those who came before us.

Another area for further development of academic integrity from a social justice perspective is decolonization and Indigenization. Many educators of settler European heritage remain unaware of Indigenous ways of knowing, teaching, and learning. Embedded within Indigenous knowledge systems are long-standing practices of how to attribute knowledge to those who came before us.
Although there has been a quiet movement underway by some educators and librarians to supplement existing referencing and style with libguides that provide additional guidance on how to attribute in ways that are respectful to Indigenous populations, this work remains on the small scale, done at the library (meso level) for use by students at that particular institution (macro level). For the work of decolonizing referencing, citation, and attribution practices to have impact, conversations must happen at a bigger scale, such as at library and other scholarly conferences. In addition, it is incumbent upon the mega-organizations that produce style and referencing manuals to be more intentional, respectful, and clear in their guidance about how to recognize the knowledge contributions of Native Americans and other Indigenous populations. Of course, such work must include Indigenous people in consultation and collaboration; decolonizing attribution practices cannot happen if members of the White dominant social classes are the only ones making decisions.

In addition, it is incumbent upon the mega-organizations that produce style and referencing manuals to be more intentional, respectful, and clear in their guidance about how to recognize the knowledge contributions of Native Americans and other Indigenous populations. Of course, such work must include Indigenous people in consultation and collaboration; decolonizing attribution practices cannot happen if members of the White dominant social classes are the only ones making decisions.
InChapter 10, I discussed the practices of how educators recognize and then report plagiarism and other breaches of academic integrity, and then how cases are resolved. The work of decolonization can—and should—extend to academic misconduct case management. The current system of student judicial affairs, rooted in administrative law, is less focused on helping students learn than it is on punishing “wrongdoers.” Research has shown over the decades that although there are a few truly rotten apples, these are not the majority. Many plagiarism cases are related to underdeveloped writing and research skills, as well as ignorance of what is expected. It will be interesting to see whether and how alternative approaches to breaches of integrity, such as restorative practices, can gain traction. If they do, it is probable that that would happen within the portfolios of senior institutional leaders, such as vice provosts of equity, diversity, and inclusion, whose role is to promote socially just academic and administrative practices and policies.

ADVANCING AND ALIGNING INSTITUTIONAL APPROACHES TO INTEGRITY

ADVANCING AND ALIGNING INSTITUTIONAL APPROACHES TO INTEGRITY
All of this points to further development of how we think about plagiarism and academic integrity broadly. Current definitions of academic integrity remain focused on students, with further attention aimed at undergraduates because they make up the majority of the student body. As undergraduate research continues to be viewed as part of a “high-impact student experience” (Lopatto, 2010),researchintegrity is likely to become more intertwined with, and inseparable from,academicintegrity. InChapter 11, I explored the topic of plagiarism among academics, researchers, and administrators. To date, plagiarism among the student body has often been dealt with differently than when it happens among other campus stakeholders. To some extent, this makes sense because the main job of students is to learn, whereas the job of professors and researchers is to mobilize knowledge from their research, as well as to teach. What does not make sense, however, is when institutions have elaborate policies, procedures, and practices for addressing student breaches of integrity and opaque and obscure processes for addressing breaches that occur beyond the student body.

Chapter 11

To date, plagiarism among the student body has often been dealt with differently than when it happens among other campus stakeholders. To some extent, this makes sense because the main job of students is to learn, whereas the job of professors and researchers is to mobilize knowledge from their research, as well as to teach. What does not make sense, however, is when institutions have elaborate policies, procedures, and practices for addressing student breaches of integrity and opaque and obscure processes for addressing breaches that occur beyond the student body.
If idiosyncratic approaches to academic integrity violations are admonished, as they have been since the 1980s (Jendrek, 1989), then so too must institutions resist the temptation to treat faculty breaches of integrity as one-time occurrences. Instead, systematic, methodical, and just ways of addressing breaches of integrity must be applied to all campus stakeholders. That is not to say that the systemscannotdiffer because after all, professors are supposed to be acculturated to the expectations of the academy, but it is imperative that the systems exist and that the processes for dealing with student academic misconduct and faculty and administrator misconduct are equitable.

It could be that over time, academic and research integrity become synonymous, or at least better aligned. This kind of synthesis makes sense, given that the word “integrity,” as I pointed out earlier in this book, comes from the Latinintegrāre(Hoad, 1993), meaning “to integrate or make whole.” Our approaches to plagiarism and academic integrity must focus on a multistakeholder approach, not only in terms of student conduct but in terms of stakeholder conduct.

CONTEMPLATING A POSTPLAGIARISM WORLD

CONTEMPLATING A POSTPLAGIARISM WORLD
So I end where I began—puzzling through definitions of words. We turn to definitions to help us make sense not only of words, but of the concepts behind them. As I draw this book to a close, I continue to reflect onRebecca Moore Howard’s (2000b) proposition that plagiarism is “inherently indefinable” (p. 473), that it “eludes definition” (p. 474), and ultimately, that we ought to discard the term entirely. As practices such as contract cheating continue to complicate and challenge academic integrity, debates about whether academic outsourcing is plagiarism or fraud cause us to get lost in the weeds.

So I end where I began—puzzling through definitions of words. We turn to definitions to help us make sense not only of words, but of the concepts behind them. As I draw this book to a close, I continue to reflect on
Rebecca Moore Howard’s (2000b) proposition that plagiarism is “inherently indefinable” (p. 473), that it “eludes definition” (p. 474), and ultimately, that we ought to discard the term entirely. As practices such as contract cheating continue to complicate and challenge academic integrity, debates about whether academic outsourcing is plagiarism or fraud cause us to get lost in the weeds.
Definitions are important to help us puzzle through what we do not understand. Once we do understand a topic, we can begin to insist on the importance of more sophisticated and nuanced approaches. It is not so much that we shoulddiscardthe term “plagiarism” astranscendit. Ultimately, the finite nature of definitions can serve as an impediment to deeper reflection about what it means to integrate the practices of learning, teaching, and ethical conduct, not only in school but in society. These reflections are inescapable if we are to commit to educational integrity as a broad concept that includes teaching, learning, research, leadership, and policy. As students, educators, and members of society think more about the normalcy of complexity and developing a tolerance for ambiguity, we will be challenged in ways that we have never seen before to define and redefine what it means to learn, work, and live ethically. It is time to contemplate what it would mean to live in a postplagiarism world.

Ultimately, the finite nature of definitions can serve as an impediment to deeper reflection about what it means to integrate the practices of learning, teaching, and ethical conduct, not only in school but in society. These reflections are inescapable if we are to commit to educational integrity as a broad concept that includes teaching, learning, research, leadership, and policy. As students, educators, and members of society think more about the normalcy of complexity and developing a tolerance for ambiguity, we will be challenged in ways that we have never seen before to define and redefine what it means to learn, work, and live ethically. It is time to contemplate what it would mean to live in a postplagiarism world.
I imagine that global citizens of a postplagiarism world might reject binary notions entirely, shaking their heads at the futility of arguments about good versus bad students or pedagogy versus policing. Those who insist on focusing on dualities might show themselves as less intellectually capable than those who can tolerate the chaos and embrace the complexity of whatever it means to integrate, to become whole, as a learner and as a person. But who knows? The odds that the current generation of academics and administrators will be around to bear witness to that world are slim.

POSTSCRIPT: A CALL TO THE NEXT GENERATION

POSTSCRIPT: A CALL TO THE NEXT GENERATION
I started this book by saying that I intended it not only for an audience of my peers, but also our protégés. By the time we reach the middle of the twenty-first century, we, the current generation of educators, scholars, and administrators, will have faded from the scene. In the Preface, I explained that I learned the importance of putting people first in this work from my PhD supervisor, Dr. J. Tim Goddard. He taught his students to listen (and read) first, and then write. As we move further into the age of complexity, I teach my own graduate students similar principles, but with a twenty-first century twist. I say: Read. Write. Read more. Write more. Repeat.

In the Preface, I explained that I learned the importance of putting people first in this work from my PhD supervisor, Dr. J. Tim Goddard. He taught his students to listen (and read) first, and then write. As we move further into the age of complexity, I teach my own graduate students similar principles, but with a twenty-first century twist. I say: Read. Write. Read more. Write more. Repeat.
With the myriad of digital tools available to us, as well as the rate at which knowledge continues to advance, the sequence of reading first,followed by writing, is too linear. Knowledge building happens as we learn and as we demonstrate that learning, be it through writing or some other form of sharing. The process of listening, reading, writing, and sharing is infinitely more complex today and iterative than it has ever been; however, the principle of listening deeply to what others have said before us still applies. We honor those who have come before us by listening to and reading their work and understanding how previous contributions influence the work that is developed later as a result.

With the myriad of digital tools available to us, as well as the rate at which knowledge continues to advance, the sequence of reading first,
followed by writing, is too linear. Knowledge building happens as we learn and as we demonstrate that learning, be it through writing or some other form of sharing. The process of listening, reading, writing, and sharing is infinitely more complex today and iterative than it has ever been; however, the principle of listening deeply to what others have said before us still applies. We honor those who have come before us by listening to and reading their work and understanding how previous contributions influence the work that is developed later as a result.
There is a continual looping back as we think forward. The future of academic integrity rests not in the hands of today’s academics and administrators, but in those of our students. Ultimately, today’s educators leave these tough topics in the hands of our youth. And so I conclude with a call to action to today’s young people: to continue puzzling through, discussing, and taking action on plagiarism and other matters related to academic integrity in an increasingly complex world.

About the Author

About the Author
Sarah Elaine Eaton, PhD, is an associate professor at the University of Calgary, Canada, where she also served as the university’s inaugural Educational Leader in Residence, Academic Integrity (2019–2021). In 2020, the Canadian Society for the Study of Higher Education conferred their prestigious Research and Scholarship Award on her. In addition, Eaton received the Teaching Excellence Award from the Werkund School of Education in 2015. She has led research projects on academic integrity at the national and local levels. She was the co-chair of the Canadian Symposium on Academic Integrity (2019) and served as the program chair for the International Center for Academic Integrity conference (2020). She serves as the editor-in-chief for theInternational Journal for Educational Integrity, published by BMC Springer Nature. Eaton regularly appears as a guest on television and radio programs to talk about academic misconduct in higher education.
